day.label: Main duties
day.text: A 3D artist builds digital models of characters, props and environments. They then unwrap UVs, paint textures and set up materials and lighting. Finally they hand off finished assets to animators, game engines or renderers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a team check-in and a review of feedback on yesterday’s work. Most hours go to modeling, sculpting or texturing in focused blocks. The day ends with exporting assets, fixing notes and updating task trackers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include modeling packages like Blender, Maya or 3ds Max, sculpting software like ZBrush, and texturing tools like Substance Painter. Many artists also work in game engines such as Unreal or Unity and use a pen tablet.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: 3D artists work closely with art directors, concept artists, animators, riggers and technical artists. In games they also coordinate with designers and programmers. In product work they may take direct notes from clients or marketing teams.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on how closely it matches the concept and art style, and on clean topology and correct scale. Efficient use of polygons and texture memory also counts. Meeting deadlines and handling feedback well matter just as much as raw skill.

qa.q: What does a 3D artist do day to day?
qa.a: A 3D artist spends most of the day modeling, sculpting, texturing or lighting assets in 3D software. They review reference and concept art, take feedback from leads, and revise their work. They also export files in the right formats and test how assets look in a game engine or final render.

qa.q: What is the difference between a 3D artist and a 3D animator?
qa.a: A 3D artist creates the look of things: the shape, surface, materials and lighting of characters, objects and scenes. A 3D animator makes those finished models move, usually after a rigger adds a skeleton and controls. Some smaller studios hire generalists who do both, but larger teams keep the roles separate.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Account executives run sales deals from the first meeting to the signed contract. They qualify leads, lead discovery calls, give product demos, write proposals, negotiate price and terms, and close deals that count toward a monthly or quarterly quota.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts by updating the sales pipeline and planning follow-ups. Then come back-to-back calls or video demos, emails to buyers, pricing questions sent to managers, and time spent preparing proposals or contract redlines for deals near closing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with sales development reps who book first meetings, sales engineers who handle technical questions, and customer success teams who take over after the sale. On the buyer side, they deal with end users, managers, procurement staff and executives who sign.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most rely on a CRM system to track contacts, deals and forecasts. Video meeting software, email sequencing tools, e-signature platforms, slide decks and pricing calculators are common. Many also use call recording tools to review conversations and coach their pitch.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is mostly measured by revenue closed against quota. Managers also watch pipeline size, win rate, average deal size, sales cycle length and forecast accuracy. Pay usually combines a base salary with commission tied to these results.

qa.q: What does an account executive do day to day?
qa.a: An account executive spends most of the day talking to potential buyers. They run discovery calls to learn a buyer’s needs, give demos, answer objections, send proposals and negotiate terms. Between calls they update the CRM, forecast which deals will close, and coordinate with sales engineers, managers and legal teams to get contracts signed.

qa.q: What is the difference between an account executive and a sales development representative?
qa.a: A sales development representative, or SDR, finds and qualifies new leads, often through cold calls and emails, then books meetings. The account executive takes those meetings and owns the deal from there, running demos, negotiating and closing the contract. SDR roles are often entry level, and many people move up into account executive jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Account managers own a set of existing customers. They handle renewals, answer questions, fix problems, and spot chances to add products or services that genuinely help the client. The goal is to keep customers happy, loyal, and growing over time.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes scheduled check-in calls, emails about billing or orders, and prep for upcoming renewals. Many account managers also run quarterly business reviews, update notes in the customer database, and chase down answers from other teams.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They are the customer’s main contact inside the company. Internally they work with sales reps who closed the deal, support and success teams, billing, product staff, and managers who approve pricing or contract changes.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use a customer relationship management system to track contacts, deals, and renewal dates. Email, video calls, shared calendars, spreadsheets, and slide decks for client reviews are everyday tools. Some roles also use contract and quoting software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is usually measured by how many customers renew, how much revenue grows within existing accounts, and how satisfied clients are. Many roles pay a base salary plus a commission or bonus tied to these goals.

qa.q: What does an account manager do day to day?
qa.a: An account manager checks in with assigned customers, answers their questions, and solves issues by working with other teams. They track renewal dates, prepare proposals, and suggest upgrades or add-ons when they fit the customer’s needs. They also log every conversation in a tracking system so the history of each account stays clear.

qa.q: What is the difference between an account manager and a sales representative?
qa.a: A sales representative mainly finds and signs new customers. An account manager takes over after the sale and looks after those customers over the long term. Account managers focus on renewals, relationships, and growing existing accounts, while sales reps focus on prospecting and closing first deals. Some smaller companies combine both jobs into one role.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Accountants record sales, bills and payroll in the general ledger, match bank and card statements to the books, post adjusting entries, and prepare financial statements. They also track what customers owe the company and what the company owes its vendors.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to entering invoices, coding expenses and answering vendor or manager questions. Afternoons may mean reconciling accounts or building a report. The pace picks up at month end, quarter end and year end, when the books must be closed on a deadline.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Accountants work with controllers, finance managers, payroll and purchasing staff, and department heads who need budget numbers. They also answer questions from outside auditors, tax preparers and banks, and sometimes from customers and vendors about payments.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include accounting or ERP software, spreadsheets with lookups and pivot tables, bank portals and expense systems. Work follows US generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), and public companies also follow SEC reporting rules and internal control requirements.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work means accounts that reconcile, a close finished on time, clean audit results and reports managers can trust. Small errors matter, because a wrong entry can flow into tax filings, loan reports and business decisions.

qa.q: What does an accountant do day to day?
qa.a: An accountant records the money coming in and going out, checks that the books match bank statements and other records, and fixes any differences. Each month they close the books, post adjusting entries such as accruals and depreciation, and prepare reports like the income statement and balance sheet for managers, owners or auditors.

qa.q: What is the difference between an accountant and a CPA?
qa.a: Anyone who does accounting work can be called an accountant, and most staff and corporate accounting jobs do not require a license. A CPA is licensed by a state board after meeting education, exam and experience rules, which vary by state. A CPA license is required to sign audit opinions on financial statements and to offer certain services to the public.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Matches each supplier invoice to its purchase order and receiving record, codes it to the right expense account, routes it for approval and schedules payment by check, ACH or card. They also catch duplicate invoices and price or quantity errors before any money goes out.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day starts with the invoice inbox and vendor emails. Next come matching and data entry, chasing managers for approvals, and answering suppliers who ask where their payment is. Payment runs happen on set days, and month-end brings accruals and reconciliations.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with buyers and receiving staff to fix mismatched orders, department managers who approve spending, and the controller or accounting manager who signs off on payment runs. They also deal daily with the billing teams of the company’s suppliers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in accounting or ERP software, plus spreadsheets, invoice scanning or capture tools, and the company’s bank portal for ACH payments. Strong ten-key skills and Excel know-how, such as lookups and pivot tables, help with matching and reconciling.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means bills paid on time and only once, early-payment discounts captured, no late fees, and clean vendor balances at month-end. Guarding against fraud matters too, such as confirming any bank detail change by calling a known vendor contact.

qa.q: What does an accounts payable specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They take supplier invoices from receipt to payment. That means checking each bill against the purchase order and delivery, getting approval, entering it in the accounting system and paying it on schedule. They also keep vendor records and W-9 forms current, answer supplier questions and help prepare year-end 1099 forms for the IRS.

qa.q: What is the difference between accounts payable and accounts receivable?
qa.a: Accounts payable handles money the company owes its suppliers, so the work is checking and paying bills. Accounts receivable handles money customers owe the company, so the work is sending invoices, applying payments and following up on overdue accounts. Both post to the general ledger, and in small businesses one person often does both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They create and send invoices, post incoming payments to customer accounts, and match each payment to the right invoice. They follow up on overdue balances by email, phone and letter. They also resolve disputes over pricing, short payments or missing paperwork.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The morning often starts with the bank deposit or lockbox file, applying checks, ACH and card payments. Later comes the aging report, a list of who owes what and for how long. Then come calls to late payers and notes on each promise to pay.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They deal with the accounts payable staff at customer companies. Inside their own company, they work with sales reps, customer service and the credit manager. Accounts that stay unpaid may go to a manager, a collection agency or an attorney, depending on company policy.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Accounting or ERP software, spreadsheets, online banking and customer billing portals are daily tools. Many teams also use collections software that sends automated reminders and tracks each call, email and payment promise.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers watch days sales outstanding, the share of invoices past due, unapplied cash and how fast disputes get closed. Accuracy matters too. A misapplied payment can trigger a wrong reminder and upset a good customer.

qa.q: What does an accounts receivable specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They bill customers, record and match incoming payments, and keep each account current. Much of the day goes to reviewing the aging report, sending reminders, calling late payers and fixing disputes or billing errors. They also reconcile receivables with the general ledger and help with the month-end close.

qa.q: Do debt collection laws apply to in-house collections specialists?
qa.a: The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act mainly covers third-party collectors of consumer debts, not a company collecting its own bills. Business-to-business debts fall outside it. Some states have laws that also cover original creditors, so the rules vary by state. Honest, respectful contact is expected either way.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Build models that estimate the chance and cost of future events like death, illness, accidents, or property damage. Use them to set insurance premiums, calculate reserves for future claims, and test whether insurers and pension plans can pay what they promise.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Pull and clean claims or policy data, update assumptions, run projections, and compare results with earlier periods. A good share of the day goes to writing memos and explaining the numbers to people who are not actuaries.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Underwriters, accountants, product managers, investment staff, pension plan sponsors, and state insurance regulators. Newer actuaries usually work under a credentialed actuary who reviews their models and signs off on the final results.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets, SQL, and programming languages such as R and Python, plus specialized actuarial projection software. Mortality tables, loss development triangles, and experience studies are everyday working materials.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether prices and reserves hold up as real claims come in, how clearly the work is documented, and whether it follows actuarial standards of practice. Some reports, such as statutory reserve opinions, must be signed by a qualified actuary.

qa.q: What does an actuary do day to day?
qa.a: An actuary spends most of the day working with data and models. That means cleaning claims data, setting assumptions about death rates or accident costs, running projections, and checking results. They then write reports and explain what the numbers mean for prices, reserves, or pension funding to managers, clients, and regulators.

qa.q: How do you become an actuary?
qa.a: Most actuaries pass a series of professional exams over several years. Life, health, and retirement actuaries usually follow the Society of Actuaries path, while property and casualty actuaries follow the Casualty Actuarial Society path. Many start in entry-level roles after passing one or two exams. Signing certain pension filings also requires federal enrollment as an Enrolled Actuary.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Additive manufacturing engineers make parts with industrial 3D printers. They pick parts that suit printing, adapt designs to the process, choose materials, set build orientation and supports, develop print parameters, oversee post-processing like heat treatment and machining, and qualify parts and machines for production.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start by checking overnight builds and printer logs. Then come preparing a new build file, reviewing CT scans or test results on printed parts and tuning parameters. Afternoons go to design reviews, supplier calls and writing process documentation.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with design engineers, materials scientists, quality and inspection staff, machine technicians and machinists who finish parts. In aerospace and medical work they also work with certification and regulatory teams, and with printer makers on service and upgrades.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include CAD like SolidWorks, Siemens NX or Fusion 360, build preparation software like Materialise Magics, and simulation tools. They run laser powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition, binder jet and polymer printers, and use CT scanners and microscopes for inspection.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Engineers are judged on part quality and repeatability: density, strength, dimensions and surface finish that meet the specification. Build success, cost per part, machine uptime and getting parts qualified for flight or medical use also count.

qa.q: What is the difference between additive manufacturing and 3D printing?
qa.a: Both terms describe building parts layer by layer from a digital model. “3D printing” is the common name, often used for hobby and prototype printers. “Additive manufacturing” is the industry term, used for production parts made under controlled processes, with qualified materials, inspection and traceability. Job titles usually use the industry term.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be an additive manufacturing engineer?
qa.a: Most engineer roles ask for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, materials, manufacturing or aerospace engineering. Research and qualification roles often prefer a master’s or PhD. Technician roles that run the printers may need only a certificate or associate degree. Hands-on printing experience and a portfolio of printed parts help a lot.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Administrative assistants keep a team or manager organized. They manage calendars and schedule meetings, book travel, process expense reports, order supplies, prepare documents and slide decks, and file records. Many also take meeting notes, track deadlines and act as the first contact for the people they support.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often begin with checking email and the day’s calendars for conflicts. Then come scheduling requests, booking a trip, drafting letters and preparing a meeting room. Afternoons go to expense reports, invoices, updating spreadsheets and setting up tomorrow’s agenda.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They support one or several managers or a whole department. They work daily with other assistants, office managers, the IT help desk, facilities and finance staff. They also deal with clients, vendors, travel agents and visitors on behalf of their team.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core tools are Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, especially Outlook, Word, Excel and shared calendars. Many also use Zoom or Teams, expense software like Concur, travel booking tools, e-signature tools like DocuSign and project trackers such as Asana.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Assistants are judged on reliability and accuracy: no double bookings, expense reports filed on time and documents free of errors. Managers also value anticipating needs, handling confidential matters with discretion and keeping things moving when plans change at the last minute.

qa.q: What is the difference between an administrative assistant and an executive assistant?
qa.a: An administrative assistant usually supports a team or several people with scheduling, documents, supplies and office tasks. An executive assistant supports one or a few senior leaders more closely, often managing their inbox, complex travel, board materials and confidential matters. Executive assistant roles usually need more experience, and many admins move up into them.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be an administrative assistant?
qa.a: Most jobs require a high school diploma or equivalent, and many employers train new hires on the job. Some prefer a certificate or associate degree in office administration. Strong skills in Microsoft Office or Google Workspace, clear writing and organization matter more than a degree. Legal and medical assistant roles may require specialized training.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan campaigns, buy media across search, social, TV, audio and digital display, and set up ads in ad servers. Ad operations staff traffic creative, set targeting and budgets, check tags and tracking, and fix delivery problems so each campaign runs as sold.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with pacing reports to see which campaigns are over or under delivering. Then come launches, creative swaps, client or sales questions, discrepancy checks between ad server and partner numbers, and end-of-day reporting on spend and results.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with account managers, sales teams, media planners, creative and design staff, data analysts and clients. Ad operations also works closely with publishers, ad tech vendors and engineers when tags break or numbers do not match.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include ad servers, demand-side and supply-side platforms, search and social ad managers, analytics dashboards, tag managers and spreadsheets. Many teams also use project trackers, insertion orders and basic HTML or JavaScript to check ad tags.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by on-time launches, accurate setup, correct pacing and spend, and results such as clicks, conversions, reach or return on ad spend. Clean billing, few errors and clear reports matter as much as campaign performance.

qa.q: What does an ad operations specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They set up and manage digital ad campaigns behind the scenes. That means loading creative into ad servers, setting targeting, flight dates and budgets, testing tags, watching delivery and pacing, solving tracking errors, and pulling reports. They also reconcile numbers with partners so billing is correct at the end of each campaign.

qa.q: What is the difference between a media buyer and a media planner?
qa.a: A media planner decides where and when ads should run, based on audience, goals and budget. A media buyer carries out that plan by negotiating prices, buying placements or bidding in programmatic platforms, and making sure the ads run as agreed. On smaller teams, one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Aerospace engineers design, analyze and test aircraft, rockets, satellites, missiles and their parts. They study structures, aerodynamics, propulsion, guidance and control. They write requirements and test plans, review drawings, and track down the cause of failures found in testing or in service.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes computer modeling, design reviews and team meetings. An engineer might run a stress or airflow analysis in the morning, check data from a test in the afternoon, and finish by updating documents. Some roles add time in labs, hangars or launch sites.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use computer-aided design software, finite element analysis for stress, and computational fluid dynamics for airflow. Programming and numerical tools help them build models. Physical tools include wind tunnels, engine test stands, vibration tables, thermal vacuum chambers and flight simulators.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with mechanical, electrical and software engineers, technicians, machinists and quality inspectors. Test pilots, mission operators and program managers are part of the team too. Many also deal with customers such as airlines, government agencies or the military.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged in design reviews and tests against requirements for safety, weight, performance, cost and schedule. Civil aircraft and parts must meet FAA airworthiness standards. Military programs follow military airworthiness processes. Defense work often requires US citizenship, a security clearance and care with export control rules.

qa.q: What does an aerospace engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days are spent at a computer building models, running analyses and checking designs against requirements. Engineers attend design reviews, work through problems with teammates, and write reports and test plans. Depending on the role, they may also visit factory floors, watch tests in labs or wind tunnels, or support flight tests and launches.

qa.q: What is the difference between aeronautical and astronautical engineering?
qa.a: Aeronautical engineering deals with aircraft that fly within Earth’s atmosphere, such as airplanes, helicopters and drones. Astronautical engineering deals with rockets, satellites and spacecraft that operate in space. Many US degree programs teach both under the name aerospace engineering, and engineers often specialize in one branch through their jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They find and sign up websites, coupon sites, bloggers and creators who promote a brand for a commission on each sale or lead. They set commission terms, approve or reject applicants, supply links and promo codes, and make sure partners get paid correctly.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with yesterday’s clicks, orders and commissions in the tracking platform. Then come partner applications, outreach emails to promising sites, planning a promotion with top partners, and reversing commissions on returned or canceled orders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Outside partners include content publishers, deal and loyalty sites, influencers and account managers at affiliate networks. Inside the company they work with ecommerce, finance, legal, brand and paid media teams so offers, payouts and messaging line up.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: An affiliate network or tracking platform, spreadsheets and web analytics are the core tools. Managers also use email outreach tools, unique promo codes, banner and product feeds, and fraud checks that flag cookie stuffing, fake leads or trademark bidding.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured by revenue from partners, cost per acquisition and return on spend. Good managers also track how many sales are truly new customers, how many active partners they have, and how much commission is lost to fraud or returns.

qa.q: What does an affiliate marketing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They review sales data from tracking software, recruit and approve new partners, and negotiate commission rates. They send partners creative assets and promo codes, plan seasonal offers, audit for fraud and policy breaks, and approve monthly payouts. They also check that partners clearly disclose their paid relationship, as Federal Trade Commission rules require.

qa.q: What is the difference between affiliate marketing and influencer marketing?
qa.a: Affiliate marketing pays partners mainly for results, such as a commission on each tracked sale or lead. Influencer marketing often pays a flat fee for content and judges it on reach and engagement. The two overlap when creators earn commission through links or codes. In both cases, US rules require clear disclosure of the paid connection.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: AI engineers build features on top of large language models. They write prompts, connect models to company data through retrieval, set up tools that agents can call, and wire everything into a working app that real users can rely on.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reviewing failed chat transcripts, then tuning a prompt or retrieval step. Afternoons often go to writing code, running evaluation sets, checking cost and speed, and shipping small fixes behind feature flags.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work in Python or TypeScript and call model APIs or self-hosted open models. They use vector databases, embedding models, orchestration libraries, evaluation harnesses, tracing and logging tools, and cloud services for deployment.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, backend and frontend engineers, and designers. They also talk with data, security and legal teams about privacy, and with support staff who report where the assistant gives wrong answers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by answer quality on test sets, user feedback, task completion rates, response time and cost per request. Teams also watch for hallucinations, unsafe outputs and leaks of private data before and after each release.

qa.q: What does an AI engineer do day to day?
qa.a: An AI engineer builds and improves products that use language models. Daily work includes writing prompts, building retrieval over documents, connecting agents to tools and APIs, running evaluations, debugging bad outputs, and tracking cost and latency. Much of the job is ordinary software engineering, with extra time spent testing how the model behaves on real user questions.

qa.q: What is the difference between an AI engineer and a machine learning engineer?
qa.a: A machine learning engineer usually trains, tunes and deploys models, working with datasets, training pipelines and model infrastructure. An AI engineer usually builds applications on top of existing language models, focusing on prompts, retrieval, agents, evaluation and product integration. The titles overlap at many companies, so the job posting’s duties matter more than the name.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They decide which problems an AI feature should solve and write the requirements. They set quality bars for model output, plan launches, and weigh tradeoffs between accuracy, speed, cost and safety. They also decide when a feature is good enough to ship.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with reviewing evaluation results or user feedback on model answers. Then come meetings with engineers about a failing test case, a roadmap discussion, and time spent reading real user conversations to spot errors and gaps.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with machine learning engineers, data scientists, software engineers and designers. They also work with legal, privacy and policy teams on risk, and with sales or support staff who hear what customers need.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use evaluation datasets, labeled test sets and dashboards that track model quality. They write prompts to probe model behavior and query data with spreadsheets or SQL. They also use ticket trackers, product specs and A/B test reports.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether the AI feature helps users and holds up in real use. Teams watch adoption, task success, error and complaint rates, and cost per use, along with avoiding harmful or embarrassing outputs after launch.

qa.q: What does an AI product manager do day to day?
qa.a: An AI product manager defines what an AI feature should do and how well it must perform. Day to day, they review model test results, read real user interactions, write specs, set launch criteria, and work with engineers and data scientists to fix weak spots. They also balance quality against speed, cost and safety risks.

qa.q: What is the difference between an AI product manager and a regular product manager?
qa.a: Both decide what to build and why. An AI product manager also deals with outputs that are not always predictable. They set measurable quality bars, build evaluation sets, plan for wrong or harmful answers, and decide how much error users can accept. They need a working grasp of how models are trained, tested and monitored.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They design tests, often called evals, that measure what an AI model can do and where it breaks. They probe for failures like made-up facts, unsafe advice, flattery and hidden goals. Then they help build fixes such as extra training, filters and refusal rules.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start by running a test set across several model versions overnight. Then comes reading transcripts, sorting failures into patterns and checking scoring code for bugs. Afternoons often go to writing up results and meeting with the team that trains the model.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in Python, using notebooks, model APIs, open-source evaluation harnesses and shared GPU clusters. Grading may use human raters, scoring scripts or another model acting as a judge. Version control and experiment tracking keep results repeatable.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with researchers who train models, product engineers and policy staff. Outside experts in fields like biology, chemistry or cybersecurity often help test risky knowledge. Contract red-teamers and data labelers supply attacks and graded examples.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work produces tests that are reliable, hard to game and repeatable by others. It is valued when findings change a training run, a safety mitigation or a release decision. Clear, honest reports about uncertainty matter as much as clever methods.

qa.q: What does an AI safety and evaluation worker do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix coding and careful reading. They write or update tests, run them on new model versions and read the model’s answers to see how it failed. They look for patterns like confident errors or unsafe help, try fixes, rerun the tests and write short reports so training and product teams can act on the results.

qa.q: What is the difference between AI evaluation and red teaming?
qa.a: Evaluation measures a model in a structured, repeatable way, using fixed test sets and scoring rules to compare versions over time. Red teaming is open-ended attack work, where people or tools try to trick the model into breaking its rules. Red team findings often become new evaluation tests once a failure is understood.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They rate and rank chatbot answers, write sample prompts and ideal replies, label images, audio or text, and flag unsafe or wrong output. Each task follows a detailed project guideline, and the results become training data for AI models.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most log in to a task platform, pick up available tasks and work through them one by one. One task may mean reading two answers, checking facts, choosing the better one and explaining why. Work comes in batches, so some days are full and others quiet.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most work from home as independent contractors and set their own hours within project limits. Some projects seek specialists such as coders, nurses, lawyers or language experts. Nearly all need a reliable computer, a steady internet connection and a quiet space.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Reviewers score each task for accuracy, guideline compliance and clear reasoning. Low quality scores can mean fewer tasks or removal from a project. Most platforms also require passing a skills test before any paid work starts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A web-based labeling or rating tool, the project guideline document, search engines for fact-checking, and sometimes a code editor or spreadsheet. Time trackers are common, since many projects pay by the hour and set time limits per task.

qa.q: What does an AI trainer do day to day?
qa.a: An AI trainer reads prompts and model answers, then rates, ranks, corrects or rewrites them according to a written guideline. Others label images, transcribe audio or write fresh examples from scratch. The work is detail-heavy, mostly solo and done on a computer, often from home on a flexible contract schedule.

qa.q: Is AI training a steady job?
qa.a: Often not. Most roles are freelance or contract, so projects can start, pause or end with little notice. Pay is usually hourly or per task, and independent contractors generally get no benefits and must handle their own taxes. Many people treat it as side income, though skilled specialists may find more regular work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Verify customer identities at account opening, collect beneficial ownership details for business customers, screen names against OFAC sanctions lists and review transaction monitoring alerts. When activity looks suspicious, they document it and escalate it so the institution can decide whether to file a Suspicious Activity Report with FinCEN.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most of the day is spent working a queue of alerts or onboarding files. An analyst pulls account history, compares activity to the customer’s stated purpose, searches public records and news, then writes a case narrative and closes or escalates it. Periodic reviews of high-risk customers fill the rest.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with onboarding teams, branch and relationship staff, financial crime investigators, the BSA/AML officer and compliance managers. They also support internal audit, and during regulatory exams they may provide case files to federal or state examiners.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include case management software, transaction monitoring systems, sanctions screening tools, identity verification services, public records databases and spreadsheets. Just as important is working knowledge of the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act, OFAC rules and red flags such as structuring.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on clear, defensible written decisions, accuracy in quality assurance reviews, and meeting deadlines. Suspicious Activity Reports generally must be filed within 30 days of initial detection. Internal audits and regulatory exams also test whether files show sound reasoning.

qa.q: What does an AML/KYC analyst do day to day?
qa.a: They review new customer files and alerts from monitoring systems. For each case they check identity documents, ownership, sanctions screening results and transaction patterns, then decide if the activity makes sense. They write up their reasoning, close cases that are explained and escalate suspicious ones. SARs are confidential, so they never tell the customer about a filing.

qa.q: What is the difference between AML and KYC?
qa.a: KYC, or know your customer, is the part focused on who the customer is: verifying identity, identifying beneficial owners, understanding the purpose of the account and assigning a risk rating. AML, or anti-money laundering, is the broader program that includes KYC plus ongoing transaction monitoring, investigations, sanctions controls, training and reporting suspicious activity to FinCEN.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Analog and mixed-signal engineers design circuits that handle real-world signals. These include amplifiers, data converters, voltage regulators, phase-locked loops, radio front ends and high-speed serial links. They set specifications, choose architectures, size transistors and check that the design meets targets for noise, power, speed and accuracy.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes circuit simulation, design reviews and debugging. An engineer might run corner and Monte Carlo simulations in the morning, review a layout with a mask designer after lunch, then measure first silicon on the lab bench to compare results with predictions.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They work in schematic capture and SPICE-type simulators, using foundry process design kits and models. In the lab they use oscilloscopes, spectrum and network analyzers, signal generators, power supplies and probe stations. Scripting in Python or similar languages helps automate simulation and test.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with layout designers, digital designers, verification engineers and system architects. They also work with test and product engineers who bring chips into production, applications engineers who support customers, and foundry contacts who supply process data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether the chip works on first silicon and meets its specifications across process, voltage and temperature variation. Yield in production, power use, die area and meeting tapeout schedules also matter a great deal.

qa.q: What does an analog and mixed-signal engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They design and verify circuits that connect chips to the physical world, such as converters, regulators, clock circuits and radio blocks. Daily work includes simulating designs, guiding layout, reviewing results with teammates and testing real chips in the lab to find and fix problems before production.

qa.q: What is the difference between analog design and digital design?
qa.a: Digital designers mostly describe logic in hardware languages and rely on automated tools to build circuits from standard cells. Analog designers work at the transistor level, hand-crafting circuits where noise, matching, temperature and layout details directly affect performance. Mixed-signal engineers handle blocks that combine both, like data converters and phase-locked loops.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Analysts gather numbers or documents in one area, such as finance, risk, operations or data. They clean and check the information, look for patterns and problems, and turn what they find into reports, charts and plain recommendations that help managers decide what to do next.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with pulling fresh data or reviewing new reports. Then come checks for errors, building or updating models, and answering questions from managers. Many analysts spend part of the afternoon writing summaries, preparing slides or joining meetings to explain results.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets are the everyday tool, often with formulas, pivot tables and charts. Many analysts also use SQL to query databases, dashboard and reporting software, and sometimes programming languages such as Python or R. Finance analysts may use accounting systems and market data services.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Analysts work with managers who need answers, team members who own the data, and specialists in IT, accounting or operations. Some present findings to senior leaders or clients, so they must explain complex results in short, clear terms that non-experts can act on.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good analysis is accurate, delivered on time and easy to understand. Managers look at whether numbers hold up under review, whether reports answer the real question, and whether recommendations lead to better decisions, lower costs or fewer risks.

qa.q: What does an analyst do day to day?
qa.a: An analyst collects data or documents, checks them for errors, and studies them to find trends, risks or problems. They build spreadsheets, models or dashboards, then write reports and present findings to managers. Much of the day is spent answering specific questions, such as why costs rose or which products sell best.

qa.q: What is the difference between a data analyst and a financial analyst?
qa.a: A data analyst works with many kinds of information, such as sales, customer or website data, and often uses SQL and dashboards. A financial analyst focuses on money matters like budgets, forecasts, investments and company performance. Both study numbers and report findings, but financial analysts usually need deeper knowledge of accounting and finance.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Analytics engineers write SQL that turns raw data into clean, well-named tables. They define business metrics once so every report agrees, add tests that catch bad or missing data, and document what each table and column means.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start by checking overnight data jobs for failures. Then comes building or fixing a data model, reviewing a teammate’s code changes, and answering questions from analysts about why two numbers do not match.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core tools are SQL, a cloud data warehouse, and a transformation framework that runs SQL models in order. They use Git for version control, scheduling tools for data pipelines, and sometimes Python for scripts and checks.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They sit between data engineers, who bring raw data in, and data analysts, who explore it. They also work with finance, marketing, and product teams to agree on what terms like active customer or revenue really mean.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means people trust the numbers. Good work shows up as fewer broken dashboards, tests that catch problems before users do, clear documentation, fast queries, and metrics that match across every team’s reports.

qa.q: What is the difference between an analytics engineer and a data analyst?
qa.a: A data analyst uses data to answer business questions, build reports, and share findings. An analytics engineer builds and maintains the clean, tested tables those analysts rely on. Analytics engineers borrow software habits like version control, code review, and automated testing, while analysts focus more on interpreting results.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to become an analytics engineer?
qa.a: No license is required, and many employers care most about strong SQL and an understanding of data modeling. Many people enter from data analyst or data engineering roles. A degree in a field like computer science, statistics, or business helps, but a portfolio showing well-built, tested data models can also make a strong case.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Android developers write and maintain app code, mostly in Kotlin. They build screens, connect the app to servers through APIs, store data on the device, fix bugs and crashes, write tests, and release updates to app stores.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team meeting. Then they code a feature or fix from the task board, review teammates’ pull requests, test on emulators and real phones, and check crash reports from the live app.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with product managers who set priorities, designers who supply screen layouts, backend engineers who build the APIs, QA testers, and often iOS developers building the same app for iPhone.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Core tools include Android Studio, Kotlin, the Gradle build system, Git for version control, and Jetpack libraries such as Jetpack Compose for building screens. Emulators, test devices, crash reporting tools and automated build pipelines round out the kit.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in a stable app with few crashes, fast load times, smooth scrolling and good battery use. Teams also look at clean, tested code, features shipped on schedule, user ratings, and following app store rules.

qa.q: What does an Android developer do day to day?
qa.a: An Android developer spends most of the day writing Kotlin code for new features and fixes. They also review other developers’ code, test the app on different phones and screen sizes, read crash reports, join planning meetings, and prepare new versions for release to app stores.

qa.q: What is the difference between an Android developer and an iOS developer?
qa.a: Android developers build apps for Android devices, mostly in Kotlin using Android Studio. iOS developers build for iPhone and iPad, mostly in Swift using Xcode on a Mac. Android work often means supporting many device makers, screen sizes and older system versions. Some developers use cross-platform tools to cover both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Angular and Vue developers build the interactive parts of web apps with one of these two frameworks. They create components and forms, manage app data and routing, connect screens to APIs, and keep the interface fast, accessible and consistent across browsers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes a standup, then building or fixing components against design files. Developers write unit tests, review teammates’ code and debug in the browser. In Angular teams some time often goes to framework upgrades, since large business apps must stay on supported versions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with UX designers, backend developers who supply the APIs, QA testers and product owners. Angular roles often sit in big enterprise teams with strict code standards. Vue roles are often at smaller companies, where the developer may also handle some backend work.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Angular work uses TypeScript, the Angular CLI, RxJS and Angular Material. Vue work uses Vite, Pinia for app state and often Nuxt for full sites. Both rely on VS Code, npm, Git, ESLint and testing tools like Jest, Vitest, Cypress or Playwright.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on screens that match the design, load quickly and work in all supported browsers. Reviewers look for clear components, tested code and correct handling of forms and errors. Keeping the app on current framework versions without breaking features also counts.

qa.q: What is the difference between Angular and Vue?
qa.a: Angular is a full framework with built-in tools for routing, forms and testing, and it uses TypeScript by default. Vue is lighter and easier to start with, and teams add only the pieces they need. Angular is common in big enterprise apps, while Vue is popular with smaller teams and in many PHP projects.

qa.q: Is AngularJS the same as Angular?
qa.a: No. AngularJS is the original framework, and its official support ended at the end of 2021. Modern Angular is a full rewrite in TypeScript and works very differently. Some companies still hire developers to keep old AngularJS apps running or to move them to modern Angular or another framework.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They design and build APIs, often REST, GraphQL or gRPC, and write SDKs in languages like Python, JavaScript, Java or Go. They handle authentication, versioning, error messages and rate limits so outside developers can connect to the product reliably.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reviewing pull requests, then writing endpoint code and tests. Later they update reference docs, fix a bug reported by a partner, and check that a new SDK release does not break existing customer code.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with product managers, backend engineers, security teams and technical writers. They also hear directly from the developers who use their APIs, through support tickets, community forums, issue trackers and partner calls.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include OpenAPI specifications, Postman or similar API clients, Git, CI pipelines, package registries like npm and PyPI, code generators, and monitoring dashboards that track latency, error rates and usage.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in how quickly outside developers get a first working call, how stable the API stays across versions, and how few breaking changes or support tickets reach the team. Clear docs and consistent design count heavily.

qa.q: What does an API and SDK developer do day to day?
qa.a: They write and test the code behind API endpoints, build client libraries that wrap those endpoints in popular languages, and keep documentation accurate. They review code, respond to bug reports from developers who use the product, plan version changes, and watch monitoring tools for errors or slow responses.

qa.q: What is the difference between an API and an SDK?
qa.a: An API is the set of rules and endpoints a program uses to talk to a service, such as sending requests and getting data back. An SDK is a packaged toolkit, usually a code library plus samples and docs, that makes calling that API easier in a specific programming language.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Application security engineers review code and designs for security flaws, run scanning tools, and test running apps for weaknesses. They help developers fix what they find and set secure coding standards the whole team follows.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with triaging new findings from automated scans. Then comes a threat modeling session for a planned feature, a code review of a risky change, and time spent explaining a fix to a developer.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with software developers and product teams. They also partner with DevOps engineers on build pipelines, with incident responders when a flaw is exploited, and with outside researchers who report bugs.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include static analysis (SAST), dynamic testing (DAST), software composition analysis for open source libraries, secret scanners, and web proxies for manual testing. Many write scripts in Python or another language to automate checks.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in fewer serious flaws reaching production, faster fix times, and developers who catch issues on their own. Good engineers are judged on accurate findings, not noise, and on keeping releases moving safely.

qa.q: What does an application security engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They look for security flaws in their company’s own software before release. That means reviewing code, running and tuning scanners, testing apps by hand, and modeling threats for new features. Much of the job is working with developers to fix issues and building security checks into the build pipeline so problems are caught early.

qa.q: What is the difference between an application security engineer and a penetration tester?
qa.a: A penetration tester usually attacks systems for a set period and writes a report of findings, often for many clients. An application security engineer works inside one company over time, reviewing code, shaping design, automating checks, and helping developers fix flaws. The engineer is focused on preventing issues, not just finding them.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They find tasks where AI can save time or money, test tools on real work, set up the winners, and train staff to use them. They also write usage guidelines and track whether the results hold up after launch.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with interviews to map a team’s workflow, then time spent writing and testing prompts or connecting an AI tool to company data. Afternoons often go to demos, training sessions, and answering questions from people trying the tools.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with department heads, frontline staff, IT and security teams, and legal or compliance staff. They often act as a translator between business people who know the problem and technical people who build or buy the tools.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include chat assistants and large language model APIs, automation platforms, spreadsheets, and data dashboards. Many roles also use basic scripting such as Python, plus documentation tools for writing guides, policies, and training material.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by real adoption and results: hours saved, fewer errors, faster turnaround, and how many people keep using the tools. Safe handling of data and following company policy on privacy and accuracy also count heavily.

qa.q: What does an applied AI specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They spend most days talking with teams about how they work, picking tasks AI can help with, and testing tools on those tasks. They set up what works, write simple guides, run training, and check results. Much of the job is people work: listening, explaining limits, and helping skeptical staff get comfortable with new tools.

qa.q: Do you need a license or degree to work in AI adoption?
qa.a: No license is required in the US. Many employers prefer a degree in business, computer science, or a related field, but proven results and a portfolio often matter more. Workers should know that rules on data privacy and on AI use in areas like hiring vary by state and city, so checking local requirements is part of the job.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Arabic-speaking staff answer calls, chats and emails in Arabic, translate documents, interpret conversations or sell to clients in the Gulf, the Middle East and North Africa. They switch between Arabic and English all day and often write case notes and reports in English.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many roles start early or run late to overlap with business hours in the Middle East, which are several hours ahead of US time. Some employers also cover days that fall on a regional workweek, since some Arab countries keep a different weekend.

day.label: Which Arabic they use
day.text: Modern Standard Arabic is used for writing, news and formal settings. Spoken dialects differ widely, so postings often ask for Gulf, Levantine, Egyptian or Maghrebi Arabic. North African customers may also mix in French, so some jobs ask for both.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include ticketing and customer record systems, an Arabic keyboard layout, and software that handles right-to-left text. Translators use translation memory programs and glossaries. Interpreters work by phone, video platforms or in person with a headset and notepad.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers check accuracy, tone, response time and customer satisfaction. Most test language skills before hiring. Court interpreting rules vary by state, medical interpreters may hold voluntary national certification, and many government linguist jobs require US citizenship and a security clearance.

qa.q: What does an Arabic-speaking customer service representative do day to day?
qa.a: They handle orders, billing questions, account issues and complaints from Arabic-speaking customers by phone, chat or email. They adjust to the customer’s dialect, explain policies clearly, log each case in English and pass complex problems to other teams. Shifts may be early, late or on weekends to match customers’ time zones.

qa.q: What is the difference between an Arabic interpreter and an Arabic translator?
qa.a: An interpreter works with spoken language, turning speech between Arabic and English in real time at hospitals, courts, meetings or on the phone. A translator works with written text, such as contracts, websites and records. Translators usually have time to research terms, while interpreters must be accurate on the spot.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: An art director decides how a project should look and feel. They set the visual style, review concepts, approve layouts and final art, and make sure every piece fits the brand, the brief and the deadline.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with team check-ins and feedback on work in progress. The rest of the day mixes client or stakeholder meetings, sketching rough ideas, building mood boards, and giving artists clear notes on what to change.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They lead graphic designers, illustrators, 3D artists, photographers and production staff. They also work closely with copywriters, creative directors, producers, marketing leads and clients, translating business goals into visual direction.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include design and image software for layouts, photo editing and vector art, plus prototyping apps and project trackers. In games, they also review work in 3D tools and game engines. Sketchbooks and style guides stay essential.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in a consistent, striking visual style that meets the brief, on time and within budget. Clients, creative directors and audiences judge the results, and a strong portfolio of shipped projects drives career growth.

qa.q: What does an art director do day to day?
qa.a: An art director spends the day guiding a team’s visual work. They review drafts, give feedback, approve final designs, and meet with clients or producers to align on goals. Some hands-on design or sketching is common, but much of the job is direction, communication and keeping projects consistent and on schedule.

qa.q: What is the difference between an art director and a creative director?
qa.a: An art director owns the visual side of a project and leads designers and artists. A creative director sits above them, setting the overall creative vision across visuals, writing and strategy, often for several projects or a whole brand. In smaller teams, one person may handle both roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They turn a chip specification into working hardware. That means defining the microarchitecture, writing RTL code in Verilog or SystemVerilog, checking it in simulation, and working with physical design teams to meet timing, power and area targets before the design goes to manufacturing.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start by reviewing overnight simulation or regression results. Engineers then debug failing tests in a waveform viewer, fix logic bugs or timing violations, update design documents, and join design reviews where teammates check each other’s blocks for errors and risks.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with chip architects, verification engineers, physical design and layout engineers, and design-for-test specialists. They also coordinate with firmware and software teams who will program the chip, and with manufacturing and packaging partners near tapeout.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include hardware description languages, logic simulators, waveform viewers, synthesis tools, static timing analysis, formal verification, and place-and-route software. Most work happens on Linux machines and shared compute farms, with scripts written in Python, Tcl or Perl and code kept in version control.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means a chip that works on first silicon and hits its performance, power and area goals on schedule. Because fixing a bug after tapeout can require costly new masks, careful verification, clean timing and thorough reviews matter as much as speed.

qa.q: What does an ASIC engineer do day to day?
qa.a: An ASIC engineer spends most of the day writing and refining hardware code, running simulations, and debugging problems found in tests. They also review timing and power reports, attend design reviews, and update specifications. As a tapeout deadline nears, work shifts toward fixing late bugs, closing timing, and signing off that the design is ready for manufacturing.

qa.q: What is the difference between an ASIC engineer and an FPGA engineer?
qa.a: Both write hardware description code, but an ASIC engineer designs a custom chip that is manufactured once and cannot be changed. An FPGA engineer configures a programmable chip that can be updated after it ships. ASIC work adds physical design, test insertion, and strict signoff steps, because a mistake found after manufacturing is far more expensive to fix.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: An associate product manager owns a small feature or part of a product. They gather user feedback, write requirements and user stories, prioritize a backlog, and help decide what gets built next. Senior product managers guide their bigger decisions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a team standup. Then come user interviews, reviewing data on how a feature is used, and writing specs. Later they may answer engineer questions, test new builds, and update stakeholders on progress.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with software engineers, designers, and data analysts. They also talk with sales, marketing, and customer support teams. A senior product manager or mentor usually reviews their work and coaches them.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include issue trackers for backlogs, shared documents for specs, design files for reviewing mockups, and analytics dashboards. Many also use spreadsheets, survey tools, and basic SQL to answer questions about user behavior.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether their features ship on time and move agreed goals, such as user engagement or retention. Managers also look at the quality of their specs, their judgment, and how well the team trusts them.

qa.q: What does an associate product manager do day to day?
qa.a: They spend the day deciding what a small part of a product should do and keeping the team moving. That means writing specs, prioritizing tasks, joining standups, talking with users, checking usage data, and answering questions from engineers and designers. In rotational programs, they may switch to a new product area after a set period.

qa.q: What is the difference between an associate product manager and a product manager?
qa.a: An associate product manager is an entry-level role. They own a smaller scope, such as one feature, and work under close guidance. A product manager owns a larger product area, sets its strategy, and makes bigger tradeoff decisions with less oversight. Many associates are promoted to product manager after gaining experience.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They record, edit and mix sound effects, dialogue and music, then build them into a finished product. In games, they also set how sounds react to play, such as footsteps changing on gravel or music shifting when a fight starts.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a new game build or video cut and a list of sound fixes. Then comes editing in audio software, a recording session for props or voices, and testing sounds in the game or final mix.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily gear includes audio editing software, microphones, portable field recorders, audio interfaces and studio speakers or headphones. Game audio adds middleware and game engines. Audio programmers write code, often in C++, for sound engines, plugins and signal processing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with game designers, video editors, directors, composers, voice actors and software engineers. Producers set the schedule, and testers report bugs such as missing, distorted or badly timed sounds.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Sound must fit the picture or gameplay, stay clear at different volumes and meet the loudness targets of each platform. In games and apps, audio also has to run within memory and processor limits without glitches.

qa.q: What does a sound designer do day to day?
qa.a: A sound designer creates and edits the sounds heard in a game, video or product. They record or source raw audio, layer and process it, and match it to picture or gameplay. Much of the day goes to testing, taking feedback from directors or designers, and fixing sounds that feel wrong, too loud or out of sync.

qa.q: What is the difference between a sound designer and an audio programmer?
qa.a: A sound designer makes the sounds and decides how they should feel and behave. An audio programmer writes the code that plays them, such as sound engines, mixing systems, effects and tools. Designers work mostly in audio software and middleware. Programmers work in code, usually with a computer science background and some knowledge of signal processing.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Internal auditors test whether a company’s controls work as designed. They review processes like purchasing, payroll and the financial close. They check samples of transactions, find weak spots and recommend fixes. At public companies, many also test controls over financial reporting that management must assess under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a walkthrough meeting with a process owner. Then comes pulling samples, inspecting invoices and approvals, and documenting results in workpapers. Later hours often go to writing findings, following up on open issues and updating the audit manager on progress.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with department managers, accounting and finance staff, IT teams and compliance officers. The head of internal audit usually reports results to the board’s audit committee. They also coordinate with outside auditors, who may rely on some internal audit testing.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets, data analytics software and audit management systems for workpapers are daily tools. Auditors also pull data from the company’s accounting and ERP systems. Many use the COSO internal control framework to judge controls and use query tools to test full data sets, not just samples.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on clear, well supported findings, solid workpapers and finishing audits on the plan’s schedule. Success also shows when management actually fixes the issues raised. Professional internal audit standards guide the work, and the function is reviewed by periodic quality assessments.

qa.q: What is the difference between internal audit and external audit?
qa.a: Internal auditors work for the company, or for a firm hired to act as its internal audit team. They review controls, risks and operations all year. External auditors are independent CPA firms that give a formal opinion on the financial statements. Firms auditing public companies must register with the PCAOB. Internal audit reports to the audit committee and management, not to outside investors.

qa.q: Do internal auditors need a CPA license?
qa.a: No law requires a license to work in internal audit. Many employers prefer candidates with a CPA license or the Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) credential. IT auditors often hold the CISA. CPA licensing rules vary by state. Credentials often matter more for promotion to senior or manager roles than for entry-level jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build links between business systems, such as a sales app and an accounting system, so data moves without anyone retyping it. They also write scripts and workflows that replace manual steps, then test, document and support them after launch.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with checking logs and alerts for failed data syncs or stalled jobs. The rest of the day mixes fixing errors, mapping fields between systems, writing code for a new connection and meeting with the team that asked for it.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include REST and SOAP APIs, webhooks, message queues, integration platforms, robotic process automation software, scripting languages like Python or PowerShell, SQL, version control, and scheduling and monitoring tools.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with business analysts, software developers, IT operations, security staff and the people whose tasks are being automated. Talking with those end users matters, since they know the exceptions and odd cases a real process has.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in hours of manual work removed, fewer data entry errors and integrations that run reliably without constant fixes. Clear documentation, good error handling and safe handling of passwords, keys and personal data also count.

qa.q: What does an integration and automation engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They connect software systems through APIs and other interfaces, and they automate repetitive tasks such as copying data, building reports or setting up user accounts. Daily work includes monitoring running integrations, fixing failures, gathering needs from business teams, writing and testing code or workflows, and documenting how each connection works.

qa.q: What is the difference between an automation engineer and an integration engineer?
qa.a: An integration engineer focuses on making separate systems exchange data correctly, through APIs, files or middleware. An automation engineer focuses on removing manual steps from a process, using scripts, workflows or bots. The roles overlap, and many employers combine them. The title “automation engineer” can also mean test automation or factory control systems, so read each posting closely.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Automotive engineers design, analyze and test parts and systems for cars and trucks, such as the body, chassis, brakes, powertrain, electrical systems and software. Most specialize in one area, like crash safety, battery systems or vehicle dynamics, and follow a part from concept through production.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may mix CAD modeling, reviewing simulation results, writing test plans and joining design reviews. Many engineers also spend time in a lab, on a dynamometer or at a test track, then solve problems with suppliers or the assembly plant.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with designers, test technicians, software and electrical teams, manufacturing and quality engineers, purchasing staff and outside suppliers. Program managers set deadlines and budgets, and engineers often present results to them and to other teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include CAD software, finite element analysis, computational fluid dynamics, data acquisition systems and vehicle network tools for reading CAN bus data. Test work uses dynamometers, crash sleds, climate chambers and instrumented prototype vehicles.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Designs must meet federal motor vehicle safety standards set by NHTSA and EPA emissions rules, with stricter rules in California and states that follow its standards. Engineers are also judged on cost, weight, durability, warranty problems and hitting program timing.

qa.q: What does an automotive engineer do day to day?
qa.a: An automotive engineer spends the day designing or improving a vehicle system, checking it with computer simulation and physical tests, and fixing problems that show up. They write reports, attend design reviews, work with suppliers on parts, and support the plant when a design moves into production. The mix of desk and test work depends on the role.

qa.q: Do automotive engineers need a PE license?
qa.a: Most do not. Engineers who work for vehicle makers and suppliers usually fall under an industrial exemption, though the exact rules vary by state. A Professional Engineer license helps more in consulting, accident reconstruction or expert witness work. Most automotive engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, electrical or automotive engineering.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Automotive sales consultants greet shoppers, learn what they need, and match them with new or used vehicles. They explain features, run test drives, help appraise trade-ins, present pricing, and hand buyers to the finance office. At delivery they walk buyers through the car and its technology.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Shifts are often long and include evenings and weekends, when most shoppers visit. Between walk-in customers, consultants answer online leads, return calls and texts, follow up with past buyers, prepare cars for delivery and study new models through manufacturer training.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Consultants work with sales managers who approve deals, finance and insurance managers who arrange loans and add-on products, and the service department. They also deal with porters, detailers and the internet sales team. Customers include first-time buyers, families, fleet buyers and repeat clients.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include dealership CRM systems such as VinSolutions or DealerSocket, inventory and pricing tools, and vehicle history reports. Consultants also use desking tools for payment quotes, texting and video apps for remote shoppers, and the manufacturer’s online training portal.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Consultants are judged on units sold each month, gross profit per deal and customer satisfaction surveys sent by the manufacturer. Managers also track closing rate, appointments that show up, follow-up activity and repeat or referral business. Pay is often mostly commission plus volume bonuses.

qa.q: Do you need a license to sell cars?
qa.a: It depends on the state. Some states require car salespeople to hold their own salesperson license, which can include an application, a fee and a background check, while others license only the dealership. A degree is not usually required. Dealers train new hires on the product, the sales process and the rules for advertising and financing.

qa.q: Is car sales a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Pay often depends heavily on commission, so a slow month means a smaller check. Shifts are long and include weekends and many holidays, and monthly sales targets add pressure. Many consultants enjoy the fast pace, meeting people and the chance to earn more as repeat and referral business grows.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Autonomous vehicle operators ride in or remotely monitor self-driving cars and trucks during testing. They watch the system and the road, take manual control when the software misbehaves or a hazard appears, log events, follow test routes and checklists, and give feedback to engineers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift starts with a briefing on the day’s tests and pre-drive checks of the vehicle and sensors. Most hours go to riding test routes in autonomous mode with hands ready, flagging events as they happen. The shift ends with written reports, data uploads and a debrief.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Operators work with test leads, fleet technicians, safety teams and the software engineers who use their notes. Some ride with a second operator who logs data. Remote operators work in a control center alongside other monitors and dispatchers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The main tools are the test vehicle, a laptop or tablet running test software, event tagging buttons and an issue logging system. Operators also use checklists, two-way radios, dash cameras and vehicle diagnostic tools. Remote operators use consoles with several screens.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Operators are judged on safety first: timely, smooth takeovers, no at-fault incidents and strict use of procedures. The quality of event notes matters because engineers rely on them. Reliability, alertness through long shifts and a clean driving record also count.

qa.q: What qualifications do you need to be an autonomous vehicle operator?
qa.a: Most employers require a valid driver’s license held for several years, a clean driving record, a background check and a drug test. Truck testing roles need a commercial driver’s license. Companies train operators in defensive driving and safe takeovers. Some states, such as California, also require the testing company to hold a permit and train its drivers.

qa.q: Is being an autonomous vehicle operator a stressful job?
qa.a: It mixes long stretches of watching the road with rare moments that need a fast, calm takeover.
