Chemists work in fume hoods, wear goggles, gloves and lab coats and follow safety data sheets. Computational and office-based chemists face almost no chemical risk.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A chief of staff helps an executive decide what matters most and makes sure it gets done. They set agendas, track goals, follow up on decisions, draft key messages and lead special projects that cut across teams.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a review of the executive’s calendar and priorities. Then come leadership meetings, prep notes for board or investor sessions, check-ins with department heads and time spent unblocking stalled projects.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with one executive, often the CEO or a senior leader. They also deal daily with the leadership team, executive assistants, finance, communications and sometimes board members or outside partners.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include shared calendars, slide decks, spreadsheets, project tracking software and dashboards for company goals. Strong writing, discretion and the ability to read people matter more than any single tool.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in how well the executive’s time is used, whether leadership decisions turn into action and how smoothly big initiatives run. Trust from the executive and from other leaders is the real measure.

qa.q: What does a chief of staff do day to day?
qa.a: A chief of staff manages an executive’s priorities, prepares and runs leadership meetings, follows up on decisions and leads special projects. They act as a link between the executive and the rest of the organization, often handling sensitive issues and making sure nothing important falls through the cracks.

qa.q: What is the difference between a chief of staff and an executive assistant?
qa.a: An executive assistant mainly handles scheduling, travel, correspondence and day-to-day logistics. A chief of staff works on strategy and operations: setting priorities, driving projects across teams and advising the executive. Many leaders have both, with the assistant running the calendar and the chief of staff shaping how that time is spent.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Use Mandarin or Cantonese to serve customers, patients or clients. Common tasks include answering calls, explaining products, bills or forms, translating short documents, and switching between Chinese and English in the same conversation.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Banks, insurance and real estate offices, hospitals and clinics, call centers, retail and travel businesses, schools, law offices, and companies that trade with mainland China, Taiwan or Hong Kong. Many roles are in cities with large Chinese communities.

day.label: Reading and writing Chinese
day.text: Some jobs need speaking only. Others need written Chinese in simplified characters, used in mainland China, or traditional characters, used in Taiwan, Hong Kong and many long-established US communities. Postings usually say which one.

day.label: How skills are checked
day.text: Employers often test language skills in an interview or a phone or written assessment. Medical interpreters may hold a voluntary national credential. Many state courts certify Mandarin and Cantonese interpreters, and the rules vary by state.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Customers who are more comfortable in Chinese, often older adults or recent immigrants, and English-speaking coworkers who rely on them to bridge the gap. Cultural sense, such as polite forms of address, matters as much as vocabulary.

qa.q: What does a Chinese speaking worker do day to day?
qa.a: It depends on the main job. A bank teller or sales rep does the usual tasks but handles Chinese-speaking customers. A call center agent takes calls in Mandarin or Cantonese. An interpreter or translator converts meaning between Chinese and English. Most spend the day explaining details clearly, answering questions, and keeping notes or records in English.

qa.q: What is the difference between Mandarin and Cantonese jobs?
qa.a: Mandarin is the official language of mainland China and Taiwan and is the more common request. Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macau and many older US Chinatowns. The spoken forms are not mutually understandable, so employers hire for the one their customers use. Written Chinese is largely shared, though character sets differ.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A CISO owns a company’s whole security program. They set the strategy and budget, hire and lead security teams, approve policies, manage risk from vendors and new projects, oversee incident response and report on cyber risk to executives and the board.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A CISO’s day is mostly meetings: briefings on threats and incidents, budget and hiring decisions, project reviews and talks with business leaders. They also prepare board updates, answer customer and auditor questions and make the final calls during serious incidents.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the CEO, CIO, general counsel, chief risk officer and the board or its audit committee. They lead security managers and engineers and deal with regulators, auditors, insurers, outside lawyers and incident response firms.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: CISOs work less with hands-on tools and more with frameworks like the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, ISO 27001 and SOC 2. They use risk registers, GRC platforms such as ServiceNow or Archer, security dashboards fed by SIEM tools, and board slide decks.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: A CISO is judged on whether the company avoids major breaches and recovers fast when one happens. Boards also look at risk reduction, audit and compliance results, budget use, team retention and how clearly the CISO explains risk in business terms.

qa.q: Who does a CISO report to?
qa.a: It varies by company. Many CISOs report to the CIO, while others report to the CEO, the general counsel or the chief risk officer. Most also brief the board or a board committee on a regular schedule. Public companies must describe in their annual reports how the board oversees cybersecurity risk, under SEC rules.

qa.q: What legal duties does a CISO have after a breach?
qa.a: Most legal duties fall on the company, but the CISO usually leads the response. Every state has its own data breach notification law, and deadlines and rules vary by state. Public companies must also disclose material cyber incidents under SEC rules, and fields like health care and banking have extra federal notice rules.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Civil engineers design roads, building sites, foundations, storm drainage, and water and sewer systems. They run calculations for loads, grades and flows, prepare plans and specifications, and review contractor submittals. During construction they check that the work matches the approved design.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Much of the day is spent at a desk on design software, calculations and reports. Some days bring site visits to check grading, pipe installation, concrete pours or soil conditions. Meetings with clients, permit reviewers and contractors fill the rest.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with surveyors, geotechnical engineers, architects, planners, drafters and construction crews. Public agency staff review their plans for permits. Clients include developers, cities, counties, state transportation departments and utilities.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use computer-aided design and civil modeling software, GIS mapping, hydraulic and stormwater models, and spreadsheets for calculations. In the field they rely on survey data, soil reports, levels, hard hats and safety vests. Design codes and local standards guide every drawing.

day.label: Licensing and sign-off
day.text: Only a licensed Professional Engineer (PE) can seal plans submitted for public approval. Licensure usually means an accredited degree, passing the FE exam, about four years of supervised experience and passing the PE exam. Exact rules vary by state.

qa.q: What does a civil engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A civil engineer spends most days designing and checking projects such as roads, site grading, drainage, foundations and water lines. That means running calculations, drawing plans in design software, writing reports and answering questions from permit reviewers. On other days they visit job sites to inspect work, solve field problems and confirm the contractor is building to the approved plans.

qa.q: What is the difference between a civil engineer and a civil engineering technician?
qa.a: A civil engineer usually holds a bachelor’s degree in engineering and is responsible for the design. Once licensed as a PE, they can seal plans. A technician often has an associate degree or training and supports the engineer by drafting, collecting field data, testing materials and inspecting work. Technicians cannot seal engineering plans.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Claims adjusters investigate insurance claims after accidents, storms, thefts or injuries. They review the policy, inspect damage, interview the people involved, gather reports and estimates, decide what is covered and negotiate the payment. They also spot possible fraud and refer it to special investigation units.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A field adjuster may drive to several homes or vehicles a day to inspect damage, take photos and write estimates. Desk adjusters work by phone and email, reviewing documents, calling claimants and repair shops, and updating files. After disasters, catastrophe adjusters travel and work long hours.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Adjusters deal with policyholders and claimants, agents, repair shops, contractors, medical providers and attorneys. Inside the insurer they work with claims supervisors, underwriters and special investigation units. Independent adjusters are hired by insurers through adjusting firms, while public adjusters represent policyholders.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include claims systems such as Guidewire ClaimCenter, estimating software like Xactimate for property damage, and auto estimating platforms. Field adjusters carry ladders, cameras, moisture meters and sometimes drones. Mobile apps, phone systems and document scanners handle the rest.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Adjusters are judged on accurate coverage decisions, fair and supported settlements, and closing claims on time. Supervisors review file quality, reserves, customer satisfaction and overpayments. Following state claims handling laws and deadlines is essential, since unfair claims practices can bring penalties.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a claims adjuster?
qa.a: It depends on the state. Most states license independent and public adjusters, many also license company staff adjusters, and a few license only public adjusters. Licensing usually means a state exam or approved course, a background check and continuing education. Adjusters from states without a license often get a designated home state license so they can work elsewhere.

qa.q: What is the difference between a staff, independent and public adjuster?
qa.a: A staff adjuster is employed by an insurance company and handles its claims. An independent adjuster works for an adjusting firm or for themselves and is hired by insurers, often after big storms. A public adjuster is hired by the policyholder, usually for a share of the claim payment, to argue for a larger settlement.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Client services managers answer client questions, fix service problems and process changes such as upgrades, cancellations or new users. They track each request until it is closed and keep clear notes on every account.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with the inbox and open tickets. Then come client calls, check-in meetings and follow-ups with internal teams. Urgent issues can reshape the plan at any hour, so juggling priorities is constant.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They are the link between clients and the company. They work with sales, billing, operations and technical support staff, and often lead a small team of client service representatives or coordinators.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work in a CRM system and a ticketing or help desk tool. Email, phone, video calls, shared calendars and spreadsheets for reporting fill out the toolkit. Industry software varies by employer.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers are usually measured on client satisfaction scores, response and resolution times, renewal or retention rates and the number of escalated complaints. Clear records and calm handling of difficult clients also count.

qa.q: What does a client services manager do day to day?
qa.a: They handle client requests and problems from start to finish. That means answering calls and emails, logging issues, working with other teams to fix them, processing service changes and following up. Many also review account health, coach junior staff and report on trends to leadership.

qa.q: What is the difference between a client services manager and an account manager?
qa.a: A client services manager focuses on keeping service running smoothly and solving problems. An account manager usually focuses more on growing the relationship, such as renewals, upsells and contract talks. At smaller companies one person often does both, so job titles and duties vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Clinical informatics specialists are often nurses, pharmacists or physicians who turn clinical needs into health technology. They design order sets, documentation templates and decision support alerts in the electronic health record, test changes, train staff and check that new tools are safe.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include meeting clinicians to gather requests, reviewing a new build in a test environment, testing workflows from start to finish and answering support tickets. During a go-live they spend time on hospital units helping staff use the new system.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with physicians, nurses, pharmacists, IT analysts and software vendors. Quality and patient safety teams, data analysts, compliance staff and informatics leaders such as the chief medical information officer also shape their work.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include electronic health record systems such as Epic or Oracle Health, clinical decision support tools, SQL and reporting tools for data, Visio for workflow diagrams and ticketing systems. They also need to understand data standards such as HL7 and FHIR.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether clinicians adopt the tools and find them easier, less documentation time, fewer ignored alerts and fewer technology-related safety events. Delivering projects and go-lives on schedule and meeting federal health IT rules also count.

qa.q: Do you need a clinical background to work in clinical informatics?
qa.a: Many roles prefer or require one, such as a nursing, pharmacy or medical license, because the job turns clinical work into software. Physicians can become board certified in clinical informatics as a medical subspecialty, and nurses can earn informatics nursing certification. Analysts without clinical degrees also work in the field, often after health IT training.

qa.q: What is the difference between clinical informatics and health IT?
qa.a: Health IT covers all technology in health care, including networks, devices, security and the help desk. Clinical informatics focuses on how clinical information and decisions move through that technology. Specialists use their clinical knowledge to design workflows, alerts and data so that care is safer and easier to deliver.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan and run clinical trials that test new drugs, devices and treatments. They screen and enroll volunteers, collect data, track side effects, and prepare filings for the FDA and ethics boards. Medical affairs staff explain study results to doctors and answer their medical questions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A coordinator might walk a new volunteer through the consent form, run a study visit, log lab results in an electronic case report form, and answer data queries from the sponsor. Regulatory staff spend more of the day on submissions, protocol changes and document reviews.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with study doctors called principal investigators, nurses, pharmacists, volunteers and their families. Outside the clinic, they deal with sponsors, contract research organizations, monitors, data managers, statisticians, institutional review boards and FDA reviewers.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: US trials follow FDA regulations in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Good Clinical Practice guidelines and HIPAA privacy rules. Most studies need approval from an institutional review board and signed informed consent before a volunteer joins. Some states add their own consent rules.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means accurate data, enrollment on schedule, few protocol deviations and clean audits or FDA inspections. A late adverse event report or a consent mistake can delay a study, so careful, complete records matter most.

qa.q: What does a clinical research coordinator do day to day?
qa.a: A clinical research coordinator runs a trial at a hospital or clinic. They screen and enroll volunteers, explain consent forms, schedule study visits, collect samples and data, and record side effects. They keep study files in order, enter data into the sponsor’s system and fix errors the monitor finds. They also work closely with the study doctor and the review board.

qa.q: What is the difference between a clinical research coordinator and a clinical research associate?
qa.a: A coordinator works at the study site and handles volunteers and daily study tasks. A clinical research associate, often called a monitor, usually works for the sponsor or a contract research organization. They visit or remotely review several sites, check records against source documents and make sure each site follows the protocol and the rules. Associates often travel.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Clinical research coordinators run trials at a hospital or clinic site. They screen and enroll eligible patients, help obtain informed consent, schedule study visits, collect data and samples, report side effects, enter data for the sponsor and keep regulatory files current.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day mixes participant visits with desk work. Coordinators check eligibility, run study procedures, process and ship lab samples, enter visit data and answer data queries. They also prepare for monitor visits and send protocol changes and reports to the ethics board.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work for a principal investigator and with sub-investigators, research nurses, lab and pharmacy staff and the study participants. They also deal with sponsor monitors, called clinical research associates, and with the institutional review board that oversees the study.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include electronic data capture systems such as Medidata Rave or REDCap, clinical trial management systems, electronic regulatory binders and electronic health records. Many also use centrifuges, specimen kits, temperature logs and online portals for review board submissions.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Coordinators are judged on enrolling patients on target, few protocol deviations, clean and timely data and fast answers to queries. Clean monitoring visits and audits matter, as does following Good Clinical Practice, FDA rules and informed consent requirements.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a clinical research coordinator?
qa.a: Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in a science or health field, though some hire people with an associate degree, nursing training or related experience. No state license is required for the role. Training in Good Clinical Practice is expected, and voluntary certifications become valuable after a couple of years of work.

qa.q: What is the difference between a clinical research coordinator and a clinical research associate?
qa.a: A clinical research coordinator works at the study site and runs the trial day to day with patients and doctors. A clinical research associate usually works for the sponsor or a contract research company and monitors several sites, checking data against medical records and making sure the protocol is followed. Many associates start as coordinators.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Builds and maintains servers, networks, databases and storage on a public cloud platform. Writes infrastructure as code, sets up access rules, automates deployments, and watches cost and uptime so applications stay fast, secure and affordable.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Starts by checking dashboards and overnight alerts. Reviews changes to infrastructure templates, helps developers ship a release, tunes an autoscaling rule, and hunts for idle resources that waste money. Many teams also rotate on-call shifts for outages.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Infrastructure as code templates, containers and Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, Python or Bash scripts, Git, the cloud provider’s console and command line, plus monitoring, logging and cost reporting tools.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Software developers, DevOps and site reliability engineers, security teams, database administrators, and finance staff who track cloud spending. They also explain tradeoffs between speed, reliability and cost to managers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By uptime and how fast systems recover after incidents, how quickly teams can deploy, whether systems pass security reviews and audits, and whether the monthly cloud bill stays on budget without hurting performance.

qa.q: What does a cloud engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A cloud engineer checks alerts and dashboards, writes and reviews code that creates cloud resources, fixes failed deployments, and adjusts settings for security and scaling. They also review spending reports, shut down unused resources, and help developers get their apps running. When something breaks, they find the cause and restore service.

qa.q: What is the difference between a cloud engineer and a DevOps engineer?
qa.a: The jobs overlap a lot. A cloud engineer focuses on the cloud platform itself: networks, accounts, access, storage and cost. A DevOps engineer focuses on how code gets built, tested and released, mainly through pipelines and automation. Many employers blend the two, so read each posting’s duties rather than relying on the title.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They set and check security settings for cloud accounts, decide who can access which systems, and write network rules that block unwanted traffic. They also review new projects before launch, fix risky configurations, and help respond when an alert points to a possible breach.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with alerts and findings from scanning tools. Then come reviews of infrastructure code, meetings with developers about a new service, and trimming access roles that grant more than needed. Some days bring incident response or requests for audit evidence.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with software developers, DevOps and platform engineers, and the wider security team. They also answer questions from compliance staff, outside auditors, and managers who need to know whether a system meets company policy or industry rules.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Identity and access management consoles, infrastructure-as-code templates, cloud posture scanners, log monitoring and alerting systems, secrets managers, and encryption key services. Scripting in Python or a shell language is common, along with each cloud platform’s command-line tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in fewer misconfigurations, access limited to what each person or service truly needs, fast fixes for critical findings, clean audits, and calm, well-documented incident response. Strong engineers add protection without slowing other teams down.

qa.q: What does a cloud security engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They review alerts and scan results, fix risky settings such as open storage or overly broad access, and check infrastructure code before it goes live. They meet with developers to design secure services, update network and access rules, collect evidence for audits, and step in when a possible security incident needs investigation.

qa.q: What is the difference between a cloud engineer and a cloud security engineer?
qa.a: A cloud engineer builds and runs the systems: servers, databases, networks, and deployment pipelines. A cloud security engineer focuses on protecting them. They set access controls, encryption, logging, and network limits, hunt for misconfigurations, and handle incidents. The two roles overlap, and many security engineers start in general cloud or systems work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They draft and negotiate sales agreements, supplier contracts, NDAs and data processing terms. They also review new products and features for legal risk before launch, covering privacy, consumer protection, advertising claims and intellectual property, and suggest practical fixes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The morning may start with redlines on a large customer deal, then a call with the other side’s lawyer. Afternoons often go to product reviews, quick questions in chat, and updates to contract templates or playbooks so sales can close routine deals without legal help.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with sales, procurement and finance teams on deals, and with product managers, engineers and designers on launches. They also partner with privacy, security and marketing staff, often report to a general counsel, and bring in outside firms for specialized issues.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their tools include word processors with tracked changes, contract management systems, e-signature tools, legal research databases and intake systems for requests. Clause libraries, fallback positions and negotiation playbooks keep terms consistent across many deals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Speed and judgment both count. They are judged on how quickly deals close, how well key risk terms like liability caps and indemnities hold up, and whether products launch on time without legal problems later.

qa.q: What is the difference between commercial counsel and product counsel?
qa.a: Commercial counsel focuses on contracts, negotiating terms with customers, vendors and partners. Product counsel works closely with product teams, spotting legal issues in features before launch, such as privacy, consumer protection and intellectual property. Many companies, especially smaller ones, combine both jobs into one role.

qa.q: Do you need a law license to work as commercial or product counsel?
qa.a: Yes. These roles call for a law degree and admission to the bar in at least one US jurisdiction. Rules for in-house lawyers working in a state where they are not admitted vary by state, and many states allow them to register as in-house counsel. Most employers also want several years of practice experience.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Communications and PR staff write press releases, announcements, speeches and internal memos. They pitch stories to reporters, answer media questions and keep the company’s message consistent. Many also manage social media posts, the newsroom page on the website and the brand voice used across materials.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a scan of news coverage and social media mentions. Then come drafting and editing, calls with reporters, and meetings with leaders to plan upcoming announcements. Plans can shift fast when a story breaks or a customer complaint spreads online.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with executives, marketing, legal and human resources. Outside the company, they deal with journalists, editors, bloggers, agency partners and sometimes community groups or investors. Internal communications roles also connect with managers who pass messages on to their teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include media monitoring and press release distribution services, media contact databases, social media scheduling platforms and shared document editors. Many teams follow AP style for writing. Basic design and video editing skills help when preparing graphics or short clips.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are judged by the quality and tone of media coverage, message reach, employee engagement and how well a crisis is handled. Teams track mentions, share of voice and audience response. Accuracy matters, because one wrong statement can damage trust or create legal trouble.

qa.q: What is the difference between PR and marketing?
qa.a: Marketing promotes products to drive sales, mostly through paid advertising and campaigns. PR manages the company’s reputation and relationships with the public, often through earned media such as news stories, interviews and statements. The two teams often share goals and work together, but PR focuses on trust and credibility rather than direct selling.

qa.q: Is communications and PR a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Deadlines are tight, news moves quickly and a crisis can arrive at night or on a weekend. Staff must stay calm while leaders, lawyers and reporters all want answers. Many people enjoy the pace and variety, and quieter periods of planning and writing balance out the busy times.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Community managers welcome new members, answer questions, and set and enforce community rules. They plan events, spark discussions, and pass user feedback to product and support teams. They also spot problems early, from bugs people report to arguments that need calming.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a scan of overnight posts, flagged messages, and open questions. Then come replies, moderation calls, and a check-in with volunteer moderators. Afternoons may hold an event, a product update announcement, or a feedback summary for the team.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with product managers, support agents, marketing, and developer relations staff. Much of the daily contact is with users themselves and with volunteer moderators or superfans who help run channels and answer newcomers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Discord, Slack, forum software, and social media apps. Many use moderation bots, community analytics dashboards, a help desk or ticket system, survey tools, and spreadsheets to track feedback and member trends.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is often measured by active members, retention, response times, event turnout, and how many questions members answer for each other. Teams also value the quality of feedback passed to product and a calm, safe tone in the space.

qa.q: What does a community manager do day to day?
qa.a: A community manager keeps a product’s user spaces healthy and useful. Day to day, that means answering questions, moderating posts, welcoming newcomers, running events, and posting updates. They also gather what users say about the product and share it with internal teams so problems get fixed and good ideas get heard.

qa.q: What is the difference between a community manager and a social media manager?
qa.a: A social media manager mainly publishes brand content on public channels and grows reach. A community manager focuses on relationships among users, often in spaces like Discord or forums. The work centers on conversation, moderation, and feedback rather than broadcasting. At small companies, one person may do both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build and maintain pay grades and salary ranges, price jobs against salary survey data, and run bonus and stock plans. They also manage health, retirement and leave benefits, and they check pay across groups for unexplained gaps.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might mean reviewing offers and raises and recommending amounts within set guidelines, answering employee questions about benefits, and fixing enrollment problems with a carrier. They also run spreadsheet analyses for budget or annual review cycles.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with recruiters, hiring managers, HR business partners, payroll and finance. Outside the company, they deal with insurance brokers, benefits carriers, retirement plan administrators and salary survey providers. Leaders and finance usually hold final approval on pay decisions.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: They apply federal laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act for overtime classification, the Equal Pay Act, ERISA for most private employer plans, COBRA and HIPAA privacy rules. Pay transparency and salary history rules vary by state and sometimes by city.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets are the core tool, along with HR information systems, payroll software, benefits administration platforms and compensation survey databases. Many also use equity management software to track stock grants and vesting schedules.

qa.q: What does a compensation and benefits specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They research market pay, place jobs in salary ranges, and review offers and raises to recommend amounts within guidelines. They help run open enrollment, answer benefits questions, work with carriers and brokers, and prepare reports for leaders who approve budgets. Much of the work is data analysis and checking that pay and plans follow the law.

qa.q: What is the difference between compensation and benefits?
qa.a: Compensation is direct pay: base salary or hourly wages, bonuses, commissions and stock awards. Benefits are the other rewards of a job, such as health insurance, retirement plans like a 401(k), paid time off, and life or disability insurance. Smaller employers often have one person handle both, while larger ones usually split them into separate teams.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Compiler engineers build the programs that turn source code or AI models into instructions a processor can run. They design intermediate representations and optimization passes, generate machine code for CPUs, GPUs or AI accelerators, and fix bugs where compiled code runs wrong or slow.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day involves reading generated assembly or intermediate code, writing and testing an optimization, and running benchmark suites to see if programs got faster. Engineers also sort through compiler crashes, review patches and discuss new chip features with hardware teams.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with hardware architects designing new chips, runtime and library engineers, and performance engineers who profile real workloads. At AI chip companies they also work with machine learning researchers. Many review code and discuss designs with open-source compiler communities.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core tools are C++, LLVM and its MLIR framework, and sometimes GCC. AI compiler work adds Python, PyTorch, Triton and XLA. Engineers use debuggers like GDB and LLDB, profilers, chip simulators, fuzzers that generate random test programs, and large automated test suites.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on correctness first: compiled programs must behave exactly as the source says. Then come the speed of the generated code, compile time, memory use and support for new chip features. Clean patches that pass review in large shared codebases also count.

qa.q: Do you need a PhD to be a compiler engineer?
qa.a: No, but many compiler engineers have a master’s degree or PhD in computer science or computer engineering. Employers mainly want deep knowledge of data structures, computer architecture and compiler theory. Accepted contributions to open-source compilers such as LLVM or GCC are a strong signal and can make up for fewer formal credentials.

qa.q: What does an AI compiler engineer do?
qa.a: An AI compiler engineer builds the software that takes a trained model, written in a framework like PyTorch, and maps it onto a GPU or custom AI chip. They fuse operations, plan memory, split work across many cores and generate fast kernels. Their work decides how much of the chip’s raw speed real models actually use.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Compliance staff read the rules that apply to the business and turn them into written policies and checks. They run anti-money-laundering reviews, screen customers against sanctions lists, track license renewals, file required reports with regulators, and train employees on what the rules require.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with alerts from monitoring systems that flag unusual transactions or customers. Staff look into each one, document what they found, and decide whether to escalate. Later they may update a procedure after a rule change, answer staff questions, or gather files for an audit.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with legal, finance, operations, risk and internal audit teams. They answer to senior managers and often report to a board committee. They also deal with outside auditors and with examiners from state or federal regulators during reviews.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include transaction monitoring software, sanctions screening tools, case management systems for tracking investigations, and spreadsheets for logs and deadlines. Staff also rely on regulator websites, rule texts, and the company’s own policy manuals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in clean audit and exam results, reports filed on time, and few findings from regulators. Good compliance work also means decisions are clearly documented, staff training is complete, and problems are caught and fixed before they grow.

qa.q: What does a compliance officer do day to day?
qa.a: A compliance officer checks that the company follows the laws and rules that apply to it. Day to day, that means reviewing flagged transactions, screening customers, updating policies, tracking licenses and filing deadlines, training staff, and preparing for audits. In banking and other financial firms, much of the work centers on anti-money-laundering rules under the Bank Secrecy Act, including filing suspicious activity reports.

qa.q: What is the difference between compliance and legal?
qa.a: Legal teams interpret the law, write and negotiate contracts, and represent the company in disputes. Compliance teams build the day-to-day controls that keep the business inside the rules, then monitor and test that those controls work. Lawyers advise on what the law means. Compliance staff make sure people actually follow it. Many compliance jobs do not require a law degree.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Compliance officers write and update company policies, check that daily work follows the laws and regulations that apply, run internal reviews and investigate complaints or tips. When they find a problem, they help fix it, keep records of what was done and report it to the right agency when the law requires.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reviewing alerts or exception reports, then answering staff questions about whether a sale, payment or contract is allowed. Later hours often go to testing a process, tracking new rule changes, updating a policy and preparing a summary for managers or a board committee.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with lawyers, internal auditors, risk managers and department heads. They meet with outside examiners and regulators during reviews. They also train front-line employees, from tellers to sales staff to nurses, so each person knows the rules that apply to their own job.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Policy manuals, compliance management software, case tracking systems and spreadsheets are everyday tools. In banks, transaction monitoring systems help flag possible money laundering for review. Ethics hotlines, online training platforms and audit checklists help them collect reports, teach staff and prove what was checked.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most work in offices at banks, insurers, hospitals, drug and device makers, investment firms, manufacturers and government contractors. Many roles allow hybrid or remote work. The rules they handle depend on the industry, and some areas, like insurance, are regulated mainly by each state, so duties vary by state.

qa.q: What does a compliance officer do day to day?
qa.a: A compliance officer spends the day checking that the company follows the laws and rules for its industry. That means reviewing reports and transactions, answering staff questions, updating policies, running training, looking into possible violations and keeping clear records. When a serious issue turns up, they work with leaders and lawyers to fix it and, when required, report it to regulators.

qa.q: What is the difference between a compliance officer and an internal auditor?
qa.a: A compliance officer builds and runs the program that keeps a company within laws and regulations, giving advice as work happens. An internal auditor stands apart from daily operations and independently tests whether controls, including the compliance program, actually work. Auditors usually report findings to an audit committee, while compliance officers often own the fixes and the contact with regulators.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Composites technicians build light, strong parts from carbon fiber, fiberglass and other reinforced materials. They cut prepreg plies, lay them on molds in a set order and direction, vacuum bag and cure parts in ovens or autoclaves, then trim, drill, bond, inspect and repair them.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift often starts with reading the work order and ply book, then taking material out of the freezer and logging its out time. Most hours go to layup, vacuum bagging and debulking. Later come loading the autoclave, removing cured parts from molds and trimming.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with composites engineers who write the layup instructions, quality inspectors, nondestructive testing technicians and production supervisors. In aerospace they may also see customer or government inspectors. In boat and wind blade shops they work alongside laminators and finishers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include ply cutters, laser projection systems, hand rollers, vacuum bagging materials, pumps, ovens and autoclaves. They also use routers, drills, sanders, ultrasonic testing gear, thermocouples and cure monitoring software. Respirators, gloves and dust collection are standard safety gear.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Technicians are judged on part quality: correct ply count and orientation, no wrinkles, voids or foreign objects, and a clean cure record. Following work instructions exactly, keeping material within its out time, working safely and finishing parts on schedule all matter.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a composites technician?
qa.a: Most composites technician jobs require a high school diploma and train on the job. Community college certificates in composites or aerospace manufacturing help. Many aerospace and defense roles require US citizenship or permanent residency because of export control rules. Good hand skills, patience, attention to detail and the ability to read drawings matter most.

qa.q: What is an autoclave in composites work?
qa.a: An autoclave is a heated pressure vessel used to cure composite parts. The part, sealed in a vacuum bag on its mold, is heated under pressure, which squeezes out air and gives strong laminates with very few voids. Out-of-autoclave methods use ovens, resin infusion or presses instead, often at lower cost.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Computer vision engineers build software that finds, sorts and tracks things in photos and video. They gather and label data, train deep learning models, test how accurate they are, and make them run fast enough on a car, robot, camera or medical scanner.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with checking overnight training runs. Then come code reviews, fixing a model that misses objects in low light or rain, and studying failed examples one by one. Afternoons may go to meetings with product and hardware teams about what the system must catch.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Python is the main language, with C++ used when code must run fast on a device. Common tools include PyTorch, TensorFlow and OpenCV, along with GPUs, cloud servers, image labeling software and small edge chips. Git and Linux are everyday basics.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with data scientists, software and embedded engineers, and the teams who label images. In medical imaging they also work with doctors and regulatory staff, since software that helps diagnose patients usually needs FDA clearance or approval before it can be sold for clinical use.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Models are judged on measures like precision, recall and speed per frame, tested on data they never saw in training. Real-world results matter most: fewer missed pedestrians, fewer false alarms and fewer wrong readings once the system is running in the field.

qa.q: What does a computer vision engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix coding and experiments. They prepare and clean image data, train and tune models, and look closely at the cases where a model fails. They also shrink models so they run quickly on cameras, robots or vehicles, write tests, review teammates’ code and explain results to product and hardware teams.

qa.q: What is the difference between computer vision and image processing?
qa.a: Image processing changes an image, for example by sharpening, removing noise or resizing it, and the result is usually another image. Computer vision tries to understand what the image shows, such as spotting a person, reading a sign or flagging a tumor. Vision systems often use image processing as an early step.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Engineers design site grading, drainage, foundations and structures. Builders turn those plans into factories, data centers and launch pads. The work spans surveying, earthwork, utilities, concrete, steel erection and finishing, and every step is checked against the drawings and specifications.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Site days often start with a safety briefing and a look at the schedule. Then come inspections of finished work, crew and delivery coordination, and answers to field questions. Engineers split time between design software in the office and visits to the site.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with owners, architects, structural and electrical engineers, surveyors, subcontractors and equipment operators. They also deal with local building inspectors, utility companies and permit offices, which set their own rules and approval steps.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include CAD and building information modeling software, scheduling programs, total stations and GPS survey gear, and laser levels. Crews also rely on excavators, cranes and concrete testing equipment, plus hard hats, safety vests and fall protection.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Projects are judged on safety, quality, schedule and budget. Work must pass inspections and meet the building codes adopted by the state or city. Owners also look at whether the finished site works as designed, such as power and cooling capacity in a data center.

qa.q: What does a civil engineer in construction do day to day?
qa.a: A civil engineer reviews and prepares design drawings and runs calculations for loads, drainage and soils. They answer contractor questions and visit the site to check that work matches the plans. They also update designs when field conditions change and coordinate with inspectors and other engineers to keep the project moving.

qa.q: What is the difference between a civil engineer and a construction manager?
qa.a: A civil engineer designs and analyzes the project. To sign and seal plans, they need a Professional Engineer license, and each state sets its own rules. A construction manager runs the building phase. They handle the schedule, budget, crews, subcontractors and site safety. Some people move from one role to the other during their careers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Construction workers and equipment operators do the hands-on work of building. Laborers clear and prepare sites, dig trenches, set forms, place and finish concrete, move materials, put up scaffolding and keep the site clean. Operators run excavators, loaders, dozers, cranes and other heavy equipment.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts early with a toolbox safety talk and the foreman’s plan. Then come hours of physical work: carrying, digging, pouring, rigging loads or running a machine. Weather, deliveries and inspections shape the schedule, and the day ends with cleanup.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work under a foreman or superintendent alongside carpenters, ironworkers, electricians, plumbers and other trades. Operators work closely with spotters, riggers and signal persons. Inspectors, safety managers, engineers and delivery drivers are part of daily site life.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Laborers use shovels, rakes, wheelbarrows, jackhammers, concrete vibrators, power saws, compactors and grade lasers. Operators run excavators, skid steers, loaders, dozers and cranes, often with GPS machine control. Hard hats, high-visibility vests, safety boots and fall protection are required gear.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Workers are judged on safety first, then on productivity, quality and showing up on time every day. Operators are judged on precise grading, smooth lifts and caring for their machines. Following plans and instructions and working well with other trades also matter.

qa.q: Do you need a license to operate heavy equipment?
qa.a: Most equipment such as excavators and loaders needs no state license, but employers must train operators and check their skills. Cranes are different: OSHA rules require certification for most construction crane operators, and some states also issue crane licenses. Driving heavy equipment on public roads may require a commercial driver’s license.

qa.q: How do you start working in construction?
qa.a: Many people start as general laborers with no experience and learn on the job. Others join apprenticeships run by unions or contractor groups, which combine paid work with classes, including operating engineer programs for heavy equipment. Employers often want an OSHA 10-hour safety card, reliable transportation and the ability to lift heavy loads.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Builds and tracks the project budget and schedule, awards and manages subcontracts, prices and negotiates change orders, coordinates permits and inspections, and leads closeout and handover to the owner. Who pulls permits depends on the contract and local rules.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Often starts with a site walk or a call with the superintendent. Then reviews submittals, logs RFIs and routes design questions to the architect or engineer, updates the schedule, checks costs against budget, and runs owner or subcontractor meetings.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Owners and their representatives, architects, engineers, the site superintendent, subcontractors, suppliers, building inspectors, and in-house estimators, schedulers and accountants. Much of the job is keeping all of these groups informed and moving in the same direction.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Scheduling software for critical path schedules, construction project management platforms, spreadsheets, drawings and specifications, cost reports, daily logs, meeting minutes, change order logs and punch lists. A phone and email inbox that rarely go quiet.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Finishing on time and within budget, a strong safety record, quality work that passes inspection, few unresolved disputes, and a clean closeout with warranties, as-built drawings and operation manuals delivered to the owner.

qa.q: What does a construction project manager do day to day?
qa.a: They keep a building project on track. A day mixes site visits, schedule updates, cost checks and meetings. They review submittals, track RFIs and send design questions to the architect or engineer, price change orders, and follow up with subcontractors. They also coordinate inspections and keep the owner informed about progress and risks.

qa.q: What is the difference between a construction project manager and a superintendent?
qa.a: The superintendent runs the field each day: crews, work sequence, site safety and quality. The project manager runs the business side: contracts, budget, schedule, change orders, paperwork and owner communication. The superintendent is usually on site full time. The project manager splits time between the office and the site. They work as a team.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Consultants meet with clients to understand a problem, gather facts, weigh options, and recommend a fix. Many also help put the plan in place, train staff, or show customers how to get the most from a product or system.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a client call, then move to staff interviews, reviewing reports or spreadsheets, and building slides or a written proposal. Afternoons often bring status meetings, follow-up emails, and logging billable hours against a project.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Consultants work with business owners, managers, and front-line staff at client organizations. Inside their own firm, they report to project leads or partners and team up with analysts, subject experts, and sales staff who bring in new accounts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets, presentation software, video meeting apps, and project tracking tools are daily staples. Depending on the field, consultants may also use data analysis software, customer relationship management systems, or the client’s own product to run demos and test fixes.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Clients judge consultants on results: whether the advice solved the problem, stayed on budget, and met deadlines. Firms also track billable hours, client satisfaction, repeat business, and how clearly consultants explain complex ideas.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a consultant?
qa.a: Most consulting work needs no special license. Some fields do. Giving investment advice for pay generally requires registration as an investment adviser with the SEC or a state. Offering engineering services to the public requires a professional engineer license, and rules vary by state. Optional certifications, such as project management credentials, can still help you stand out.

qa.q: Is consulting a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Consultants often juggle several clients, tight deadlines, and high expectations for quick results. Travel is frequent at some firms, though many roles now work remotely part of the time. Independent consultants also have to find their own clients and manage uneven income. Many people find the variety and problem solving worth the pressure.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Content designers write and shape the words people see inside apps and websites. That means button labels, form hints, error messages, empty screens, onboarding steps and notifications. They decide what to say, when to say it and sometimes whether words are needed at all.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a design review, then move to drafting copy for a new sign-up flow. Later they test two versions of an error message, update a voice and tone guide, and answer quick wording questions from engineers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product designers, product managers, engineers and user researchers. They often check wording with legal, support and marketing teams, and with localization teams who translate the product into other languages.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in shared design files, where they write directly on screen mockups. They also use content style guides, spreadsheets of interface strings, usability testing sessions, analytics dashboards and readability checks for plain language.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether people finish tasks without confusion. Teams look at completion rates, fewer support tickets, test results and accessibility. Clear, consistent, inclusive words that fit the space on a small screen are the goal.

qa.q: What does a content designer do day to day?
qa.a: A content designer writes and edits the words inside a digital product, such as buttons, instructions and error messages. They join design meetings, map out user flows, test wording with real users, keep terms consistent across screens and make sure text works for screen readers and in translation.

qa.q: What is the difference between a UX writer and a content designer?
qa.a: The titles overlap and many companies use them interchangeably. UX writer often points to writing interface copy like labels and messages. Content designer can be broader, covering content strategy, information structure and research to decide what content a product needs before any words are written.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Content writers and editors research topics, draft articles, guides, newsletters and web pages, and edit copy for clarity, accuracy and tone. They follow a style guide, check facts and sources, and revise drafts based on feedback before work is published.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with checking the content calendar and briefs. Then comes research, outlining and drafting, with breaks to edit a colleague’s piece, answer reviewer comments, update older pages and load finished copy into the publishing system.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with marketing managers, subject matter experts, designers, SEO specialists and other editors. Freelancers often report to a single client contact or an agency editor who sends briefs and approves final drafts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include word processors, shared document editors, content management systems, grammar and readability checkers, keyword research tools and email newsletter platforms. Many teams also use project boards and a written house style guide.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on accuracy, clear writing, meeting deadlines and following the brief. Many employers also track results such as page traffic, search ranking, time on page, newsletter open rates and how often readers take a desired action.

qa.q: What does a content writer and editor do day to day?
qa.a: They plan and research topics, write drafts of articles, guides, newsletters and web copy, and edit their own and others’ work. They check facts, apply a style guide, add headings and links, respond to feedback and publish or schedule finished content in a content management system.

qa.q: What is the difference between a content writer and a copywriter?
qa.a: A content writer mainly creates informative material such as articles, guides and newsletters that build trust and answer reader questions. A copywriter focuses on short persuasive text meant to drive a sale or signup, such as ads, product pages and email subject lines. Many jobs blend both skills.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Contract managers draft and review agreements with customers and suppliers. They negotiate terms such as price, payment, liability and termination. Then they track deadlines, renewals and obligations so nothing lapses or gets missed.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with redlining a supplier’s draft and answering questions from sales. Later comes a negotiation call, an update to the contract database and a check on agreements nearing renewal or expiry.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with sales, procurement, finance and operations teams. They bring in the company’s lawyers on unusual risks and deal directly with the other side’s contract staff or counsel.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use word processors with track changes, contract lifecycle management software, e-signature platforms and spreadsheets. Clause libraries and approved templates help them draft quickly and keep terms consistent across deals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in deals closed on time, risky terms kept out, renewals handled before deadlines and few disputes. Clean records that pass internal and external audits also matter, especially in government contracting.

qa.q: What does a contract manager do day to day?
qa.a: A contract manager drafts, reviews and negotiates agreements with customers and suppliers. They flag risky clauses, get internal approvals and keep signed contracts organized. They also watch key dates like renewals and deliverables, and they help resolve disagreements over what a contract requires.

qa.q: What is the difference between a contract manager and a contract attorney?
qa.a: A contract attorney is a licensed lawyer who can give legal advice. A contract manager usually does not need a law license and focuses on the business side: drafting from templates, negotiating terms and tracking performance. Many contract managers escalate complex legal questions to attorneys. Some contract managers do have law degrees, but it is not required.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Oversees the general ledger, the monthly and year-end close, account reconciliations and the financial statements. Designs and tests internal controls, leads the accounting staff and makes sure the books follow generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Early in the month is close season: reviewing journal entries, accruals and reconciliations, then checking the statements before they reach leadership. Later weeks go to variance analysis, budget support, audit requests and fixing weak spots in accounting processes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Reports to the CFO or owner and leads staff accountants plus payables, receivables and payroll teams. Works with outside auditors, tax advisers and bankers, and with department heads who need budget and spending numbers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Accounting or ERP software, spreadsheets, reconciliation and close-checklist tools, and reporting dashboards. Written policies for approvals, access rights and segregation of duties are just as important as the software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Accurate statements delivered on time, audits with few adjustments, and controls that catch errors and prevent fraud. At public companies, the work also supports management’s required assessment of internal control over financial reporting under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

qa.q: What does a financial controller do day to day?
qa.a: A controller reviews and approves journal entries, checks reconciliations, answers questions from the accounting team and keeps the close on schedule. They prepare or review financial statements, explain results to leadership, respond to auditors and improve processes and controls. The first days of each month are usually the busiest, since the close has a firm deadline.

qa.q: What is the difference between a controller and a CFO?
qa.a: A controller focuses on the accuracy of the numbers: the books, the close, controls and financial reporting. A CFO looks ahead, handling strategy, financing, cash planning and relationships with investors and lenders. The controller often reports to the CFO. At smaller companies, one person may cover parts of both roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Writes, tests and fixes PLC programs, often in ladder logic or other IEC 61131-3 languages. Builds operator screens, sets up the networks linking sensors, drives and robots, and traces faults when a line, boiler or building system stops working.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may open with a call about a machine that is down. Then comes code work at a desk, a review of wiring drawings, and testing changes on the floor with operators. New start-ups can mean long shifts, weekend work or travel.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Electricians, maintenance technicians, mechanical and process engineers, machine operators and plant managers. They also deal with outside integrators, equipment vendors and safety staff who check guarding, interlocks and emergency stops.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A laptop with vendor programming software, PLCs, HMI touch screens, variable frequency drives and SCADA systems. Industrial networks such as EtherNet/IP, Profinet and Modbus. A multimeter, electrical schematics and P&ID drawings round out the kit.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By uptime, start-ups that finish on schedule, and safety logic that works every time. Good code is clean, commented and easy for the next person to maintain. Machine wiring and controls are often expected to follow NFPA 79.

qa.q: Is being a controls and PLC engineer a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. When a line or plant stops, every minute costs money and people wait on you to find the fault. Start-ups bring tight deadlines and long hours. Between those moments, much of the work is calm design, coding and testing. Those who like solving puzzles under pressure tend to do well.

qa.q: Do controls engineers need a PE license?
qa.a: Most controls engineers working inside a factory or plant do not need one, because many states exempt industrial employers. A PE license matters if you sign drawings or offer engineering services to the public, which can apply to some building and utility projects. Rules vary by state. A PE exam in Control Systems is offered for those who want it.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A chief operating officer runs a company’s day-to-day operations and turns the CEO’s strategy into plans, goals and processes. Depending on the company, the COO may oversee operations, supply chain, customer service, people teams and sometimes sales or finance.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A COO’s day is mostly meetings: leadership team sessions, one-on-ones with department heads and reviews of operating dashboards. In between they solve problems between teams, approve budgets and hires, meet key customers or suppliers and prepare updates for the CEO and board.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with the CEO and CFO, other executives and the heads of each department. They also deal with the board of directors, investors, major customers, suppliers and outside advisors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include business intelligence dashboards such as Tableau or Looker, ERP systems such as SAP or NetSuite, goal-tracking software for OKRs, spreadsheets, project management tools, Slack and video conferencing.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: A COO is judged on whether the company hits its goals for revenue, margins and growth, and on efficiency, on-time delivery and customer satisfaction. Retaining good staff and delivering major projects on schedule also count.

qa.q: What is the difference between a COO and a CEO?
qa.a: The CEO sets the company’s vision and strategy, makes final decisions, answers to the board and is the public face of the company. The COO runs internal operations and makes sure the strategy gets done, and is often second in command. Not every company has a COO, and the role is shaped by what the CEO needs.

qa.q: What does a COO do day to day?
qa.a: A COO spends the day making sure the company runs well. They review operating results, meet department heads, fix problems that cross teams, set priorities and approve spending and hiring. They also design processes so the company can grow, lead major projects and report progress to the CEO and board.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Coordinators keep a team’s work on track. They book meetings, track orders and deliveries, plan events, update spreadsheets and file paperwork. They also answer emails and calls and follow up when tasks or replies run late.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with the inbox and the calendar. Then come scheduling changes, vendor calls, a supply order, notes from a team meeting and a status update for a manager. Small surprises fill whatever time is left.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Coordinators work closely with a manager or team lead. They also deal with coworkers in other departments, outside vendors, clients and guests. Being the person everyone checks with means clear, polite communication matters every day.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most of the work happens on a computer. Common tools are email, shared calendars, spreadsheets, word processing, video meeting software and project tracking apps. Some roles also use ordering systems, a CRM or basic invoicing software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good coordinators are judged by what goes smoothly. Meetings happen on time, orders arrive, events run without gaps and files are easy to find. Managers notice accuracy, quick follow-up and how well problems get flagged early.

qa.q: What does a coordinator do day to day?
qa.a: A coordinator handles the details that keep a team organized. On a normal day that means scheduling meetings, tracking orders, answering emails and calls, updating records, preparing documents and helping plan events. Many coordinators also act as the go-between for their team and vendors, clients or other departments.

qa.q: What is the difference between a coordinator and an administrative assistant?
qa.a: The roles overlap a lot, and titles vary by employer. An administrative assistant often supports one person or office with general clerical tasks. A coordinator usually owns a specific area, such as events, projects, scheduling or purchasing, and tracks it from start to finish. Both are common first office jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Corporate secretaries and governance specialists keep a company’s legal entities in good standing. They schedule board and committee meetings, prepare agendas and board books, take minutes, draft resolutions and consents, file annual reports with states, track directors and officers, and keep bylaws and charters current.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include drafting minutes from a committee meeting, collecting signatures on written consents and updating the entity database. Specialists also handle state annual reports, registered agent changes and qualifications to do business in other states, answer questions about signing authority, and prepare the next board book.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the general counsel, CFO, CEO and board members, plus tax, finance and legal teams. They also deal with outside counsel, registered agents, auditors, transfer agents at public companies, and state business filing offices.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include entity management software, board portals such as Diligent Boards for secure board books, e-signature tools, state online filing systems and document management systems. Public companies also use the SEC’s EDGAR system for proxy statements and insider reports.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on entities that stay in good standing, filings made on time, accurate and complete minutes, and smooth board meetings. Leaders also value clean records during audits, financings and acquisitions and, at public companies, timely SEC filings and a well-run annual shareholder meeting.

qa.q: Do you need to be a lawyer to be a corporate secretary?
qa.a: Not always. At many public companies the corporate secretary is a lawyer, often the general counsel or a deputy. But governance specialists, paralegals and entity managers who do much of the daily work often hold a paralegal certificate or a bachelor’s degree instead. Strong organization, discretion and a working knowledge of corporate law matter most.

qa.q: What is the difference between a corporate secretary and an executive assistant?
qa.a: A corporate secretary is a company officer responsible for governance: board meetings, minutes, legal records, state filings and, at public companies, parts of SEC compliance. An executive assistant supports one or more executives with calendars, travel and correspondence. Despite the similar title, the corporate secretary role carries legal duties and often sits in the legal department.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Corporate trainers find out what employees need to learn, then design and deliver sessions on skills, software, company processes and compliance topics. They also onboard new hires, update course materials and track who has completed required training.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a morning workshop for new hires, followed by a virtual session on a software update. Afternoons often go to building slides, editing an online module, answering learner questions and meeting with managers about upcoming needs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Trainers work closely with human resources, department managers and subject matter experts who know the technical details. They teach employees at every level, from front-line staff to supervisors, and sometimes coordinate with outside vendors who supply courses or platforms.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include presentation software, video meeting platforms and a learning management system to assign courses and record completions. Many trainers also use e-learning authoring tools, survey forms, quizzes, screen recording software and simple video editing programs.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by learner feedback, quiz and assessment results, course completion rates and whether employees apply the skills on the job. Managers may also look at changes in errors, productivity, safety incidents or customer complaints after training.

qa.q: What does a corporate trainer do day to day?
qa.a: A corporate trainer spends the day teaching and preparing to teach. That means leading classroom or online sessions, building slides, videos and quizzes, and updating courses when processes change. They also meet with managers to learn what skills teams lack, track completions in a learning system, and review feedback to improve their next session.

qa.q: What is the difference between a corporate trainer and an instructional designer?
qa.a: A corporate trainer mainly delivers training, standing in front of learners in person or online and guiding them through the material. An instructional designer mainly creates training, planning learning goals and building courses, modules and assessments. In smaller companies one person often does both jobs, while larger companies tend to split them into separate roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Cost accountants work out what it really costs to make each product or deliver each service. They track materials, labor and overhead, set standard costs, analyze variances, value inventory, and support pricing and make-or-buy decisions. In tech companies they also allocate cloud and software costs to teams and products.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may start with production or cloud usage reports and posting cost entries. Then comes investigating why actual costs differ from standards, updating overhead rates and answering questions from plant managers. Month-end brings inventory reconciliations, cost of goods sold reports and closing entries.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Cost accountants work with plant controllers, production and operations managers, purchasing teams and supply chain planners. They also support general ledger and FP&A teams, and in tech firms partner with engineering and FinOps staff on cloud spending. Auditors review their inventory and cost records.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work inside ERP systems such as SAP, Oracle or NetSuite, using their costing and inventory modules. Excel is used constantly for variance analysis and models. BI tools like Power BI or Tableau, and cloud billing and cost management dashboards, are common in tech settings.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Cost accountants are judged on accurate inventory values and product costs, a clean and timely month-end close, and clear variance explanations. Leaders value savings they help find, sound pricing support, and records that pass internal and external audits without adjustments.

qa.q: What does a cost accountant do day to day?
qa.a: A cost accountant tracks what goes into making products or running services: materials, labor, machine time, overhead and, in tech, cloud usage. They compare actual costs to standards or budgets, explain the differences and suggest fixes. They also value inventory, post month-end entries, and give managers cost data for pricing and budgets.

qa.q: Do you need a CPA to be a cost accountant?
qa.a: No. Most cost accountant jobs ask for a bachelor’s degree in accounting or finance, not a CPA license. Many cost accountants earn the Certified Management Accountant, or CMA, credential, which focuses on cost and management accounting. A CPA can still help with promotion to controller roles, and CPA licensing rules vary by state.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: C++ developers write and maintain code where speed and memory use really matter. They build new features, fix crashes and memory bugs, profile slow code paths and tune them, and review teammates’ changes before they merge.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team check-in, then hours of focused coding. Much time goes to debugging, reading crash reports, running tests, and measuring performance after each change to confirm it actually got faster.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use compilers such as GCC, Clang or MSVC, build tools like CMake, debuggers like GDB or LLDB, profilers, sanitizers that catch memory errors, Git for version control, and continuous integration systems that build and test every change.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with other engineers, testers and product managers. Depending on the field, they also work with game designers and artists, traders and quants, hardware and firmware engineers, or robotics and controls specialists.
