They also report to senior leaders and coordinate with other departments so their team’s work fits the wider goals of the organization.

qa.q: What is the difference between a director and a manager?
qa.a: A manager usually runs a single team and focuses on daily work and short-term goals. A director often oversees several managers or an entire department and focuses on longer-term strategy, budgets and staffing. Directors typically report to executives, while managers often report to directors. Exact titles and duties vary from one employer to another.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They design and build services that spread work and data across many machines. They handle replication, partitioning and consensus so the system stays correct when servers crash, networks split or messages arrive late or twice.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with dashboards and alerts from overnight. Then come design reviews, writing code, testing failure cases and reading traces to find why one request was slow. Some weeks include on-call shifts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include languages like Go, Java, Rust or C++, container platforms such as Kubernetes, message queues, distributed databases, and tracing and metrics systems. Many teams also use chaos testing and formal specs to check designs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with site reliability engineers, backend developers, database specialists and product teams. They often write design documents that other engineers review before major changes ship.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by uptime, latency, data correctness and how well the system scales under load. Teams track service level objectives and review outages in blameless postmortems to prevent repeats.

qa.q: What does a distributed systems engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They write and review code for services that run across many servers. They test how the system behaves when machines or networks fail, tune performance, and investigate slow or failed requests using logs, metrics and traces. Many also take on-call shifts and write design documents for new features or scaling changes.

qa.q: What is the difference between a distributed systems engineer and a site reliability engineer?
qa.a: A distributed systems engineer mainly designs and builds the software that coordinates many machines, such as storage, messaging or scheduling layers. A site reliability engineer focuses on keeping production services running through monitoring, automation, capacity planning and incident response. The roles overlap a lot, and titles vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: .NET developers write business software in C# on the .NET platform. They build web APIs and websites with ASP.NET Core, background services and internal tools. They connect these to databases, write automated tests, fix bugs and keep older applications running on supported versions of .NET.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days start with a team standup and a look at the ticket board. Then come focused hours writing C# code, reviewing pull requests from teammates and debugging issues. Some time goes to deployments, database changes and questions from testers or business users.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with other developers, QA testers, product owners and business analysts who explain what the software must do. They also coordinate with database administrators and DevOps or cloud engineers who run the servers. In consulting roles they may talk to client staff directly.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core kit is C#, Visual Studio or Rider, and ASP.NET Core for web work. Entity Framework Core handles database access, usually against SQL Server or PostgreSQL. Common extras are Git, NuGet packages, xUnit or NUnit for tests, Docker and Azure cloud services.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether features ship working and on time, and on code that other developers can read and change. Reviewers look at tests, performance, security issues like injection flaws, and how well the code fits the team’s architecture.

qa.q: What is the difference between .NET Framework and modern .NET?
qa.a: .NET Framework is the older version that runs only on Windows and is now kept up mainly for existing applications. Modern .NET, which grew out of .NET Core, is open source and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. New projects usually use modern .NET, while many company jobs still involve maintaining or migrating .NET Framework code.

qa.q: Is C# only used for Windows software?
qa.a: No. C# started out closely tied to Windows, but modern .NET runs on Linux and macOS too. Today C# is widely used for web APIs and cloud services, many running on Linux servers and containers. It also powers desktop apps, mobile apps through .NET MAUI, and games built in the Unity engine.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Drivers pick up passengers or goods on schedule and get them where they need to go safely. They plan routes, help with luggage or packages, keep the vehicle clean and fueled, log each trip, and report any vehicle problems or incidents to dispatch.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a pre-trip inspection of tires, lights, brakes, and fluids. Then comes a review of the schedule or delivery list. Hours are spent driving, waiting at airports or offices, adjusting for traffic, and updating dispatch, then fueling, cleaning, and paperwork at the end.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: GPS and route apps, dispatch phones or tablets, and two-way radios keep drivers on track. Many commercial vehicles use electronic logging devices to track driving hours. Shuttle drivers may run wheelchair lifts, and delivery drivers use hand trucks and scanners.

day.label: Licenses they need
day.text: A standard driver’s license covers most sedans, SUVs, and small vans. A commercial driver’s license with a passenger endorsement is required for vehicles built to carry 16 or more people, including the driver. Some states and cities also require a chauffeur or for-hire license, so rules vary by location.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers look at on-time pickups and drop-offs, a clean driving record, and no accidents or damaged goods. Passenger ratings and courtesy matter, and executive chauffeurs are also judged on discretion, appearance, and knowing the area well.

qa.q: What does a driver or chauffeur do day to day?
qa.a: They inspect their vehicle, check the day’s schedule, and drive passengers or goods to set destinations on time. Between trips they wait at pickup points, handle luggage or packages, stay in touch with dispatch, and adjust routes for traffic. The day ends with fueling, cleaning the vehicle, and logging trips.

qa.q: Do you need a CDL to be a chauffeur?
qa.a: Usually not. Most chauffeurs drive sedans, SUVs, or smaller vans that only need a standard license, though some states require a chauffeur license or for-hire permit. A commercial driver’s license with a passenger endorsement is required for vehicles designed to carry 16 or more people, including the driver, such as large shuttles, party buses, and motorcoaches.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Drone engineers and operators design, build, test or fly uncrewed aircraft. Engineers work on airframes, propulsion, flight controllers, sensors and software. Operators plan missions, check airspace, fly drones for mapping, inspection, filming, delivery or defense, and process the data they collect.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: An operator’s day starts with checking weather, airspace and permissions, then preflight checks of the aircraft and batteries. Then come flights, data downloads and logbook updates. An engineer’s day mixes design work, bench tests, flight test planning and fixing problems found in testing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with visual observers, test engineers, software and hardware teams, and data analysts who turn imagery into maps or models. Field operators deal with clients, site managers, air traffic control when needed, and sometimes local police or property owners.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Operators use flight planning apps, the FAA’s B4UFLY app, LAANC for airspace approval and processing software like Pix4D or DroneDeploy. Engineers use CAD, PX4 or ArduPilot autopilot software, flight simulators, MATLAB and Python, and motor and thrust test stands.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Operators are judged on safe flights with no incidents, following FAA rules, and delivering clean, accurate data on time. Engineers are judged on flight performance, reliability, endurance, payload capacity and passing test and certification milestones. Good documentation and logs matter for both.

qa.q: Do you need a license to fly drones for work?
qa.a: Yes. Anyone flying a drone for business in the US needs an FAA Remote Pilot Certificate under Part 107. You earn it by passing an FAA knowledge test, then keep it current with free online recurrent training. Drones flown for work must be registered with the FAA. Some flights, such as beyond visual line of sight, need extra FAA approval.

qa.q: What is the difference between a drone engineer and a drone pilot?
qa.a: A drone engineer designs and improves the aircraft: structure, motors, electronics, autopilot software and sensors. A drone pilot or operator flies missions and collects data, such as photos, maps or inspection footage. Engineers usually need an engineering degree, while pilots need an FAA Remote Pilot Certificate. Test pilots often bridge both roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Answer customer calls, emails and chats in Dutch. Solve order, billing, account and technical problems. Some roles also sell to or manage accounts for clients in the Netherlands and Belgium, or translate and review written content.

day.label: Hours and time zones
day.text: The Netherlands and Belgium are usually six hours ahead of US Eastern time. Shifts that cover their business day often start very early in the morning in the US, especially for live phone and chat support.

day.label: Language skills used
day.text: Most roles ask for native or near-native spoken and written Dutch, plus fluent English for internal work. Agents switch between formal u and informal je to match the brand’s tone. Belgian accounts may also ask for French.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Jobs sit in customer support centers, sales teams, travel and software companies, and translation or localization agencies. Many US-based Dutch speaking roles are remote or hybrid, working from home with a headset and company systems.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Support roles track customer satisfaction scores, response and resolution times, and quality reviews of calls and tickets. Translation roles are judged on accuracy and natural tone. Handling customer data must follow EU privacy rules under GDPR.

qa.q: What does a Dutch speaking customer support agent do day to day?
qa.a: They log in to a ticket or phone system and handle a queue of Dutch-speaking customers. They answer questions, fix account or order issues, process returns, and write clear notes. Tricky cases go to a specialist or supervisor. Many also translate help articles or flag common complaints to the team.

qa.q: What is the difference between Dutch and Flemish for these jobs?
qa.a: Flemish is the Dutch spoken in Flanders, the northern part of Belgium. Both use the same standard written language, but accents, some words and expressions differ. Most employers accept speakers of either. Belgian customers may notice Netherlands word choices, so some roles ask for familiarity with Belgian usage.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They decide which products go live, write and fix listings, set prices and promotions, and watch what sells. They also manage stock levels, product photos, categories and search filters so shoppers find items fast.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with yesterday’s sales, traffic and conversion numbers. Then come listing updates, price checks against competitors, planning the next promotion, and sorting out problems like out-of-stock items or wrong product details.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Store platforms and marketplace seller dashboards, spreadsheets, web analytics, product information systems, inventory software and email marketing tools. Many also use simple photo editing and basic HTML to tidy up product pages.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Buyers and suppliers, warehouse and fulfillment staff, designers and photographers, marketing teams and customer service. On marketplaces they also deal with platform rules and seller support when listings get flagged.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Mostly by numbers: revenue, conversion rate, average order value, margin, return rate and how often items sell out. Clean, accurate listings and promotions that launch on time also count.

qa.q: What does an e-commerce merchandiser do day to day?
qa.a: They review sales and traffic data, update product listings, adjust prices and promotions, and decide which items to feature on the home page or in emails. They also fix listing errors, track stock with the warehouse, and plan seasonal launches with buyers and marketing.

qa.q: What is the difference between an e-commerce merchandiser and a buyer?
qa.a: A buyer chooses which products to purchase from suppliers, negotiates terms and orders stock. An e-commerce merchandiser takes that stock and makes it sell online by deciding how it is listed, priced, grouped and promoted on the site. In small companies one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Economists study how markets, prices, wages and policies work. They gather and clean data, build statistical and economic models, forecast trends, estimate what a tax, rule or business decision will change, and write reports and briefs that explain their findings to decision makers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes cleaning data, running regressions or forecasting models and checking results against economic theory. Economists read new research and official data releases, write memos or papers, and present findings to policymakers, managers or clients.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with policymakers, lawyers, business leaders, statisticians and data scientists. In government they brief officials and legislators. In consulting they support legal cases such as antitrust or damages. In companies they advise pricing, strategy and finance teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Economists mainly use Stata, R and Python, plus Excel for quick work. Some use MATLAB or EViews for forecasting and macro models, and SQL for large datasets. They rely on public data from federal statistical agencies and often write papers in LaTeX.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on sound methods, correct data and clear reasoning that survives review by other economists. Forecast accuracy matters in some roles. Explaining results simply to non-economists, and on deadline, counts as much as technical skill.

qa.q: Do you need a PhD to be an economist?
qa.a: Many economist jobs ask for at least a master’s degree, and most research, academic and senior government roles require a PhD. A bachelor’s degree in economics can lead to research assistant or analyst roles. Some federal economist jobs accept a bachelor’s degree that includes enough economics and statistics coursework.

qa.q: What is the difference between an economist and a financial analyst?
qa.a: An economist studies how whole markets, industries or economies behave and what policies or events will do to them. A financial analyst studies specific companies, investments or budgets to guide buying, selling or spending decisions. Economists lean on economic theory and statistical models, while financial analysts lean on accounting and valuation.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan lessons, teach live or recorded classes, and grade student work. Many also write course content, build quizzes and practice activities, and turn learning goals into clear, step-by-step materials for online courses or education products.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might mix teaching a video class, answering student questions on a discussion board, and giving feedback on assignments. Course builders may spend hours drafting a module, scripting a video, or revising lessons after reviewing learner results.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include learning management systems, video meeting software, screen recording and editing programs, slide decks, and course authoring tools. Shared documents, gradebooks, and online quiz builders are used almost every day.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with students and often parents, plus subject matter experts, editors, video producers, and other teachers. In education companies, they may also work with product managers and engineers who build the learning platform.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is judged by whether learners actually learn. Employers look at test and quiz results, course completion, student feedback, and how accurate, clear, and engaging the materials are. Meeting content deadlines also matters for course builders.

qa.q: What is the difference between a teacher and an instructional designer?
qa.a: A teacher works directly with students, delivering lessons, answering questions, and grading work. An instructional designer plans and builds the course itself, deciding learning goals, the order of lessons, activities, and assessments. Designers often never meet the learners. Many people in education do both, especially in online courses.

qa.q: Do you need a teaching license to teach online?
qa.a: It depends on the job. Many public K-12 schools require a state teaching license, but rules vary by state, some charter schools are exempt, and emergency or alternative permits exist. Tutoring platforms, private education companies, and adult or corporate training usually set their own requirements, often a degree and subject knowledge.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Education program managers run learning programs for students, employees, customers or the public. They plan content with experts, recruit participants and instructors, manage budgets and schedules, work with partners and measure whether people learn and finish.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include checking enrollment and attendance data, meeting instructors and course designers, answering participant questions and handling session logistics. Managers also meet partners such as schools or nonprofits and write reports for leaders or funders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with instructional designers, teachers and facilitators, subject experts, school and district staff, community partners and funders. In companies they also work with marketing, customer success and product teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include learning management systems such as Canvas, Moodle or Docebo, survey tools such as Google Forms or Qualtrics, project management software, spreadsheets, a CRM and Zoom. Many also build data dashboards to track results.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers are judged on enrollment, completion and learning results, such as assessment scores or skills gained, and on participant satisfaction. Staying on budget, keeping partners happy and meeting grant reporting rules also count.

qa.q: What does an education program manager do day to day?
qa.a: An education program manager keeps a learning program running. They schedule courses and instructors, track enrollment and completion, answer questions from learners and partners and fix problems with content or logistics. They also review survey and assessment data, report results to leaders or funders and plan improvements for the next session.

qa.q: Do you need a teaching license to be an education program manager?
qa.a: Usually not. A state teaching license is required to teach in most public school classrooms, but program managers at nonprofits, colleges, companies and museums typically need a bachelor’s degree and experience in education, training or program management. Some school district roles prefer or require an educator license, so check each posting.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: EHS staff inspect work areas, check compliance with OSHA and EPA rules, run safety training, and investigate injuries and spills. They also keep injury logs, environmental permits, and hazardous waste records current and ready for an agency inspection.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a floor walk to spot hazards like blocked exits, missing guards, or poor lockout/tagout. Later come training sessions, permit paperwork, air or noise sampling, contractor safety reviews, and follow-up on open corrective actions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with plant managers, supervisors, and frontline workers, plus maintenance crews, contractors, and HR. They also deal with outside parties such as OSHA or state plan inspectors, environmental regulators, insurers, and waste haulers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include gas detectors, noise dosimeters, and air sampling pumps. They rely on safety data sheets, OSHA 300 injury logs, audit checklists, and EHS software that tracks incidents, training, permits, and inspection findings.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in fewer recordable injuries and lost-time cases, clean audits, permits kept in compliance, and no regulatory citations. Leaders also watch whether hazards get fixed quickly and whether workers actually report near misses.

qa.q: What does an EHS specialist do day to day?
qa.a: An EHS specialist walks the site looking for hazards, trains workers on topics like hazard communication and lockout/tagout, and investigates incidents to find root causes. They keep OSHA injury records, track environmental permits and waste shipments, and work with supervisors to fix problems before they cause harm or a citation.

qa.q: Is EHS a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Serious injuries, spills, and surprise agency inspections bring pressure and long days. EHS staff must also push for safety when production schedules are tight, which takes tact. Many find the work rewarding because it protects people, and routine tasks like training and audits balance out the urgent moments.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Electrical engineers design and test electrical systems. They plan power distribution, size wiring and protection, choose batteries and chargers, and lay out circuit boards or radio parts. They write specs, run calculations, review drawings and fix problems found in testing or in the field.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes desk work and lab or site time. An engineer might run load or circuit calculations, update a schematic, check a prototype with test gear, answer questions from builders or technicians, and join a design review with other engineers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use computer-aided design software for schematics and building drawings, circuit simulation, and circuit board layout tools. In the lab they rely on multimeters, oscilloscopes, power supplies, spectrum analyzers and battery testers. Building work follows the National Electrical Code as adopted by each state or city.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with mechanical and software engineers, drafters, technicians, project managers and electricians. On building and utility projects they deal with architects, contractors and code inspectors. In product work they talk with manufacturing teams, suppliers and test labs.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on safety, code compliance, reliability, cost and schedule. Only a licensed Professional Engineer can seal engineering drawings, and the license comes from each state. Many building and utility jobs need sealed drawings, so those roles often ask for a PE or a path to one.

qa.q: What does an electrical engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days involve design and problem solving. An electrical engineer runs calculations, draws schematics or wiring plans, picks parts like breakers, batteries or radio components, and tests prototypes. They also review others’ work, answer questions from technicians or contractors, and write reports. Some roles add site visits to check installations or troubleshoot equipment.

qa.q: What is the difference between an electrical engineer and an electrician?
qa.a: An electrical engineer designs systems and usually holds a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering. An electrician installs, maintains and repairs wiring and equipment, often following an engineer’s plans. Electricians usually train through apprenticeships and need a license, with rules that vary by state and sometimes by city. Engineers who seal drawings need a state Professional Engineer license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build electrical and electronic assemblies by hand from drawings. They cut, strip and crimp wire, route cable harnesses, solder parts onto circuit boards, mount components in enclosures, then test each unit and fix any faults they find.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The shift starts with a work order and a build packet. Most hours go to soldering, wiring and assembly at a bench. Finished units go through power-up and function tests, and results are logged before parts move to inspection.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Temperature-controlled soldering irons, desoldering tools, wire strippers, crimpers and heat guns are used daily. Testing relies on multimeters, power supplies and oscilloscopes. Magnifiers or microscopes help with small parts, and grounding straps and mats protect static-sensitive components.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most work happens in manufacturing plants, repair depots and lab or prototype shops. Benches are usually indoors, clean and well lit. Some areas are static-controlled, and some jobs require safety glasses, gowns or other protective gear.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is checked against schematics, wiring diagrams and written workmanship standards. Inspectors look at solder joints, wire routing and labeling. Units must pass electrical tests, and first-pass yield, rework counts and on-time completion are commonly tracked.

qa.q: What is the difference between an electrical technician and an electrician?
qa.a: An electrical and electronics technician builds and tests equipment, usually at a bench in a plant or lab. An electrician installs and repairs wiring in buildings and on job sites. Electricians generally need a state or local license, and rules vary by state. Bench assembly technicians usually do not need a license, though employers often require workmanship training or certification.

qa.q: Is electrical technician work a stressful job?
qa.a: It is usually steady rather than high stress. The pressure comes from fine detail, tight tolerances and production deadlines, since a single bad joint can fail a unit. Long hours of close-up work can strain eyes, hands and posture. Good lighting, magnification and regular breaks help.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Electricians read blueprints, run conduit and cable, and install panels, outlets, switches and lighting. They connect motors and controls, find and fix faults, replace worn parts, and test circuits so systems work safely and pass inspection.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days start with a job briefing and a look at the plans. Then comes pulling wire, bending conduit, mounting boxes and making connections. On service calls, they trace a fault with a meter, fix it and explain the repair to the customer.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common hand tools include wire strippers, lineman’s pliers, screwdrivers, fish tape and a conduit bender. Multimeters, clamp meters and insulation testers check circuits. Lockout devices and arc-rated clothing protect them around energized equipment.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Job sites range from new homes and remodels to offices, hospitals, factories and power sites. Work can be outdoors, on ladders and lifts, or in tight attics and crawl spaces. Many work for contractors, while others maintain one plant or campus.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work must meet the electrical code adopted by the state or city, usually based on the National Electrical Code, and the edition in force varies by location. Inspectors often check work before walls are closed and again at the end.

qa.q: What does an electrician do day to day?
qa.a: An electrician plans the job from drawings, installs wiring, boxes, panels and fixtures, and connects equipment. They test circuits, troubleshoot problems with meters and replace faulty parts. Many days also include working with other trades, ordering materials, keeping the site safe and getting work ready for inspection.

qa.q: How do you become a licensed electrician?
qa.a: Most people start with an apprenticeship that usually lasts four or five years and combines paid on-the-job hours with classroom training. Licensing rules vary by state, and some states leave licensing to cities or counties. Where a license is required, you typically log set hours, pass a journeyman exam, and can later qualify for a master license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Embedded engineers write and debug firmware, mostly in C and C++, for the microcontrollers and processors inside products. They build drivers for sensors, displays and radios, manage memory and power use, and make sure code meets strict timing limits on chips with little memory.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes coding with bench work. An engineer might flash new firmware to a prototype board, chase a bug with a logic analyzer, review a teammate’s code, then meet with hardware and test colleagues about the next build.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include C and C++, cross-compilers, Git, JTAG or SWD debuggers, oscilloscopes, logic analyzers and multimeters. Many projects run a real-time operating system, while larger chips often run embedded Linux. Some teams also use Python for test scripts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with electrical engineers who design the circuit boards, plus test, manufacturing and product teams. Reading schematics and chip datasheets is a daily skill, because software bugs and hardware faults can look alike.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Code must be reliable, fit in limited memory and respond on time. Regulated fields set a higher bar: automotive work often follows ISO 26262, medical device software commonly follows IEC 62304, and avionics follows DO-178C. Most roles need no state license.

qa.q: What does an embedded engineer do day to day?
qa.a: An embedded engineer writes and tests the low-level code that controls a device’s hardware. Daily work includes coding in C or C++, loading firmware onto test boards, tracing bugs with debuggers and oscilloscopes, reading datasheets, and working with hardware engineers to fix problems before a product ships.

qa.q: What is the difference between an embedded engineer and a software engineer?
qa.a: A general software engineer usually builds apps or web services that run on computers or servers with plenty of memory. An embedded engineer writes code for a specific device with tight limits on memory, power and timing. Embedded work needs more hardware knowledge, like reading schematics and using lab tools.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Employee experience managers design how it feels to work at a company. They shape onboarding for new hires, run engagement and pulse surveys, plan culture programs and events, and improve the office and hybrid work setup so people feel welcome and supported.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reviewing survey comments, then a meeting with HR about a new onboarding step. Afternoons often go to planning an all-hands event, checking in with office staff, and drafting messages about upcoming programs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with HR, recruiting, people managers and company leaders. They also partner with facilities, IT, internal communications and outside vendors such as caterers, event venues and survey software providers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include HR information systems, survey and feedback platforms, onboarding checklists, chat and video tools, project trackers and spreadsheets. Many also use simple dashboards to track survey scores, event turnout and new hire feedback.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is often measured by engagement survey results, new hire feedback, retention trends and participation in programs. Leaders also look at whether action plans from surveys were actually carried out and whether employees noticed the changes.

qa.q: What does an employee experience manager do day to day?
qa.a: They spend the day improving how employees experience work. That includes updating onboarding, reading and sharing survey results, planning events and recognition programs, fixing office or hybrid work pain points, and meeting with managers and HR to turn employee feedback into concrete changes.

qa.q: What is the difference between employee experience and HR?
qa.a: HR covers the full set of people functions, including hiring, pay, benefits, compliance and employee relations. Employee experience is usually a focused part of HR or a partner team. It concentrates on how work feels day to day, through onboarding, feedback, culture, events and the workplace itself.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Employee relations specialists handle workplace complaints and conflicts. They investigate claims of harassment, discrimination, retaliation and misconduct, interview witnesses, write findings, and advise managers on discipline and terminations. They also interpret policies, track case trends and help keep decisions consistent, fair and lawful.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include intake calls about new complaints, witness interviews and writing an investigation report. Specialists also coach a manager on a performance plan, review a termination with legal counsel and update case files. Some days bring training sessions on respectful workplace conduct.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with HR business partners, managers, employees who raise concerns and the people accused. They also consult employment lawyers, compliance and ethics teams, and sometimes union representatives. The EEOC or state civil rights agencies may be involved when charges are filed.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include case management software for investigations, the HRIS, ethics hotline and reporting platforms, and secure document storage. Specialists use interview templates, investigation report formats, policy handbooks, and Excel or dashboards to track case volume and trends.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on thorough, unbiased and well-documented investigations, timely case closure and consistent outcomes. Leaders also look for fewer repeat issues, fewer legal claims and how well managers follow advice. Protecting confidentiality and preventing retaliation are essential.

qa.q: What does an employee relations specialist do day to day?
qa.a: An employee relations specialist takes in workplace complaints, decides how to handle them, and runs investigations by interviewing people and gathering evidence. They write up findings, recommend actions, and advise managers on discipline, performance plans and terminations. They also spot patterns across cases and suggest policy changes or training to prevent future problems.

qa.q: What laws do employee relations specialists need to know?
qa.a: They need a working knowledge of federal laws such as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act and the National Labor Relations Act. Many states and cities add broader protections, so the rules vary by state and location.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Employment lawyers advise employers on hiring, offer letters, employment contracts, handbooks and terminations. They review restrictive covenants, wage and hour rules, leave and accommodation requests. They also defend discrimination, harassment and retaliation claims, and they coordinate advice for staff based in other countries.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a call from HR about a planned firing. Then comes a separation agreement to draft and a policy update to review. There may be a position statement to write for a charge filed with the EEOC or a state agency.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with HR teams, managers, executives and payroll. They also deal with outside law firms, local counsel in other countries, opposing lawyers, mediators and government investigators. Some represent employees instead of employers, and they meet with workers who believe their rights were violated.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their core tools are legal research databases, contract and document templates, and matter management software. Federal laws such as Title VII, the ADA, the ADEA, the FLSA and the FMLA guide much of the work. State and city laws often add stricter rules.

day.label: Rules for the job
day.text: Employment lawyers need a law degree and a license from at least one state bar. In-house lawyers working in a state where they are not licensed may need to register there, and the rules vary by state. Advice on foreign staff usually relies on locally licensed counsel.

qa.q: What does an employment lawyer do day to day?
qa.a: An employment lawyer answers workplace legal questions as they come up. That can mean reviewing an offer letter, checking whether a worker is properly classified, advising on a termination or leave request, and drafting agreements. They also investigate complaints, respond to agency charges, negotiate settlements and, when needed, defend or bring lawsuits in court or arbitration.

qa.q: What is the difference between an employment lawyer and a labor lawyer?
qa.a: Employment lawyers focus on individual workplace rights, such as discrimination, wages, leave, contracts and firing. Labor lawyers focus on unions and collective bargaining under the National Labor Relations Act. Their work includes union elections, bargaining and unfair labor practice charges. Many lawyers practice both, and job titles often use the terms loosely.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Builds and maintains the settings, apps and security rules that every company laptop, desktop, tablet and phone receives. Automates enrollment so new devices set themselves up, pushes updates and patches, enforces encryption and passcodes, and can lock or wipe a lost or stolen device remotely.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with compliance reports showing which devices missed updates or fell out of policy. The rest of the day mixes testing a new configuration on a small pilot group, packaging an app for deployment, handling escalated help desk tickets, and planning the next operating system rollout.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with help desk staff, the security team, network engineers and HR, who flag new hires and departures. They also coordinate with purchasing and device resellers so new hardware ships already linked to the company’s management system.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A unified endpoint management or mobile device management console, vendor zero-touch enrollment programs, directory and identity services, patch management tools and endpoint protection software. Scripting skills help automate fixes and reports across hundreds or thousands of devices running different operating systems.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in how fast a new hire gets a ready device, how many devices stay encrypted and up to date, fewer repeat help desk tickets, and clean results when auditors or security reviewers check device controls.

qa.q: What is the difference between an endpoint engineer and a help desk technician?
qa.a: A help desk technician fixes problems for individual users, one ticket at a time. An endpoint engineer designs the policies, app packages and automated setup that apply to every device at once. When the help desk sees the same issue again and again, the endpoint engineer usually fixes the cause for the whole fleet.

qa.q: Is endpoint and device management a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. A bad policy or update pushed to every device can disrupt the whole company, so careful engineers test changes on pilot groups first. Pressure peaks during major operating system releases, security incidents and large hiring waves. Much of the work is planned, though, and good automation cuts down on after-hours emergencies.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They install, run and maintain equipment that makes, stores or saves power. This includes solar panels, wind turbines, battery systems and efficient heating and cooling. Others audit buildings, track energy use, plan projects and help customers lower their bills.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A field tech might climb a roof or turbine, test wiring and log readings. An office worker might review utility data, estimate savings, prepare permit or rebate paperwork, and meet with clients or crews to plan the next job.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: They work on rooftops, solar farms, wind sites, power plants, battery facilities, factories, homes and utility offices. Many jobs mix outdoor work in all kinds of weather with desk time and driving between sites.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with electricians, engineers, project managers, utility staff, building owners and inspectors. Customer-facing workers explain options to homeowners and businesses. Field crews coordinate closely to stay safe on roofs, towers and live electrical equipment.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Field tools include multimeters, infrared cameras, blower door testers, power tools, lifts and fall protection harnesses. Office roles use energy modeling software, spreadsheets, monitoring dashboards and utility billing data to find where power is made, stored or wasted.

qa.q: What does an energy and sustainability worker do day to day?
qa.a: It depends on the role. Installers and technicians mount, wire, test and repair solar, wind, battery or efficient heating and cooling systems. Auditors inspect buildings for energy waste. Analysts and project managers study usage data, plan upgrades, handle permits and incentive paperwork, and report on savings to clients or managers.

qa.q: Do you need a license to work in solar or energy jobs?
qa.a: It depends on the job and the location. Electrical work on solar and battery systems usually must be done or supervised by a licensed electrician. Licensing rules are set by states and sometimes cities, and some states have separate solar contractor licenses. Many helper, sales, audit and analyst roles need no license, though employers may prefer industry certifications and safety training.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Engagement managers set and guard the scope of a client project, staff the team, build the timeline and budget, and keep the client informed. They spot risks early, handle change requests, and make sure the work delivered matches what the contract promised.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a team check-in on progress and blockers. Then come client calls, status reports, budget and hours reviews, and talks about new requests. Late in the day they may review deliverables or plan the next project phase.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They sit between the client and their own firm. On the client side they work with sponsors and project leads. Inside the firm they work with consultants, analysts, delivery leads, partners or account executives, and finance staff who track billing.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include project tracking software, shared timelines and Gantt charts, spreadsheets for budgets and forecasts, time tracking systems, and slide decks for steering meetings. Statements of work, change orders and status reports are core documents.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is judged by on-time, on-budget delivery, client satisfaction, and project margin. Repeat work or follow-on contracts from the same client are a strong sign of a well-run engagement. Team retention and morale also count.

qa.q: What does an engagement manager do day to day?
qa.a: An engagement manager runs client projects for a consultancy or vendor. Day to day, they lead team check-ins, meet with the client, track hours and budget against the contract, handle scope changes, and review work before it goes out. They also flag risks to firm leaders and look for chances to extend or grow the client relationship.

qa.q: What is the difference between an engagement manager and a project manager?
qa.a: A project manager focuses mainly on delivery: tasks, schedules and resources. An engagement manager does that too but also owns the client relationship and the commercial side, such as scope, contracts, billing and margin. Engagement managers usually work at consulting or service firms, while project managers can work anywhere, including internal company teams. Titles vary by firm.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Engineering interns work on a defined project, such as testing a design, writing code, drafting parts in CAD or analyzing test data. They join team meetings, document their work and present results at the end of the term.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a team check-in or a short meeting with a mentor. The rest of the day goes to project work, lab or field tasks, reading specs and asking questions. Interns often end the day by noting progress and next steps.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: A mentor or supervising engineer guides the intern and reviews their work. Interns also work with technicians, designers, project managers and other interns. On some projects they meet clients, suppliers or plant staff.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Tools depend on the field. Mechanical and civil interns often use CAD and simulation software. Software and electrical interns use code editors, version control and lab test equipment. Spreadsheets are common everywhere, and safety gear is standard on plant floors and job sites.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Interns are judged on the quality of their project, how fast they learn and how clearly they communicate. A final report or presentation is common. Strong interns often get a return offer for another term or a full-time job after graduation.

qa.q: What does an engineering intern do day to day?
qa.a: An engineering intern spends most of the day on an assigned project under a mentor’s guidance. That can mean modeling parts, writing and testing code, running lab tests, collecting field data or checking drawings. They attend team meetings, ask questions, keep notes on their work and usually present what they built or learned at the end of the internship.

qa.q: What is the difference between an engineering internship and a co-op?
qa.a: An internship usually lasts one summer or one semester. A co-op often includes several work terms, sometimes alternating with school terms, and is usually arranged through a university program, which can add time before graduation. Both give real engineering work with a mentor. Co-ops tend to give deeper, longer experience with the same employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Engineering managers lead a team of engineers. They hire new people, plan and prioritize the team’s work, run one-on-one meetings, give feedback and handle performance reviews. They also remove blockers so the team can ship work on time.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team stand-up. Then come one-on-ones, planning sessions, interviews with candidates and meetings with product partners. Between meetings, managers review designs, answer questions and update leaders on progress and risks.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with their own engineers, product managers, designers and other engineering managers. They also report to a director or senior leader and coordinate with recruiters, HR and teams that depend on their work.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include issue trackers, shared documents, calendars, chat and video apps, and code hosting platforms. Many managers still read code and design documents so they can judge technical trade-offs and give useful feedback.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by the team’s results, not personal output. Leaders look at whether projects ship reliably, quality stays high, people grow and stay, open roles get filled with strong hires and the team works well with others.

qa.q: What does an engineering manager do day to day?
qa.a: An engineering manager spends most of the day with people. That means one-on-ones, team planning, hiring interviews and meetings with product and business partners. They set priorities, track progress, give feedback and help engineers solve problems. Some still write code, but most time goes to guiding the team rather than building features alone.

qa.q: What is the difference between an engineering manager and a tech lead?
qa.a: A tech lead guides the technical side of a team, such as design choices, code quality and architecture, and usually codes a lot. An engineering manager is responsible for the people. They handle hiring, growth, performance reviews and team health. At some companies one person does both, but the focus of each role is different.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Enterprise account executives find, pursue and close large deals with major companies. They map who decides and who influences, run discovery calls, build business cases, negotiate pricing and contract terms, and forecast which deals will close each quarter.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a forecast review, then a call with a champion inside a target account. Afternoons often go to drafting a proposal, prepping a demo with a sales engineer, and answering legal or security questions that keep a deal moving.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: On the buyer side, they deal with executives, procurement, legal, IT and security teams, and end users. Internally, they lean on sales development reps, sales engineers, customer success managers, deal desk staff and their own sales leadership.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They live in a CRM to track accounts, contacts and pipeline. Video calls, email sequencing tools, contract and e-signature software, and mutual action plans shared with buyers help them keep long, complex deals organized.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is measured mainly against a quota, usually annual or quarterly revenue closed. Managers also watch pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, deal size, win rates and how cleanly deals move from stage to stage.

qa.q: What does an enterprise account executive do day to day?
qa.a: They spend most days advancing a small number of large deals. That means meeting stakeholders, running discovery and demos with sales engineers, writing proposals, handling procurement and security reviews, negotiating terms, and updating the CRM so leaders can trust the forecast. Some time also goes to prospecting new accounts in their territory.

qa.q: What is the difference between an enterprise account executive and a mid-market account executive?
qa.a: Enterprise reps sell to the largest companies, so deals are bigger, sales cycles often run many months, and many more people weigh in. Mid-market reps handle more accounts with faster cycles and fewer approvers. Enterprise roles usually expect prior closing experience and stronger skills in negotiation and managing complex buying committees.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Enterprise architects map a company’s business processes, applications, data and technology, then decide how they should fit together over the coming years. They set standards, review major projects, plan which systems to retire or replace and turn business strategy into a technology roadmap.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day mixes meetings with business and IT leaders, reviews of solution designs from project teams and updates to architecture models. Enterprise architects also run or attend an architecture review board, write standards and principles and assess new vendors or cloud services.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the CIO and other executives, business unit leaders, solution and security architects, project managers and finance teams. They also deal with vendors, and sometimes with auditors or regulators who ask how key systems and data are managed.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include EA platforms like LeanIX, Ardoq or Sparx Enterprise Architect, plus diagram tools like Visio and Lucidchart. Many use frameworks and notations such as TOGAF, ArchiMate and BPMN. Spreadsheets and slide decks remain key for roadmaps and executive briefings.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether the company’s systems become simpler, cheaper to run and better at supporting strategy. Leaders look for fewer duplicate applications, projects that follow the roadmap and lower risk from outdated technology. Influence counts, since architects rarely control budgets directly.

qa.q: What is the difference between an enterprise architect and a solution architect?
qa.a: A solution architect designs the technology for one project or product, deciding how its parts work together. An enterprise architect looks across the whole company, setting standards and long-term plans that every project should follow. Many enterprise architects started as solution or software architects and moved up as their scope widened.

qa.q: Do enterprise architects need TOGAF certification?
qa.a: No license is required, and TOGAF certification is optional, though many job postings list it as preferred. Employers care more about long hands-on experience in software, infrastructure or business analysis, plus the ability to talk with executives. Cloud architecture certifications are also common in this field.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They prepare and track environmental permits, run site studies, and design systems that treat water, air or soil. They also plan clean-up of contaminated sites and check that projects meet federal, state and local environmental rules.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start in the field taking soil, groundwater or stormwater samples. The rest goes to reviewing lab results, modeling how pollutants move, drafting reports and answering questions from regulators or project managers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with civil engineers, geologists, lab staff, contractors and property owners. They deal often with state environmental agencies and sometimes the EPA, and may explain findings to residents at public meetings.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Field tools include sampling pumps, water quality meters, air monitors and GPS units. At the desk they use spreadsheets, GIS mapping, CAD and software that models groundwater flow, air dispersion or treatment processes.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Engineers who seal plans need a Professional Engineer license, issued by each state. Work draws on laws like the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, RCRA and Superfund. Hazardous waste site work usually requires OSHA HAZWOPER training.

qa.q: What does an environmental engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They split time between the field and the office. In the field they sample soil, water or air and inspect sites. In the office they review data, design treatment or clean-up systems, write permit applications and reports, and coordinate with regulators, clients and contractors to keep projects compliant and on schedule.

qa.q: What is the difference between an environmental engineer and an environmental scientist?
qa.a: Environmental scientists mostly study and measure. They collect samples, assess impacts and write findings. Environmental engineers use that data to design solutions, such as treatment systems or remediation plans. Engineers who sign final designs need a state Professional Engineer license, while scientists generally do not. On real projects the two roles overlap and work side by side.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They set up and maintain the ERP system, manage user roles and permissions, build saved searches and reports, fix data errors, and test updates. They also turn requests from finance, sales and warehouse teams into system changes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a queue of support tickets, such as a stuck sales order or a user locked out. Later come meetings on a new workflow, testing a change in a sandbox, and checking that overnight integrations ran cleanly.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with accountants, controllers, buyers, warehouse leads and sales operations. They also deal with IT staff, outside consultants and the software vendor’s support team when a problem goes beyond their own access.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Beyond NetSuite or Oracle itself, they use spreadsheets, CSV import tools, SQL for queries, and ticketing systems. NetSuite work may involve SuiteScript, which is JavaScript, while Oracle work may involve PL/SQL and its own reporting tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in clean data, a smooth month-end close, accurate inventory counts and few user complaints. Changes that go live without breaking orders, invoices or reports are the clearest sign of good work.

qa.q: What does an ERP specialist do day to day?
qa.a: An ERP specialist keeps a company’s core business system running. They answer user questions, fix records, adjust forms and workflows, build reports, manage access, and test changes before they go live. Much of the day is spent translating what finance or operations staff need into settings, scripts or searches inside NetSuite, Oracle or a similar platform.

qa.q: What is the difference between an ERP specialist and an ERP consultant?
qa.a: An ERP specialist usually works inside one company and supports its system over the long term, handling daily fixes and improvements. An ERP consultant often works for an outside firm or as a contractor and moves between clients, focusing on new rollouts, migrations or large projects. Many specialists start in-house and later move into consulting, or the other way around.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They take over cases that frontline agents could not resolve, plus formal written complaints. They investigate what went wrong, decide on a fair fix within their authority, explain it to the customer, and record the outcome and root cause.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day mixes callbacks to upset customers, reading account histories and call notes, chasing other teams for answers, and writing clear response letters or emails. Many cases stay open for days or weeks, so tracking deadlines and follow-ups takes steady attention.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with frontline agents who hand cases up, team leads, and billing, shipping or technical teams. Sometimes they also work with legal or compliance staff. In regulated fields such as banking, insurance or healthcare, they may answer complaints routed through government agencies.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use ticketing or case management software, customer account records, phone and email systems, call recordings, and policy knowledge bases. Templates help, but most replies need careful custom wording that is accurate, calm and easy to follow.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Common measures include time to resolve, deadlines met, customer satisfaction after closing, repeat complaints, and quality reviews of calls and letters. Strong specialists also spot patterns and report them, so the same problem stops happening.

qa.q: Is escalations work a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Most contacts start with someone who is already frustrated, angry or worried. Some cases involve threats of legal action or complaints to regulators. A few things make the job much more manageable: clear authority to fix problems, solid support from managers, and the habit of not taking anger personally. Many people find closing a hard case very satisfying.

qa.q: What is the difference between an escalations specialist and a customer service representative?
qa.a: A customer service representative handles a high volume of everyday questions and simple problems, often following scripts. An escalations specialist takes the cases those agents cannot solve. They spend more time per case and dig deeper, and they usually have more authority to grant refunds, credits or exceptions. The role often requires frontline experience and stronger writing skills.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Cost estimators and project controls staff work out what a project will cost before it starts and track cost and schedule while it runs. They take off quantities from drawings, price labor, materials and equipment, gather subcontractor bids, build budgets, then report progress, forecasts and earned value.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: An estimator’s day may include taking off quantities from plans, calling suppliers and subcontractors for prices and finishing a bid before a deadline. Project controls staff update schedules, review cost reports, track change orders and prepare monthly forecasts for project managers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with project managers, engineers, architects, superintendents, schedulers, purchasing and accounting staff. Outside the company they deal with subcontractors, suppliers and the owner’s representatives. Senior estimators often review bids with company leaders before submission.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Estimators use takeoff software like Bluebeam, PlanSwift or On-Screen Takeoff, estimating software like HCSS HeavyBid or Sage Estimating, and Excel. Project controls staff use Primavera P6 or Microsoft Project for schedules and cost systems or Procore for budgets.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Estimators are judged on accuracy: how close bids come to final costs and how many bids win work at a profit. Project controls staff are judged on reliable forecasts, early warnings about overruns and delays, and clean, on-time reports.

qa.q: What is the difference between a cost estimator and a quantity surveyor?
qa.a: In the US, “cost estimator” is the usual title, and estimators both measure quantities and price the work. “Quantity surveyor” is the common title in the UK and many Commonwealth countries, where the role also covers contracts and payment valuations. In US postings, those tasks are often split between estimators, project controls and contract administrators.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a cost estimator?
qa.a: Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in construction management, civil engineering or a related field, though some estimators move up from the trades with strong field experience. No license is required. Optional credentials, such as the Certified Cost Professional or Certified Estimating Professional, can help with hiring and promotion.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: EV charging specialists plan, install, commission and maintain charging stations for electric cars and trucks. Depending on the role they assess sites, size electrical service, design layouts, handle permits and utility connections, install and test chargers, troubleshoot faults and manage networked charger software.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A field technician’s day may include driving to sites, diagnosing a down charger, swapping a cable or board and confirming it talks to the network again. Design and project staff spend days on site surveys, load calculations, permit drawings and calls with utilities and contractors.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with electricians and electrical engineers, utility representatives, site hosts such as property owners and fleet managers, permitting offices and charger maker support teams. Network operations and customer support staff handle driver complaints and remote resets.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Field tools include multimeters, insulation testers, EV charger test adapters, laptops for firmware updates and standard electrician’s hand tools. Office staff use AutoCAD, charger network management software built on the OCPP protocol, utility load data and project management tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on charger uptime, first-time fix rate and how fast faults are cleared. Projects are judged on getting stations powered on schedule and budget, passing electrical inspections, and meeting uptime rules for federally funded stations and accessibility requirements.

qa.q: Do you need to be an electrician to install EV chargers?
qa.a: In most states, wiring a hardwired EV charger must be done by a licensed electrician or under an electrical contractor, with a permit and inspection. Many installers also take the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program course, which some public funding programs require. Licensing rules vary by state and city, so check local requirements.

qa.q: What is the difference between Level 2 and DC fast charging?
qa.a: Level 2 chargers supply alternating current, usually at 240 volts in homes or 208 volts in many commercial buildings, and the car’s onboard charger converts it, so a full charge takes hours. DC fast chargers convert power inside the station and charge much faster, but they need larger electrical service, more cooling and more maintenance.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Events managers set goals and budgets for conferences, meetups and trade-show stands. They book venues, hire vendors, build schedules, manage registration and run the event on the day. Afterward they settle invoices and report results.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Months out, the day is mostly emails, calls and spreadsheets: contracts, speaker confirmations and shipping deadlines. During event week it turns physical, with early setup, long hours on their feet and quick fixes when something goes wrong.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with marketing and sales teams, speakers, sponsors and executives. Outside the company they deal with venue staff, caterers, audiovisual crews, exhibit builders, freight carriers, hotels and the trade-show organizer’s service desk.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include event registration platforms, project management software, shared calendars, budget spreadsheets and badge scanners for capturing leads. Many also use floor-plan tools, virtual event platforms and survey software to collect attendee feedback.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by attendance, leads gathered at stands, sponsor and attendee satisfaction, and staying on budget. A smooth event where guests never notice the problems behind the scenes is often the best sign of good work.

qa.q: What does an events manager do day to day?
qa.a: Most days involve planning work at a desk: negotiating with venues, tracking budgets, confirming speakers and vendors, and updating timelines. Close to an event they coordinate shipping, staffing and setup. On site they oversee check-in, keep sessions on time, solve last-minute problems and make sure the trade-show stand is staffed and stocked.

qa.q: Is being an events manager a stressful job?
qa.a: It often is, especially in the weeks before an event. Deadlines are fixed, budgets are tight and problems like late freight or a missing speaker need fast answers. Travel, early mornings and long on-site days are common. Many people enjoy the pace, and strong planning and backup plans make the pressure easier to handle.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Exchange operations staff keep a crypto exchange running. They process deposits and withdrawals, reconcile balances between hot and cold wallets, support new token listings and network upgrades, watch trading for manipulation and work with compliance on suspicious activity.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Crypto markets never close, so teams work in shifts. A shift includes reviewing withdrawal queues and flagged transactions, checking blockchain confirmations, fixing stuck transfers, reconciling the ledger with on-chain balances and answering escalations from customer support.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with compliance and anti-money laundering teams, customer support, engineers, treasury and custody staff, market surveillance and listings teams. They also deal with finance, legal, banking partners and the teams behind listed tokens.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include internal admin consoles, block explorers such as Etherscan, blockchain analytics tools such as Chainalysis, wallet and custody systems, SQL, monitoring dashboards, Jira, Zendesk and Slack.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on accurate fund movements and reconciliations, fast processing, few incidents and quick fixes when they happen. Following anti-money laundering rules and state licensing conditions, and resolving customer escalations quickly, also count.

qa.q: Do crypto exchanges in the US need a license?
qa.a: Yes. Exchanges serving US customers generally register with FinCEN as money services businesses and must run anti-money laundering programs under the Bank Secrecy Act. Most states also require a money transmitter or similar license, and New York requires its own virtual currency license. Some activities can also fall under SEC or CFTC rules, and the details vary by state.

qa.q: What does a crypto exchange operations specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They make sure money and tokens move correctly. They review deposits and withdrawals, investigate stuck or flagged transactions, reconcile wallet balances with the exchange ledger and help launch new tokens or handle network upgrades. They also answer escalations from support and pass suspicious activity to compliance.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Executives set strategy and goals, approve budgets, hire and lead senior managers, and make the final call on major decisions. A VP usually owns one area, such as sales, finance, operations or engineering, and answers for its results.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Meetings fill much of the day: leadership team syncs, one-on-ones with direct reports, customer or partner calls and budget reviews. Between meetings they read reports, handle escalated problems, review key hires and prepare updates for the CEO or board.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Executives work with the CEO, other senior leaders, the board of directors and the managers who report to them. Many also deal with key customers, investors, lenders, auditors, outside lawyers and regulators, depending on their function and the company’s size.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Dashboards, financial reports, spreadsheets, slide decks and planning documents are daily tools. Most rely on email, video calls and company systems for sales, finance or human resources, often with an executive assistant managing schedules and travel.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured against goals such as revenue, profit, growth, cost control, customer retention and team health. A board or CEO typically reviews performance at least yearly, and pay often includes bonuses or equity tied to those results.

qa.q: What does a VP do day to day?
qa.a: A VP leads one function, such as marketing, finance or operations. Day to day they meet with their managers, track key numbers, approve spending and hires, solve problems that get escalated, and report progress to the CEO or another senior executive. They also plan the coming quarter and year for their team.

qa.q: Is being an executive a stressful job?
qa.a: It often is. Executives answer for results they cannot fully control, work long hours and may travel often. At public companies, the CEO and CFO must personally certify financial reports under federal law. Stress varies with company size, industry and how well the leadership team works together, and many find the work rewarding.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They manage calendars, book travel, schedule meetings and handle correspondence. They prepare documents, track deadlines, process expense reports and screen calls and emails so the executive or team can focus on decisions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a check of the inbox and calendar. Then come scheduling changes, meeting prep, notes or minutes, travel bookings and follow-ups. Urgent requests often reshape priorities by midday.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They support one executive, several leaders or a whole team. They deal daily with other assistants, clients, vendors, travel agents and colleagues in finance, HR and IT, often acting as the first point of contact.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Email and shared calendars, word processing and spreadsheet software, video meeting platforms, expense and travel booking systems, and file sharing tools. Strong typing and clear writing matter as much as any software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By how smoothly the executive’s schedule runs, how few things fall through the cracks, and how well confidential information is protected. Discretion, accuracy and anticipating needs before they are asked are what set strong assistants apart.

qa.q: What does an executive assistant do day to day?
qa.a: An executive assistant keeps a leader’s work organized. Day to day, they manage the calendar, arrange travel, prepare meeting materials, draft emails and reports, handle expense reports and screen requests. They often decide what reaches the executive and what can be handled elsewhere, so judgment and discretion are central to the job.

qa.q: What is the difference between an administrative assistant and an executive assistant?
qa.a: An administrative assistant usually supports a team or office with general tasks like answering phones, filing, scheduling and ordering supplies. An executive assistant typically supports one or a few senior leaders, handles more confidential matters, manages complex calendars and travel, and often acts on the executive’s behalf. Titles and duties vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They fill senior and specialist roles, such as chief financial officer, sales director or in-house counsel. They write the role brief, find and approach candidates, run screening interviews, present a shortlist, check references and help close the offer.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to research and outreach calls to people who are not job hunting. Afternoons bring candidate interviews, debriefs with hiring managers and updates to the search tracker. Early or evening calls are common, since senior candidates are busy during work hours.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: On the client side, they work with CEOs, boards, department heads and HR leaders. On the other side are candidates, references and sometimes background check providers. Researchers and sourcers often support the lead recruiter on larger searches.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use an applicant tracking system or search database, professional networking sites, phone and video calls, and market maps of target companies. They also use structured interview guides, assessments and background checks that must follow federal and state consumer reporting rules.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by placements made, time to fill, shortlist quality and whether hires stay and perform. In agency roles, pay is often tied to placement fees. In-house recruiters are judged more on hiring manager satisfaction and cost per hire.

qa.q: What does an executive recruiter do day to day?
qa.a: They spend much of the day on calls. They contact potential candidates, interview them and pitch the role. They meet hiring managers to agree on what the job needs, share shortlists, gather feedback and schedule interviews. Later in a search, they check references, discuss pay expectations and help both sides reach an offer.

qa.q: What is the difference between retained and contingency search?
qa.a: In a retained search, the client pays the firm in stages, often starting up front, and the firm usually runs the search exclusively. This is common for top leadership roles. In contingency search, the firm is paid only if its candidate is hired, and several firms may compete. It is common for mid-level sales, finance and legal roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They design A/B tests, choose the metrics that define success, and work out how many users and how many days a test needs. After launch, they check the data, measure the effect with confidence intervals, and write a clear ship or no-ship recommendation.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with checking live tests for broken logging or uneven traffic splits. Then come planning meetings with product teams, SQL queries on event tables, and analysis in Python or R. Many afternoons end with a readout explaining what changed and why.

day.label: When tests aren’t possible
day.text: Some questions can’t be randomized, like a price change in one region or a policy rollout. Then they use observational methods such as difference-in-differences, synthetic control, regression discontinuity, or matching, and state the assumptions each result depends on.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include SQL, Python or R, notebooks, and statistics libraries for power analysis and regression. Many teams also use an in-house or vendor experimentation platform that assigns users to groups, plus dashboards that monitor sample ratio, guardrail metrics, and results.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work is judged by trust, not by wins. Teams value tests that were sized correctly, metrics decided before launch, honest reporting of flat or negative results, and recommendations that hold up when the change rolls out to everyone.

qa.q: What does an experimentation data scientist do day to day?
qa.a: They help teams test ideas before rolling them out.
