That means setting up A/B tests, choosing metrics, calculating sample sizes, watching for data problems while tests run, and analyzing results at the end. They also explain findings to product managers and engineers, and push back when someone wants to stop a test early or read too much into a small, noisy difference.

qa.q: What is the difference between correlation and causation in A/B testing?
qa.a: Correlation means two things move together, like users who see a feature also spending more. Causation means the feature made them spend more. Random assignment in an A/B test is what separates the two, because it makes the groups alike except for the change. Without randomization, other factors can explain the gap, so stronger methods and assumptions are needed.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fabrication technicians turn drawings into finished parts. They lay out and mark material, cut it to size, bend or roll it into shape, join pieces by welding, bolting or riveting, then grind, deburr and finish the work so it fits and meets spec.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The shift often starts with reviewing a work order and blueprint. Then comes pulling stock, setting up machines, cutting and forming parts, fitting and tacking assemblies, and checking dimensions. Much of the day is spent standing, lifting and working with loud, hot equipment.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include band saws, shears, plasma or laser cutters, press brakes, rolls, drill presses, MIG and TIG welders, and grinders. Tape measures, squares, calipers and levels check the work. Safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection and welding helmets are standard gear.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most work in metal fabrication shops and manufacturing plants that build equipment, structural parts, enclosures, trailers or machinery. Some work in maintenance departments or on job sites. Shops can be hot, noisy and dusty, and many run multiple shifts.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on accuracy to the drawing, staying within tolerances, weld and finish quality, and keeping pace with production schedules. Parts may be inspected by a supervisor or quality inspector before they move on, and safe work habits matter as much as speed.

qa.q: What does a fabrication technician do day to day?
qa.a: A fabrication technician reads blueprints, measures and marks metal, and cuts, bends and joins it into parts or assemblies. They set up and run shop machines, weld or fasten pieces together, grind and finish surfaces, and check their work against the drawing. They also keep the work area clean and follow shop safety rules.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fabrication technician and a welder?
qa.a: A welder focuses mainly on joining metal with welding processes. A fabrication technician does a wider range of work, including layout, cutting, forming, fitting, welding and finishing, often building a whole part from raw stock. Many fabrication jobs include welding, and some employers ask candidates to pass a welding test before hiring.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Plan and track maintenance, cleaning, security and energy use for one or more buildings. Hire and oversee contractors, run office moves and space planning, manage a budget, and keep the site in line with fire, safety and accessibility codes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a walk through the site and a review of open work orders. Then come vendor calls, quotes to compare, a leak or broken cooling unit to sort out, and planning for upcoming projects or moves.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Maintenance technicians, custodial and security staff, outside contractors such as HVAC, electrical and roofing firms, landlords or property managers, IT teams during moves, and department heads who need space, repairs or furniture.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Maintenance management software for work orders and preventive schedules, building automation systems for heating, cooling and lighting, floor plans, budget spreadsheets, and access control and camera systems for security.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By how reliably building systems run, how fast work orders get closed, staying on budget, energy use, passed inspections, a clean safety record, and whether people in the building can work without disruption.

qa.q: What does a facilities manager do day to day?
qa.a: A facilities manager keeps buildings safe, working and comfortable. Day to day, that means checking on repairs, assigning work orders, meeting contractors, reviewing invoices and quotes, watching energy use, handling security or cleaning issues, and planning moves or renovations. They also respond to surprises like power outages, floods or equipment failures.

qa.q: What is the difference between a facilities manager and a property manager?
qa.a: A property manager usually works for the owner and focuses on the building as an investment: leasing, rent collection and tenant relations. A facilities manager focuses on how the building runs for the people using it: maintenance, cleaning, security, energy and space. In smaller organizations, one person may do parts of both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fellows and residents do real project work inside a host organization, such as a research lab, government office, nonprofit, or university. Tasks can include collecting and analyzing data, drafting reports or policy memos, supporting programs, and presenting findings, while also learning the field through structured training.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes focused project work with meetings. Fellows check in with a mentor, join team meetings, and attend seminars or skill workshops. Many programs add cohort events, site visits, or guest speakers so participants build a network as well as experience.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: The closest working tie is usually a mentor or supervisor who guides the project. Fellows also work with project teams, a program coordinator, and fellow members of their cohort. Depending on the role, they may deal with community members, agency staff, or outside researchers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Many programs set goals at the start and review progress with the mentor during the term. Completion often depends on a final product, such as a report, presentation, publication, or capstone project. Feedback from supervisors can also shape references for the next job.

day.label: Terms of the program
day.text: These roles last a fixed term, often a few months to two years, and usually start on a set date with a cohort. Pay may come as a salary or a stipend, and benefits and employee status vary by program.

qa.q: What does a fellow do day to day?
qa.a: Most of the day goes to an assigned project, such as research, data analysis, program support, or policy writing. Fellows also meet with mentors, join team meetings, attend training sessions, and share progress with their cohort. Near the end of the term, many present a final report or project that sums up what they built or learned.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fellowship and a residency?
qa.a: Usage varies by field. In medicine, residency is the graduate training doctors complete after medical school in a chosen specialty, and a fellowship is optional further training in a subspecialty after residency. Outside medicine, a fellowship is often a funded research or public service role, while a residency often places an artist, writer, or professional at a host site for a set time.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fiber and telecom technicians install, splice, test and repair the cables and equipment that carry internet, phone and TV traffic. They pull fiber and copper, fusion splice strands, mount cabinets and racks, run drops to homes and businesses, and test links with power meters and OTDRs.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a work order and a safety talk, then driving to a route, pole, vault or customer site. Most hours go to splicing in a trailer or bucket truck, placing cable or tracking down a cut. The day ends with test reports and closeouts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with crew leads, splicers, linemen, underground and aerial crews, and engineers who design routes. They coordinate with network operations centers, utility locators, permitting offices, property managers and customers. Tower technicians also work with RF engineers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include fusion splicers, cleavers, OTDRs, power meters, visual fault locators and fiber cleaning kits. Field crews use bucket trucks, ladders, cable pullers and cable locators. Tower work adds climbing harnesses and fall protection. Work orders and maps live on tablets.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Technicians are judged on clean, low-loss splices, passing test results, correct documentation and work finished on schedule. Safety around power lines, traffic, heights and trenches matters a lot. Repair speed during outages and repeat trouble calls also count.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to be a fiber optic technician?
qa.a: A state license is usually not needed for outside fiber splicing, but many employers prefer industry certifications such as Certified Fiber Optic Technician, or maker training on specific splicers. Tower climbers need fall protection and climber safety training. Some states require a low-voltage or telecommunications license for cabling inside buildings, so rules vary.

qa.q: Is fiber technician a physically demanding job?
qa.a: Yes, often. Technicians work outdoors in heat, cold and rain, climb poles and ladders, lift cable reels and equipment, and work in tight vaults or attics. Splicing also needs steady hands and good color vision to match fiber color codes. Tower roles involve serious heights and strict safety training.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Field marketing managers plan and run marketing for one region or customer segment. They organize events, trade show booths, roadshows and local campaigns. They track the leads each program brings in and make sure sales follows up on them.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a call with regional sales reps about which accounts to target. Then come vendor emails about a venue or booth shipment, a review of event registrations, and updates to the campaign budget and lead reports.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with sales reps and sales leaders in their region. They also partner with product marketing, demand generation, marketing operations, channel partners, agencies, and event vendors such as venues, caterers and print shops.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM to track leads and pipeline, a marketing automation platform for invitations and follow-up emails, event registration software, spreadsheets for budgets, and dashboards that tie each program to meetings, opportunities and revenue.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually measured by pipeline and revenue influenced in the region. Leads generated, meetings booked, event attendance, cost per lead and return on spend also count. Strong relationships with the sales team matter as much as the numbers.

qa.q: What does a field marketing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They plan and run marketing programs for a specific region or segment. Daily work includes meeting with sales about target accounts, booking venues and vendors, building event invitations and campaigns, managing a budget, and reporting on leads and pipeline. Many weeks include travel to run events in person and make sure attendees get timely follow-up from sales.

qa.q: What is the difference between field marketing and demand generation?
qa.a: Demand generation usually runs broad, often digital programs such as paid ads, webinars and email campaigns to create leads at scale across the whole market. Field marketing is more local and hands-on. It focuses on one region or segment, relies heavily on in-person events, and works side by side with regional sales teams on specific accounts and deals.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Field sales representatives find and visit prospects, present products in person, answer questions, and close orders. They also check in on existing accounts, take reorders, and fix problems so customers keep buying.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with planning a route and confirming appointments. Then come back-to-back visits, product demos, and cold calls on new businesses or homes. Evenings may go to logging notes, sending quotes, and preparing for tomorrow.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A reliable car, a smartphone, and a laptop or tablet are standard. Reps use CRM software to track leads and visits, mapping apps to plan routes, and samples, brochures, and price sheets for demos.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most of the work happens on the road within an assigned territory. Reps visit offices, stores, job sites, clinics, or homes. Some territories cover one city. Others span several states and need overnight travel.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is measured mainly against sales quotas. Managers also track new accounts opened, visits made, customer retention, and how accurate the sales forecast is. Pay often includes commission or bonuses tied to these results.

qa.q: What is the difference between field sales and inside sales?
qa.a: Field sales reps meet customers face to face and spend much of their time traveling a territory. Inside sales reps sell by phone, email, and video from an office or home. Field roles often suit relationship-heavy or hands-on products, while inside roles usually handle more contacts per day with shorter conversations.

qa.q: Do door-to-door sales reps need a license?
qa.a: It depends on where and what you sell. Many cities and counties require a solicitor or peddler permit, and rules vary by state and locality. Selling insurance, securities, or real estate needs a state license. The FTC Cooling-Off Rule also lets buyers cancel many sales made at their home within three business days, and reps must give written notice of that right.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Field service technicians install, start up, maintain and repair equipment at the place where it runs. That can mean medical devices, industrial machines, HVAC systems, kiosks or telecom gear. They test, diagnose faults, replace parts, calibrate settings and confirm the equipment works before they leave.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a dispatch list on a phone or tablet. Techs drive to several sites, check in with the customer, do the job, log hours and parts, and update the ticket. Urgent breakdown calls can reshuffle the plan. Some roles include on-call nights or weekends.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Hand and power tools, multimeters, laptops with diagnostic software, and manufacturer manuals are standard. Most techs drive a company van or their own vehicle stocked with parts. Field service apps handle work orders, customer signatures and parts requests.

day.label: Rules and safety
day.text: Techs follow OSHA lockout/tagout procedures before servicing powered equipment. Anyone who handles refrigerants needs EPA Section 608 certification. Electrical, plumbing or HVAC work may need a state or local license, and the rules vary by state. Many employers require a valid driver’s license and a clean driving record.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers track first-time fix rate, response time, repeat visits and customer satisfaction. Accurate paperwork matters too, since service reports drive billing, warranty claims and parts orders. Being reliable and polite on site counts as much as technical skill.

qa.q: What does a field service technician do day to day?
qa.a: They travel to customer sites to install, start up, maintain and repair equipment. A day usually mixes scheduled maintenance with breakdown calls. They diagnose problems, swap parts, test the system, explain the fix to the customer and close out the work order. A good part of the day is spent driving between jobs.

qa.q: What is the difference between a field service technician and a bench technician?
qa.a: A field service technician goes to the equipment, working in hospitals, factories, offices or homes. A bench technician works in a shop or repair center, and the equipment is shipped or brought in. Field work involves more travel, customer contact and working alone. Bench work usually offers a steadier schedule and a controlled workspace.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Answer calls, chats and emails in Filipino and English, solve account or order problems, and log every case. Many roles are customer support, billing, data entry or other back-office work, either for clients in the Philippines or for Filipino-speaking customers in the US.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Log in, check the queue and work through contacts one by one. Agents often switch between Filipino, English and Taglish within a single call. Notes are usually written in English. Since the Philippines is many hours ahead of the US, overnight or early morning shifts are common.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Customers and their families, team leads, quality reviewers and other departments such as billing or claims. In health care, social services or court settings, Filipino speakers may work beside nurses, doctors, caseworkers and attorneys to help clients understand what is happening.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A headset and computer, a ticketing or customer records system, chat software, a searchable knowledge base, call scripts and approved glossaries for tricky terms. Remote roles usually need a quiet room, a steady internet connection and sometimes a backup power source.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Supervisors and quality reviewers score recorded calls and chats for accuracy, tone and following policy. Common measures include customer satisfaction, issues solved on first contact and time per contact. Many employers also give a spoken and written language test before hiring.

qa.q: What does a Filipino speaking customer service agent do day to day?
qa.a: They take calls, chats or emails from Filipino-speaking customers, find out what the customer needs, and fix it or pass it to the right team. They explain bills, orders or policies in plain Filipino or English, keep a polite tone, and write clear case notes, usually in English, so coworkers can follow up.

qa.q: Do Filipino speaking jobs require a certification?
qa.a: Most support and back-office roles only require passing the employer’s own language test. Medical interpreter certification is generally voluntary, though some employers ask for it. Court interpreting rules are set by each state, and some states, such as California, certify Tagalog court interpreters. Check the rules where you plan to work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A finance manager builds the annual budget, updates forecasts, and tracks spending against plan. They explain variances to leaders, prepare monthly reports, watch cash flow, and help decide where money should go next.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with checking cash and reviewing the latest numbers. The rest of the day mixes spreadsheet modeling, meetings with department heads about costs, answering questions from executives, and reviewing work from staff accountants or analysts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with owners, executives, and department managers who spend the budget. They also coordinate with accountants, payroll, banks, outside auditors, and tax preparers, and may supervise a small finance team.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets are the core tool, used for models, forecasts, and what-if scenarios. Most also use accounting or ERP software, budgeting and planning tools, reporting dashboards, and sometimes a database query language for pulling data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in accurate forecasts, on-time monthly closes and reports, and costs kept within budget. Leaders also value clear explanations of the numbers and sound advice that helps the business make better decisions.

qa.q: What does a finance manager do day to day?
qa.a: A finance manager reviews financial results, updates budgets and forecasts, and explains why actual spending differs from plan. They meet with managers about costs, prepare reports for leadership, monitor cash, and often check the work of accountants or analysts. In a small company they may also handle banking, insurance, and audit preparation.

qa.q: What is the difference between a finance manager and an accountant?
qa.a: An accountant records transactions and prepares accurate statements of what already happened. A finance manager uses those results to plan ahead: building budgets, forecasting, and advising leaders on spending and investments. Many finance managers start as accountants. A CPA license is required only for certain work, such as signing audit opinions, and rules vary by state.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build the annual budget, update rolling forecasts, and compare actual results to plan each month. They explain why numbers moved and model what a new hire, a price change, or a new project would cost or earn.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to pulling data from the accounting system and refreshing reports. Afternoons bring meetings with department heads about spending, followed by updates to models. Month end and budget season mean longer days and tight deadlines.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with accounting, department managers, and finance leaders such as the controller and chief financial officer. Much of the job is turning managers’ plans into numbers, then turning the numbers back into plain advice.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets are the core tool for models, scenarios, and quick checks. Most teams also use an accounting or ERP system, a planning and budgeting platform, and business intelligence dashboards. Some analysts write SQL to pull their own data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work shows in forecasts that land close to actual results, models others can follow and trust, and clear explanations of variances. Leaders also judge whether the analysis helped them make a better decision in time.

qa.q: What does an FP&A analyst do day to day?
qa.a: An FP&A analyst updates forecasts, checks actual spending and revenue against the budget, and explains the gaps. They answer questions from managers, such as what a new hire or price change would do to profit. They build and maintain spreadsheet models and prepare reports and slides for finance leaders.

qa.q: What is the difference between FP&A and accounting?
qa.a: Accounting records what already happened, closes the books, and prepares financial statements under set rules such as GAAP. FP&A looks ahead, using those results to budget, forecast, and weigh decisions. Public accountants who sign audits need a state CPA license; FP&A roles need no license, though employers often value finance or accounting degrees.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They prepare monthly, quarterly and annual financial statements and footnotes under US GAAP. At public companies they draft the 10-Q and 10-K filed with the SEC. They also research how the accounting rules apply to new contracts, acquisitions, leases and financing deals, then write memos that document the conclusions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The morning might go to reviewing consolidation entries or a draft footnote. Later, a deal team asks how a new customer contract affects revenue timing. The accountant reads the FASB Accounting Standards Codification, drafts a position memo and talks it through with the controller. Close weeks and filing deadlines bring long hours.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the controller, CFO, tax, treasury, legal and financial planning teams. They answer questions from the external auditors, who review their memos and test the statements. At public companies, their work also goes to the audit committee before filings are released.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include the ERP general ledger, consolidation and close software, and heavy spreadsheet work. Public company filings are built in disclosure management software that produces XBRL-tagged reports. Research relies on the FASB Codification, SEC rules and staff guidance, and accounting guides published by audit firms.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means accurate statements filed on time, audits without significant findings, and no restatements. Technical memos must hold up when auditors or SEC staff review them. Clear, complete disclosures and solid internal controls over financial reporting also count heavily.

qa.q: Is technical accounting and financial reporting a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be, especially around quarter-end and year-end. Public companies face fixed SEC filing deadlines, and an error can lead to a restatement or an audit finding. Complex deals often arrive with little warning and need fast answers. Outside close and filing periods, the pace is usually steadier, with time for research, policy updates and preparing for new standards.

qa.q: What is the difference between technical accounting and financial reporting?
qa.a: Financial reporting focuses on producing the statements, footnotes and regulatory filings accurately and on schedule. Technical accounting focuses on deciding how GAAP applies to specific transactions, such as an acquisition, a lease or complex debt, and documenting that judgment in a memo. Many companies combine both in one team, since the reporting depends on those technical conclusions.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fire protection and emergency response staff prevent fires and respond to emergencies at a plant, campus, airport or other site. They inspect and test alarms, sprinklers, extinguishers and fire pumps, enforce hot work permits, give first aid and emergency medical care, respond to spills and rescues, and train workers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift starts with a crew briefing and checks of trucks, breathing apparatus and medical gear. Then come scheduled inspections, hydrant or sprinkler tests, hot work permits and training drills. Alarms, medical calls or chemical spills can interrupt at any moment.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with safety managers, facilities and maintenance teams, security, environmental staff and plant operators. They coordinate with local fire departments, mutual aid partners and hospitals, and work with fire protection engineers, sprinkler contractors and insurance inspectors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include fire trucks, hoses, self-contained breathing apparatus, gas monitors, extinguishers, rescue gear, AEDs and first aid kits. Inspection staff use test equipment for alarm and sprinkler systems and log results in software. Radios and incident reporting systems are constant.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on readiness and results: response times, inspections and tests done on schedule to NFPA standards and the local fire code, clean audits by insurers and fire marshals, and no preventable losses. Training records, safety and calm leadership in real emergencies count too.

qa.q: What certifications do fire protection and emergency response workers need?
qa.a: Requirements vary by state and employer. Industrial firefighters often need Firefighter I and II certificates and hazardous materials training, and EMT certification is common. Inspection technicians often hold NICET certification in sprinkler or alarm systems, and some states license fire sprinkler and alarm contractors or their technicians.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fire protection engineer and a firefighter?
qa.a: A fire protection engineer designs systems that prevent and control fire, such as sprinklers, alarms, smoke control and safe exit routes, using codes and fire modeling. A firefighter or emergency responder answers fires, medical calls and rescues and keeps equipment ready. Engineers usually need an engineering degree, and some states require a PE license to seal designs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Firmware engineers write and debug the low-level code that boots a device and drives its hardware. They configure microcontrollers, write drivers for sensors and peripherals, manage memory and power use, and build safe ways to update the code in the field.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes coding in C or C++ with time at the bench. An engineer might trace a timing bug with a logic analyzer, review a teammate’s code, step through a crash with a debugger, then test a new build on prototype boards.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include compilers and toolchains for embedded chips, JTAG or SWD debug probes, oscilloscopes, logic analyzers and multimeters. Engineers read datasheets and schematics closely and use version control, build scripts and sometimes a real-time operating system.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with hardware engineers who design the circuit boards, plus software and app teams who rely on the device’s data. Test engineers, manufacturing staff and product managers also depend on their code being stable and on schedule.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good firmware boots reliably, responds on time, fits in limited memory and handles errors without bricking the device. In regulated fields such as medical devices, cars or aircraft, the code must also meet strict documentation and safety standards.

qa.q: What is the difference between a firmware engineer and a software engineer?
qa.a: A firmware engineer writes code that runs directly on a chip, often with little memory and no full operating system, and must understand the hardware closely. A software engineer usually builds applications that run on computers, phones or servers, where resources are larger and the hardware is hidden behind an operating system.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to become a firmware engineer?
qa.a: Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering or computer science. No state license is required for most firmware jobs. Strong C skills, comfort reading schematics and hands-on projects with microcontroller boards can help candidates stand out, especially for entry-level roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fleet managers buy or lease vehicles, set maintenance schedules, control fuel spending, keep registrations and insurance current, handle accidents and repairs, and decide when to sell or replace each vehicle based on its total cost of ownership.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with telematics alerts and fuel reports. Then come repair approvals, checks on which vehicles are due for service or inspection, driver questions, record updates, and talks with finance or operations about costs and upcoming purchases.

day.label: Safety and compliance
day.text: For commercial vehicles, they help the company follow federal FMCSA rules on things like driver qualification files, hours of service, electronic logs and drug and alcohol testing for CDL drivers. Rules on registration, emissions and inspections vary by state.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Fleet management software, GPS and telematics tracking, fuel card systems, maintenance and work order records, budget spreadsheets, and driver safety tools such as dash cameras and driving scorecards.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results show in cost per mile, vehicle uptime, preventive maintenance done on time, accident and violation rates, fuel use, and clean results on audits and roadside inspections.

qa.q: What does a fleet manager do day to day?
qa.a: A fleet manager keeps a company’s vehicles safe, legal and running at the lowest sensible cost. Day to day, that means scheduling maintenance, approving repairs, watching fuel and GPS data, handling accidents, keeping driver and vehicle records current, and planning when to buy, lease or retire vehicles.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fleet manager and a dispatcher?
qa.a: A dispatcher assigns drivers, routes and jobs in real time and stays in contact with drivers during the shift. A fleet manager looks after the vehicles themselves over the long term: purchasing, maintenance, costs, safety programs and compliance. In small companies, one person may do both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Write, test and fix the code that runs on flight computers. This covers guidance, navigation and control, command handling, telemetry, fault detection and recovery, and device drivers. The code must meet strict timing, memory and reliability limits.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Reviewing a teammate’s code, running tests on a hardware-in-the-loop bench or simulator, and digging through telemetry logs to find a bug. They also update requirements and test records and join meetings with systems and hardware engineers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Guidance and control engineers, avionics hardware engineers, systems engineers, test engineers, mission operators and quality or safety reviewers. On launch or test days they may support operations teams in a control room.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Mostly C and C++, sometimes Ada, Rust or Python for test scripts. They use real-time operating systems or embedded Linux, debuggers, logic analyzers, oscilloscopes, static analysis tools, version control and flight simulators.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether every requirement is traced to code and tests, how much code is covered by tests, and passing formal reviews. Civil aircraft software usually follows DO-178C guidance, which the FAA accepts. NASA projects follow NASA software engineering requirements.

qa.q: Is flight software engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. A single bug can damage hardware or end a mission, and launch dates and test campaigns bring deadlines and long days. Teams manage the risk with heavy testing, peer reviews and simulation, so the pace is often slower and more careful than in other software jobs. Stress tends to peak near launches, flight tests and anomaly investigations.

qa.q: Do flight software engineers need to be US citizens?
qa.a: Often, but not always. Much flight software falls under ITAR export rules, so many employers require US person status, which includes citizens, permanent residents and certain protected individuals. Defense and some government space programs also require a security clearance, which generally requires US citizenship. Check each job posting for its exact requirement.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Food service workers prepare simple foods, set up serving lines, serve meals, run cash registers, wash dishes and clean dining and kitchen areas. They work in school cafeterias, hospitals, workplace canteens, senior living communities and catering.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Workers arrive early to prep food and set up the line. During meal rushes they serve, restock and take payment. Between meals they check and log hot and cold food temperatures, then clean, wash dishes and close down.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with cooks, food service supervisors and cashiers, and with customers such as students, patients, employees or residents. In hospitals they follow dietitians’ orders for special diets, and in schools they work with school staff.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include steam tables, ovens, slicers, commercial dishwashers, food thermometers, cash registers and tray lines. Workers also use gloves, hairnets, sanitizer test strips and cleaning chemicals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Workers are judged on food safety and hygiene, correct portions, speed during rushes, friendly service and a clean work area. Following allergy and special diet rules and showing up reliably for shifts also matter.

qa.q: What does a food service worker do day to day?
qa.a: A food service worker spends the day preparing, serving and cleaning up food. They set up serving lines, portion meals, restock items, take payments and check food temperatures. After each meal they clean tables, wash dishes and get ready for the next service. In hospitals they may also deliver meal trays to patients.

qa.q: Do you need experience to be a food service worker?
qa.a: Usually not. It is an entry-level job with on-the-job training. Some states and cities require a food handler card, and hospital or school jobs may require a background check or health screening. Federal law also limits what workers under 18 may do, such as banning them from using power-driven meat slicers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They sit with a customer’s team, learn the real problem, and shape their company’s product to solve it. That means writing integration code, connecting data sources, building custom workflows, and fixing issues fast so the customer sees results.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a call to scope a new use case. Then comes writing Python or SQL to clean customer data, and it ends with a demo for users. Bugs and missing features get reported back to the core product team.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work daily with the customer’s engineers, analysts, and managers. They also work with their own company’s account leads, product managers, and core engineers. They act as a bridge, turning needs from the field into clear product requests.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Some work fully on-site at a customer office, plant, hospital, or government facility. Others mix remote work with frequent travel. Roles serving defense or intelligence customers often require a US security clearance, which generally requires US citizenship.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether the customer adopts the product and gets value from it. Fast delivery, stable deployments, renewed or expanded contracts, and useful feedback that improves the product all count.

qa.q: What is the difference between a forward deployed engineer and a solutions engineer?
qa.a: A solutions engineer usually works before the sale, running demos and showing the product fits. A forward deployed engineer usually works after or alongside the deal, embedded with the customer for weeks or months, writing production code so the product works in their setting. Titles overlap between companies, so read each posting closely.

qa.q: Is forward deployed engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. The work brings tight deadlines, shifting customer needs, and pressure to show results in front of the people paying for the product. Travel can be heavy in some roles. Many people enjoy the variety and direct impact, but the job suits those who stay calm with unclear problems and like talking with customers as much as coding.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Takes on whatever the founder needs most right now, such as running a product launch, filling key hires, preparing fundraising materials, or fixing a broken process. Priorities change whenever the founder’s needs change, not on a set schedule.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Often starts with a check-in with the founder on what matters most. The rest of the day moves between meetings, analysis, writing memos, chasing open items across teams, and preparing materials for board or investor meetings.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Works closely with the founder or CEO, plus department heads, finance, and recruiting. Depending on the project, they may also deal with investors, board members, outside advisors, and key customers or partners.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets for financial models and tracking, slide decks for investor and board updates, project management tools, shared documents, and team chat. Clear writing and short, sharp summaries matter as much as any software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether projects ship and goals are met, how much time the founder gets back, and how well the person earns trust across teams while handling confidential information with discretion.

qa.q: What does someone in a founder’s office role do day to day?
qa.a: They work on the founder’s current top priorities. One day might mean building a hiring plan, the next might mean drafting an investor update or coordinating a launch across teams. They run meetings, analyze data, write memos, follow up on decisions, and step in wherever a project is stuck. The mix changes as the company’s needs change.

qa.q: What is the difference between a chief of staff and a founder’s office role?
qa.a: Titles overlap and vary by company. A chief of staff is often a more senior role that manages the leadership team’s meetings, goals, and communication, and may lead a small team. Founder’s office roles, common at startups, are often more project based and can suit earlier career people who want broad exposure to how a company is built.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Build the first version of the product or a whole function, such as engineering, sales or operations, with no playbook to follow. Pick the tools, set up the first processes, ship work fast and fix what breaks. Many founding hires also help hire the people who come next.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day can mix writing code or drafting a sales pitch with customer calls, a quick planning talk with the founders and an urgent bug or deadline. Priorities shift often as the company learns what customers want and how long its money will last.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work every day with the founders and a small group of other early hires. They often talk directly with early customers and outside contractors, and sometimes with advisers or investors. There are few managers, so most decisions happen in quick, informal talks.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Shared documents, chat apps, task boards and video calls hold the small team together. Engineers use code repositories and cloud services. Sales and operations hires lean on a CRM and spreadsheets. The team usually chooses and sets up these tools itself.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in shipped features, first paying customers, growth and whether the company can raise its next round. Pay often mixes a salary with stock options that vest over several years, so the final value depends on how the company does.

qa.q: What does a founding team member do day to day?
qa.a: They do whatever the young company needs most that week. That usually means building the core product or setting up a function like sales or operations from scratch, talking with early customers, solving problems with the founders and handling tasks outside their title. The work is fast, hands-on and changes often as the startup learns what works.

qa.q: What is the difference between a co-founder and a founding team member?
qa.a: Co-founders start the company, usually own a larger share and often sit on the board. Founding team members are among the first employees hired after that. They usually get a salary plus a smaller equity grant, often stock options that vest over time. “Founding team” is a job label, not a legal title, so its meaning varies by company.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: FPGA engineers turn system requirements into digital logic. They write register transfer level code in VHDL, Verilog or SystemVerilog, simulate it, then synthesize, place and route the design. They work to meet timing, fit the chip’s resources and stay within power limits.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often splits between the desk and the lab. Mornings may go to writing code and testbenches or reading timing reports. Afternoons may mean loading a new build onto a board and chasing a bug with an on-chip logic analyzer or an oscilloscope.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use vendor design suites for synthesis and place and route, logic simulators, and verification methods such as UVM or Python-based testbenches. Tcl and Python scripts automate builds. Version control, development boards, signal generators and oscilloscopes round out the kit.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with board designers on pinouts and signal integrity, and with firmware and software engineers on drivers and register maps. Systems engineers set the requirements. Verification and test engineers check the design before it ships.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Common employers include defense and aerospace contractors, satellite and radio makers, telecom equipment firms, test and measurement companies, medical imaging, data centers and high-frequency trading. Many defense roles require US citizenship and the ability to get a security clearance.

qa.q: What does an FPGA engineer do day to day?
qa.a: An FPGA engineer writes hardware description code, builds testbenches and runs simulations to prove the logic works. They then compile the design, fix timing problems the tools report, and test it on real boards in the lab. Much of the day goes to debugging, code reviews and talking with board and software teams about interfaces.

qa.q: What is the difference between an FPGA engineer and an ASIC engineer?
qa.a: Both write similar hardware code, but an ASIC engineer designs a custom chip that is manufactured once and cannot be changed, so mistakes are very costly and verification takes longer. An FPGA engineer targets a ready-made chip that can be reprogrammed, even after it ships. FPGA work usually has faster cycles and more lab time on real hardware.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fraud analysts review alerts on suspicious orders, logins and payments. They decide whether to approve, block or hold a transaction. They close fake accounts and look for patterns behind stolen card use, account takeovers, scams and promo abuse. They also write up cases and suggest new detection rules.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a queue of flagged cases. Analysts check order details, device and location data, and account history, then make a call. Between cases they may contact customers to verify activity, work on chargeback disputes, and pull reports on new fraud trends.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in case management and fraud detection software that scores risk. Analysts use spreadsheets, SQL queries and dashboards to dig into data. They also rely on address and phone lookups, device fingerprinting, and bank or card network dispute portals.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with customer support, payments and chargeback teams, engineers who build detection rules, and data scientists who tune risk models. At banks, they pass suspicious activity to compliance staff, who decide whether to file reports with regulators. Some cases are referred to law enforcement.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Teams track fraud losses, chargeback rates, false positives that block good customers, and how quickly cases get reviewed. Accuracy and clear case notes matter, since decisions may be audited or used as evidence in disputes.

qa.q: What does a fraud analyst do day to day?
qa.a: A fraud analyst works through flagged transactions, new accounts and logins that look risky. For each case, they check data such as location, device, payment details and past behavior, then approve, block or escalate it. They also spot new fraud patterns, help shape detection rules, handle chargebacks and keep clear notes for audits or investigations.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fraud analyst and an AML analyst?
qa.a: A fraud analyst protects a company and its customers from being cheated, such as through stolen cards, fake accounts or scams. An anti-money laundering (AML) analyst looks for criminals moving or hiding money through the system, under federal rules like the Bank Secrecy Act. Both review suspicious activity, and at banks the two roles often work closely together.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They review flagged transactions, accounts and claims to decide what is fraud and what is normal. They measure how much money is at risk, find patterns behind losses, and write or tune the rules that block, hold or approve activity.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a queue of alerts and chargebacks. Between cases, they pull data, check how yesterday’s rules performed, look into new fraud trends, and adjust thresholds so real customers are not blocked by mistake.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include SQL, spreadsheets, and sometimes Python for analysis. They also use case management systems, rules engines, dashboards, device and identity checks, and model risk scores that rank how likely an event is to be fraud.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with customer support, compliance, product and engineering teams, and data scientists. At banks and some other financial firms, their findings may feed suspicious activity reports that the institution must file under federal anti-money laundering rules.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by losses prevented, fraud caught early, and how few good customers get declined or delayed. Managers also look at case accuracy, clear notes for audits, and how quickly new fraud patterns turn into working rules.

qa.q: What is the difference between a fraud analyst and a risk analyst?
qa.a: A fraud analyst focuses on deliberate deception, such as stolen cards, fake accounts or account takeover, and works case by case. A risk analyst looks more broadly at possible losses, including credit, operational or market risk, and builds models and limits. Many jobs blend both, which is why titles like fraud and risk analyst are common.

qa.q: Is fraud and risk analysis a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Fraud attacks can spike without warning, queues grow fast, and every decision trades losses against upset customers. Some roles include on-call or weekend shifts. Many analysts like the puzzle-solving side, though, and stress is usually lower in teams with good tools, clear rules and steady staffing.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Get rates from carriers, quote prices to customers, and book space on vessels, flights and trucks. Prepare shipping documents, track cargo along the route, and fix problems such as delays, rolled bookings, missed cutoffs or missing paperwork.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with overnight updates from overseas agents and carriers. Then come customer emails, new quotes, booking confirmations, chasing documents before cutoffs, and arranging pickup or delivery trucks. Time zones can mean early or late calls.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Shippers and importers, ocean and air carriers, trucking companies, warehouses, customs brokers, overseas partner agents, and port or airport cargo terminals. Sales staff and accounting teams inside the company also rely on them for quotes and billing.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Forwarding or transport management software, carrier booking portals, email and spreadsheets. Daily paperwork includes commercial invoices, packing lists, bills of lading and air waybills. Knowing Incoterms, which set who pays and who carries risk, is part of the job.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: Ocean forwarders and NVOCCs in the US need a license from the Federal Maritime Commission. Air forwarders follow TSA cargo security programs. Many exports need electronic export information filed in the government’s ACE system, and hazardous goods have strict packing and paperwork rules.

qa.q: Is freight forwarding a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Forwarders juggle many shipments at once, and each has hard cutoffs for bookings and documents. Weather, port congestion, equipment shortages and customs holds can upset plans with little warning. Customers often want answers fast. People who stay organized, communicate clearly and stay calm when plans change tend to handle the pressure well.

qa.q: What is the difference between a freight forwarder and a customs broker?
qa.a: A freight forwarder arranges the movement of goods, booking carriers and managing the shipment from pickup to delivery. A customs broker prepares and files customs entries, classifies goods and calculates duties for imports. In the US, customs brokers must hold a license from U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Many companies offer both services.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They handle customer calls, chats and emails in French, often switching to English in the same shift. Depending on the role, that means solving support tickets, selling, managing accounts, translating documents or checking French content for accuracy and tone.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Customers and partners in France, Quebec and the rest of Canada, Belgium, Switzerland, and French-speaking countries in Africa and the Caribbean. Inside the company, they pass issues to English-speaking teams and explain what local customers expect.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Shifts often start early, since Paris is six hours ahead of New York for most of the year. The day mixes live conversations, written replies, notes in a ticketing or CRM system, and quick translations for coworkers.

day.label: Language skills that matter
day.text: Employers usually test spoken and written French before hiring. Regional differences matter, since Quebec French and European French differ in vocabulary and expressions. The formal vous is the safe default with customers unless they set a casual tone.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Reviewers check accuracy, grammar and tone in both languages. Support roles also track response time, resolution rates and customer satisfaction scores, while sales roles track pipeline and closed deals.

qa.q: What does a French speaking customer service agent do day to day?
qa.a: They answer French-language calls, chats and emails, solve account or order problems, and log each case in a ticketing system. Many also cover English queues. When an issue needs another team, they summarize it in English and follow up with the customer in French.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to work in a French speaking job?
qa.a: Most bilingual jobs do not require a license. Employers test fluency with their own spoken and written assessments. Court interpreting is different, and credential rules vary by state. Translator and medical interpreter certifications from national bodies are often preferred but are voluntary in most cases.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Turns designs into working pages and screens using HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript. Builds reusable components, connects them to data from backend APIs, fixes bugs, and makes sure pages load fast and work well on phones, tablets and desktops.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Often starts with a short team standup, then coding on assigned tickets. Reviews teammates’ code changes, tests work in several browsers, and checks with designers when a layout or interaction is unclear. Some time goes to planning meetings for upcoming work.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Works closely with product designers, backend engineers and product managers. Also works with QA testers who find bugs, and sometimes with support staff who pass along problems that users report.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A code editor, Git for version control, browser developer tools, and frameworks or libraries such as React, Vue or Angular. Also uses build tools, automated testing tools, shared design files and a ticket tracker.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether features ship on time and match the design, how fast pages load, how few bugs reach users, and whether the site works with a keyboard or screen reader under accessibility guidelines like WCAG.

qa.q: What is the difference between a frontend engineer and a backend engineer?
qa.a: A frontend engineer builds what users see and use in a browser or app, such as buttons, forms and page layouts. A backend engineer builds the servers, databases and APIs behind it that store data and run the business logic. A full-stack engineer does some of both.

qa.q: Do you need a degree or license to be a frontend engineer?
qa.a: No license is required in any state. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, but plenty hire based on skills shown through a portfolio, code samples and technical interviews. Bootcamp graduates and self-taught developers also work in this field.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Full-stack engineers build features from end to end. They write the screens and forms users touch, the APIs behind them, and the database queries that store and fetch data. They also fix bugs, review code and ship updates.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team standup. Then comes coding a feature, writing tests, reviewing a teammate’s pull request and checking why a page loads slowly. Some days include a planning meeting or helping fix a problem in production.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript for the browser, plus a front-end framework. On the server, they use languages such as Python, Java, Go or JavaScript running on Node.js. They also rely on Git, SQL databases, cloud services and a code editor.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, designers and other engineers. They may also talk with quality testers, data teams and support staff who report bugs from customers. On small teams, they often handle tasks that larger companies split among specialists.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged by whether features ship on time, work correctly and stay reliable. Teams also look at code quality, test coverage, page speed, security and how easily others can read and maintain the code.

qa.q: What does a full-stack engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A full-stack engineer builds and maintains both the user-facing part of an app and the server and database behind it. Daily work usually mixes writing code, testing it, reviewing others’ code, fixing bugs and joining short team meetings to plan and track progress.

qa.q: What is the difference between a full-stack engineer and a back-end engineer?
qa.a: A back-end engineer focuses on servers, APIs, databases and system performance. A full-stack engineer covers that work too, but also builds the front end that users see in the browser or app. Full-stack roles trade some depth in one area for breadth across the whole product.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Fund accountants keep the books for mutual funds, hedge funds, private equity funds and other pooled investments. They record trades, income and expenses, reconcile cash and positions, price holdings, and calculate the net asset value, or NAV. They also allocate gains and losses to each investor’s capital account.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: In mutual funds, the day builds toward a daily NAV struck after the market closes, so earlier hours go to reconciling trades and cash. Hedge fund and private equity teams work on monthly or quarterly cycles, processing capital calls, distributions, fees and investor statements.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Fund accountants work with portfolio managers and traders, custodian banks and prime brokers, transfer agents and investor services teams. They also deal with auditors at year-end, tax preparers who issue investor tax forms, and compliance staff. Many work at fund administrators that serve many funds.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include fund accounting systems such as Geneva, Investran or eFront, and Excel for reconciliations and NAV checks. Accountants also use prices from Bloomberg terminals or other data vendors, custodian portals, and reporting tools for financial statements.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Accuracy comes first, since a wrong NAV can force reprocessing and payments to make investors whole. Fund accountants are judged on meeting NAV and reporting deadlines, clean reconciliations, few errors and audits without findings. Clear answers to investor and manager questions also count.

qa.q: What does a fund accountant do day to day?
qa.a: A fund accountant records every trade, income item and expense in a fund’s books, then reconciles cash and holdings with the custodian or prime broker. They check the price of each security and calculate the fund’s net asset value. They also prepare investor allocations, financial statements and reports for managers, auditors and regulators.

qa.q: Do you need a CPA to be a fund accountant?
qa.a: No. Entry-level fund accountant jobs usually ask for a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance or a related field. A CPA license helps for senior, controller and audit-facing roles, and some people later earn the CFA charter or other credentials. Strong Excel skills and attention to detail often matter most at the start.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Nonprofit fundraising and grants staff raise money for a cause or give it away through a foundation. They find and cultivate donors, write grant proposals and reports, plan campaigns and events, record and thank gifts, and on the grantmaking side, review applications and monitor how funds are used.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include a call or lunch with a major donor, research on new prospects and drafting a grant proposal due soon. Afternoons go to entering gifts in the database, writing thank-you letters, planning an event and preparing reports for funders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the executive director, board members, program staff who supply results and stories, and finance teams who track restricted funds. Outside they deal with individual donors, foundation program officers, corporate giving staff, volunteers and event vendors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use donor databases like Raiser’s Edge, Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud, Bloomerang or DonorPerfect. Grant research tools like Foundation Directory, Grants.gov for federal grants, email platforms, online giving pages and prospect research tools are common.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Fundraisers are judged on money raised against goals, donor retention, the number of meaningful donor contacts and grant success rate. Grant staff are also judged on accurate, on-time reports. Grantmakers are judged on funding strong projects and tracking their impact.

qa.q: What is the difference between a development officer and a grant writer?
qa.a: A development officer builds relationships with individual and major donors and asks for gifts, often meeting donors in person. A grant writer researches foundations and government funders, writes proposals that follow each funder’s rules, and prepares reports on how grants were spent. Small nonprofits often have one person doing both jobs.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to work in fundraising?
qa.a: No license is needed to work as a staff fundraiser. The Certified Fund Raising Executive credential is optional and is usually earned after several years of experience. Many states require charities to register before asking the public for money, and outside paid solicitors or fundraising counsel may have to register too, so rules vary by state.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Concept artists sketch and paint characters, creatures, props and environments before anything is built. Game artists turn approved designs into final art, such as textures, sprites, icons, backgrounds and interface elements, ready for use in the game engine.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team check-in. Then come hours of quick thumbnail sketches, refining the strongest idea and painting a finished version. Artists share work for review, take notes from an art director and revise, often several times, before a piece is approved.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with art directors, game designers, writers, 3D modelers, animators and programmers. Concept art guides the rest of the team, so artists often explain a design’s shape, scale, materials and how it should move.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use a drawing tablet or pen display, digital painting software and often 3D sculpting and texturing programs. Many also use photo reference, rough 3D blockouts and a game engine to check how art looks in play. Sketchbooks still help for quick ideas.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Art is judged on whether it fits the game’s style, reads clearly at the size players see it, solves the design brief and arrives on time. For hiring, a strong portfolio usually matters more than a degree, and many artists work as freelancers or contractors.

qa.q: What is the difference between a concept artist and a game artist?
qa.a: A concept artist works early, making fast sketches and paintings that show what characters, places and objects should look like. A game artist, sometimes called a production artist, makes the finished assets that appear in the game, such as textures, sprites, 2D art and models, based on approved concepts. On small teams, one person often does both.

qa.q: Is being a game artist a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Tight deadlines, frequent revisions and crunch periods before a release can mean long hours. Layoffs and canceled projects also happen in the industry. Many artists still find the creative work very rewarding. Studios differ a lot, so ask about overtime, how feedback is given and contract length before accepting a role.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Game designers decide how a game plays. They write the rules, plan levels and missions, balance rewards and in-game economies, and shape how the story unfolds through play. They write it all down in design documents so the rest of the team can build it.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes playtesting a new build, tuning numbers in spreadsheets, and writing or updating design specs. Designers meet with artists and programmers to solve problems, review player feedback, and decide what to cut or change before the next milestone.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Designers work closely with programmers, artists, writers, sound designers, producers and quality assurance testers. On live games they also work with data analysts and community teams who report what players actually do and say.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include game engines, spreadsheets for balance and economy math, visual scripting systems, level editors, and task trackers. Many designers also sketch on paper, build quick prototypes, and use simple scripting languages to test ideas.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: The work is judged by whether the game is fun, clear and fair. Teams look at playtest reactions, player retention, completion rates, reviews and bug reports, and whether features ship on schedule within scope.

qa.q: What does a game designer do day to day?
qa.a: A game designer spends most days testing builds, adjusting rules and numbers, and writing design documents. They meet with artists, programmers and producers to plan features and fix problems. Much of the job is playing the game over and over, watching others play, and making small changes until the experience feels right.

qa.q: What is the difference between a game designer and a game developer?
qa.a: A game designer decides what the game is and how it plays, such as rules, levels and progression. Game developer is a broader term for anyone who helps make games, and it often means programmers who write the code. Designers may script or prototype, but their main focus is the player’s experience rather than engineering.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Game developers write the code that makes a game run. They build gameplay systems, controls, cameras, menus and save files. Depending on the team, they may also design levels, create art or tune how the game feels. Fixing bugs and improving performance take up much of the work.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team meeting to review tasks and blockers. Then comes focused work: coding a feature, testing it in the game, and fixing what breaks. Developers review each other’s code, play recent builds and log bugs for the next round.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Developers work with designers, artists, animators, sound designers, producers and quality assurance testers. On small indie teams, one person may cover several of these roles. Larger studios split the work into specialties such as gameplay, graphics, networking, tools and user interface programming.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include game engines, code editors, version control systems and bug trackers. Languages such as C++ and C# are widely used. Developers also use profilers to find slow code, debuggers to trace crashes, and art or level tools to bring assets into the game.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether features ship on schedule, run smoothly on target hardware and feel fun to play. Teams look at crash rates, frame rate, bug counts and playtest feedback. A strong portfolio of finished, playable projects matters a great deal when hiring.

qa.q: What does a game developer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days are spent writing and testing code for game features, then fixing bugs found by testers or players. Developers attend short team meetings, review teammates’ code and play the latest build to check how changes feel. On smaller teams they may also design levels, make art or handle sound.

qa.q: What is the difference between a game developer and a game designer?
qa.a: A game designer decides how the game should work: its rules, levels, goals and balance. A game developer, often a programmer, builds those ideas in code so they run on a computer, console or phone. The titles overlap, and at small studios one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Game programmers write and maintain the code that makes a game run. That can mean player controls, enemy behavior, physics, graphics rendering, audio systems, editor tools for designers, or the servers behind online play and matchmaking.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team standup, followed by focused coding on a feature or bug. Programmers test new builds, review teammates’ code, track down slow frames, and fix crashes that QA testers report.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with game designers, artists, animators, sound designers, producers and QA testers. A programmer often turns a designer’s idea or an artist’s model into something that actually works inside the game.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include C++ and C#, commercial or in-house game engines, version control, debuggers and performance profilers. Scripting languages such as Python and Lua are used for tools and gameplay. Console work needs special developer kits.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Code is judged on whether features work as designed, keep a steady frame rate and fit memory limits on every target platform. Teams also weigh crash rates, how readable the code is for others, and meeting milestone dates.

qa.q: What does a game programmer do day to day?
qa.a: A game programmer spends most of the day writing and testing code for a game. They build features like combat or menus, fix bugs found by testers, speed up slow parts of the game, review other programmers’ code, and meet with designers and artists to plan how new ideas will work.

qa.q: What is the difference between a game programmer and a game designer?
qa.a: A game designer decides what the game should be: rules, levels, characters and how it feels to play. A game programmer writes the code that makes those ideas work on a computer or console. Designers may do light scripting, but programmers handle the engine, systems and technical problems.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Leads the company’s legal function. Advises the CEO and board on risk, deals, disputes and regulation. Oversees contracts, litigation, compliance, employment matters, intellectual property and corporate governance. Often also serves as corporate secretary, keeping board minutes and records.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a call on a pending lawsuit, then a review of a major customer contract. Later come meetings with HR on an employee issue, a check-in with outside law firms, and prep for a board or committee meeting.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Reports to the CEO and works closely with the board, often attending its meetings. Partners with finance, HR, sales and product leaders. Manages in-house lawyers, paralegals and compliance staff, and hires and supervises outside law firms and their budgets.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Contract management and e-signature systems, legal research databases, matter and spend tracking software, and board portals. Much of the real work is judgment: weighing legal risk against business goals and explaining it in plain terms to executives.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether the company avoids costly surprises, closes deals on sound terms, resolves disputes efficiently and stays compliant. Legal spend and trust from the CEO and board count too. Ethics duties run to the company as the client, not to any one executive.

qa.q: Do you need a law license to be a general counsel?
qa.a: Yes. A general counsel needs a law degree, usually a JD, and admission to the bar in at least one state. Rules for in-house lawyers working in a state where they are not licensed vary by state; many states offer a limited registered in-house counsel status. Most general counsel spend years at law firms or in junior in-house roles first.

qa.q: What is the difference between a general counsel and a chief legal officer?
qa.a: At many companies they are the same job with different titles. At some larger companies, the chief legal officer is the top legal executive with a broader scope, such as compliance, government affairs or ethics, and a general counsel may report to that person. The exact split depends on the company.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A general manager owns the results of a business unit, site or country. They set targets, approve budgets, hire and lead the managers who report to them, and answer to senior leaders or owners for revenue, costs and profit.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a look at sales, costs and key numbers from the day before. The rest goes to meetings with department heads, decisions on spending or staffing, customer or partner calls, and fixing problems that others could not settle.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They lead heads of sales, operations, finance, HR and other functions. They report up to a regional leader, president, owner or board. They also deal with key customers, suppliers, landlords, regulators and sometimes union representatives.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Profit and loss statements, budgets and forecasts are the core tools. Most also use spreadsheets, reporting dashboards, ERP or accounting systems, CRM software and performance reviews to track how the business and its people are doing.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured mainly by profit against budget, revenue growth and cost control. Owners also look at customer satisfaction, staff turnover, safety records and whether the unit hits the goals set in the yearly plan.

qa.q: What does a general manager do day to day?
qa.a: A general manager reviews the unit’s numbers, meets with the managers who report to them, and makes calls on pricing, staffing and spending. They solve escalated problems, talk with major customers or partners, and report results to senior leaders or owners. Much of the job is setting priorities and holding department heads to their targets.

qa.q: What is the difference between a general manager and an operations manager?
qa.a: An operations manager runs the daily work, such as production, service delivery or logistics, and focuses on efficiency and quality. A general manager oversees every function, including sales, finance and operations, and is accountable for the whole unit’s profit and loss. In many companies the operations manager reports to the general manager.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Geologists and mining engineers study rock, soil and water to find minerals, judge whether ground is safe and plan how mines are built. Geologists map, log drill core and model ore bodies. Mining engineers design pits and underground workings, plan production, ventilation and blasting, and plan mine closure.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Field days may mean mapping outcrops, supervising a drill rig, logging core and taking samples. Mine site days include pit or underground inspections, survey checks and short-range planning. Office days go to geologic models, mine plans, reports and permit work.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with drillers, surveyors, geotechnical and environmental engineers, metallurgists, mine operators and safety staff. They also deal with assay labs, consultants, regulators such as MSHA and state agencies, and landowners or communities near projects.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include rock hammers, hand lenses, GPS units and core logging tablets, plus GIS software like ArcGIS and QGIS. Geology and mine planning software such as Leapfrog, Vulcan, Deswik or Surpac is standard, along with drones and laser scanners for surveys.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Geologists are judged on accurate maps, reliable resource models and good drilling decisions. Mining engineers are judged on safe, efficient mine plans that hit production and cost targets. Both are judged on safety, environmental compliance and how well their results hold up under audit.

qa.q: Do geologists and mining engineers need a license?
qa.a: It depends on the state. Many states require a Professional Geologist license to sign geology work for the public, and engineers who seal designs need a Professional Engineer license. Work at active mines also requires MSHA safety training. Resource reports from public mining companies must be signed by a qualified person under SEC rules.

qa.q: What is the difference between a geologist and a mining engineer?
qa.a: A geologist studies the earth itself: rock types, structures and where minerals or water are found, and estimates how much is there.
