A mining engineer takes that model and plans how to extract the material safely and at a profit, designing pits, tunnels, blasting and haulage. On mine sites they work side by side.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They answer customer emails, chats and calls in German. They solve order, billing, account and technical problems. They often write case notes in English, so US teams can follow up, and they may review or translate German content.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Shifts often start early in the US morning to overlap with business hours in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, which usually run six hours ahead of US Eastern time. Mornings bring the most German contacts. Later hours go to follow-ups and internal English work.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They serve customers and business partners in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Inside the company, they work with US colleagues in support, sales, billing and product teams, who rely on them to explain what German-speaking customers need.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Ticketing systems, CRM software, chat and phone platforms, and video calls are daily tools. Many also use glossaries, translation memory and a brand style guide that says whether to address customers with the formal Sie or the informal du.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers check the accuracy and tone of their German, how fast cases get resolved, and customer satisfaction scores. They must also handle personal data from Germany and Austria under GDPR rules, and from Switzerland under Swiss data protection law.

qa.q: What does a German speaking customer support rep do day to day?
qa.a: They handle questions from customers in Germany, Austria and Switzerland by email, chat and phone. They fix orders, refunds, logins and product issues in clear, polite German. They log each case in English for US coworkers. They also adjust for regional differences, such as Swiss spelling that uses ss instead of ß, and Austrian word choices.

qa.q: Do German speaking jobs require native fluency?
qa.a: Many postings ask for native or near-native German, often described as C1 or C2 on the European CEFR scale, plus strong English. Employers usually test skills with a German interview or writing sample. A certificate can help, but it is not always required. Written accuracy matters most in email and chat roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They collect, clean and update location data, then turn it into map layers. They run spatial analysis such as route planning, service coverage or site selection. They also build maps, web apps and dashboards that other teams use to make decisions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with fixing errors in a road or parcel dataset. Then comes a request for a custom map, a script to automate a weekly update, and a check of new imagery or GPS data against existing layers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Desktop and web GIS software, spatial databases, and scripting in Python or SQL are core tools. Many also work with GPS receivers, aerial and satellite imagery, lidar point clouds and street-level sensor data for detailed or high-definition maps.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with city planners, engineers, surveyors, logistics managers, emergency managers and software developers. On self-driving and navigation projects, they often support data scientists and testing teams who need accurate, current map data.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Employers include city and county governments, utilities, transport agencies, logistics and delivery firms, engineering consultancies and mapping or autonomous vehicle companies. Most work happens at a computer, in an office or remotely, with occasional field trips to collect or verify data.

qa.q: What does a GIS and mapping specialist do day to day?
qa.a: Most of the day is spent at a computer. They import and clean location data, edit map layers, check accuracy, and run analysis like finding the best delivery routes or mapping who lives near a service. They also answer map requests from coworkers and write small scripts to automate repeated tasks.

qa.q: What is the difference between a GIS specialist and a land surveyor?
qa.a: Land surveyors are licensed by each state and can certify legal property boundaries and official survey plats. GIS specialists compile, manage and analyze map data, but their maps are generally not legal survey documents. Rules on which mapping tasks require a surveyor’s license vary by state. Voluntary GIS certifications exist but are not a license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They design guidance laws, navigation filters and control loops that keep a vehicle on its path. They model vehicle motion, combine sensor data from IMUs, GPS or star trackers, tune autopilots, and prove the software works before it ever flies.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Much of the day goes to running simulations and reviewing plots of how far the vehicle drifted. There are also code reviews, design meetings with propulsion, avionics and flight software teams, and debugging on a hardware-in-the-loop test bench.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: MATLAB and Simulink, Python, and C or C++ for flight code. Kalman filters, PID and optimal control methods, six-degree-of-freedom simulations, Monte Carlo runs, and lab benches with real sensors and flight computers.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Aerospace and defense firms, space launch companies, government labs, drone makers and self-driving vehicle teams. Much of the work falls under export control rules, so many employers require US citizenship or permanent residency, and defense roles may need a security clearance.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether the vehicle reaches its target within error limits and stays stable when sensors are noisy or parts fail. Strong test evidence, passed design reviews and clean flight data count more than lines of code written.

qa.q: What does a guidance, navigation and control engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They write and test the math that lets a vehicle know where it is and steer itself. Most days involve simulation runs, tuning filters and control gains, reviewing test data, and working with hardware and software teams. Around flight tests or launches, they often sit in the control room watching their algorithms perform live.

qa.q: What is the difference between guidance, navigation and control?
qa.a: Navigation estimates where the vehicle is and how it is moving. Guidance decides where it should go and works out the path to get there. Control turns those commands into actions, such as moving fins, tilting an engine or changing motor speed, while keeping the vehicle stable. Many engineers specialize in one area, but all three must work together.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Go developers build and maintain backend services, APIs and command-line tools written in Go. They design how services talk to each other, use goroutines and channels to handle many requests at once, and fix bugs found in testing or production.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team stand-up. Then come code reviews of teammates’ pull requests, writing new features with unit tests, and checking dashboards for errors or slow responses. Some days include an on-call shift for live systems.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They rely on the Go toolchain, including go build, go test, go vet and gofmt. They also use Git, containers, Kubernetes, gRPC and REST APIs, SQL and key-value databases, message queues, and logs, metrics and traces for monitoring.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with other backend engineers, site reliability and DevOps staff, and frontend or mobile developers who call their APIs. Product managers set priorities, and security reviewers check code that handles sensitive data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good Go code is simple, readable and well tested. Teams also judge the work by how the services run: uptime, response time and error rates measured against agreed targets, plus how fast problems get fixed.

qa.q: What does a Go developer do day to day?
qa.a: A Go developer writes and reviews code for server software, such as APIs, background workers and cloud tools. They write tests, deploy changes through automated pipelines, watch monitoring dashboards, and investigate slow or failing requests. Many also take turns on call to respond when a live service has a problem.

qa.q: What is the difference between a Go developer and a Java developer?
qa.a: Both usually build backend systems. Go compiles to a single fast binary with no separate runtime to install, has a small language, and builds concurrency into the core with goroutines. Java runs on the Java Virtual Machine and has a larger, older ecosystem, common in big enterprise systems. Go is popular for cloud infrastructure and networked tools.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: People in this field win and deliver government contracts. Roles include engineers, analysts, proposal writers, contract managers, program managers and business development staff. All of them must meet the contract’s terms and federal buying rules such as the Federal Acquisition Regulation.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes project work, status meetings with the government customer, written reports and compliance tasks. Many staff record hours against specific contract charge codes. Proposal teams work toward firm due dates set in each solicitation.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with government contracting officers, agency program offices, military personnel and other contractors. Companies often team up, with a prime contractor leading the work and subcontractors handling parts of it.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Work happens in offices near military bases and agency headquarters, and in labs, factories and shipyards. Classified work is done in secure facilities where personal phones and devices are usually not allowed. Some roles involve travel or time on base.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by meeting contract deliverables on schedule and within cost. Agencies rate contractor performance, and those past performance records count when future contracts are awarded. Following security and export control rules is also closely checked.

qa.q: Do I need a security clearance to work in government and defense?
qa.a: Only some roles need one. Clearances are granted by the federal government, usually after an employer sponsors you for a specific job, so you generally cannot apply on your own. US citizenship is normally required. The background check looks at finances, foreign contacts, drug use and criminal history. Many postings ask for the ability to obtain a clearance.

qa.q: What is the difference between a government contractor and a federal employee?
qa.a: A contractor works for a private company that the government pays under a contract. A federal employee is hired directly by an agency under civil service rules. Contractor jobs depend on contract funding and can end when a contract ends. Contractors also cannot perform inherently governmental tasks, such as making final decisions on spending public money.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Government contracts specialists manage the contracts a company holds with federal, state or local agencies. They review solicitations, help prepare proposals, negotiate terms, track deliverables and modifications, and make sure the company follows the rules that apply, such as the Federal Acquisition Regulation and agency supplements.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include reading a new solicitation on SAM.gov, flagging risky clauses and checking proposal compliance. Specialists also process contract modifications, answer contracting officer questions, review subcontract terms, track invoices and reports, and keep registrations and certifications current.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: On the government side they work with contracting officers and their representatives. Inside the company they work with program managers, proposal writers, pricing analysts, legal counsel and finance teams. They also coordinate with subcontractors and with auditors such as the Defense Contract Audit Agency.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include SAM.gov for registration and opportunities, the FAR and agency supplements such as the DFARS, contract management systems, and government contract accounting systems such as Deltek Costpoint. Excel and document tools help track deliverables, modifications and compliance deadlines.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Specialists are judged on compliant contracts, clean audits, on-time deliverables and accurate records. Missed clauses or false statements can bring penalties, False Claims Act liability or suspension from future awards. Leaders also value well-negotiated terms, fast modifications and good relationships with contracting officers.

qa.q: What is the FAR in government contracting?
qa.a: The FAR, or Federal Acquisition Regulation, is the main set of rules for how federal executive agencies buy goods and services. It covers competition, contract types, pricing, required clauses and contractor duties. Many agencies add their own supplements, such as the DFARS for defense. State and local governments follow their own procurement laws, which vary by state.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a government contracts specialist?
qa.a: Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, law, finance or a related field, and some senior roles prefer a law degree. Experience matters a lot, especially with the FAR, proposals and audits. Optional contract management certifications can help. Federal contracting officers on the government side follow their own training and certification requirements.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Find where software spends its time and make it faster. They write and tune GPU kernels, cut memory traffic, overlap computation with data movement, and spread AI training or inference across many chips so jobs finish sooner and cost less.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Profile a slow model or job, read the timeline, and form a guess about the bottleneck. Change the code, benchmark again, and confirm the numerical results still match. Then review teammates’ code and write up what changed and why.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: C++ and Python, GPU programming toolkits, profilers and tracing tools, machine learning frameworks and compilers, benchmark suites, and clusters of servers with many GPUs linked by fast networks. Strong knowledge of memory hierarchies and parallel computing matters as much as any tool.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Machine learning researchers, model and infrastructure engineers, compiler teams, and hardware architects. They often act as translators, explaining what a model needs from the hardware and what the hardware can realistically deliver.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By measured gains in throughput, latency, memory use, and cost per run, and by how close code gets to the chip’s peak capability. Faster code only counts if results stay correct, reproducible, and maintainable by others.

qa.q: What does a GPU and performance engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They measure how software runs on GPUs and other processors, find the slowest parts, and rewrite or tune them. Much of the day goes to profiling, writing low-level kernel code, running benchmarks, and checking that faster code still gives correct results. They also review code and share findings with AI researchers and infrastructure teams.

qa.q: What is the difference between a GPU performance engineer and a machine learning engineer?
qa.a: A machine learning engineer builds, trains, and deploys models, focusing on data and model quality. A GPU performance engineer focuses on how efficiently that work runs on hardware, working on kernels, memory use, and parallelism across chips. The roles overlap, and many people move between them, but performance engineers usually work closer to the hardware.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Graphic and brand designers create logos, ads, social posts, illustrations, slide decks and web page layouts. They choose fonts, colors and images, then prepare final files for print or screen. Many also write and maintain brand guidelines so every team uses the look the same way.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a brief from a client or manager. Designers sketch ideas, build drafts, and share them for feedback. Afternoons go to revisions, resizing a design for different formats, and exporting files that meet print or web specs before a deadline.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with marketing managers, copywriters, web developers, photographers and printers. In agencies they answer to an art director and talk with clients. In-house designers serve sales, HR and leadership teams that need materials fast and on brand.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include vector, photo editing and page layout software, plus browser-based design and prototyping apps. Designers use drawing tablets, color-calibrated monitors and font libraries. A growing number also use AI image tools, while checking usage rights and licenses for fonts and stock images.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether it fits the brand, meets the brief and lands on time. Clean files, correct sizes, readable text and accessible color contrast matter. Results such as campaign response or client approval often count more than personal style.

qa.q: What does a graphic and brand designer do day to day?
qa.a: They turn requests into visuals. That means reading a brief, sketching options, building drafts in design software, and revising after feedback. They resize designs for print, social media and websites, and keep logos, colors and fonts consistent across everything a company publishes. Much of the day is spent on small, deadline-driven tasks alongside larger projects like a new logo or campaign.

qa.q: What is the difference between a graphic designer and a brand designer?
qa.a: A graphic designer makes individual pieces, such as a flyer, ad or web banner. A brand designer shapes the overall identity: the logo, color palette, typography and rules that guide every piece. In practice the roles overlap, and many job postings ask for both skills. No license is required for either role in the US; a strong portfolio matters most.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Write and optimize the code that turns 3D data into images, either in real time or offline. Build lighting, shading, shadows, and post-processing effects, and keep frame rates steady on every target device.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Capture a slow frame in a GPU profiler and find the costly pass. Fix a shader bug, review a teammate’s code, and test a new effect on several devices. Then meet with artists about how it should look.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: C++ plus shading languages such as HLSL, GLSL, or Metal Shading Language. Graphics APIs like Vulkan, DirectX 12, Metal, and OpenGL. GPU debuggers and profilers, linear algebra, and version control.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Technical artists, 3D artists, engine and gameplay programmers, and simulation developers. They also work with hardware and driver teams. Much of the job is turning an artistic goal into code that fits a strict memory and time budget.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Game studios, film and animation houses, and virtual and augmented reality teams. Others work in automotive and flight simulation, CAD and medical imaging software, or at GPU and chip makers. Many roles are hybrid or remote.

qa.q: What does a graphics and rendering engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They write and tune code that draws 3D scenes on the GPU. A day often mixes building features like shadows or reflections, chasing visual bugs, and profiling to keep each frame within its time budget. They also review code, test on different hardware, and talk with artists about the look they want.

qa.q: What is the difference between a graphics engineer and a technical artist?
qa.a: A graphics engineer builds the rendering engine itself. That means low-level GPU code, graphics APIs, and core shaders. A technical artist bridges art and engineering. They make art tools, material setups, and asset pipelines, and they help artists stay within performance limits. The roles overlap, but engineers usually need deeper programming and math skills.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Grocery store associates stock shelves, coolers and freezers, rotate older products to the front, check dates and pull expired items. They face shelves so labels line up, set out sale tags, help shoppers find products, and may bag orders or run a register when lines get long.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many shifts start early or overnight, unloading the delivery truck and working pallets onto the floor. Later hours bring serving at the deli or bakery counter, weighing and slicing orders, restocking busy aisles and answering questions. Closing shifts include cleaning, recovering messy shelves and returning items left in the wrong place.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Associates use handheld scanners, price guns, box cutters, carts and manual pallet jacks. Counter staff use scales, label printers and slicers. Federal child labor rules bar workers under 18 from operating power-driven meat slicers, so younger associates are kept to other tasks.

day.label: Food and age rules
day.text: At deli and bakery counters, workers wear hair restraints and avoid bare-hand contact with ready-to-eat food, using gloves, tongs or deli paper, under their state’s food code. Where stores sell beer or wine, associates check ID, and states set their own minimum age for clerks who make alcohol sales.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: They work in supermarkets, neighborhood grocers, warehouse clubs and natural food stores, often in one department such as produce, dairy, frozen, meat, deli or bakery. The job means hours on their feet, regular lifting, and time inside walk-in coolers and freezers.

qa.q: What does a grocery store associate do day to day?
qa.a: They keep the store full and easy to shop. That means unloading deliveries, stocking and rotating products, checking dates, and tidying shelves. They also help customers find items, serve at deli or bakery counters, bag groceries, and clean their area. Tasks depend on the department and shift, with overnight crews focused on stocking and day crews on customers.

qa.q: What is the difference between a grocery store associate and a cashier?
qa.a: A cashier mainly works the register, scanning items, taking payment and bagging orders. A grocery store associate has a wider role across the store, stocking shelves, working counters and helping shoppers on the floor. In many stores the jobs overlap, and associates are trained to cover a register when checkout gets busy.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Group and principal product managers set the strategy and roadmap for a whole product area. They decide which problems to solve first, align goals across teams, and make the hard tradeoffs on scope, timing and investment. Group managers also hire, coach and review a team of product managers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes strategy reviews, one-on-ones with product managers, and meetings with engineering and design leads. They read customer research and usage data, unblock decisions that cross teams, and prepare updates or planning documents for executives.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with engineering and design leaders, data analysts, and user researchers. They also partner with sales, marketing, customer support, legal and finance, and they report to a director or vice president of product.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include roadmap and backlog software, product analytics dashboards, spreadsheets, shared documents and slide decks. Many also use experiment platforms, customer feedback tools and team chat to keep large groups aligned.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by business and customer outcomes for the whole area, such as adoption, retention, revenue or reliability. Leaders also look at the quality of decisions, how well teams ship together, and how product managers on the team grow.

qa.q: What is the difference between a group product manager and a principal product manager?
qa.a: A group product manager usually manages people. They lead several product managers and own the combined direction of their areas. A principal product manager is often a senior individual contributor. They take the most complex or high-stakes product problems and influence many teams without direct reports. Titles and duties vary by company, so job seekers should read each posting closely.

qa.q: Is group product management a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. These leaders answer for results across several teams, juggle competing demands from executives and customers, and make calls with incomplete information. Meetings can fill the calendar, and launches or planning cycles bring pressure. Many find it rewarding because they shape strategy and grow other product managers. Good delegation and clear priorities help keep the load manageable.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Growth staff find the points where users drop off or revenue stalls. They form ideas to fix them, run tests, and measure the results. They scale what works and drop what does not, whether the change sits in marketing, the product or the sales process.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a check of key metrics such as signups, activation and conversion. Then come planning test ideas, writing briefs, reviewing results from running experiments, and meeting with designers or engineers to ship the next change.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, engineers, designers, data analysts, marketers and sales teams. Because growth cuts across departments, much of the job is persuading others to make room for tests and agreeing on how success will be measured.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include web and product analytics, A/B testing platforms, SQL and spreadsheets, email and ad managers, and CRM systems. Many also use dashboards to track funnels and simple scripts or no-code tools to launch quick experiments.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are judged by measurable lifts in users, retention or revenue, not by activity. Good growth staff are also judged on how many sound experiments they run, how clearly they document what they learned, and whether wins hold up over time.

qa.q: What does a growth marketer do day to day?
qa.a: A growth marketer studies data to see where people leave the funnel, then designs small tests to keep them. That can mean new landing pages, onboarding emails, pricing pages or ad audiences. They launch tests, wait for enough data, read the results, and share what they learned with the team before picking the next idea.

qa.q: What is the difference between growth and traditional marketing?
qa.a: Traditional marketing usually focuses on brand, campaigns and bringing in new leads. Growth covers the whole customer journey, from first visit to activation, retention, referral and revenue. It relies heavily on rapid, measured experiments and often changes the product itself, not just the messaging, so growth staff work closely with engineers and product teams.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Growth engineers build and test product changes that bring in new users and keep them coming back. They code sign-up and onboarding flows, referral programs, pricing pages, email triggers and in-app prompts, then measure whether each change moved the numbers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reading results from last week’s A/B test. Then comes shipping a new variant of a checkout screen, adding event tracking, fixing a broken funnel step and planning the next experiment with a product manager.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use web and mobile frameworks, feature flag systems, experimentation platforms and product analytics tools. SQL is common for pulling data. They also work with email and push notification services, attribution tools and dashboards that track sign-ups, activation and retention.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, designers, data analysts and marketers. They also coordinate with core product engineers, since growth changes often touch shared code like login, payments and account settings.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by experiment results and business metrics such as conversion, activation, retention and referral rates. Speed matters too. Teams value engineers who run many clean, well-instrumented tests and learn from failed ones without breaking the product.

qa.q: What does a growth engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A growth engineer writes code for experiments meant to raise sign-ups, activation or retention. Daily work includes building test variants behind feature flags, adding analytics events, checking test results, cleaning up losing variants and planning new ideas with product, design and data teammates.

qa.q: What is the difference between a growth engineer and a software engineer?
qa.a: A growth engineer is a software engineer focused on user acquisition and retention rather than core features. The work is more experiment-driven, with short cycles, heavy use of A/B testing and analytics, and success measured by metric changes. A general software engineer usually builds and maintains longer-lived product features and systems.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A growth manager finds the biggest levers for more users or revenue. They study the funnel from first visit to paying customer, spot where people drop off, and run experiments to fix those weak points. They then roll out the tests that win.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with dashboards and the results of running tests. Then come writing test ideas, ranking them by likely impact and effort, and briefing designers or engineers. Late in the day they may check a new email flow, a landing page, or a pricing change.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, engineers, designers, data analysts and marketers. They also talk with sales and customer support to learn why people buy, stay or leave. Most report to a head of growth, marketing or product.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include product analytics software, A/B testing platforms, spreadsheets and SQL for pulling data. They also use email and messaging tools, ad managers and customer data platforms. Basic statistics helps them tell a real result from noise.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by movement in key metrics such as sign-ups, activation, retention, conversion to paid and revenue per user. Managers also look at how many solid experiments ship and how well the team learns from tests that fail.

qa.q: What does a growth manager do day to day?
qa.a: A growth manager reviews data to see where users get stuck, comes up with ideas to fix it, and runs controlled tests such as A/B tests. They work with engineers and designers to launch changes, read the results, and keep what works. Much of the day is spent prioritizing ideas and sharing findings with the team.

qa.q: What is the difference between a growth manager and a marketing manager?
qa.a: A marketing manager usually focuses on brand, campaigns and bringing new people in. A growth manager looks at the whole customer journey, including onboarding, retention and upsells, and often changes the product itself. Growth roles lean heavily on experiments and data, while marketing roles may also cover messaging, events and creative work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Growth marketers plan and run paid ads on search and social platforms, build email campaigns, and test landing pages. They track how many customers each channel brings in and what each one costs, then move budget toward what works.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a dashboard check on spend, clicks, sign-ups and sales. The rest of the day goes to adjusting bids, writing ad copy, setting up A/B tests, reviewing results and reporting numbers to the team.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include ad managers for search and social platforms, web analytics software, email marketing platforms, spreadsheets and testing tools. Many roles also use SQL, tag managers and CRM systems to follow a customer from first click to purchase.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with designers and copywriters on creative, with product and engineering teams on sign-up flows and tracking, and with sales or finance on targets. Agency roles add regular calls with clients.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured in numbers such as cost per acquisition, return on ad spend, conversion rate and customer lifetime value. Good marketers also run clean experiments and explain clearly why a result happened.

qa.q: What does a growth marketer do day to day?
qa.a: A growth marketer checks campaign data, adjusts ad budgets and targeting, writes and tests ads and emails, and runs experiments on landing pages or sign-up steps. They report which channels bring customers at the best cost and decide what to try next.

qa.q: What is the difference between growth marketing and performance marketing?
qa.a: Performance marketing focuses on paid channels where every click or sale is tracked and paid for. Growth marketing is broader. It covers paid ads plus email, referrals, onboarding and retention, using experiments across the whole customer journey. Many job titles mix the two.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Growth product managers find the steps where users drop off, from signup to first use to paying. They write hypotheses, plan A/B tests, set priorities with engineers and designers, and ship changes to onboarding, pricing pages, trials and referral flows.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a dashboard check on signups, activation and retention. The rest of the day goes to reviewing test results, writing specs for the next experiment, sitting in on user interviews and deciding which ideas to drop or scale.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with engineers, product designers and data analysts. They also coordinate with marketing, sales, customer support and finance, since changes to pricing, emails or trials touch many teams and must not break other parts of the product.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include product analytics software, A/B testing and feature flag platforms, SQL for pulling data, spreadsheets, session recordings and survey tools. Many also use email and in-app messaging systems to test lifecycle campaigns.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by movement in agreed metrics such as activation rate, conversion to paid, retention and revenue per user. Good growth managers are also judged on test quality: clear hypotheses, sound sample sizes and honest reporting of failed experiments.

qa.q: What does a growth product manager do day to day?
qa.a: They study where users stall in the product, then design and run experiments to fix it. A day might include reading test results, writing a spec for a new onboarding step, meeting with engineers and designers, checking metrics with an analyst and talking to customers about why they did or did not upgrade.

qa.q: What is the difference between a growth product manager and a core product manager?
qa.a: A core product manager builds and improves the main features users come for. A growth product manager focuses on the path around those features: getting people to sign up, reach value quickly, pay and stay. Growth work runs more small, fast experiments and is tied closely to conversion and retention numbers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Hardware engineers design the circuit boards, chips and electronics inside products. They turn requirements into schematics, choose components, guide board layout, build prototypes and test them until the design works reliably and can be made at a sensible cost.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a short team meeting, then hours at the lab bench probing a prototype board. Afternoons often go to design reviews, updating schematics, reading component datasheets, or helping the factory solve a build problem.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use schematic capture and PCB layout software, circuit simulators such as SPICE, and hardware description languages like Verilog or VHDL for chip and FPGA work. On the bench they rely on oscilloscopes, logic analyzers, power supplies, multimeters and soldering stations.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with firmware and software engineers, mechanical engineers who design the enclosure, test engineers and manufacturing partners. They also deal with component suppliers and with test labs that check products against FCC and safety requirements.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work means boards that power up, pass testing and hit targets for speed, power use, heat, size and cost. Most electronic products sold in the US must meet FCC rules on radio frequency emissions, so passing compliance testing without redesigns matters a lot.

qa.q: What does a hardware engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix design and testing. A hardware engineer draws or updates schematics, reviews board layouts, and reads datasheets to pick parts. Then they bring up prototype boards in the lab, measure signals with an oscilloscope, track down bugs, and work with firmware and manufacturing teams to fix problems before the product ships.

qa.q: What is the difference between a hardware engineer and an electrical engineer?
qa.a: Electrical engineering is the broad field. It covers power grids, motors, controls and electronics. A hardware engineer focuses on computer and electronic hardware such as chips, circuit boards and devices. Many hardware engineers hold electrical or computer engineering degrees. A state PE license is rarely required for hardware design jobs, though it is more common in power and utility work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Builds and owns the master schedule for a hardware product, from early prototypes through EVT, DVT and PVT builds to mass production. Tracks risks, costs and open issues, runs build readiness reviews, and makes sure every team knows what must be done before the next gate.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with calls to factory teams in other time zones about yield, part shortages or test failures. The rest of the day goes to status meetings, updating the build plan, pushing for engineering decisions and writing clear summaries for leadership.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Mechanical, electrical, firmware and test engineers, plus supply chain, quality, operations and product managers. Outside the company, they work daily with contract manufacturers, component suppliers and labs that run safety, regulatory and reliability testing.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Scheduling and issue tracking software, shared spreadsheets, product lifecycle management systems for the bill of materials and engineering changes, and build reports with yield and failure data. Clear written updates and well run meetings matter as much as any software.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Mostly office or hybrid roles at companies that make consumer electronics, networking gear, medical devices, vehicles or industrial equipment. Many jobs involve travel to factories and supplier sites, sometimes overseas, especially around prototype and production builds.

qa.q: What does a hardware program manager do day to day?
qa.a: They keep a hardware product moving toward launch. That means checking build status with factories, tracking part supply and test results, running meetings with engineering teams, updating schedules and risk lists, and deciding with others which problems must be fixed before the next build stage. They also report progress, cost and quality to leadership.

qa.q: What is the difference between a hardware program manager and a product manager?
qa.a: A product manager decides what to build and why, based on customer needs and business goals. A hardware program manager figures out how and when it gets built, coordinating engineering, suppliers and factories to hit schedule, cost and quality targets. The two work closely, and the roles can overlap at smaller companies.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Engineers draw harness layouts, choose wire gauges, connectors and terminals, and plan routing paths through a vehicle or machine. Technicians cut, strip, crimp and bundle wires on formboards, then test each finished harness for continuity and correct pinout.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Electrical CAD software for schematics and 3D routing, wire cutting and stripping machines, crimp presses and hand crimpers, heat guns for shrink tubing, pull testers for crimp strength, and electrical testers that check every circuit before a harness ships.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Most work in plants and engineering offices serving automotive, aerospace, defense, farm and construction equipment, medical devices and appliances. Engineers split time between a desk and the build floor. Technicians usually stand at benches or formboards for a full shift.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with mechanical designers who control the space a harness must fit, electrical engineers who define the circuits, connector and terminal suppliers, quality inspectors and production staff. Field service teams often report failures back to them.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is checked against the drawing and workmanship standards, most often IPC/WHMA-A-620. Inspectors look at crimp height, pull strength, labels and routing. Engineers are judged on harnesses that fit on the first build, pass electrical tests and survive heat, vibration and moisture.

qa.q: What is the difference between a wire harness engineer and a wire harness technician?
qa.a: The engineer designs the harness: schematics, routing, wire sizes, connector choices and the build drawing. The technician builds, repairs or tests it from that drawing by crimping terminals, inserting pins into connectors, taping or sleeving bundles and running electrical tests. Engineers usually hold an engineering degree. Technicians often learn on the job or through a technical program.

qa.q: Do wire harness technicians need a license or certification?
qa.a: No state license is required to build wire harnesses. Many employers, especially in aerospace and defense, ask for IPC/WHMA-A-620 training or certification, which covers accepted workmanship for crimping, soldering and assembly. Some customer contracts require it. Employers often pay for the course, and the certificate must be renewed on a set schedule.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Sets the marketing strategy and yearly plan, owns the marketing budget, and decides which channels get money. Hires and leads the marketing team, approves brand and messaging, and reports results to the CEO and often the board.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a look at pipeline, traffic and campaign numbers. The rest of the day mixes one-on-ones with team leads, reviews of creative and launch plans, budget calls, and meetings with sales and product leaders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Works closely with the CEO, the head of sales, product leaders and finance. Manages marketing managers, content, design and analytics staff, and oversees outside agencies, freelancers and vendors such as media buyers and PR firms.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Uses CRM and marketing automation platforms, web and ad analytics, dashboards and spreadsheets for budgets and forecasts. Also relies on project management software, customer research, and brand guidelines the team maintains.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Judged on business results more than activity. Common measures include revenue or pipeline sourced by marketing, customer acquisition cost, return on ad spend, brand awareness, and whether the team hits its plan within budget.

qa.q: What is the difference between a head of marketing and a CMO?
qa.a: A CMO, or chief marketing officer, is an executive title. CMOs usually sit on the leadership team and often present to the board. Head of marketing is a common title at smaller or growing companies for the top marketing leader. The daily work can be very similar. A CMO role is often broader and more strategic.

qa.q: Is being a head of marketing a stressful job?
qa.a: It often is. The role answers for results that depend on many factors, including sales, product and the economy. Budgets get questioned, targets rise, and launches run on tight deadlines. Turnover in top marketing jobs is known to be high. Leaders who build a strong team and agree on clear goals with the CEO usually find the pressure easier to manage.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A head of product sets the product strategy and roadmap, decides which features and bets get funded, and hires, coaches and manages the product managers who carry out that plan.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to one-on-ones with product managers and roadmap reviews. Afternoons bring meetings with engineering and design leads, a few customer calls, and time spent reading usage data before making tradeoff decisions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the chief executive, engineering and design leaders, sales, marketing and customer support. They often present plans to the executive team or board and explain why some requests will wait.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include roadmap and backlog software, product analytics dashboards, spreadsheets, shared documents, customer research notes and slide decks. Many also use experiment results, such as A/B tests, to check whether a change worked.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by business results tied to the product, such as customer adoption, retention and revenue, plus how reliably teams ship. The strength and growth of the product management team also counts.

qa.q: What does a head of product do day to day?
qa.a: They decide what the company builds next and make sure teams build it well. Day to day, that means coaching product managers, reviewing roadmaps, weighing customer feedback and data, settling priority conflicts between teams, and reporting progress and plans to company leadership.

qa.q: What is the difference between a head of product and a product manager?
qa.a: A product manager owns one product area or feature set and works directly with a single team. A head of product leads all of the product managers, sets the overall strategy across products, and answers to company leadership for the results. Titles vary by company, and smaller firms may combine the two roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Dietitians assess nutrition needs and plan diets for conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease or food allergies, then teach people how to follow them. Health coaches help clients set goals for eating, exercise, sleep and stress, and keep them motivated through regular check-ins.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days mix one-on-one sessions in person, by phone or by video with charting and follow-up messages. Hospital dietitians review charts, visit patients on the wards and recommend tube or IV feeding plans. Coaches may also run group classes or workplace wellness sessions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Dietitians work with doctors, nurses, pharmacists, diabetes educators and food service staff. Health coaches often work inside primary care teams, employer wellness programs or health plans. Both talk with clients’ families, who often shop and cook for them.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include nutrition analysis software, food logging apps, scales and body composition analyzers, electronic health records and telehealth platforms. Coaches often review data from fitness trackers and use messaging apps. Both rely on motivational interviewing, a structured way of talking about change.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on client results, such as changes in weight, blood sugar or blood pressure, and on how many clients stay with the program. Client satisfaction and clear notes also count. Coaches must stay in scope and not diagnose or prescribe diets to treat disease.

qa.q: What is the difference between a health coach and a dietitian?
qa.a: New registered dietitians need a graduate degree, supervised practice hours and a national exam, and most states license or certify dietitians. Dietitians can provide medical nutrition therapy for diseases. A health coach needs no state license, though certifications exist. Coaches focus on habits and motivation and should refer clients with medical needs to a dietitian or doctor.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a dietitian?
qa.a: In most states, yes. Most states license or certify dietitians, and some limit who may give medical nutrition advice or use the title. The national registered dietitian credential now requires a graduate degree, supervised practice and a national exam. The title nutritionist is less regulated in many states, and health coaching has no state license, so check your state’s rules.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Clinicians at health-tech and biotech companies see patients by video, phone or in clinics, review lab results and write care notes. Others support care by running clinical trials, checking product safety, training users on medical tools or advising engineers on how real clinics work.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A telehealth nurse or doctor may work through a queue of virtual visits and patient messages. A clinical research coordinator may screen trial volunteers, collect data and log adverse events. Most days also include charting, team meetings and follow-up with patients or study sites.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with patients, physicians, nurses and pharmacists, plus colleagues outside medicine such as product managers, software engineers, data scientists and regulatory staff. Biotech roles often involve trial sites, investigators and ethics review boards.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include electronic health records, telehealth video platforms, e-prescribing systems, clinical trial data systems and remote patient monitoring devices. Staff follow HIPAA privacy rules when handling patient information and good clinical practice standards in research.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Patient-facing clinicians need an active license in the state where the patient is located during the visit. Compacts for nurses and physicians make multistate practice easier, but membership and rules vary by state. Prescribing controlled substances by telehealth carries extra federal and state requirements.

qa.q: What does a clinician at a health-tech company do day to day?
qa.a: Most see patients through video or phone visits, answer secure messages, order tests, prescribe within their license and document care in an electronic health record. Many also give feedback on the product, help write clinical protocols and review quality or safety issues. The mix depends on whether the role is mainly patient care or mainly advising the company.

qa.q: What is the difference between clinical work at a hospital and at a biotech company?
qa.a: Hospital clinicians mainly treat patients in person. At a biotech company, clinical staff more often support research, such as running or monitoring trials, tracking drug safety or explaining study data to doctors. Some biotech roles involve direct patient contact at trial sites, but many focus on data, protocols and regulatory requirements rather than daily bedside care.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Healthcare administrators manage the business side of a clinic, hospital department, nursing home or practice. They hire and schedule staff, set and track budgets, oversee billing, improve patient flow and make sure the facility follows health, safety and privacy rules.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with reports on patient volume, staffing and finances. Then come meetings with department leads, staff issues, patient complaints and calls with vendors. Larger projects, such as new software, a new service or an upcoming inspection, fill the rest.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with physicians, nurse managers, finance, human resources, IT and compliance staff. Outside the building they deal with insurers, vendors, state inspectors and accrediting bodies. Senior administrators also report to boards or owners.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include electronic health record and practice management systems, staff scheduling software, Excel, budgeting tools and dashboards in Tableau or Power BI. They also use payroll and HR systems, incident reporting software and policy management tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Administrators are judged on financial results against budget, patient satisfaction, wait times, staff turnover and quality and safety measures. Passing state inspections and accreditation surveys without serious findings matters a great deal.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a healthcare administrator?
qa.a: Most healthcare administrator jobs do not need a license, but employers usually want a bachelor’s or master’s degree in health administration, business or public health. Nursing home administrators are the exception: every state requires them to hold a license, which usually involves education, supervised training and exams. Many states also license assisted living administrators.

qa.q: What does a healthcare administrator do day to day?
qa.a: A healthcare administrator spends the day keeping a clinic or department running. They review staffing, finance and patient reports, meet with doctors and managers, solve scheduling gaps, handle complaints and approve spending. They also prepare for inspections, update policies to match new rules and lead projects to make care faster or cheaper.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Hebrew speaking staff handle calls, chats and emails in Hebrew, often for customers in Israel. Depending on the role, they also translate documents, review Hebrew content, sell products or explain policies. Most switch between Hebrew and English many times a day.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many shifts follow Israeli business hours, which are usually seven hours ahead of US Eastern time. That can mean very early mornings. The Israeli workweek generally runs Sunday through Thursday, so Sunday shifts are common and Friday or Saturday coverage may be lighter.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Typical tools include ticketing systems, customer databases, phone and chat software, and a Hebrew keyboard layout. Workers must handle right-to-left text cleanly. Translators often use translation memory software and glossaries to keep terms consistent.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They serve Israeli customers, clients or partners and pass clear notes to US teams who may not read Hebrew. They often explain cultural context, such as Israeli holidays, direct communication styles, or local norms around dates and addresses.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers usually test Hebrew fluency before hiring. On the job, work is judged on accuracy, tone, response time and customer satisfaction. Native speakers or quality reviewers often check samples of calls, chats or translations.

qa.q: What does a Hebrew speaking employee do day to day?
qa.a: Most days involve answering Hebrew calls, chats or emails, solving account or order problems, and writing notes in English for coworkers. Some roles add sales, translation or content review. Many shifts line up with Israeli business hours, so early mornings and Sunday work are common.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to work in Hebrew?
qa.a: Usually not for customer service or sales jobs. Employers often give their own fluency test instead. There is no single national license for translators. Court interpreting rules vary by state and by court, and medical interpreting often calls for extra training or credentials, so check the rules where you plan to work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Help desk technicians answer calls, chats and tickets from employees with IT problems. They reset passwords, unlock accounts, fix printer and laptop issues, install approved software and pass harder problems to senior IT staff.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day starts with the ticket queue. Technicians work through requests by priority, take live calls and chats, and log every step. Some walk to desks to swap hardware or set up a new hire’s laptop.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use a ticketing system, remote desktop software, and directory tools for user accounts and passwords. They also rely on a knowledge base of known fixes, plus basic hardware like spare laptops, docks, cables and printers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They help employees in every department, many of whom are not technical. They hand off complex issues to system administrators and network staff, and work with managers on equipment for new and departing employees.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is often tracked by tickets closed, response and resolution times, issues fixed on first contact, and user satisfaction surveys. Clear notes in each ticket and a polite, patient manner also count.

qa.q: What does a help desk technician do day to day?
qa.a: A help desk technician works through a queue of IT requests. They reset passwords, unlock accounts, troubleshoot laptops, printers and email, and install software. They take calls and chats, connect remotely to fix problems, and record each fix in a ticket. Issues they cannot solve go to more senior IT staff.

qa.q: Is help desk a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Technicians often handle many requests at once, and callers may be frustrated or under deadline. Outages can flood the queue in minutes. Stress is lower with good documentation, clear escalation paths and reasonable ticket targets. Many people find it a solid entry point into an IT career.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Prepping and cooking food, setting up dining areas, taking orders, and serving meals and drinks. Staff also greet and check in guests, answer questions, handle complaints, clean as they go and keep food at safe temperatures from delivery to plate.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Shifts often start with deliveries, prep lists and a short pre-shift meeting. Then comes the breakfast, lunch or dinner rush. Quiet stretches go to restocking, cleaning and prep for the next shift. Early mornings, late nights, weekends and holidays are common.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Cooks, servers, dishwashers, hosts and bartenders work side by side under a chef, kitchen manager or shift lead. In company kitchens and on travel teams, they also coordinate with event planners, facility staff and the guests or employees they feed.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Knives, ovens, grills, fryers, mixers and commercial dishwashers in the kitchen. Thermometers and sanitizer test strips for food safety. Point-of-sale systems, handheld order devices and reservation software out front, plus trays, carts and steam tables for service.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Many states, counties or cities require a food handler card, and many also require a certified food protection manager on site. Serving alcohol has a minimum age, and some states require server training. Rules vary by state and locality, so check where you work.

qa.q: What does a food and hospitality worker do day to day?
qa.a: It depends on the role. Cooks prep ingredients, cook to recipes and keep stations clean. Servers greet guests, take orders, bring food and drinks, and handle payment. Most staff set up before service, work through busy rushes, then clean, restock and prep for the next shift. Food safety and teamwork run through every task.

qa.q: Is hospitality a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Meal rushes move fast, kitchens are hot, and you spend long hours on your feet. Demanding guests, short staffing and irregular schedules add pressure. Many people still enjoy the pace, the teamwork and seeing results right away. Good prep, clear systems and a supportive crew make busy shifts much easier.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Guest services staff check guests in and out, manage reservations, take payments and answer questions. They also arrange requests such as extra towels, rides or dinner bookings and resolve complaints. Housekeeping and concierge teams keep rooms ready and guests looked after.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many hotels staff the front desk around the clock. Mornings bring check-outs and billing questions, afternoons bring check-ins, and night staff run the audit. Throughout the shift, agents take calls, update reservations and check with housekeeping on which rooms are ready.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with housekeeping, maintenance, bell staff, concierges, reservations agents, security, sales and events staff, restaurant teams and managers. They also deal with guests, travel agents and tour groups.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a property management system such as Oracle Opera, key card encoders, payment terminals, phone systems and online booking channel portals. Many hotels also use guest messaging apps and CRM software for loyalty members.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Staff are judged on guest satisfaction scores and online reviews, quick check-ins, accurate billing and how they handle complaints. Many hotels also track room upgrades sold and loyalty program sign-ups.

qa.q: What does a hotel front desk agent do day to day?
qa.a: A front desk agent greets guests, checks them in and out, assigns rooms and takes payment. Between arrivals they answer phone calls and emails, update reservations, handle requests and complaints and pass messages to housekeeping and maintenance. On night shifts they also balance the day’s accounts and help with security.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to work in hotel guest services?
qa.a: No. Most entry-level guest services jobs need a high school diploma or equivalent, good communication skills and comfort with computers, and training happens on the job. A second language helps in many places. A hospitality or business degree can help later when applying for front office or hotel management roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: An HR business partner advises the leaders of one department or business unit on people decisions. They help plan reorganizations, guide performance reviews, weigh in on pay and promotions, and handle difficult employee cases such as complaints, investigations and terminations.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a leadership meeting, then moves to one-on-one coaching with managers. In between, they review a pay request, talk through a performance problem, check headcount plans and follow up on an open employee relations case.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with a department head and the managers below them. They pull in HR specialists for recruiting, compensation, benefits, learning and employee relations, and they consult legal counsel on risky cases.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their daily tools include an HR information system, people data dashboards, spreadsheets for org and budget planning, performance review software and case tracking tools. Clear writing and calm, direct conversation matter as much as any system.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in whether leaders trust their advice and act on it. Common measures include turnover and retention in their group, how smoothly reorganizations land, fair and consistent pay decisions, and employee cases resolved without legal trouble.

qa.q: What does an HR business partner do day to day?
qa.a: They spend most of the day in conversations. They coach managers on feedback and performance plans, advise leaders on team structure and staffing, review pay and promotion requests, and work through sensitive employee issues. They also study people data, such as turnover, to spot problems early and suggest fixes.

qa.q: What is the difference between an HR business partner and an HR generalist?
qa.a: An HR generalist usually handles a broad mix of day-to-day HR tasks, such as onboarding, records, benefits questions and policy enforcement. An HR business partner is more of an adviser to one group’s leaders, focusing on strategy, org design, performance and complex cases, and often relies on specialists or generalists for routine work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: HR coordinators and assistants keep HR paperwork and systems moving. They prepare offer letters, schedule interviews, run new hire onboarding, collect I-9 and tax forms, update employee records in the HRIS, process changes like address or title updates, and answer routine employee questions.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may start with checking the HR inbox and new hire paperwork. Then come interview scheduling, background check requests, onboarding sessions and data entry for job changes or terminations. Coordinators also file documents, run reports and help plan training or employee events.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They support HR generalists, recruiters, HR managers and payroll staff. They work daily with hiring managers, new hires and current employees, and sometimes with background check vendors, benefits providers and IT teams who set up accounts and equipment.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include HRIS platforms such as Workday, BambooHR or ADP Workforce Now, applicant tracking systems like Greenhouse, e-signature tools, E-Verify where the employer uses it, and scheduling tools. Microsoft Office or Google Workspace and shared drives fill the rest of the day.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Coordinators are judged on accurate and complete records, forms filed on time, smooth onboarding for new hires and quick replies to questions. Handling confidential information carefully matters greatly. Reliable, organized coordinators often move up to generalist, recruiter or HR specialist roles.

qa.q: Is HR coordinator an entry-level job?
qa.a: Often, yes. Many HR coordinators and assistants are in their first HR job, some with a bachelor’s degree in HR or business and some after an internship or office experience. The role teaches HR systems, employment paperwork and policies. With experience, many move into generalist, recruiting, benefits or payroll roles.

qa.q: What is an I-9 form and why does HR handle it?
qa.a: Form I-9 is the federal form employers use to verify that each new hire can legally work in the United States. The employee completes their section by the first day of work, and the employer reviews identity and work authorization documents within three business days. HR coordinators often manage the forms, deadlines and record keeping.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They set the company’s people strategy. That covers hiring plans, pay structures, benefits, policies and performance reviews. They also guide managers on hard cases such as discipline, layoffs and employee complaints, and they lead the HR team.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with hiring updates and leadership meetings. Afternoons may bring an employee relations issue, a policy review, budget work for raises or a benefits renewal, and one-on-ones with HR staff. An urgent complaint or investigation can reset the whole schedule.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the CEO, other executives, department managers and their own HR team. Outside the company they deal with benefits brokers, payroll providers, recruiting agencies and employment lawyers when legal questions come up.

day.label: Laws they follow
day.text: They keep the company in line with federal laws such as Title VII, the ADA, the FMLA and the Fair Labor Standards Act. State and local rules on paid leave, pay transparency and final paychecks vary, so employers in several states need extra care.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Leaders look at turnover, time to fill open roles, employee survey results, payroll and benefits costs, and legal risk. A good HR director is also judged on whether managers trust them for clear, practical advice.

qa.q: What does an HR director do day to day?
qa.a: An HR director spends the day in meetings and decisions. They review hiring progress, approve pay and job offers, update policies, and advise managers on discipline or performance problems. They handle serious employee complaints, plan budgets for salaries and benefits, and coach their HR staff. They also report to senior leaders on staffing, costs and risks.

qa.q: What is the difference between an HR manager and an HR director?
qa.a: Titles vary by company. Usually an HR manager runs daily HR work, such as hiring, onboarding, employee questions and policy enforcement, often for one site or area. An HR director sets strategy for the whole HR function, manages HR managers, controls the HR budget and reports to senior leadership. In small companies, one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: HR generalists handle a wide range of people tasks. They support hiring and onboarding, answer employee questions on pay, benefits and policies, manage leave requests, help with performance reviews, handle employee relations issues, and keep the company compliant with federal, state and local employment laws.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include onboarding new hires, answering a stream of employee emails and processing a leave of absence. Generalists also advise managers on a performance problem, update the handbook, check that I-9 forms are complete, and prepare data for payroll or open enrollment.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with employees at every level, managers and executives, plus payroll, recruiting, benefits and legal teams. Outside the company they deal with benefits brokers, insurance carriers, payroll or PEO providers, and sometimes employment lawyers or state agencies.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include HR information systems such as Workday, BambooHR, ADP Workforce Now or Rippling, applicant tracking systems, benefits platforms and e-signature tools. Excel helps with reports, and help desk or ticketing tools track employee questions.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Generalists are judged on accurate records, quick and fair answers to employees, smooth onboarding and compliance with employment laws. Leaders also watch turnover, engagement survey results, and how well HR issues are prevented or resolved before they become legal claims.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to be an HR generalist?
qa.a: No license is required to work in HR. Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business or a related field, or equal experience. Certifications such as the SHRM-CP or PHR are optional but often preferred for generalist roles, since they show knowledge of HR practice and employment law.

qa.q: What is the difference between an HR generalist and an HR specialist?
qa.a: An HR generalist covers many areas at once: hiring, onboarding, policies, leave, benefits and employee relations. An HR specialist focuses on one area in depth, such as compensation, benefits, recruiting, payroll or employee relations. Smaller companies often rely on generalists, while larger companies build teams of specialists alongside generalists and HR business partners.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They keep the HR information system running. They set up new hires, job changes, pay grades and org charts, fix data errors, manage user access and test updates. They also build reports and dashboards on headcount, hiring, pay and turnover.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The morning often starts with a ticket queue: a manager can’t see a report, or a promotion didn’t flow to payroll. Midday may go to cleaning data and building a turnover dashboard. Afternoons can bring system testing or a meeting with HR leaders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with HR generalists, recruiters, compensation and benefits staff, payroll, IT and finance. They often act as the bridge between HR and the software vendor. They also explain numbers to managers and executives who are not data experts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core HRIS plus linked systems for payroll, applicant tracking and benefits. Spreadsheets, SQL and business intelligence tools are used for reports and dashboards. Some use Python or R for deeper analysis. Data imports, integrations and role-based security settings are routine work.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means accurate, on-time data that people trust. Clean audits, smooth upgrades and protected employee privacy matter as much as polished charts. Strong specialists also help leaders act on findings, such as where turnover is rising or pay looks uneven.

qa.q: What does an HRIS and people analytics specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They maintain employee records in the HR system, fix data problems, manage who can see what, and test system changes. They pull and clean data to report on headcount, hiring, pay and turnover. They also help prepare required reports, such as the federal EEO-1 report for employers that meet the size rules, and answer data questions from HR and managers.

qa.q: What is the difference between an HRIS specialist and an HR generalist?
qa.a: An HR generalist works directly with employees on hiring, policies, benefits questions and workplace issues. An HRIS specialist runs the software and data behind those tasks and turns that data into reports. The generalist handles people problems one at a time. The HRIS specialist looks at patterns across the whole workforce. In small companies, one person may do both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: HR staff handle hiring paperwork, onboarding, employee records, benefits enrollment, leave requests and workplace policies. They answer employee questions, help managers deal with performance problems, investigate complaints and keep the company in line with federal and state employment laws.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with new-hire paperwork and Form I-9 checks. Then come a benefits question, a manager asking how to document poor performance, and interviews to schedule. Some days bring a harassment complaint or a termination meeting that needs careful notes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: HR works with employees at every level, from front-line staff to executives. They partner with managers on hiring and discipline, payroll on pay and deductions, outside benefits brokers and insurers, and employment lawyers when a dispute could turn into a legal claim.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most HR teams use an HR information system to store records, an applicant tracking system for hiring, and payroll and benefits software. Employee handbooks, job descriptions, spreadsheets and required federal and state workplace posters are everyday tools too.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good HR work shows up as jobs filled on time, accurate records, fair and consistent handling of complaints, and few legal problems. Keeping things confidential matters a lot. Mistakes with leave, overtime rules or discrimination complaints can lead to lawsuits or government penalties.

qa.q: What does a human resources specialist do day to day?
qa.a: An HR specialist spends the day answering employee questions, processing new hires and departures, updating records, and helping with benefits and leave. They advise managers on policies and discipline, look into complaints, and make sure the company follows wage, leave and anti-discrimination laws. In small companies one person may do all of this. Larger companies split it among recruiters, benefits staff and employee relations staff.

qa.q: Do you need a license or certification to work in human resources?
qa.a: No state requires a license to work in HR. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in HR, business or a related field, but entry-level roles often accept relevant experience instead. Voluntary certifications from national HR professional groups can help with hiring and promotions. The laws HR must follow, such as leave and wage rules, vary by state, so local knowledge is valuable.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: HVAC technicians install, maintain and repair heating, cooling and ventilation systems. These include furnaces, boilers, heat pumps, rooftop units, chillers and air handlers. They diagnose faults, replace parts, charge refrigerant and test that systems run safely and efficiently.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days start with a list of service calls or a project site. A tech might run preventive maintenance on rooftop units, chase down a no-heat call, then help set new equipment. Notes and photos for each job, often logged on a tablet, close out the day.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Manifold gauges, multimeters, refrigerant recovery machines, vacuum pumps, leak detectors, brazing torches and combustion analyzers. Commercial and data center work adds building automation software, where techs read alarms and adjust controls from a laptop.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Homes, offices, schools, hospitals, factories and data centers. The work happens in attics, crawl spaces, mechanical rooms and on rooftops in all kinds of weather. Data center and hospital roles often include on-call shifts, because a cooling failure cannot wait.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Federal law requires EPA Section 608 certification to service or repair equipment in ways that could release refrigerant. HVAC licensing is set by states and sometimes cities, so the rules differ widely. Many states license contractors, and some also license individual technicians.

qa.q: What does an HVAC technician do day to day?
qa.a: An HVAC technician drives to job sites or works in one large building, checking and fixing heating, cooling and ventilation equipment.
