Typical tasks include cleaning coils, changing filters and belts, testing electrical parts, finding refrigerant leaks and installing new units. They also explain problems to customers or facility managers and record the work done.

qa.q: Is HVAC technician a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Heat waves and cold snaps bring long hours and back-to-back emergency calls. The work is physical, with lifting, ladders, tight spaces and exposure to electricity and refrigerant. Many techs still find it satisfying because the problems are concrete and solvable. Commercial maintenance roles tend to be more predictable than residential service work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They create, change and remove user accounts as people join, move or leave. They set up single sign-on and multi-factor authentication, manage roles and permissions, and make sure each person can reach only the systems their job requires.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with access requests and tickets: locked accounts, new hires, role changes. Later they may connect a new app to single sign-on, review who holds admin rights, tune a password policy or script a cleanup of stale accounts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the help desk, HR, security analysts, app owners and auditors. HR events like hires and terminations drive much of their work. Managers are asked to approve access and confirm it during periodic reviews.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include directory services, identity providers for single sign-on, multi-factor authentication apps, identity governance platforms and privileged access vaults. Standards like SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect and SCIM come up daily, along with scripting in PowerShell or Python.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means people get the access they need quickly, and lose it promptly when they leave. Clean audit results, few orphaned or overprivileged accounts, and smooth logins without constant lockouts show the work is done well.

qa.q: What does an identity and access management specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They handle account setup and removal, reset access problems the help desk can’t solve, and connect apps to single sign-on. They also run access reviews, manage admin and service accounts, and gather evidence for audits. Much of the job is automating these steps so access follows HR changes without manual work.

qa.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
qa.a: Authentication proves who you are, such as entering a password and approving a multi-factor prompt. Authorization decides what you may do once you’re in, such as reading a file or approving a payment. Identity and access management teams handle both, using roles, groups and policies to control authorization.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Implementation specialists set up a new customer on a product. They map the customer’s current process, configure settings, connect other systems, move data from old tools, and train users until the customer can run on their own.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes kickoff or status calls, configuring an account, cleaning a spreadsheet of customer records before import, testing an integration, answering questions in a shared channel, and updating the project plan with tasks and dates.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the customer’s project lead, IT staff and end users. Inside the company they hand off with sales, pull in engineers or support for technical problems, and pass the finished account to a customer success manager.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include project trackers, the product’s admin console, spreadsheets for data mapping, CSV import tools, API documentation and testing tools, video meeting software, screen recorders for training clips, and a ticketing system for issues.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually measured by time to go live, hitting the agreed launch date, clean data after migration, how many users actually adopt the product, customer satisfaction scores, and how few problems come back after handoff.

qa.q: What does an implementation specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They run onboarding projects for new customers. That means leading calls, gathering requirements, configuring the product, importing and checking data, testing connections to other systems, and training users. Most juggle several customers at once, each at a different stage, and keep plans, tasks and deadlines on track until each account goes live.

qa.q: What is the difference between implementation and customer success?
qa.a: Implementation is a project with a start and end. It covers setup, data migration, integrations and training until the customer goes live. Customer success is ongoing. It starts after launch and focuses on adoption, renewals, and growing the account over time. At smaller companies one person may do both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They make sure a company charges, collects and pays sales, use, VAT and similar taxes correctly. They also set and defend the prices that related companies in the same group charge each other for goods, services, loans and intellectual property.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might mean deciding whether a new product is taxable in several states, fixing a tax code in the billing system, reviewing a return before filing, updating a benchmarking study, or gathering records for an auditor.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with accounting, finance, IT, sales and procurement teams, plus legal staff and outside advisors. They also deal with state tax auditors, foreign tax authorities and IRS examiners during audits and reviews.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include ERP systems, sales tax calculation software, exemption certificate tracking, and spreadsheets. For transfer pricing they use databases of comparable company financials, Section 482 regulations under the Internal Revenue Code, and the OECD transfer pricing guidelines.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means returns filed on time, tax charged correctly on each sale, few surprises in audits, and avoided penalties and interest. Transfer pricing work is judged on clear documentation that shows intercompany prices meet the arm’s length standard.

qa.q: What does an indirect tax and transfer pricing specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They answer questions about what is taxable and where, keep tax software settings accurate, review sales tax and VAT filings, and track rule changes. On the transfer pricing side, they set intercompany prices, test them against comparable companies, prepare documentation, and support audits by state, federal or foreign tax authorities.

qa.q: What is the difference between indirect tax and transfer pricing?
qa.a: Indirect tax covers taxes on transactions, like state and local sales and use tax in the US or VAT abroad. The US has no federal VAT, and sales tax rules vary by state. Transfer pricing is about the prices related companies charge each other, which affects how income tax is split among countries under the arm’s length standard.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They use Indonesian or Malay to help customers, translate documents, interpret conversations, or review content. Common roles include customer support, sales, localization, content moderation, and interpreting in hospitals, courts, or community settings.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A support agent answers chats, emails, and calls in the customer’s language and logs each case. Indonesia and Malaysia are many hours ahead of the continental US, so many roles involve early morning, evening, or overnight shifts.

day.label: Language skills that count
day.text: Indonesian and Malay are closely related and largely understood by each other’s speakers. They still differ in vocabulary, some spelling, and everyday phrasing. Employers often ask which one you speak natively and expect strong English as well.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Workers use ticketing and chat systems, call software, shared glossaries, and style guides. Translators often use computer-assisted translation tools. Remote interpreters work over phone or video platforms with a headset and a quiet space.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Accuracy, clear tone, and response time matter most. Support teams track customer satisfaction and quality reviews. Court interpreter credentials are set by each state, and healthcare interpreter requirements vary by state and employer.

qa.q: What does an Indonesian and Malay speaking worker do day to day?
qa.a: Most spend the day talking with or writing for people who use Indonesian or Malay. That can mean solving customer problems, translating product text, interpreting for patients or clients, or checking content for accuracy. They switch between English and the target language, follow company glossaries, and record their work in shared systems.

qa.q: What is the difference between Indonesian and Malay?
qa.a: Both come from the same Malay language. Indonesian is the national language of Indonesia, while Malay is official in Malaysia, Brunei, and Singapore. Speakers usually understand each other, but vocabulary, some spelling, and borrowed words differ. Indonesian has more Dutch loanwords, and Malaysian Malay has more English ones, so employers may want one variety specifically.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Industrial designers shape the look, feel and function of physical products. They research users, sketch concepts, build models and prototypes, choose materials and finishes, and work out how a product will be made. They refine designs until they meet cost, safety and manufacturing limits.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day mixes sketching and 3D CAD work with design reviews. Designers may build a foam model, check a 3D print, or test how a handle fits the hand. Meetings with engineers about parts, tolerances and costs often fill the afternoon.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with mechanical engineers, product managers, user researchers and marketing teams. They also talk with model makers, suppliers and factories, often overseas, about materials, colors and finishes. In design consultancies, they present concepts directly to clients.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include sketchbooks and pen tablets, CAD software such as SolidWorks, Rhino, Fusion 360 or Creo, and rendering tools like KeyShot. Adobe Photoshop and Illustrator help with presentations. Many studios use 3D printers, foam and shop tools to build physical models.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether users find the product easy and pleasant to use, whether it can be made at the target cost, and whether it fits the brand. Clear presentations, meeting design milestones and products that sell well also count.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be an industrial designer?
qa.a: Most employers expect a bachelor’s degree in industrial design or a related field, and a strong portfolio is usually the deciding factor. No state license is required to work as an industrial designer. A portfolio shows sketching, 3D modeling, prototypes and the thinking behind each design, so proven skills often weigh more than the school.

qa.q: What is the difference between an industrial designer and a mechanical engineer?
qa.a: An industrial designer focuses on how a product looks, feels and is used: form, ergonomics, materials and finish. A mechanical engineer focuses on how it works inside: structure, mechanisms, heat, strength and tolerances. The two work side by side, and both must agree on the design before tooling for mass production starts.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Industrial security specialists protect classified information and manage security clearances at defense and government contractors. They process clearance requests, brief and debrief cleared staff, control classified documents and areas, report required events to the government and prepare for government security reviews.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes starting clearance paperwork for new hires, handling visit requests, reviewing reports of foreign travel or other reportable events and giving security briefings. Specialists also check secure areas, update records in government systems and keep staff training current.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with the Facility Security Officer, program managers, human resources, IT staff who protect classified systems, and cleared employees. Outside the company they work with Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency representatives, contracting officers and background investigators.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily work runs on the government’s online systems for clearance records and investigation forms such as the SF-86. Specialists follow 32 CFR Part 117, known as the NISPOM rule, and the DD Form 254 security requirements on each contract. Visitor logs, approved safes and alarm systems are part of the job.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on clean government security reviews, accurate clearance records and prompt reporting of required events. Preventing security violations and data spills, and handling any that happen correctly, matters most. Fast clearance processing that keeps programs staffed also counts.

qa.q: What does a Facility Security Officer do?
qa.a: A Facility Security Officer, or FSO, is the employee a cleared contractor must appoint to run its security program under federal rules. The FSO must be a US citizen, hold a clearance at the facility’s level and complete required training. They oversee clearances, classified material, reporting and self-inspections, and are the main contact with the government.

qa.q: Do you need a security clearance to work in industrial security?
qa.a: Usually yes. Most industrial security roles at cleared contractors require an active clearance or the ability to get one, which requires US citizenship. Clearances are sponsored by an employer or agency, so individuals cannot apply for one on their own. Experience with clearance processing, the NISPOM rule and government security reviews counts most in hiring.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They turn a company’s offerings, often several products bundled together, into solutions for one or more target industries or audiences. They write messaging, build use cases, plan campaigns and give sales teams pitch decks and talking points in the buyer’s own language.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a sales call about a banking prospect, then move to editing a solution brief. Later they might review a webinar script for developers and check how a campaign aimed at startups is performing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product marketing, product management, sales, partner teams and content writers. They also talk with customers and industry experts to learn the rules, workflows and terms that matter in each vertical.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM, marketing automation software, slide and design apps, and analytics dashboards. Many also rely on industry reports, analyst briefings and customer interview notes to keep their messaging accurate and current.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is often measured by pipeline and revenue influenced in target segments, win rates, campaign results and how much sales teams use the materials. Strong customer stories and positive analyst coverage also count.

qa.q: What does an industry and solutions marketing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They study the problems of a target industry or audience, then show how the company’s products solve them. Most days mix writing solution briefs and case studies, coaching sales teams, planning events or webinars, meeting customers and partners, and reviewing campaign results for each segment they cover.

qa.q: What is the difference between product marketing and industry marketing?
qa.a: Product marketing starts from a product: its features, positioning and launches for all buyers. Industry or solutions marketing starts from a market segment, such as healthcare or developers, and shows how one or more products solve that segment’s needs. Titles and scope vary by company, and the two roles often overlap.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They explain how a product fits the problems of one industry, such as healthcare, banking or manufacturing. They join key sales calls, shape solution strategies, speak at events and bring customer feedback to product teams.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with prep for an executive meeting, then a whiteboard session with a customer’s technical leaders, then a deal strategy call with account executives. Afternoons often go to writing, building demos or briefing product managers on what buyers ask for.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: On the vendor side they partner with account executives, solutions engineers and sales leaders. On the customer side they meet CIOs, CTOs, architects and business unit heads. They also work with partners, analysts, and product and marketing teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their main tool is deep knowledge of the industry’s workflows, rules and buying habits. Day to day they use CRM systems, slide decks, demo environments, architecture diagrams and video calls, plus industry reports and standards documents.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually tied to influenced revenue, win rates on strategic deals and the pipeline they help build. Many are also judged on thought leadership, the strength of their customer relationships and the quality of feedback they give product teams.

qa.q: What does a field CTO do day to day?
qa.a: A field CTO meets senior technical buyers as a peer, explains the vendor’s technology direction and helps close large or complex deals. They travel to customer meetings, speak at conferences, and carry what customers need back to engineering and product leaders. Unlike a company’s main CTO, they rarely manage engineering teams directly.

qa.q: What is the difference between an industry specialist and a solutions engineer?
qa.a: A solutions engineer focuses on the product itself. They run demos, technical discovery and proofs of concept across many deals. An industry specialist focuses on one sector’s business problems, rules and language, and usually joins fewer, larger deals. Many specialists come from that industry, such as former clinicians, bankers or plant engineers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Inference engineers take models that are already trained and make them serve user requests quickly and cheaply. They tune batching, caching and memory use, shrink models with quantization, and write or choose faster GPU code, all without lowering answer quality.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include profiling a slow model, reading GPU traces, testing a lower-precision version against quality benchmarks, reviewing code, and watching dashboards for latency spikes. Some days bring an outage or a new model launch that must be ready to serve at scale.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with research scientists who train the models, infrastructure engineers who run GPU clusters, product teams who set speed and cost targets, and site reliability engineers who share on-call duty when serving systems break.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Python and C++, deep learning frameworks, GPU programming and kernel languages, open-source model serving engines, performance profilers, container orchestration, and monitoring dashboards that track tokens per second, time to first token and cost per request.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by latency, throughput, GPU utilization and cost per token, while keeping model accuracy within agreed limits. Reliability also counts, including uptime, error rates and how well the system holds up during sudden traffic spikes.

qa.q: What does an inference engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They find out why a model is slow or expensive to run, then fix it. That means profiling GPU use, trying tricks like quantization, smarter batching and key-value caching, and checking that answers stay accurate. They also deploy new models, watch production dashboards and help during outages.

qa.q: What is the difference between an inference engineer and a machine learning engineer?
qa.a: A machine learning engineer often builds data pipelines and trains and evaluates models. An inference engineer focuses on what happens after training: running models in production fast, reliably and cheaply. The role goes deeper into GPU hardware, memory limits, low-level kernels and serving systems. Titles overlap, and many companies blend the two jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Find creators whose audience fits the brand and check their past posts and audience data. Negotiate fees, deliverables, timing and usage rights. Then write briefs, review content before it goes live, track results and make sure creators get paid on time.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to email and DMs: answering creator questions, chasing drafts and confirming post dates. Later come contract edits, content reviews against the brief, and pulling numbers from live posts into a report for the brand or client.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Creators and their managers or agents, brand and product managers, social media and paid ads teams, legal staff who review contracts, and finance teams who process creator payments. At agencies, they also work closely with client account leads.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Influencer discovery and campaign platforms, spreadsheets, email outreach tools, e-signature software, and each social platform’s analytics and branded content features. Tracking links and discount codes help tie a creator’s posts to clicks and sales.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: FTC rules require creators to clearly disclose paid, gifted or other material connections to a brand, for example with #ad or a platform’s paid partnership label. Brands are expected to brief creators on this and monitor posts, so disclosure checks are part of every content review.

qa.q: What does an influencer marketing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They search for creators who fit a campaign, send outreach messages and negotiate deals. They write briefs, review drafts for brand fit and proper ad disclosure, and keep posting schedules on track. They also gather results like reach, engagement and sales from codes or links, and report what worked to the brand or client.

qa.q: What is the difference between influencer marketing and social media marketing?
qa.a: Social media marketing runs a brand’s own accounts: planning, posting and replying to followers. Influencer marketing works through other people’s accounts. It involves finding creators, negotiating contracts and usage rights, and managing outside partners. At small companies one person often does both, while larger teams usually split them into separate roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They write and update security policies, review who has access to which systems, scan for weaknesses and make sure patches get applied. When something goes wrong, they investigate the incident, contain it and document what happened and how to prevent a repeat.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with reviewing alerts from monitoring tools and deciding which ones are real threats. The rest of the day may mix access reviews, follow-up on vulnerability scans, answering staff questions about suspicious emails and preparing evidence for audits.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Analysts use security information and event management (SIEM) systems, firewalls, endpoint detection software, vulnerability scanners and identity management tools. They also rely on written frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, to organize security controls and measure progress.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with IT administrators, software developers, legal and compliance staff, and outside auditors. During a serious incident they may also coordinate with senior managers, outside response specialists, cyber insurers and, in some cases, law enforcement.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows up as fewer incidents, faster detection and response, clean audit results and staff who follow the rules. Analysts are also judged on clear reporting, since leaders need plain explanations of risk to decide where to spend.

qa.q: What does an information security analyst do day to day?
qa.a: They watch for threats, review alerts and check that systems and people follow the company’s security rules. They manage access, track weaknesses until they are fixed, train staff on risks like phishing and respond when an incident happens. Much of the job is documentation and explaining risk to managers in plain language.

qa.q: Is an information security analyst job stressful?
qa.a: It can be. Routine weeks are often steady, but a breach or ransomware attack can bring long hours, pressure from leadership and legal deadlines, since state breach notification laws set rules for telling affected people and they vary by state. Many teams use on-call rotations. Practiced response plans and supportive management make the stress easier to handle.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Inside sales representatives find and qualify leads, make outbound calls, answer inbound inquiries and run product demos over video. They send quotes and follow-up emails, handle objections and either close the deal or pass qualified prospects to an account executive.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many reps start with a focused block of calls and emails to new prospects. Midday often brings scheduled video demos. Between conversations they log notes in the CRM, prepare proposals and finish the day with follow-ups on open deals.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core kit is a headset, a CRM system, a dialer and a video meeting platform. Reps also use email sequencing tools, contact databases, e-signature software and team chat to work fast and keep every customer touch on record.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Most reps carry a quota. Managers track calls made, emails sent, meetings booked, pipeline created and revenue closed. Pay is commonly a base salary plus commission, so results directly shape earnings.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: Calls to consumers must respect the National Do Not Call Registry. The federal TCPA limits autodialed or prerecorded calls and texts to cell phones without consent. Commercial email must follow CAN-SPAM. Call recording consent rules vary by state, and some states require every party to agree.

qa.q: What does an inside sales representative do day to day?
qa.a: An inside sales representative spends most of the day talking with prospects and customers by phone, video and email. They research leads, make calls, run online demos, send quotes and follow up on open deals. They also update the CRM after each conversation so the team can see where every deal stands.

qa.q: What is the difference between inside sales and outside sales?
qa.a: Inside sales reps sell remotely from an office or home, using phone, video and email. Outside sales reps travel to meet customers in person and often manage a geographic territory. Inside reps usually handle more conversations per day and travel little, while outside reps spend more time on the road building face-to-face relationships.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Instructional designers decide what a course or training must teach, then plan the order of lessons. They write learning objectives, build activities and practice, and create quizzes or tasks that show whether people actually learned the material.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a call to a subject matter expert, then move to writing a storyboard or script. Afternoons often go to building modules in an authoring tool, reviewing feedback and fixing content before launch.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with subject matter experts, trainers, teachers or faculty, and project managers. They may also work with graphic designers, video producers, learning management system administrators and the managers who asked for the training.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include e-learning authoring software, learning management systems, slide and video editing programs, and survey tools. Many designers use models such as ADDIE or Bloom’s taxonomy to plan objectives and assessments.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether learners can do what the course promised. Designers look at quiz results, completion rates, learner feedback and, in workplaces, changes in job performance after the training.

qa.q: What does an instructional designer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix planning, writing and building. An instructional designer interviews experts, writes objectives and scripts, builds online modules or classroom materials, and designs quizzes and practice tasks. They also review drafts with stakeholders, test courses for errors and accessibility, and revise content based on learner data and feedback.

qa.q: What is the difference between an instructional designer and a trainer?
qa.a: An instructional designer plans and builds the learning: the objectives, sequence, materials and assessments. A trainer delivers it, usually by teaching live sessions in person or online. Some people do both, especially at smaller organizations, but the designer’s focus is creating the course rather than presenting it.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Underwriters review applications, decide whether to offer coverage, and set the price and terms. Claims staff investigate reported losses, check what the policy covers, estimate the damage or injury, and decide what the insurer pays.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: An underwriter reads applications, inspection reports and loss histories, then approves, declines or adjusts a policy. An adjuster returns calls from claimants, reviews photos and repair estimates, may inspect a damaged home or car, and writes up findings.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with agents and brokers, policyholders, people filing claims, actuaries, appraisers, contractors, auto body shops, medical providers, fraud investigators and attorneys. Underwriters and claims staff also share what they learn so pricing reflects real losses.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in policy and claims management software. Underwriters use rating guidelines and risk reports. Adjusters use estimating software, cameras, phones and sometimes drones or aerial images for roof damage, plus mileage logs for field visits.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Underwriters are judged on whether their accounts stay profitable over time. Adjusters are judged on accurate payments, file closing speed and following state claims handling rules, which set deadlines and fair treatment standards that vary by state.

qa.q: What is the difference between an underwriter and a claims adjuster?
qa.a: An underwriter works before a loss. They decide whether to insure a person or business and what to charge. A claims adjuster works after a loss. They investigate what happened, confirm coverage and settle the claim. Many states require adjusters to hold a license, with rules that vary by state, while underwriters usually do not need one.

qa.q: Is insurance claims work a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Adjusters often talk with people who are upset after an accident, fire or storm, and they juggle many open files with deadlines. After big disasters, workloads and travel can spike. Underwriting is usually calmer, though it has volume targets and pressure to price risk correctly.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Insurance agents learn what risks a person or business faces, compare policies, and recommend coverage such as auto, home, life, health or commercial lines. They quote prices, complete applications, explain policy terms, bind or submit coverage, and review policies with clients at renewal.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day mixes prospecting calls and emails with quotes and client meetings. Agents gather details, run quotes and explain options. They also handle policy changes, billing questions and renewals, and help clients start claims, though adjusters decide the claim itself.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Agents serve individuals, families and business owners. Captive agents represent one insurer, while independent agents and brokers place business with several carriers. They also work with underwriters, customer service staff, agency owners, and lenders or car dealers who need proof of coverage.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Agents use agency management systems, carrier quoting portals and comparative rating software to price policies across insurers. A CRM, e-signature tools, phone and video calls, and online continuing education courses that keep the license current are also common.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Agents are judged on new policies written, premium volume and retention, meaning how many clients renew. Pay often mixes salary with commission, or is all commission. Accurate applications, suitable recommendations and following state insurance rules also matter, since they keep the agent licensed.

qa.q: Do you need a license to sell insurance?
qa.a: Yes. Every state requires a producer license from its insurance department for each line sold, such as life and health or property and casualty. Getting one usually means prelicensing study, a state exam and a background check, often with fingerprints. Agents must complete continuing education and hold a license in each state where they sell.

qa.q: What is the difference between a captive and an independent insurance agent?
qa.a: A captive agent represents one insurance company and sells only its policies, often with leads, training and brand support from that company. An independent agent is appointed with several insurers and can compare their quotes for each client. Independent agents often own their agency or work for one, and may control their own book of clients.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Intellectual property specialists help protect inventions, brands and creative work. They prepare and track patent and trademark filings, manage deadlines and renewals, search for conflicting marks or prior art, register copyrights, and support cease-and-desist letters and takedown notices when others copy the company’s products or content.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include docketing new office actions, reminding attorneys of response deadlines and preparing filing documents. Specialists also run trademark searches, check online marketplaces for knockoffs, file takedown requests, and update the portfolio database with registrations and renewal dates.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with patent attorneys and agents, trademark counsel, inventors and engineers, and marketing teams naming new products. They also coordinate with outside law firms, foreign associates who file abroad, the US Patent and Trademark Office, and online platforms that handle infringement complaints.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include IP docketing and portfolio management software, the USPTO’s Patent Center and trademark filing systems, patent search databases and trademark watch services. Excel, document management systems and e-filing portals for foreign patent offices are also used daily.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: The biggest test is never missing a deadline, since a missed response or maintenance fee can cost rights. Specialists are also judged on accurate filings, clean records, timely searches and how quickly they act against copies. Attorneys value clear status reports on the whole portfolio.

qa.q: Do you need to be a lawyer to work in intellectual property?
qa.a: No. Many IP roles, such as paralegals, docketing specialists and brand protection analysts, do not require a law degree. To represent inventors before the US Patent and Trademark Office, you must pass the patent registration exam, which requires a science or engineering background. Patent agents can prosecute patents but cannot handle trademarks for others or give general legal advice.

qa.q: What is the difference between a patent, a trademark and a copyright?
qa.a: A patent, granted by the US Patent and Trademark Office, protects a new invention, such as a device or process, for a limited term. A trademark protects a brand name, logo or slogan that identifies goods or services. A copyright protects original creative work, such as writing, music, software or images, from the moment it is fixed.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Intelligence analysts collect and study information about threats, groups, people and events, then write assessments that help leaders decide what to do. They check sources for reliability, connect pieces of evidence, judge what is likely to happen next and brief their findings clearly and on time.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day starts with reading overnight reporting and open-source news on assigned topics. Analysts then update databases, map links between people or events, draft short assessments and brief supervisors or customers. Many also respond to urgent requests when a situation changes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with collectors, investigators, other analysts, military or law enforcement officers and the policymakers who use their products. In companies they support security, fraud, legal and executive teams. Many share information with partner agencies under strict rules.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include link analysis software like i2 Analyst’s Notebook, mapping tools like ArcGIS, and secure databases and message systems. Analysts use structured analytic techniques, open-source research tools and Excel. Private sector threat intelligence teams also use threat intelligence platforms and SIEM data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on accuracy, timeliness and how useful assessments are to decision makers. Good analysts state confidence clearly, separate facts from judgments and cite sources. In the US intelligence community, written products are checked against formal analytic standards.

qa.q: Do intelligence analysts need a security clearance?
qa.a: Government and defense contractor intelligence analysts almost always need a clearance, often Top Secret with access to sensitive compartmented information. Some agencies also require a polygraph. Clearances require US citizenship and a background investigation. Private sector analysts who work on fraud, brand or cyber threats usually do not need one.

qa.q: What degree do you need to be an intelligence analyst?
qa.a: Most roles ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in international relations, political science, criminal justice, a foreign language, regional studies or computer science. Military intelligence experience is a common path in. Language skills and regional knowledge are highly valued, and some agencies accept relevant work experience in place of a degree.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Interns and new grads take on real but scoped tasks inside a team. These include research, data entry, drafting reports, writing code, supporting customers or helping run events. The exact mix depends on the field, from engineering and finance to marketing and healthcare.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days start with a check-in with a manager or mentor to set priorities. Then comes focused work on assigned tasks, a few meetings and time spent learning the team’s tools and processes. Many programs end with a final project or presentation.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They report to a supervisor and often have a mentor or buddy for everyday questions. They work alongside full-time staff, other interns and, in some roles, clients or customers. Recruiters or HR staff usually run onboarding and check on progress.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers look at reliability, the quality of finished work, willingness to ask questions and how fast skills grow. Many internships include a midpoint and a final review. Strong performers may receive a return offer for another term or a full-time job.

day.label: Rules on pay
day.text: Under federal law, most for-profit employers must pay interns at least minimum wage unless the intern, not the company, is the primary beneficiary of the arrangement. Some states add stricter rules, so terms vary by state. Academic credit alone does not settle the question.

qa.q: What does an intern do day to day?
qa.a: An intern spends the day on assigned tasks that support a team, such as research, analysis, drafting documents, coding or helping customers. They attend team meetings, check in with a supervisor or mentor and learn the tools the team uses. Many also join training sessions and work toward a final project shown at the end of the term.

qa.q: What is the difference between an intern and a new grad hire?
qa.a: An intern is usually still in school and works a fixed term, often a summer or a semester, sometimes for academic credit. A new grad hire has finished a degree and joins in an entry-level role, often permanent and sometimes through a rotational or training program. Both get structured training, but new grads carry fuller responsibility.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan and write messages that keep employees informed. This includes the staff newsletter, intranet posts, leadership emails and talking points. They also run the all-hands meeting and explain big changes like reorganizations, new policies or office moves.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with editing a leader’s weekly note, then a meeting to plan an upcoming change announcement. Afternoons often go to drafting intranet stories, checking engagement numbers and answering managers who need help explaining news to their teams.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with executives, human resources, legal and the external communications or PR team. They also lean on people managers, who pass messages down to their teams, and on IT for the tools that deliver them.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include the company intranet, email newsletter platforms, team chat apps and video meeting software for town halls. Many also use pulse surveys, basic design tools, video editing and a shared content calendar.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether employees understand and act on key messages. Managers look at newsletter open rates, intranet views, survey results, town hall questions and how smoothly staff take in major changes without confusion or leaked news.

qa.q: What does an internal communications manager do day to day?
qa.a: They write and edit messages for employees, coach leaders on what to say and plan the timing of announcements. They run newsletters, the intranet and all-hands meetings. When big news hits, such as layoffs, mergers or new benefits, they coordinate with HR and legal so staff hear it clearly, accurately and in the right order.

qa.q: What is the difference between internal communications and public relations?
qa.a: Internal communications speaks to a company’s own employees. Public relations speaks to outside audiences such as the media, customers and the public. The two teams work together because internal news often becomes public. Many companies coordinate timing so employees hear important announcements before they appear in the press.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They map how money moves through processes like sales, purchasing and payroll. They write down the key controls in each one and test whether those controls work. When a test fails, they help the process owner fix the gap and then retest it.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a walkthrough of the payables process. Then they pull samples of approved invoices, check approvals and system logs, and write up the results. Afternoons often go to answering document requests from the outside audit team.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with process owners in accounting, finance and IT, plus internal audit, the controller and the CFO. They also deal often with the company’s outside auditors. Their findings may reach the audit committee of the board, which oversees financial reporting.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets, flowcharts, risk and control matrices, and governance, risk and compliance software. Most US companies use the COSO internal control framework. They also review reports from the company’s ERP system and check IT general controls such as user access and change management.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means controls hold up when the outside auditor tests them. Problems are rated as deficiencies, significant deficiencies or material weaknesses. A material weakness must be disclosed in the public company’s annual report, so catching and fixing issues early matters a great deal.

qa.q: What does a SOX and internal controls specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They document business processes, identify the risks of errors or fraud, and list the controls that address those risks. Much of the day goes to testing those controls by pulling samples and checking evidence. They also track fixes for failed controls, update documentation when processes change, and gather evidence for the outside auditors.

qa.q: What is the difference between a SOX specialist and an external auditor?
qa.a: A SOX specialist works for the company or a consulting firm. They help management design, document and test controls for its own assessment under Section 404(a). The external auditor works for an independent firm registered with the PCAOB. For larger public companies, that auditor gives a separate opinion on the controls under Section 404(b) and must stay independent of management.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Counts stock by hand or with scanners, runs scheduled cycle counts, compares the counts with the inventory system, investigates any gaps, and corrects records once the cause of a discrepancy is found or approved.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Starts with a list of bins or aisles to count, scans shelves, checks receiving and shipping paperwork, tracks down mismatched items, and updates the system before the shift ends. Busy days add full physical inventories or audit prep.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Handheld barcode scanners, inventory or warehouse management software, spreadsheets and label printers. Some roles also use forklifts or powered pallet jacks, and OSHA requires employers to train and evaluate anyone who operates that powered equipment.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Receiving and shipping crews, warehouse or store supervisors, purchasing staff and accounting teams. Each group depends on accurate counts to place orders, fill customer requests and keep financial records correct.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By inventory accuracy, how fast discrepancies get resolved, shrink trends and clean audit results. Bad records lead to stockouts, overordering and wrong numbers in financial reports, so attention to detail matters most.

qa.q: What does an inventory specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They count stock in assigned locations, compare the counts with what the system says, and look into anything that does not match. That can mean checking receiving logs, finding misplaced items or spotting damage and theft. They then fix records, report problems to supervisors and help prepare for audits or full physical counts.

qa.q: What is the difference between an inventory specialist and a stock clerk?
qa.a: A stock clerk mostly moves goods: unloading, unpacking and shelving items. An inventory specialist focuses on the records: counting, reconciling the system with the shelves and explaining discrepancies. Titles vary by employer, and in smaller workplaces one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Review tips and complaints about fraud, abuse, data leaks or misconduct. Plan each inquiry, gather records and documents, interview witnesses and the people involved, and write a clear, factual report of what happened.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to reviewing case files, emails, transaction records or system access logs. Afternoons bring interviews, follow-up calls and careful notes. The day usually ends with updating case files and drafting findings.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Investigators work closely with human resources, legal counsel, compliance, security, IT and auditors. When a case involves a crime or a reporting duty, findings may be shared with law enforcement or regulators.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Case management software, spreadsheets, data analysis tools and public records databases are common. Some use digital forensic tools. Recording an interview or call must follow state law, since some states require consent from everyone on the call.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work is fair, thorough and well documented. Evidence must be handled so its integrity can be shown, details must stay confidential, and reports must be clear enough to support discipline, claims decisions or legal action.

qa.q: What does an investigations specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They read complaints and tips, pull records such as emails, payments or access logs, and look for patterns. They interview witnesses and the people accused, keep careful notes, and protect evidence. Then they write reports that state the facts, what the evidence shows, and whether the claim was supported, so managers or lawyers can decide what to do.

qa.q: What is the difference between an investigations specialist and a private investigator?
qa.a: An investigations specialist usually works in-house for one employer, insurer or agency and looks into internal matters. A private investigator is hired by outside clients. Most states require private investigators to hold a license, but rules vary by state, and many states exempt employees who only investigate for their own employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They find, test and close investments. That means screening companies to buy or fund, building financial models, running due diligence, negotiating terms and reporting results to investors, a board or an investment committee.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with market news and a review of the deal pipeline. Most hours go to valuation models, investment memos and calls with company leaders, bankers and lawyers. Work speeds up sharply when a deal nears signing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with executives, boards, investment committees, investment bankers, lawyers, accountants and consultants. In funds they answer to investors who put in the money. After a purchase, they hand off to the teams that run and integrate the business.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheet financial models and slide decks are daily tools. They also use market data terminals, virtual data rooms for due diligence, deal and investor tracking software, and company financial statements read line by line.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Roles at broker-dealers often require FINRA exams such as the SIE plus the Series 79 or Series 7, and many states require the Series 63. In-house corporate development usually needs no license. Investment advisers register with the SEC or their state, depending on firm size.

qa.q: What does an investment and corporate development professional do day to day?
qa.a: They look for companies or assets worth buying or funding, then test them. They build financial models, read financial statements, meet management teams and write investment memos. When a deal moves ahead, they coordinate lawyers and accountants, negotiate terms and present the case to decision makers. After closing, they track how the investment performs and report to investors or the board.

qa.q: What is the difference between corporate development and investment banking?
qa.a: Corporate development works inside one company. The team buys, sells or partners with other businesses to serve that company’s own strategy and often helps with integration after a deal. Investment bankers are outside advisers. They work for many clients, help them sell, buy or raise capital, and are usually paid fees tied to completed deals. Many corporate development hires start in banking.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Analysts build financial models such as discounted cash flow, merger and leveraged buyout models. They run valuation comparisons, draft pitch books and offering memorandums, and gather data for due diligence on mergers, acquisitions, stock offerings and debt deals.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with updating models and slide decks from the night before. Analysts take comments from senior bankers, fix numbers, join client calls, and keep working into the evening. Long hours and weekend work are common, especially when a deal is close to signing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Analysts report to associates, vice presidents and managing directors on a deal team. They exchange information with client finance staff, outside lawyers, accountants and the bank’s capital markets and compliance groups.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Excel and PowerPoint are the core tools, used for models and client presentations. Analysts also use financial data terminals, company filings on the SEC’s EDGAR system, and virtual data rooms where deal documents are shared.

day.label: Licenses and rules
day.text: Analysts at FINRA member broker-dealers usually must register and pass the SIE and Series 79 exams, often soon after starting and with firm sponsorship. Some firms also require the Series 63. Strict rules govern confidential deal information and insider trading.

qa.q: What does an investment banking analyst do day to day?
qa.a: Most of the day goes to building and checking financial models, preparing slides for client pitches and live deals, and pulling company and market data. Analysts also manage due diligence requests, update deal documents, and turn around comments from senior bankers, often late into the night and on weekends when a deal is active.

qa.q: What is the difference between an investment banking analyst and an associate?
qa.a: An analyst is the entry-level role, often hired straight from college for a program of about two to three years. Analysts do most of the modeling and slide work. An associate is the next level up, often hired after an MBA or promoted from analyst. Associates review analysts’ work, manage the deal workflow, and have more client contact.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Investor relations managers explain a company’s results, strategy and outlook to shareholders and analysts. They prepare quarterly earnings releases, scripts and slides, run earnings calls, organize investor meetings and conferences, track who owns the stock, and bring market feedback back to the CEO and CFO.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Outside earnings season, a day may include calls with analysts, setting up investor meetings, updating the investor website and studying peer companies. During earnings season, work shifts to drafting the release, script and Q&A prep, then handling a wave of calls after results come out.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: IR managers work most closely with the CFO, CEO, FP&A and accounting teams, legal counsel and corporate communications. Outside the company, they deal with sell-side analysts, buy-side portfolio managers, proxy advisors and IR agencies. They also report shareholder feedback to the board.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include shareholder data and analytics platforms, investor CRM systems, webcast services for earnings calls, and the SEC’s EDGAR system. Bloomberg terminals or FactSet help track the stock, peers and analyst estimates. PowerPoint and Word fill much of the rest of the day.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: IR is judged on clear, consistent messages, well-run earnings calls, useful investor meetings and honest feedback to leaders. Leaders also watch analyst coverage and the shareholder base. Above all, the team must follow Regulation FD and securities laws so no investor gets material news before others.

qa.q: What does an investor relations manager do day to day?
qa.a: An investor relations manager answers questions from analysts and shareholders, sets up meetings between investors and executives, and tracks how the stock and peer companies are trading. They write or edit earnings materials, update investor presentations and the website, and report market feedback to leadership. Every message must follow disclosure rules such as Regulation FD.

qa.q: What background do you need for investor relations?
qa.a: Most IR managers come from finance, equity research, corporate development, accounting or corporate communications. A bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting or business is typical, and an MBA or CFA charter can help. No license is required for the role itself. Employers look for financial modeling, writing and presentation skills plus sound judgment about disclosure.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: iOS developers write Swift code for iPhone and iPad apps. They build screens, connect apps to servers through APIs, store data on the device, fix bugs, and update apps when new iOS versions change how features work.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a short team check-in. Then comes coding a feature, reviewing a teammate’s pull request, testing on a simulator and real devices, and chasing crash reports from the live app.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core tool is Xcode, which runs only on a Mac. Developers use SwiftUI or UIKit for screens, Git for version control, Instruments for performance checks, and TestFlight to send test builds to users.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with designers on layouts, backend developers on APIs, QA testers on bugs, and product managers on priorities. Many teams also include Android developers building the same app for other phones.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in a stable app with few crashes, smooth scrolling, fast launch times, and good App Store ratings. Code must also pass team review and the App Store’s review rules before each release.

qa.q: What does an iOS developer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix writing Swift code, testing it, and fixing problems. An iOS developer builds new features, reviews other people’s code, tests on simulators and real iPhones and iPads, reads crash reports, and joins planning meetings. Near a release, they prepare builds, send them to testers, and submit the app for App Store review.

qa.q: What is the difference between an iOS developer and an Android developer?
qa.a: An iOS developer builds apps for iPhone and iPad, mainly in Swift using Xcode on a Mac. An Android developer builds apps for Android phones, mainly in Kotlin using Android Studio. The goals are similar, but the languages, tools, design rules, and app store review processes differ. Some developers learn both or use cross-platform frameworks.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: An IT manager leads the team that keeps a company’s technology running. They plan the IT budget, approve purchases, manage software licenses and vendor contracts, set security rules, and make sure laptops, accounts and networks work for every employee.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a check of open help desk tickets and any overnight outages. The rest of the day mixes team check-ins, vendor calls, project planning, approving access requests, and meetings with department heads about upcoming needs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They supervise help desk staff, system administrators and network technicians. They also work closely with finance on budgets, HR on new hires and departures, outside vendors and contractors, and senior leaders who set company priorities.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a ticketing system, device management software for laptops and phones, identity and access tools for user accounts, network monitoring dashboards, backup systems, and spreadsheets for tracking licenses, assets and spending.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by system uptime, how fast tickets get resolved, staying within budget, passing security audits, and keeping software licenses compliant. Leaders also judge how well the IT team supports company goals and how smoothly new projects launch.

qa.q: What does an IT manager do day to day?
qa.a: An IT manager runs the company’s IT team and its technology. Day to day, they review support tickets, assign work to staff, handle escalated problems, approve purchases, track software licenses and spending, plan upgrades, and meet with other departments. They also review security alerts and make sure new employees get working accounts and equipment quickly.

qa.q: What is the difference between an IT manager and a system administrator?
qa.a: A system administrator does hands-on technical work, such as configuring servers, managing user accounts and applying updates. An IT manager oversees the whole IT function. They lead people, set priorities, manage the budget and vendors, and report to company leaders. In smaller companies, one person may do both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Defines scope, builds the schedule and budget, assigns tasks, and tracks progress on technology projects such as system upgrades, cloud migrations and software rollouts. Manages risks, issues and change requests, and keeps the project moving from kickoff to go-live.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Often starts with a stand-up or status check, then moves between meetings with developers, vendors and business owners. Updates the plan, clears blockers, follows up on late tasks and writes status reports. Near go-live, the focus shifts to testing sign-offs, cutover planning and off-hours deployment support.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Works with developers, system administrators, network and security staff, business analysts, testers and outside vendors. Reports to project sponsors and IT leaders, and works closely with the end users whose daily work the new system will change.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Project tracking software, Gantt charts, task boards, ticketing systems, shared documents and video meetings. Uses waterfall, Agile or Scrum methods, often a mix. Common documents include the project charter, RACI chart, risk register and cutover plan.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether the project goes live on time, within budget and with the agreed scope. Smooth user adoption, few defects after launch and stakeholders who felt informed along the way also count.

qa.q: What does an IT project manager do day to day?
qa.a: They run meetings, update the project plan, and check that tasks are on schedule. They remove blockers for the technical team, manage vendor work, track the budget and log risks. They also send status updates to sponsors. Before go-live, they coordinate testing, training and the cutover, and they may support launches at night or on weekends.

qa.q: Do IT project managers need a certification?
qa.a: No license is required in the US. Many employers prefer or ask for a credential such as the PMP or a Scrum certification. The PMP requires documented project experience, training hours and a passed exam. Hands-on experience leading technology projects and some technical knowledge often matter as much as any certificate.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: IT support staff set up laptops and phones for new hires, reset passwords, unlock accounts and fix printers, Wi-Fi and email problems. They install updates, manage software licenses and take back equipment when people leave the company.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days start with the ticket queue. They answer calls and chats, walk people through fixes, visit desks or connect remotely, and log each step. Planned work like imaging new laptops or moving an office fits around urgent requests.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They work in a help desk ticketing system, remote access software and admin consoles for user accounts, email and device management. A basic toolkit, spare cables, adapters and loaner laptops are kept close at hand.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Their users are coworkers in every department, from new hires to executives. They escalate harder issues to network, security or systems administrators and deal with outside vendors for hardware repairs, phone lines and software support.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers look at how fast tickets are answered and closed, how often problems come back, and feedback from users. Clear notes, careful handling of passwords and data, and staying calm with frustrated coworkers matter as much as technical skill.

qa.q: What does an IT support specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They work through requests from coworkers who can’t log in, print, connect or use an app. They fix what they can by phone, chat or remote session, visit desks for hardware issues, set up equipment for new staff and pass complex problems to senior IT teams.

qa.q: What is the difference between IT support and a help desk job?
qa.a: The terms overlap. Help desk usually means the first point of contact, answering calls and tickets and solving common problems. IT support can be broader, including hands-on hardware work, setting up devices, managing accounts and handling issues escalated from the help desk. Small companies often combine both in one role.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Handle calls, emails and chats in Italian with customers, clients or partners in Italy, or with Italian speakers in the US. Most roles also use English for internal notes, reports and team meetings.

day.label: Common job types
day.text: Customer support agent, account manager, sales rep, interpreter, translator, travel agent, tour guide and hotel staff. Italian is the key skill, but the job title usually describes the main work.

day.label: Working across time zones
day.text: Italy is usually six hours ahead of US Eastern time. Roles that serve customers in Italy may start very early in the morning in the US, or follow a European schedule when fully remote.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Headsets, ticketing and CRM systems, chat platforms and video calls. Translators often use translation memory software and glossaries. Typing accented letters like à, è and ò quickly matters in written support.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers often test spoken and written Italian before hiring. On the job, managers track response time, customer satisfaction and quality reviews, including correct grammar and polite tone, such as the formal Lei with customers.

qa.q: Do I need a certificate to get an Italian speaking job?
qa.a: Most support, sales and travel employers give their own language test instead of asking for a certificate. Interpreting is different. Many states require a credential to interpret in state courts, and rules vary by state. Medical interpreter certification is usually voluntary, but some employers ask for it. A recognized proficiency exam result can still help your application.

qa.q: What is the difference between an Italian interpreter and an Italian translator?
qa.a: An interpreter works with spoken language in real time, in person, by phone or by video, for meetings, hospitals or courts. A translator works with written text, such as contracts, websites or manuals, and has time to research and edit. Translators usually work into their native language. Some people do both, but the skills and tests differ.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: IT service management staff run the system and rules that handle IT requests, incidents and changes. They configure the ticketing platform, set up workflows and service level targets, manage the service catalog, run change approval meetings and report on how well IT serves the business.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes reviewing open incidents and overdue tickets, running a change advisory board meeting and fixing workflow problems in the platform. ITSM staff also build reports on response times, update knowledge articles and gather requirements for new request forms.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with service desk agents, IT support and infrastructure teams, application owners and security staff. They also meet business managers who request new services, and auditors who check that changes and access follow policy.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: ServiceNow is the best-known platform, with Jira Service Management, BMC Helix and Freshservice also widely used. Many teams follow the ITIL framework. Daily work includes building forms and workflows, scripting in JavaScript inside ServiceNow, and creating dashboards and reports.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether tickets are resolved within service level targets, how few changes cause outages and how satisfied users are. Managers also look at repeat incidents, knowledge base use, audit findings and how smoothly new workflows roll out.

qa.q: What is ITIL and do I need it for an ITSM job?
qa.a: ITIL is a widely used framework of good practices for running IT services, covering areas such as incident, problem, change and request management. It is not a law or a license. Many ITSM job postings ask for an ITIL Foundation certificate, and it is a common first step into the field.

qa.q: What is the difference between ITSM and the IT help desk?
qa.a: The help desk, or service desk, is the team that answers users and works tickets. ITSM is the wider practice that designs how all IT work is requested, tracked, approved and measured, including the ticket system itself. ITSM roles focus on processes, platform setup and reporting rather than fixing individual user problems.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Janitors and cleaners keep buildings clean, stocked and safe. They sweep, mop, vacuum, empty trash and recycling, clean restrooms and break rooms, dust and disinfect surfaces, restock paper and soap, and report repairs. Some also strip and wax floors, shampoo carpets and handle minor maintenance.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many work evening or night shifts after offices close. A shift starts with picking up a cart and a route list, then moving through restrooms, offices and common areas. Spills, event setups and urgent calls interrupt the route, and the shift ends with cleaning logs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with a lead or supervisor, other cleaners on the crew and building maintenance staff. In hospitals they work with nurses and infection control teams, and in hotels with housekeeping managers. They also see tenants, office staff and security guards.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include carts, mops, microfiber cloths, vacuums, auto scrubbers, floor buffers and carpet extractors. Cleaners use chemicals with safety data sheets, gloves and other protective gear. Many crews log work on a phone app or scan codes posted in each area.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Cleaners are judged on clean, safe spaces with no missed areas, full supplies and few complaints in inspections. Using chemicals safely, following hospital or food safety rules where they apply, showing up reliably and respecting tenants’ property and privacy also count.

qa.q: What is the difference between a janitor and a housekeeper?
qa.a: A janitor or custodian usually cleans offices, schools, factories and common areas and may handle trash, floor care and light maintenance. A housekeeper usually cleans rooms where people stay or live, such as hotel rooms, hospital patient rooms or private homes, including making beds and changing linens. Duties overlap, and titles vary by employer.

qa.q: Do you need training to be a janitor?
qa.a: Most janitor jobs need no degree and train on the job. Employers must train workers on the hazardous chemicals they use under OSHA’s hazard communication standard, and hospital cleaners learn infection control steps. Optional certificates in floor care or green cleaning can help. Some jobs require a background check or a driver’s license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They answer calls, emails and chats in Japanese, explain products or services, and solve customer problems. Many also translate documents, write business email in polite Japanese, and pass messages between Japanese clients and English-speaking coworkers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Japan is 13 to 14 hours ahead of US Eastern time, and Japan does not use daylight saving time. So many workers take early morning or late evening calls, then spend the rest of the day on tickets, reports and translation.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They deal with customers, suppliers and partner companies in Japan, Japanese travelers and residents in the US, and US teams in sales, support, engineering or management who need someone to bridge language and business customs.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include a Japanese keyboard input method, ticketing and customer record systems, video meeting software, shared glossaries and style guides. Translators often use translation memory software and review machine translation output by hand.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers look at accuracy, natural wording, and correct use of keigo, the polite and honorific forms Japanese business expects. Response time, customer satisfaction scores, and clear notes in English for the US team also count.

qa.q: What does a Japanese speaking employee do day to day?
qa.a: Most handle customer or client contact in Japanese by phone, email or chat. They answer questions, fix account or order problems, and translate messages and documents. Because of the time difference with Japan, they often work early or late hours and write English summaries so US coworkers know what the customer needs.

qa.q: Do I need a certificate to get a Japanese speaking job?
qa.a: No license is required for most of these jobs. Many employers ask for JLPT level N2 or N1, the top levels of the Japanese Language Proficiency Test, or test you in the interview. Court and medical interpreting are different. Their credential rules vary by state and by setting, so check before applying.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Java developers write and maintain server-side code for business systems, such as payment processing, account services and order handling. They build APIs, fix bugs, write unit tests and review teammates’ code before it is released.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team stand-up meeting. Then comes coding on an assigned ticket, running tests and reading logs to trace a problem. Afternoons may bring code reviews, a design discussion or help with a release.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include an IDE for writing code, build tools like Maven or Gradle, Git for version control and frameworks such as Spring Boot. Many teams also use JUnit for tests, SQL databases, containers and automated build pipelines.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with other developers, QA testers, product owners and business analysts who explain what the system must do. In banks and large companies they also coordinate with security, operations and database teams before changes go live.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether code is correct, readable, tested and secure. Teams track production incidents, slow performance and missed deadlines. In regulated fields like banking, code changes often need documented review and sign-off before release.

qa.q: What does a Java developer do day to day?
qa.a: A Java developer spends most of the day writing and testing code for back-end systems. That includes adding features, fixing bugs, connecting services to databases and other systems, and reviewing teammates’ code. Short meetings to plan work and discuss designs are common, and some developers take turns on call to fix urgent problems in live systems.

qa.q: What is the difference between a Java developer and a JavaScript developer?
qa.a: Java and JavaScript are separate languages despite the similar names. Java developers mostly build server software that runs business logic, handles data and talks to databases. JavaScript developers often build what runs in the web browser, though JavaScript can also run on servers. The syntax, tools and typical job duties are different.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: JavaScript and TypeScript developers write code for the browser and the server. On the frontend they build interactive pages, and on the backend they write APIs with Node.js. Many work full stack, adding features end to end, writing tests and fixing bugs on both sides.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day starts with a standup and a look at assigned tickets. Then comes writing and reviewing code, often moving between frontend components and backend endpoints. Debugging in browser developer tools, updating packages and checking test results in the build pipeline fill much of the rest.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with designers, product managers, QA testers and other developers. On smaller teams they may cover frontend, backend and some deployment work themselves. On larger teams they coordinate with specialists in mobile, data, security and DevOps.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include VS Code, TypeScript, Node.js and npm, plus a frontend framework like React, Angular or Vue. Build tools like Vite or webpack, testing tools like Jest or Playwright, linters like ESLint, and Git are part of daily work.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on features that work in every supported browser, code others can read and strong tests. Teams also watch page speed, error rates in monitoring tools and how often old bugs come back. Catching type errors early with TypeScript is valued.

qa.q: What is the difference between JavaScript and TypeScript?
qa.a: TypeScript is JavaScript with added type labels for variables and functions. A tool checks those types before the code runs, then turns TypeScript into plain JavaScript that browsers and Node.js can run.
