Many also deal with outside study investigators, health plans, partner hospitals, and regulators such as the FDA or state health agencies.

day.label: What the role requires
day.text: Most roles require an MD or DO, and many ask for an active, unrestricted state medical license and board certification. Licensing needs vary by state and by role. Clinical experience plus leadership, research or industry background is usually expected.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is judged by patient safety, quality measures, clean audits and inspections, and sound medical decisions that hold up under review. In biotech, meeting trial milestones and supporting regulatory submissions also matter. Trust from clinicians and leadership is a key measure.

qa.q: What does a medical director do day to day?
qa.a: A medical director reviews cases and safety data, approves clinical protocols and content, and answers medical questions from staff. They meet with clinical, regulatory and business teams, advise leaders on medical risk, and keep policies current with new evidence and rules. Some still see patients part time, depending on the employer.

qa.q: What is the difference between a medical director and a chief medical officer?
qa.a: A medical director usually oversees one program, site, product or function. A chief medical officer is a top executive who sets medical strategy for the whole company, often reports to the CEO, and may supervise several medical directors. At small companies one person can hold both roles, and titles vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Medical science liaisons are scientific experts at drug, biotech and device companies. They build relationships with leading doctors and researchers, discuss clinical data, answer unsolicited medical questions, support investigator-led studies and bring insights from the field back to the company.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days involve travel within an assigned region to meet physicians at hospitals and academic centers, plus virtual meetings. Liaisons prepare to present new study results, answer questions, write up insights from each meeting and keep up with new publications.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Outside the company they meet physicians, pharmacists, nurse practitioners and researchers. Inside, they work with medical affairs, clinical development, health economics and medical information teams. They train sales colleagues on science but keep their own work separate from promotion.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM such as Veeva CRM for logging interactions, approved scientific slide decks on a tablet, PubMed and journal databases, video meeting software and conference abstract libraries. Many also use internal insight reporting platforms.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Liaisons are judged on the quality and number of scientific exchanges with experts, useful insights reported, depth of scientific knowledge and support for research. They are not measured on sales and must follow FDA rules and company policies on promotion.

qa.q: Do you need a doctorate to be a medical science liaison?
qa.a: Most employers prefer a doctoral degree such as a PharmD, PhD, MD or DNP. Some hire nurse practitioners, physician assistants or people with a master’s degree and deep experience in a disease area. The role itself needs no license, though pharmacists and nurses often keep theirs. Strong presentation skills and clinical research knowledge matter as much as the degree.

qa.q: What is the difference between a medical science liaison and a pharmaceutical sales rep?
qa.a: A pharmaceutical sales rep promotes approved uses of a medicine and has sales goals. A medical science liaison sits in medical affairs, has no sales goals and holds peer-level scientific discussions with experts. Liaisons may answer unsolicited questions about uses not yet approved, which sales reps are not allowed to discuss.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Medical writers produce documents about drugs, devices and diseases. Regulatory writers draft clinical study protocols, study reports and parts of submissions to the FDA. Others write journal articles, conference posters, continuing education for doctors, training for staff and plain-language materials for patients.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Writers read study data tables and published research, draft or revise sections, and work through review comments from scientists, statisticians and lawyers. They check every number and reference against the source. Many work remotely, and many freelance for several clients.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with clinical scientists, biostatisticians, physicians, regulatory affairs and medical affairs staff. Editors and quality reviewers check their drafts. Promotional pieces also go through medical, legal and regulatory review before release.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Microsoft Word with company templates, PowerPoint, reference managers such as EndNote or Zotero, PubMed for literature searches, document management systems such as Veeva Vault and medical style guides. Some writers use Adobe Acrobat and statistical output viewers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on accuracy against the source data, clarity for the reader, following templates and regulatory guidelines, and meeting deadlines. Fewer review rounds and claims that hold up to legal and regulatory review also count.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a medical writer?
qa.a: No license is required, but most medical writers hold a degree in life sciences, pharmacy, nursing or medicine, and many have a PhD, PharmD or MD. Employers look for writing samples, accuracy and knowledge of study design and regulatory documents. Voluntary certifications and short courses exist, and many writers move into the field from research or clinical work.

qa.q: What is the difference between regulatory and medical communications writing?
qa.a: Regulatory writers create documents for health authorities such as the FDA, including protocols, clinical study reports and submission summaries, following strict international guidelines. Medical communications writers create content for doctors, patients and the public, such as journal articles, slide decks, education and promotional materials, which must still be accurate and approved by compliance reviewers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Therapists assess new clients, identify problems such as anxiety, depression or trauma, and build a treatment plan. They hold talk therapy sessions using methods like cognitive behavioral therapy, track progress, adjust goals, and refer clients to a higher level of care when needed.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days are a series of scheduled sessions, often about 50 minutes each, by video or in person. Between sessions, therapists write progress notes, return messages, handle insurance paperwork and coordinate care. Crisis calls or safety checks can change the plan at short notice.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Therapists work in private practices, community mental health centers, hospitals, schools, addiction programs and online therapy services. Many see clients from a home office. For online work, therapists generally must be licensed in the state where the client is located, and rules vary by state.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include secure, HIPAA-compliant video platforms, electronic health records and scheduling software. Therapists use the DSM-5-TR for diagnosis and short screening questionnaires such as the PHQ-9 for depression and the GAD-7 for anxiety to measure symptoms over time.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Therapists work with individuals, couples, families and groups of all ages. They often coordinate with psychiatrists, primary care doctors, school staff and case managers. Newer clinicians working toward full licensure meet regularly with a clinical supervisor, as most states require.

qa.q: What does a therapist do day to day?
qa.a: A therapist spends most of the day in scheduled sessions with clients, by video or in person. They listen, help clients understand thoughts and patterns, teach coping skills and check on goals. Outside sessions, they write clinical notes, update treatment plans, handle insurance tasks and talk with other providers about shared clients.

qa.q: What is the difference between a therapist and a psychiatrist?
qa.a: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who diagnoses mental health conditions and can prescribe medication. A therapist, such as a licensed counselor, clinical social worker, marriage and family therapist or psychologist, mainly provides talk therapy. Most therapists cannot prescribe, though a few states let specially trained psychologists prescribe. Many clients see both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Mental health counselors assess clients, write treatment plans and lead individual or group therapy for problems such as depression, anxiety, trauma and addiction. Mental health technicians work on hospital or residential units, where they observe patients, take vital signs, lead activities and help calm crises.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Counselors see a series of clients in person or by video, then write progress notes and coordinate care with other providers. Technicians work shifts on a unit, checking on patients at set intervals, helping with meals and hygiene, leading groups and reporting changes in behavior to nurses.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, social workers, case managers and peer support specialists. With a client’s written consent, counselors may also talk with families, schools, courts or probation officers. Technicians report to nurses and join team meetings about each patient’s care.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Counselors use electronic health record systems for notes and treatment plans, standard screening questionnaires for depression, anxiety and substance use, telehealth video platforms and written safety plans. Technicians use observation logs, vital sign equipment and trained de-escalation and restraint-avoidance techniques.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on client progress toward treatment goals, keeping people safe during crises and writing accurate, timely notes that meet insurance and legal rules. Protecting confidentiality under HIPAA and the stricter federal rules for addiction treatment records is required.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a mental health counselor?
qa.a: To practice as a counselor on your own, every state requires a license, often called LPC or LMHC. It usually takes a master’s degree in counseling, supervised clinical hours after graduation and a passing score on a national exam. Details vary by state. Technician jobs usually need a high school diploma and on-the-job training, though a few states license psychiatric technicians.

qa.q: What is the difference between a mental health counselor and a psychologist?
qa.a: A licensed counselor usually holds a master’s degree and provides therapy. A clinical psychologist holds a doctoral degree, provides therapy and can give formal psychological tests. Counselors cannot prescribe medication, and psychologists can only in a few states after extra training. Psychiatrists and psychiatric nurse practitioners are the main prescribers of mental health medication.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Answer calls, chats and emails from shops, restaurants and drivers who use a platform. Fix account settings, explain missing or late payouts, update menus or listings, help with onboarding and verification, and pass complex cases to specialist teams.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Work through a queue of tickets and live contacts. One hour might bring a restaurant whose tablet stopped taking orders, a driver locked out of the app, and a seller asking why a payment was held for review.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Business owners, store managers and independent drivers or couriers on the outside. Inside the company, agents work with payments, risk and trust teams, engineering, account managers and sales to solve problems they cannot fix alone.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A ticketing or CRM system, internal admin tools to view and edit partner accounts, a knowledge base of policies, and chat and phone software. Many teams also use dashboards that track queues, response times and open cases.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Common measures include response and resolution times, partner satisfaction surveys, quality reviews of a sample of contacts, and accuracy in following policy. Correct handling of payouts, refunds and account actions matters because errors cost partners real money.

qa.q: What does a merchant support specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They spend most of the shift handling partner contacts by phone, chat or email. They check account details, trace orders and payouts, update listings, walk new partners through setup, and document each case. When an issue needs another team, such as a fraud review or a software bug, they escalate it and follow up with the partner.

qa.q: What is the difference between merchant support and customer support?
qa.a: Customer support helps the people who buy or order through a platform. Merchant support helps the businesses and drivers who sell or deliver on it. Merchant issues often involve money and livelihoods, such as payouts, fees, account holds and deactivation appeals, so the work leans more on policy, payments knowledge and careful escalation.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Mid-market account executives run the full sales cycle with medium-sized companies. They qualify leads, run discovery calls, give demos, write proposals, negotiate pricing and close contracts. Many also handle a book of existing accounts and look for upsell chances.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes back-to-back video calls with prospects, follow-up emails, and updates to deal notes in the CRM. Reps prep for demos, chase signatures, answer security or legal questions, and review their pipeline against the monthly or quarterly quota.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with sales development reps who book meetings, solutions engineers who handle technical demos, and customer success managers who take over after the sale. On the buyer side, they often deal with several decision makers, such as department heads, finance and IT.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Core tools include a CRM, a video meeting platform, email sequencing software, and e-signature tools. Many teams also use call recording and conversation analysis, sales intelligence databases for contact data, and forecasting dashboards to track deal stages.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is mostly measured against a revenue quota, usually set monthly, quarterly or yearly. Managers also watch pipeline coverage, win rate, average deal size, sales cycle length and forecast accuracy. Pay usually combines a base salary with commission tied to closed deals.

qa.q: What is the difference between a mid-market and an enterprise account executive?
qa.a: Mid-market reps sell to medium-sized companies, so deals are smaller and close faster, often in weeks to a few months. They carry more accounts at once. Enterprise reps sell to large organizations with bigger contracts, longer cycles, heavier procurement and legal review, and many more stakeholders. Company size cutoffs for each segment vary from one employer to another.

qa.q: Is mid-market account executive a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Reps live with a quota, and income depends partly on commission, so a slow quarter hurts. Deal volume is higher than in enterprise sales, which means juggling many calls and follow-ups. People who like competition, clear targets and fast feedback often enjoy the pace, while others find the constant pressure tiring.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan each ground station contact, build and check command loads, and send them to the spacecraft. During passes they watch telemetry for power, temperature, attitude and communications. When something looks wrong, they follow approved procedures to make the spacecraft safe and report the fault.

day.label: A typical shift
day.text: Many missions are staffed around the clock, so shifts can include nights, weekends and holidays. A shift starts with a handover briefing and a review of the pass schedule. Then comes a cycle of pre-pass checks, live contacts, post-pass reviews and careful log entries.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with flight dynamics staff who plan orbits and maneuvers, and with subsystem engineers for power, thermal, guidance and communications. They also coordinate with ground station operators, payload or science teams, and a flight director or mission manager who approves major activities.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their main tools are command and control software, telemetry displays with limit alarms, and written flight procedures. They also use voice loops, contact schedules, orbit prediction tools, anomaly tracking systems and console logs that record every command sent.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means commands go up correctly, passes are not missed and the spacecraft stays healthy. Controllers usually must pass training and a console certification before working alone. Clear handovers, accurate logs and calm, by-the-book responses to anomalies matter as much as speed.

qa.q: Is mission operations a stressful job?
qa.a: Most of the time the work is steady and routine, with planned passes and checklists. Stress rises during launches, maneuvers and unexpected faults, when decisions are time critical and a spacecraft may be at risk. Rotating shifts and overnight work can also be tiring. Strong training, rehearsed procedures and team support help keep pressure manageable.

qa.q: What is the difference between a flight controller and a flight dynamics engineer?
qa.a: A flight controller runs the spacecraft in real time: planning passes, sending commands, watching telemetry and responding to faults. A flight dynamics engineer focuses on the orbit itself, predicting where the spacecraft will be, planning maneuvers and calculating burns. The controller often executes the maneuver commands that the flight dynamics team designs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build and run the systems that train, test, ship and monitor machine learning models. That covers training pipelines, GPU clusters, model registries, serving endpoints and the alerts that fire when a model slows down, breaks or drifts.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a failed overnight training job, then move to tuning a Kubernetes cluster, reviewing a pull request for a deployment pipeline, and helping a data scientist package a model so it can serve live traffic safely.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Python, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, cloud platforms, GPU drivers and CUDA, workflow schedulers, experiment trackers, feature stores, model serving frameworks, and monitoring dashboards for latency, cost and model quality.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with data scientists and ML researchers who build models, data engineers who feed them, software engineers who call them, and security and finance teams who care about access controls and compute spending.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in how fast teams can go from experiment to production, how reliably models stay up, how well expensive GPUs are kept busy, and how quickly problems like data drift or bad releases get caught and rolled back.

qa.q: What does an MLOps engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They keep the path from model idea to live product running smoothly. Daily work includes fixing broken training or data pipelines, automating model testing and deployment, managing GPU and cloud resources, and watching dashboards for slow responses, errors or falling accuracy. Much of the job is writing infrastructure code and helping data scientists ship their work.

qa.q: What is the difference between MLOps and DevOps?
qa.a: DevOps automates building, testing and releasing regular software. MLOps applies the same ideas to machine learning, but adds problems DevOps rarely faces: versioning data and models along with code, scheduling costly GPU training runs, tracking experiments, and monitoring models whose accuracy can quietly decline as real-world data changes over time.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Mobile engineers write, test and ship apps that run on iPhone and Android devices. They build screens, connect the app to back-end services through APIs, fix bugs, and improve speed, battery use and stability.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team standup. Then comes coding a feature, reviewing teammates’ code, and testing on simulators and real phones. Later hours may go to fixing crash reports, meeting with designers, or preparing a release for app store review.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: iOS work uses Swift and Xcode, with some older code in Objective-C. Android work uses Kotlin, some Java, and Android Studio. Many teams also use cross-platform frameworks such as React Native or Flutter, plus Git for version control.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, designers, back-end engineers and QA testers. They also read user reviews, analytics and crash data to help decide what to build or fix first.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in app ratings, crash rates, load times and how smoothly releases pass store review. Clean, tested code that teammates can maintain also counts, as does shipping features on schedule.

qa.q: What does a mobile engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A mobile engineer spends most of the day writing and testing code for iPhone or Android apps. Typical tasks include building new screens, connecting to servers, reviewing code from teammates, fixing bugs found in crash reports, and working with designers and product managers. Before each release, they test on many devices and submit the build for app store review.

qa.q: What is the difference between a mobile engineer and a web developer?
qa.a: A mobile engineer builds apps that people install on phones and tablets, using tools like Swift, Kotlin or cross-platform frameworks. A web developer builds sites and apps that run in a browser. Mobile work adds device limits such as battery life, screen sizes, offline use and app store review, while web updates can usually go live right away.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Mortgage loan officers help people buy or refinance homes. They explain loan types, check income, assets, debts and credit, preapprove borrowers, take the application and lock rates. They then guide the file through processing, underwriting, appraisal and closing, keeping borrowers and agents updated.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often includes calls with new leads and real estate agents, reviewing pay stubs, tax returns and bank statements, and running loan scenarios. Officers update borrowers on underwriting conditions, chase missing documents and schedule closings. Evening and weekend calls are common.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with borrowers, plus real estate agents, builders and financial advisors who send referrals. Inside the lender they rely on processors, underwriters, closers and secondary marketing staff who price loans. They also deal with appraisers, title companies, escrow officers and closing attorneys.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include loan origination systems such as Encompass, pricing engines, automated underwriting systems such as Desktop Underwriter and Loan Product Advisor, credit reports and a CRM for leads. Document portals, e-signature tools and mortgage calculators are used daily.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Loan officers are judged on loan volume funded, how many applications reach closing, and on-time closings. Pay is often commission based, but federal rules bar paying loan officers based on a loan’s interest rate or terms. Lenders also check file quality, lending law compliance and borrower reviews.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a mortgage loan officer?
qa.a: It depends on where you work. Loan officers at banks and credit unions must register in the NMLS but do not need a state license. Those at nonbank lenders and mortgage brokers need a state license, which requires prelicensing education, the SAFE national exam, background and credit checks, and continuing education every year.

qa.q: What is the difference between a loan officer and a mortgage underwriter?
qa.a: A loan officer works with the borrower, explains options, takes the application and guides the deal toward closing. A mortgage underwriter usually does not talk to borrowers. Instead, the underwriter reviews the file to decide whether the loan meets the lender’s and investor’s guidelines, then approves, suspends or denies it, often with conditions.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Motion designers turn scripts, storyboards and brand guidelines into moving graphics. They animate logos, titles, icons, characters and interface elements, time movement to voiceover or music, and export finished files in the formats each video platform, app or game engine needs.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a review of feedback from a director or client. Then come hours of keyframing, adjusting timing curves, building or tweaking character rigs, rendering previews, and posting drafts for comments before the next deadline.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include motion graphics and compositing software, vector and image editors, 3D animation packages, and video editing programs. Many also use scripting or expressions to automate repetitive work, plus a pen tablet and a fast computer with a strong graphics card.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with art directors, graphic designers, video editors, copywriters, sound designers and producers. In app and game teams they also hand off animations to developers, so clear file setup and naming matter as much as the visuals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on smooth, purposeful movement, consistency with the brand or art style, clear storytelling, and hitting deadlines. A strong demo reel and portfolio usually count more than a degree when people are hired or win freelance clients.

qa.q: What is the difference between a motion designer and an animator?
qa.a: A motion designer usually animates graphic elements like type, logos, shapes and interface pieces, often for ads, explainers and apps. An animator more often brings characters to life with acting, weight and expression, as in games or film. The roles overlap a lot, and many people do both.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to become a motion designer?
qa.a: No license or degree is legally required. Many motion designers study graphic design, animation or film, but others are self-taught through courses and practice. Employers and clients mostly look at a demo reel showing strong timing, design sense and software skill, plus the ability to take feedback and meet deadlines.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Network engineers design, build and maintain the networks that link offices, data centers, cloud services and the internet. They configure routers, switches, firewalls and wireless gear, plan IP addressing, fix outages and keep the network fast, reliable and secure.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with checking monitoring alerts and the ticket queue. The rest of the day may mix troubleshooting a slow link, reviewing firewall rules, planning an upgrade and writing documentation. Larger changes are usually scheduled for nights or weekends to avoid disrupting users.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They work from the command line on routers and switches, use network monitoring dashboards and packet capture tools, and manage firewalls and VPNs. Many now write scripts in Python or use automation tools to push configurations across many devices at once.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Network engineers work closely with system administrators, security teams, cloud engineers and help desk staff. They also deal with internet service providers, equipment vendors and project managers when installing new circuits, opening sites or moving workloads to the cloud.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by uptime, speed and security. Managers look at how quickly outages are resolved, whether changes go in without breaking anything, and how well the network is documented so others can support it.

qa.q: What does a network engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A network engineer keeps an organization’s network running. Day to day, that means watching monitoring tools, resolving connectivity tickets, configuring routers, switches and firewalls, and planning upgrades. They also document the network, apply security patches and test changes. Big changes often happen after hours, and many engineers take turns being on call for emergencies.

qa.q: What is the difference between a network engineer and a network administrator?
qa.a: The titles overlap, and employers use them differently. In general, a network engineer focuses more on designing and building networks and planning how they grow. A network administrator focuses more on daily operation, such as managing users, devices, backups and routine troubleshooting. In small companies, one person often does both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: NLP and speech engineers build systems that turn speech into text, text into speech, and one language into another. They train and fine-tune language models, clean and label data, measure accuracy, and ship models into apps like chat tools, voice assistants and transcription services.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with checking overnight training runs. Then come error reviews on misheard words or wrong answers, a code review, and tuning prompts or model settings. Later they write evaluation scripts or fix a slow model in production.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in Python with deep learning libraries, transformer models, and GPU servers in the cloud. They use audio processing tools, tokenizers, vector databases, experiment trackers, and version control. Many also call large language models through APIs.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with data scientists, software and backend engineers, product managers, and linguists or annotators who label data. On voice products they also work with audio and hardware teams. Privacy and legal staff weigh in on how user data is handled.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by numbers like word error rate for transcription, translation quality scores, and task success rates for chat. Speed, cost per request, fairness across accents and dialects, and safe, accurate answers also count heavily.

qa.q: What does an NLP and speech engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They gather and clean text or audio data, train or fine-tune models, and test how well those models understand and produce language. Much of the day goes to finding errors, such as misheard names or wrong translations, and fixing them. They also write code that puts models into real products and keeps them fast and reliable.

qa.q: What is the difference between an NLP engineer and a data scientist?
qa.a: A data scientist usually analyzes data to answer business questions and builds general predictive models. An NLP engineer specializes in language and speech, building and deploying models that read, write, listen or talk. The NLP role leans more on software engineering, model training, and production systems, while data science leans more on statistics and reporting.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Node.js developers write the server side of web and mobile apps in JavaScript or TypeScript. They build REST or GraphQL APIs, connect to databases and outside services, handle logins and permissions, write background workers, and keep services fast and stable in production.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day mixes writing API endpoints, reviewing teammates’ code and writing tests. Developers trace bugs through logs, fix slow database queries and update npm packages with security warnings. Standups, planning and talks with frontend developers about API shapes fill the rest.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with frontend and mobile developers who call their APIs, and with product managers who set priorities. They also coordinate with DevOps or platform engineers on deployments, and with security staff when a package or endpoint has a known flaw.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Core tools are Node.js, npm or pnpm, TypeScript and frameworks like Express, NestJS or Fastify. Data usually lives in PostgreSQL, MongoDB or Redis. Common extras include Jest or Vitest for tests, Docker, Git, and cloud services such as AWS Lambda for serverless code.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on reliable APIs that return correct data quickly and handle errors well. Teams look at uptime, response times, tests and clean code reviews. Keeping packages patched and avoiding blocking code that stalls the server also matter.

qa.q: Is a Node.js developer a backend developer?
qa.a: Mostly, yes. Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, so a Node.js developer usually builds servers, APIs and background jobs. Many also know a frontend framework like React and work as full-stack developers. Node.js also runs build tools and command-line programs, so frontend developers use it every day too.

qa.q: Do Node.js developers need to know TypeScript?
qa.a: It is not strictly required, but many job postings now ask for it. TypeScript adds types to JavaScript, which catches many mistakes before code runs and makes large codebases easier to change. A developer who knows JavaScript well can usually pick up TypeScript on the job.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They answer customer emails, chats and calls in Swedish, Norwegian, Danish or Finnish. They handle orders, billing questions, returns and technical problems. Some translate or review product text, manuals or marketing copy. Most also write case notes and reports in English for US colleagues.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The Nordic countries are several hours ahead of US time zones, so shifts often start very early in the morning. The first hours bring the most live calls and chats. Later in the day they work through written tickets, follow-ups and internal notes.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use ticketing systems, customer relationship software, live chat tools and headsets for phone work. Translators add translation memory tools, glossaries and style guides. A keyboard set up for letters such as å, ä, ö, æ and ø is a daily basic.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They serve customers, clients and business partners in Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Inside the company they work with team leads, product and billing teams, and other language specialists. They often pass local feedback and common complaints back to US managers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Support roles track response time, how many cases are solved on first contact and customer satisfaction scores. Quality reviewers check spelling, grammar and a natural, polite tone in the target language. Translation work is judged on accuracy, consistency with glossaries and meeting deadlines.

qa.q: What does a Nordic language speaker do day to day?
qa.a: Most work in customer support, sales or account management for Nordic customers. They answer messages and calls in Swedish, Norwegian, Danish or Finnish, solve problems, and record each case in English. Others translate, localize or review written content. Many start early in the morning because of the time difference with the Nordic countries.

qa.q: Do I need to speak all the Nordic languages for these jobs?
qa.a: Usually not. Most postings ask for native or near-native fluency in one language plus good English. Swedish, Norwegian and Danish are closely related, so speakers often understand each other, but employers still want correct writing in one specific language. Finnish is not related to the other three, so it is almost always hired for separately.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Nurse practitioners take health histories, examine patients, order and interpret lab tests and imaging, diagnose illnesses and prescribe medicines. They also manage long-term conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure, give preventive care and teach patients how to care for themselves.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day usually runs on a schedule of booked visits, in person or by video. Between visits, the NP reviews test results, approves refills, answers patient messages, refers people to specialists and finishes chart notes in the electronic health record.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: NPs work in primary care clinics, hospitals, urgent care, specialty practices, nursing homes, schools and telehealth services, sometimes from home. Each NP is certified in a population focus, such as family, adult-gerontology, pediatrics, women’s health or psychiatric-mental health.

day.label: Rules of practice
day.text: Each state sets the scope. Some grant full practice authority, while others require a collaborative agreement with or supervision by a physician. Prescribing controlled substances requires a DEA registration and, in some states, a state permit. For video visits, NPs generally need a license in the state where the patient is.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: NPs work alongside physicians, registered nurses, medical assistants, pharmacists and therapists. They refer patients to specialists, coordinate with labs and imaging centers, and talk with family members and caregivers about treatment plans.

qa.q: Is nurse practitioner a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. NPs carry real responsibility for diagnoses and prescriptions, and many face full patient schedules, heavy charting and a steady flow of patient messages. Stress varies a lot by setting. Emergency and hospital roles tend to be more intense, while some clinic and telehealth roles offer more predictable hours and flexibility.

qa.q: What is the difference between a nurse practitioner and a physician assistant?
qa.a: Both examine, diagnose and prescribe. NPs are registered nurses with a graduate nursing degree, certified in a specific patient population and licensed by a state board of nursing. PAs train in a general medical model through a PA master’s program. In most states PAs practice in collaboration with physicians, while some states let NPs practice independently.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Nurses assess patients, give medications and treatments, check vital signs, and record care in the health record. They watch for changes, alert the provider when a patient gets worse, and teach patients and families how to manage care at home.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Hospital shifts often run 8 or 12 hours, including nights, weekends and holidays. A shift starts with a handoff report, then moves through patient checks, medication passes, charting, admissions and discharges, and ends with a report to the next nurse.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Nurses work with physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, pharmacists, therapists, case managers and social workers. RNs may delegate tasks to licensed practical nurses and nursing assistants, within limits set by each state’s nurse practice act.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Nurses work in hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, schools, home health and telehealth services. Telehealth nurses triage patients by phone or video and generally need a license that is valid in the state where the patient is located.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include electronic health records, IV pumps, cardiac monitors, glucose meters, barcode medication scanners and video visit software. Nurses also follow written care plans, facility protocols and provider orders.

qa.q: What does a nurse do day to day?
qa.a: A nurse checks on assigned patients, gives medications and treatments, tracks symptoms and vital signs, and documents everything in the chart. Nurses coordinate with doctors and other staff, answer patient and family questions, prepare people for discharge, and act fast when a patient’s condition changes. The exact mix depends on the setting and the nurse’s license.

qa.q: What is the difference between an RN and an LPN?
qa.a: An LPN, called an LVN in California and Texas, finishes a state-approved practical nursing program and passes the NCLEX-PN. An RN finishes an approved diploma, associate, bachelor’s or direct-entry master’s program and passes the NCLEX-RN. RNs have a broader scope, including care planning and complex assessment. LPN scope varies by state.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Observability engineers set up how software reports on itself. They collect logs, metrics and traces, build dashboards, and write alerts that fire when something breaks. They also tune noisy alerts, control data costs, and help teams add useful signals to their code.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with reviewing overnight alerts and checking which ones were false alarms. Then come pipeline fixes, new dashboards for a service launch, and code changes to add tracing. Afternoons often include helping another team debug a slow request or writing up an incident review.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include metrics systems like Prometheus, dashboards in Grafana, tracing built on OpenTelemetry, and log stores such as Elasticsearch or Loki. They work in Kubernetes and cloud platforms, write code in Go or Python, and manage setups with infrastructure-as-code tools.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with site reliability engineers, platform and DevOps teams, and the software developers who own each service. They also talk with on-call responders, security teams who need audit logs, and managers who track uptime goals.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows up as faster detection and fixes when systems fail, fewer pointless pages, and dashboards engineers actually use. Teams also watch how well service level objectives are tracked and whether monitoring costs stay under control as data grows.

qa.q: What is the difference between an observability engineer and a site reliability engineer?
qa.a: A site reliability engineer owns overall uptime, including deployments, capacity, incident response and reliability goals. An observability engineer focuses on the visibility layer: the logs, metrics, traces and alerts that SREs and developers rely on. In smaller companies one person often does both jobs, and the line between them can blur.

qa.q: Is observability engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. When outages happen, everyone needs the monitoring to work, and broken dashboards draw quick attention. Many observability engineers also join an on-call rotation. Day to day, the work is often calmer project work, and good alert tuning reduces late-night pages for everyone, including the engineer who built them.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Office managers keep the workplace running. They order supplies, manage vendor contracts, oversee reception and visitors, handle mail and deliveries, track office budgets, and fix problems with the space, from broken printers to heating complaints.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a walk through the office to check that rooms, kitchen and equipment are ready. Then come emails, supply orders, vendor calls, meeting room bookings, new hire setup and a steady stream of quick questions from staff.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with almost everyone. That includes leadership, HR, IT, receptionists and assistants, plus outside vendors such as cleaners, caterers, building management, movers and equipment repair services. In small offices they may also supervise front desk staff.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include email and calendar software, spreadsheets, room booking and visitor sign in systems, purchasing or expense software, and shared drives. They also keep vendor lists, inventory logs, budgets and emergency contact plans up to date.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good office management is often noticed only when something goes wrong. Success means supplies never run out, visitors are welcomed smoothly, events run on time, spending stays within budget and staff feel the office is comfortable and safe to work in.

qa.q: What does an office manager do day to day?
qa.a: An office manager handles the practical side of a workplace. Day to day, that means ordering supplies, greeting or routing visitors, booking rooms, coordinating repairs and cleaning, onboarding new staff, planning events and tracking office spending. They solve many small problems so other employees can focus on their own work.

qa.q: What is the difference between an office manager and an administrative assistant?
qa.a: An administrative assistant usually supports one person or a team with calendars, travel, documents and correspondence. An office manager looks after the whole office, including the space, vendors, budgets and often other support staff. In small companies one person may do both jobs, and titles vary between employers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Oil and gas engineers find, produce, move or refine oil and natural gas. Reservoir engineers estimate reserves, drilling engineers plan wells, production engineers keep wells flowing, pipeline engineers design and maintain lines, and process engineers run refineries and gas plants safely and efficiently.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Office days mix data analysis, well or plant models, cost estimates and meetings with field crews. Field days start with a safety meeting, then checking a rig, well site, pipeline or unit, solving problems and reporting. Some roles work rotations offshore or at remote sites.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with geologists and geophysicists, field operators, drilling contractors, service crews, land and regulatory staff, and health, safety and environment teams. Refinery engineers work with operators, maintenance crews and inspectors. Managers review budgets and plans with them.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Petrel for subsurface models, reservoir simulators like Eclipse, well design software and SCADA systems for monitoring production. Process engineers use Aspen HYSYS and piping engineers use CAESAR II. Excel, Python and Spotfire are everyday analysis tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Engineers are judged on safety first, then on production, reserves added, cost per well or barrel and uptime. Meeting environmental permits and regulations, avoiding spills and leaks, and delivering projects on schedule and budget all count.

qa.q: What is the difference between a petroleum engineer and a chemical engineer in oil and gas?
qa.a: Petroleum engineers work upstream: finding and producing oil and gas from reservoirs, designing wells and managing production. Chemical engineers usually work downstream in refineries and gas processing plants, designing and running the units that turn crude oil and gas into fuels and chemicals. Both also work in midstream pipeline and processing jobs.

qa.q: Do oil and gas engineers need a license?
qa.a: Many do not need a Professional Engineer license to work for an operator, because many states exempt engineering done for the employer’s own facilities. A PE license matters for engineers who seal designs or work as consultants, and rules vary by state. Field roles also require safety training, such as rig safety and hydrogen sulfide courses.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Operations analysts track how daily processes perform, such as order handling, scheduling, billing or support queues. They pull data, spot delays or errors, and suggest fixes. Associates often run the routine steps themselves, update records and keep reports current.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with checking dashboards and overnight reports for problems. Then come data pulls, spreadsheet work, a few meetings with team leads, and documenting a process change. Urgent issues, like a stuck batch or missed deadline, can reshape the plan.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Excel or Google Sheets is the core tool, often with pivot tables and lookups. Many roles also use SQL, a dashboard tool like Tableau or Power BI, a ticketing system, and sometimes simple automation scripts or workflow software.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with operations managers, frontline team leads, finance, and IT or data teams. Much of the job is translating between people who do the work and people who build the systems, then getting both to agree on a fix.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows up as fewer errors, faster turnaround, lower costs or hours saved through automation. Managers also value accurate, on-time reports and clear write-ups that let others act on the findings without extra explanation.

qa.q: What does an operations analyst do day to day?
qa.a: An operations analyst checks how a team’s processes are performing, using reports and data. They find bottlenecks, errors or wasted steps, then recommend or build fixes, such as a new checklist, a cleaner report or an automated task. They also keep recurring reports running and answer questions from managers about what the numbers mean.

qa.q: What is the difference between an operations analyst and a business analyst?
qa.a: Titles overlap and vary by employer. An operations analyst usually focuses on how existing daily work runs, measuring and improving it. A business analyst more often gathers requirements for new systems or projects and works between business teams and software developers. Both use data and process mapping, but operations roles tend to be closer to the daily work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Operations managers oversee the daily running of a business. They schedule staff, track budgets and costs, manage suppliers and inventory, fix process problems, and make sure products or services go out on time and to standard.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with reports on yesterday’s output, sales or service levels. Then come team check-ins, supplier calls, approving orders or invoices, solving staffing gaps, and planning changes that save time or money.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with department leads, frontline supervisors, finance, HR and senior leaders. Outside the company, they deal with vendors, contractors, landlords and sometimes key customers or inspectors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include spreadsheets, ERP and inventory systems, scheduling software, project management apps and dashboards that track key performance indicators. Strong written communication and basic accounting skills matter as much as software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured by cost control, on-time delivery, quality, safety records, staff turnover and customer satisfaction. Meeting budget targets and showing steady process improvement are usually central to performance reviews.

qa.q: What does an operations manager do day to day?
qa.a: An operations manager keeps the business running smoothly. Day to day, that means reviewing performance numbers, scheduling and supporting staff, managing suppliers and orders, controlling costs, and solving problems as they come up. They also plan improvements to processes and report results to senior leaders.

qa.q: What is the difference between an operations manager and a general manager?
qa.a: An operations manager focuses on how the work gets done: processes, staff, suppliers and costs. A general manager usually has wider responsibility, including sales, strategy and overall profit for a business or location. In smaller companies, one person may hold both roles, and titles vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Operators and drivers run equipment such as forklifts, buses, delivery trucks, production machines, cranes or plant control panels. They start up, watch and shut down equipment, follow safety checks, log readings or trips, and report problems before they turn into breakdowns.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift often starts with a pre-use inspection of the vehicle or machine and a handoff from the previous crew. Then comes steady running: loading, driving routes, adjusting settings or watching gauges. The shift ends with logs, cleanup and notes for the next person.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Warehouses, factories, construction sites, ports, transit agencies, water and power plants, and delivery routes. Many jobs run around the clock, so nights, weekends, rotating shifts and overtime are common. Drivers may spend most of the day alone in a cab.

day.label: Licenses and training
day.text: Driving a heavy truck or a bus, or hauling placarded hazardous materials, needs a commercial driver’s license issued by a state under federal rules. Forklift operators must be trained and evaluated by their employer under OSHA rules. Most construction crane operators need nationally accredited certification. Water treatment operator licenses are set by each state.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Safety comes first: no crashes, injuries or spills. After that, on-time runs, output, uptime, fuel use and accurate logs matter. Commercial drivers also face federal drug and alcohol testing and hours-of-service limits on how long they can drive.

qa.q: What does an operator do day to day?
qa.a: An operator checks a machine, vehicle or control system before use, then runs it through the shift. That can mean moving loads, driving a route, feeding a production line or watching plant readings. They follow safety rules, spot warning signs, fix small issues or call maintenance, and record what happened so the next shift can pick up smoothly.

qa.q: Is operator and driver work a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Stress comes from tight schedules, traffic, long or overnight shifts, and the need to stay alert around heavy equipment where one mistake can hurt someone. Many people like that the work is hands-on and ends when the shift ends. Good training, steady routines and clear safety rules help lower the pressure.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Optics and photonics engineers design lens systems, lasers, fiber links and light sensors. They model how light moves through a design, choose glass, coatings and detectors, set tolerances, and test prototypes to confirm they meet targets for sharpness, power and noise.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Part of the day often goes to running ray-trace or wave-optics simulations and checking the results. The rest may be spent aligning parts on an optical table, measuring a prototype, writing a test report, or meeting other engineers about fit, heat and cost.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Optical design and simulation software, interferometers, spectrometers, beam profilers, power meters and oscilloscopes. Lab work happens on vibration-isolated optical tables, sometimes in cleanrooms. Laser labs follow strict safety rules, including eyewear rated for the laser’s wavelength and power.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Mechanical engineers who design mounts and housings, electrical engineers who handle detectors and drivers, software teams who process images and signals, technicians who build and align assemblies, and outside suppliers who make lenses and apply coatings.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Makers of cameras, phones, medical imaging devices, chipmaking equipment, fiber networks, lidar, satellites and defense systems, plus government and university labs. Some defense roles need a security clearance, which generally requires US citizenship.

qa.q: What does an optics and photonics engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They split time between computer and lab. On screen, they simulate how light passes through lenses, fibers or sensors and adjust the design. In the lab, they align optics, measure prototypes and track down problems like blur, stray light or power loss. They also write specs and reports and work closely with mechanical, electrical and software engineers.

qa.q: What is the difference between optics and photonics?
qa.a: Optics is the broad study of light and how lenses, mirrors and prisms shape it. Photonics focuses on making, controlling and detecting light in devices such as lasers, optical fiber, LEDs and photodetectors. The two fields overlap heavily, and many job postings use both words for the same role.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Organizational development specialists design how a company structures its teams and grows its people. They build leadership programs, run performance review cycles, map career paths and skills, and guide restructurings, mergers or culture change. They also run engagement surveys and turn the results into action plans.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a meeting with a business leader about a team that is struggling. Later come designing a workshop, analyzing survey data, coaching a new manager and updating the review calendar. Running a training session or leadership offsite can take a whole afternoon.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They partner with senior leaders, HR business partners, managers and recruiting teams. They also work with learning and development staff, compensation analysts who link reviews to pay, and outside coaches, survey vendors or consultants brought in for large projects.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include performance and learning systems like Workday, Lattice or Cornerstone, and survey platforms like Qualtrics or Culture Amp. They also use PowerPoint, Excel, org chart software, personality and 360-degree feedback assessments, and Zoom or Teams for virtual workshops.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is judged by change over time: better engagement scores, fewer regretted departures, more internal promotions and ready successors for key roles. Leaders also watch whether review cycles finish on time and whether managers say the programs actually helped their teams.

qa.q: What is the difference between organizational development and training and development?
qa.a: Training and development focuses on teaching specific skills through courses and programs. Organizational development looks at the whole system: team structure, roles, leadership, culture and how performance is managed. It often uses training as one tool, but it may also redesign teams or processes. In many companies one team covers both.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to work in organizational development?
qa.a: Most jobs ask for a bachelor’s degree in psychology, HR, business or a related field, and many senior roles prefer a master’s in organizational development, industrial-organizational psychology or HR. No license is required. Experience leading groups, coaching managers and analyzing survey data often matters as much as the degree.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: OT and product security engineers protect industrial control systems, power and water systems, vehicles and connected devices from hacking. They map assets, segment networks, assess risks, test devices for weaknesses, build security into products and respond when attacks or flaws are found.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include reviewing alerts from passive network monitoring at a plant, threat modeling a new product feature or testing firmware for flaws. Engineers also plan patches around production schedules, write security requirements and work through findings with plant or engineering teams.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with control engineers, plant operators, maintenance staff and IT security teams. In product roles they work with embedded developers, hardware engineers and product managers. They also deal with regulators, customers and outside researchers who report flaws.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include passive OT monitoring platforms, Wireshark with industrial protocol support, firewalls and data diodes. Product security uses firmware analysis tools, fuzzers, JTAG debuggers and threat modeling tools. Engineers rely on standards like IEC 62443, NIST SP 800-82 and, at power utilities, NERC CIP.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on keeping operations safe and running while cutting risk. Plants and utilities look at asset visibility, network segmentation, patch progress and audit results. Product teams look at flaws caught before release, response time to reported issues and passing customer and regulator security reviews.

qa.q: What is the difference between OT security and IT security?
qa.a: IT security protects office systems and data, where keeping information confidential often comes first. OT security protects machines that control physical processes, such as pumps, turbines and assembly lines, where safety and uptime come first. OT systems may run for decades, patching can need a shutdown, and even a careless scan can disrupt production.

qa.q: What rules apply to OT and product security in the US?
qa.a: It depends on the industry. Owners of the bulk power system must follow mandatory NERC CIP standards. Makers of connected medical devices must meet FDA cybersecurity requirements before selling new devices. Pipelines and drinking water systems have their own federal requirements, while many factories follow voluntary standards such as IEC 62443.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Packaging engineers design packages that protect products, keep costs down, ship well and meet rules. They choose materials, design boxes, trays and cushioning, build prototypes, run drop, vibration and compression tests, and improve recyclability. In semiconductors, packaging engineers design the package that holds, cools and connects a chip.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include CAD work on a new tray or carton, a test run in the packaging lab and reviewing results after a damage claim. They also meet suppliers about material samples, update specifications and visit the line to see how packing really goes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with product designers, supply chain and logistics teams, manufacturing engineers, quality staff, marketing and regulatory teams. Outside they work with packaging suppliers, test labs and carriers. Chip packaging engineers work with chip designers and assembly and test factories.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include CAD like SolidWorks or ArtiosCAD, drop testers, vibration tables and compression testers used to ISTA and ASTM methods. Chip packaging engineers use simulation tools like Ansys or Cadence for thermal, stress and signal analysis, plus X-ray and microscope inspection.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether products arrive undamaged, whether packages pass required tests, and the total cost of materials, freight and labor. Sustainability goals, line speed and labeling rules also matter. For chips, the judges are reliability, heat handling and manufacturing yield.

qa.q: What is the difference between consumer packaging and semiconductor packaging engineering?
qa.a: Consumer packaging engineers design the boxes, bottles, trays and cushioning that protect and sell products during shipping and on the shelf. Semiconductor packaging engineers design the tiny package around a computer chip that connects it to a circuit board, removes heat and protects it. The titles match, but the skills, materials and employers are very different.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a packaging engineer?
qa.a: Most packaging engineer jobs ask for a bachelor’s degree in packaging science, mechanical engineering, materials science or a related field. Few US universities offer packaging degrees, so many engineers come from other branches of engineering. Semiconductor packaging roles often prefer a master’s or PhD. The Certified Packaging Professional credential is optional.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Draft routine documents such as contracts, discovery requests and corporate filings for lawyer review. Track court deadlines and contract renewal dates. Organize case files, summarize records and keep the legal team’s systems accurate and current.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a check of the deadline calendar. Then comes a mix of drafting, e-filing with courts, logging new contracts and answering lawyer requests. Rush work often appears before a filing deadline or deal closing. In law firms, time is usually recorded for billing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Attorneys and legal assistants are the closest partners. In-house teams also work with sales, procurement, finance and HR staff who need contracts handled. Outside contacts include court clerks, outside counsel, opposing counsel’s staff, clients and legal software vendors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Document management and contract management systems, e-discovery platforms, matter management and e-billing software, court e-filing portals and legal research databases. Strong skills in Word, Excel and PDF tools, including redaction, are expected almost everywhere.

day.label: Limits of the role
day.text: Paralegals work under a lawyer’s supervision. In general they cannot give legal advice, set fees, sign court filings or represent clients in court. A few states license limited legal paraprofessionals with defined rights, so the exact rules vary by state.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a paralegal?
qa.a: In most states no license is required, and certification is voluntary. Employers often look for an associate degree, bachelor’s degree or paralegal certificate, and national associations offer voluntary credentials. California sets education or experience requirements for anyone using the paralegal title, and a few states have separate licensed paraprofessional roles. Check your state’s rules.

qa.q: What is the difference between a paralegal and a legal operations specialist?
qa.a: A paralegal supports lawyers on legal matters by drafting documents, managing files and tracking deadlines. Legal operations focuses on running the legal department like a business, covering budgets, outside counsel spending, vendors, technology and workflows. Many in-house jobs blend both, so a paralegal may also run contract tools and reporting.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Partner managers recruit and onboard new partners, set joint goals, and run regular business reviews. They track deals partners bring in, settle conflicts over who owns a customer, and help partners sell and support the company’s product well.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a pipeline review in the CRM, then a call with a reseller about a stalled deal. Later comes planning a co-marketing campaign with an agency and updating training material in the partner portal.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Outside the company, they work with resellers, agencies, technology and integration partners. Inside, they coordinate with direct sales, marketing, product, legal and finance teams so partner deals, contracts, payouts and product roadmaps line up.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM, a partner relationship management platform, shared dashboards, and video calls. They also use deal registration systems, partner tiers, enablement content, and written partner agreements that set terms like discounts, referral fees and responsibilities.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually measured by revenue sourced or influenced by partners, the number of active partners, deal registration volume, and partner satisfaction. Many roles carry a quota and a variable pay plan tied to these results.

qa.q: What does a partner manager do day to day?
qa.a: A partner manager spends the day keeping partners productive. That means calls with resellers and agencies, reviewing shared deals, answering product questions, planning joint marketing, and running training. They also work with internal sales and product teams so partners get support, leads and integrations they need to sell more.

qa.q: What is the difference between a partner manager and an account manager?
qa.a: An account manager looks after end customers who buy the product directly. A partner manager looks after other businesses, such as resellers, agencies and integration partners, that sell, recommend or build on the product. The partner manager grows revenue indirectly, through those partners, rather than by selling to each customer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan joint campaigns with partners, manage market development funds, build co-branded content and track the leads partners generate. They also write partner marketing guides and approve how partners use the company’s brand.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with partner calls to review campaign plans. Then come fund requests to approve, a webinar or event to prep, and a look at pipeline reports. Afternoons may go to updating the partner portal or briefing sales on a new joint offer.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with channel and alliance managers, field sales, product marketing and demand generation. Outside the company, they deal with marketing contacts at resellers, distributors, systems integrators, technology partners and online marketplace teams.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include partner relationship management software, a CRM, marketing automation platforms, partner portals and through-channel marketing tools that let partners send ready-made campaigns. Spreadsheets and dashboards help track fund spending and results.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by partner-sourced and partner-influenced pipeline, revenue from joint deals, how many partners actively run campaigns and return on co-marketing funds. Managers also watch whether partners file proof of spend on time and follow brand rules.

qa.q: What does a partner marketing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They help partners sell the company’s products. Day to day, that means planning joint campaigns, handing out and auditing marketing funds, creating co-branded materials, running webinars and events with partners, and tracking the leads and deals that result. Much of the job is coordination across sales, channel teams and partner staff.

qa.q: What is the difference between partner marketing and channel sales?
qa.a: Channel sales managers own the business relationship and revenue targets with resellers and other partners. Partner marketing managers create the demand that feeds those deals, through joint campaigns, content and marketing funds. The two roles work side by side, and in smaller companies one person may do both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Payments staff make sure money moves correctly between customers, merchants and banks. They process card, ACH and wire transactions, reconcile settlement files, investigate failed or returned payments, handle chargebacks and disputes, and fix mismatches before money goes missing.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with matching yesterday’s settlement totals against bank statements. Then come exception queues: rejected transfers, ACH returns, duplicate charges and open disputes. Later hours often go to answering merchant or bank questions, testing a payment change, and getting files to the bank before cutoff times.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: Card work follows the PCI DSS security standard and card network rules. ACH payments follow the ACH network’s operating rules. Consumer electronic transfers fall under Regulation E, and Bank Secrecy Act anti-money laundering checks apply. Money transmitter licensing is set by each state, so requirements vary by state.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include processor and gateway dashboards, online banking portals, reconciliation software, spreadsheets, ticketing systems and SQL for pulling transaction data. Technical roles also work with payment APIs, tokenization, and message formats such as ISO 20022.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with accounting and finance, customer support, fraud and risk teams, compliance officers and software engineers. Outside the company, they deal with partner banks, card processors, and the merchants or customers whose payments they handle.

qa.q: What does a payments specialist do day to day?
qa.a: A payments specialist checks that each day’s transactions settled correctly, matches records against bank statements, and works through problems like failed transfers, returns and chargebacks. They answer questions from customers, merchants and partner banks, watch cutoff times for sending payment files, and flag anything that looks like fraud or a compliance issue.

qa.q: What is the difference between authorization and settlement?
qa.a: Authorization is the real-time check when a card is used. The card issuer confirms the account is valid and funds or credit are available, then places a hold. Settlement comes later, often in batches, when money actually moves from the issuer to the merchant’s bank. A payment can be authorized but never settled, such as when an order is canceled.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Payments engineers build and maintain the code that authorizes card charges, sends bank transfers, and handles refunds and disputes. They record every money movement in a double-entry ledger. They also make sure a retried request never charges a customer twice.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might mix writing code for a new payment method, reviewing a teammate’s change, and digging into a report where the ledger and a bank’s settlement file disagree by a few cents. Some days include on-call duty for failed payouts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with product managers, finance and accounting teams, fraud and risk analysts, compliance staff and customer support. They also work with outside payment processors and banks whose APIs and settlement files their systems connect to.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a backend programming language, relational databases with strong transaction support, message queues, processor and bank APIs, ACH and card settlement files, tokenization services, and monitoring and alerting dashboards. Idempotency keys and audit logs are everyday building blocks.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means correctness and uptime. Balances reconcile to the cent, authorization rates stay high, and duplicate charges do not happen. Incidents get fixed fast. Systems that touch card data must also pass reviews under PCI DSS, the card industry’s security standard.

qa.q: Is payments engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Bugs move real money, so mistakes are costly and visible to customers and finance teams. Many teams run on-call rotations for outages and failed settlements. Careful testing, code review, idempotent design and clear runbooks lower the pressure, and many engineers find the precision of the work satisfying.

qa.q: What is the difference between a payments engineer and a backend engineer?
qa.a: Both build server-side systems. A payments engineer also needs domain knowledge: card authorization and capture, ACH timing and returns, chargebacks, double-entry accounting, reconciliation, and security rules like PCI DSS. The bar for correctness is higher, since a rounding error or a duplicate request can cost customers real money.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Payroll staff gather hours worked, figure gross pay and overtime, and subtract deductions. They withhold federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare, plus state and local taxes where they apply. Then they send pay by direct deposit, paycard or check on the scheduled payday.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with reviewing timecards and fixing missed punches with managers. Next comes entering new hires, raises, terminations and updated W-4 forms. Before each deadline, they run a payroll preview, check it for errors, and answer employee questions about their paychecks.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use payroll software, timekeeping systems, HR databases and spreadsheets. Common forms include the W-4 for withholding, the quarterly Form 941, the annual Form 940 and W-2s at year end. State withholding and unemployment filings vary by state.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Payroll works closely with human resources, accounting and department managers. They also deal with benefits providers, retirement plan administrators and tax agencies. Employees come to them with questions about pay, deductions, wage garnishments and missing hours.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means every employee is paid correctly and on time. Tax deposits and filings must meet government deadlines to avoid penalties. Payroll staff must also follow federal and state wage laws, including overtime rules, and keep salary and personal data strictly confidential.

qa.q: Is payroll a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be, mostly around deadlines. Payday cannot move, so late timecards or last-minute changes create pressure. Quarter end and year end, when tax forms and W-2s are due, are the busiest times. Between those peaks the work is steady and routine. People who like accuracy and clear schedules often do well.

qa.q: What is the difference between payroll and accounts payable?
qa.a: Payroll pays the company’s own employees. It handles wages, overtime, tax withholding, benefits deductions and payroll tax filings. Accounts payable pays outside vendors and suppliers for goods and services, based on invoices. Both are part of finance or accounting, and in small companies one person may do both jobs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Turns a schematic into a physical board. Places parts, routes copper traces, plans the layer stackup, and checks the design against electrical and manufacturing rules. Then prepares fabrication files, drill data, assembly drawings, and a bill of materials for the board and assembly shops.

day.label: A typical day
