Many also answer questions from users and community members, and coordinate with legal or compliance staff when a product touches regulated areas like securities or payments.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means code that does exactly what it should and nothing more. Teams look at test coverage, audit findings, gas efficiency, clear documentation, and above all whether deployed contracts stay safe from exploits and lost funds over time.

qa.q: Is smart contract engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Deployed code often holds large sums, and many contracts cannot be changed once live, so a single bug can lead to permanent loss. Engineers manage this pressure with careful reviews, heavy testing, outside audits and staged launches. Incident response after an exploit can mean long, urgent hours. People who enjoy precision and security thinking tend to handle it best.

qa.q: What is the difference between a smart contract engineer and a smart contract auditor?
qa.a: A smart contract engineer builds the contracts, from design through testing and deployment. An auditor reviews code someone else wrote, hunting for security flaws and logic errors, then writes a report with findings and fixes. Engineers own the product over time. Auditors usually work on short, focused reviews. Many people move between the two roles, since each skill sharpens the other.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: An SMB account executive runs sales conversations with small and medium businesses and startups. They hold discovery calls, give product demos, send proposals and close deals. Most deals are small and move fast, so they juggle many at once.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day is packed with back-to-back calls and demos. Between them, they send follow-up emails, update deal notes, answer pricing questions and chase signatures. Many end the week by reviewing their pipeline with a sales manager.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They talk mostly with business owners, founders and office managers who make quick buying decisions. Inside the company, they work with sales development reps who book meetings, plus customer success and support teams who take over after the sale.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They live in a CRM, where every call, email and deal stage is logged. Video meeting software, a sales email sequencing tool, e-signature software and a calendar booking link are standard. Some use call recording tools for coaching.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured against a monthly or quarterly sales quota. Managers also watch activity numbers, such as calls and demos held, plus win rate, deal size and how accurate the rep’s forecast is.

qa.q: What does an SMB account executive do day to day?
qa.a: They spend most of the day on short calls and demos with small business owners and startup founders. They qualify each lead, show how the product solves a problem, handle objections, send quotes and close deals. They log every step in a CRM and follow up quickly, because small deals often close within days or a few weeks.

qa.q: What is the difference between an SMB account executive and an enterprise account executive?
qa.a: An SMB account executive sells to smaller companies, usually with one or two decision makers, and closes many smaller deals each month. An enterprise account executive sells to large organizations, where deals involve many stakeholders, legal and security reviews, and sales cycles that can run many months. SMB is often a stepping stone toward mid-market and enterprise roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: SOC analysts watch alerts from security tools, decide which ones are real threats, and act on them. They investigate suspicious logins, malware and unusual network traffic, contain confirmed attacks, document every step, and escalate serious incidents to senior analysts or incident responders.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift starts with a handoff from the previous team and a review of open tickets. Most of the day is spent triaging alerts in a queue, closing false positives, digging into suspicious events, and writing clear notes so the next shift can pick up where they left off.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: The core tool is a SIEM, which gathers logs from across the company into one searchable place. Analysts also use endpoint detection and response software, firewalls, email security filters, threat intelligence feeds, ticketing systems and written playbooks that spell out how to handle each type of alert.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: They work in a security operations center at a company, a government agency or a managed security provider that watches many clients. Because attacks happen at any hour, many SOCs run 24/7 with rotating day, night and weekend shifts. Some teams work fully or partly remote.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Teams track how fast alerts are picked up and resolved, how accurately analysts separate real threats from noise, and how well incidents are documented. Missing a real attack matters most. Clear escalation and good shift notes count as much as technical skill.

qa.q: What does a SOC analyst do day to day?
qa.a: A SOC analyst works through a queue of security alerts, checks logs and devices to see if each one is a real threat, and closes or escalates it. When an attack is confirmed, they help contain it, such as isolating a computer or disabling an account, and record what happened in a ticket.

qa.q: Is being a SOC analyst a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Entry-level analysts often face a high volume of repetitive alerts, night or weekend shifts, and pressure not to miss a real attack. Stress rises during active incidents. Good playbooks, reasonable alert tuning and a supportive team make a big difference, and many analysts move into higher tiers or specialist roles over time.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan and publish posts, write captions, reply to comments and messages, and track results across platforms. They also find creators, agree on terms, and review sponsored content before it goes live.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with checking overnight comments, mentions and analytics. Then come scheduling posts, editing short videos, briefing a creator and joining a team meeting. Later, a trending topic or customer complaint may need a fast, careful reply.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with marketing, design, customer service and sales teams. Outside the company, they deal with creators, talent agents, freelance photographers and sometimes ad agencies. Legal or compliance staff may review contracts and claims in sponsored posts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include each platform’s own apps and ad managers, scheduling and analytics dashboards, social listening software, and simple photo and video editors. A shared content calendar keeps posts, campaigns and creator deadlines in order.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by reach, engagement, follower growth, clicks, and sales or sign-ups traced to posts. Bosses also watch how fast customers get answers and whether creator campaigns delivered what was agreed and paid for.

qa.q: What does a social media manager do day to day?
qa.a: A social media manager plans, posts and monitors content on a company’s accounts. Day to day, they write captions, schedule posts, answer comments and messages, and review analytics. They also brief creators, check sponsored posts before launch, and change plans when a trend or problem appears.

qa.q: Do creators have to label sponsored posts?
qa.a: Yes. Under FTC rules, creators must clearly disclose any material connection to a brand, such as payment, free products or a family tie. Labels like “ad” or “sponsored” should be easy to see. Social media managers are expected to tell creators about this and monitor their posts, since brands can also be held responsible.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They decide how a large system is split into parts, how those parts talk to each other, and which technologies to use. They write down these decisions so many teams can build pieces that fit together and keep working as the system grows.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to design reviews and questions from team leads. Afternoons may mean drawing diagrams, writing decision records, testing an idea with a small prototype, or reading code to check that a design is being followed.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with software engineers, engineering managers, product managers, security staff, and operations teams. They also explain tradeoffs to business leaders who need to understand cost, risk, and timelines in plain terms.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include diagramming software, modeling notations, cloud provider consoles, code repositories, and shared documents for architecture decision records. Many also use monitoring dashboards to see how the running system actually behaves under load.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows over time. Teams can ship changes without breaking each other’s work, the system handles growth, outages are rare and contained, and costs stay reasonable. Clear, well-kept documentation is also a sign of good work.

qa.q: What does a software architect do day to day?
qa.a: A software architect spends much of the day in conversations. They review designs, answer questions from teams, and weigh choices like which database or messaging approach to use. They record decisions and the reasons behind them. Many still write some code or prototypes to test ideas and stay close to how the system really works.

qa.q: What is the difference between a software architect and a senior software engineer?
qa.a: A senior engineer usually owns the design and code of one part of a system. A software architect looks across many parts and teams, setting the structure, standards, and interfaces that let those parts fit together. Architects often write less production code and spend more time on planning, reviews, and explaining tradeoffs.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Software engineers design, write, test and fix the code behind apps, websites and internal systems. They turn feature requests into working code, review teammates’ changes, track down bugs, and keep older code readable and secure as the product grows.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team check-in. Then come blocks of focused coding, reviewing pull requests, answering questions in chat, and testing changes before they ship. Some days bring design discussions, planning meetings or an urgent production issue.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with other engineers, product managers, designers and quality testers. They also talk with data, security and operations teams, and sometimes with support staff who pass along problems customers report.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include a code editor or IDE, version control such as Git, a ticket tracker, automated test suites and build pipelines. Most engineers also use cloud consoles, command-line tools, logs and monitoring dashboards to see how code behaves in production.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether features ship working and on time, how few bugs reach users, and how easy the code is for others to read and change. Peer code reviews, test results and system reliability all count.

qa.q: What does a software engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A software engineer spends most of the day writing and changing code, testing it, and reviewing code from teammates. They also join short planning meetings, read tickets that describe new features or bugs, investigate problems in live systems, and write notes so others can understand their work.

qa.q: What is the difference between a software engineer and a software developer?
qa.a: The titles overlap heavily, and many employers use them for the same job. When a difference is drawn, engineer tends to suggest more focus on system design, scale and reliability, while developer may point to building specific features or apps. Read the duties in each posting rather than relying on the title.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Solar energy specialists plan, build or make solar power systems. They size systems to match energy use, mount racking and panels, run wiring to inverters and batteries, and test the finished system. In factories, they assemble, inspect and test solar modules before shipping.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Install crews often start early to beat the heat. They load the truck, hold a short safety talk, and put on fall protection before climbing. Designers spend the day on site surveys, shade checks, layout drawings and permit packages.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Field workers use drills, impact drivers, torque wrenches, crimpers, multimeters and harnesses with roof anchors. Commissioning techs may use insulation testers and I-V curve tracers. Designers rely on solar design software, aerial imagery and electrical calculation tools.

day.label: Rules they follow
day.text: Work must meet the National Electrical Code, mainly Article 690, plus local building and fire codes. Most jobs need a permit, an inspection and utility approval before the system turns on. Licensing rules vary by state, and NABCEP certification is voluntary.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: They work on home rooftops, commercial roofs, carports and large ground-mounted solar farms, often outdoors in heat and sun. Utility-scale projects can mean travel and long stays near remote sites. Others work indoors in design offices or module factories.

qa.q: What does a solar energy specialist do day to day?
qa.a: It depends on the role. Installers mount racking and panels, wire inverters and test systems on roofs or solar farms. Designers survey sites, study shade and draw system plans for permits. Factory workers assemble and inspect panels. Most days involve following electrical codes, safety rules and checklists closely.

qa.q: Do you need a license to install solar panels?
qa.a: It varies by state. Many states require a licensed electrician to make the electrical connections, and some have a separate solar contractor license. Helpers who carry panels or mount racking often work under a licensed lead. NABCEP certification is not required by law in most places, but many employers value it.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They learn how a customer’s current systems work, then design how the product will connect to them. They draw architecture diagrams, map data flows, answer security and integration questions, and write the technical plan that sales and delivery teams follow before and after the contract is signed.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes discovery calls, whiteboard sessions and demos with quieter design work. They may build a proof of concept in the morning, review a security questionnaire after lunch, and later help an implementation team solve a problem a new customer hit during rollout.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with account executives, product managers, engineers and support staff. On the customer side, they talk with IT leaders, developers, security reviewers and business owners who must agree that the design fits their needs, budget and rules.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include diagramming software, cloud consoles, API testing tools, code editors and scripting languages. They also use the company’s CRM, shared documents for proposals, and demo or sandbox environments where they can show the product working with sample customer data.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether deals close on a design that actually works. Leaders look at win rates on deals they support, smooth handoffs to delivery, fewer surprises during implementation, customer satisfaction, and whether the product is adopted and renewed.

qa.q: What does a solutions architect do day to day?
qa.a: A solutions architect spends the day turning customer needs into a workable technical design. That means asking questions on discovery calls, sketching how systems connect, running demos or proofs of concept, answering security and integration questions, and guiding the team that installs the product. After the sale, they help fix design gaps and plan expansions.

qa.q: What is the difference between a solutions architect and a sales engineer?
qa.a: The roles overlap, and titles vary by company. A sales engineer usually focuses on demos and technical questions to help close a deal. A solutions architect often goes deeper into overall system design, covers more complex or larger accounts, and stays involved after the sale to make sure the design works in practice.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Solutions engineers run product demos, answer technical questions, and design how the product will fit a customer’s systems. They build proof-of-concept setups, fill out security questionnaires, and help with early configuration so the deal can close.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a discovery call to learn a prospect’s needs, then a tailored demo, then building a test environment. Afternoons often go to internal planning with sales reps and follow-up emails answering detailed technical questions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They pair closely with account executives, who own the deal and the relationship. They also work with product managers, support staff, and implementation teams, and talk directly with the customer’s engineers, IT staff, and decision makers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM system, video meeting software, demo and sandbox environments, and APIs. Many use scripting languages, cloud platforms, and diagramming tools to show how data and systems will connect.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually tied to the sales team’s results, such as deals won and revenue closed. Managers also look at demo quality, how well technical risks are spotted early, and whether customers launch smoothly after signing.

qa.q: What does a solutions engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A solutions engineer meets with potential customers to understand their technical problems, then shows how the product solves them. Daily work includes live demos, building proof-of-concept setups, answering technical and security questions, and planning how the product connects to existing systems. They work alongside a sales rep, who handles pricing and the business side of the deal.

qa.q: What is the difference between a solutions engineer and a sales engineer?
qa.a: The two titles often describe nearly the same job, and many companies use them interchangeably. Both support sales with technical expertise. Some companies use solutions engineer for roles focused on complex software, custom integrations, or cloud architecture, while sales engineer is common in hardware and industrial sales. Always check the posting’s duties rather than relying on the title.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Sourcers find people who could fit open roles, often people who are not job hunting. They build search strings, review profiles and portfolios, write personal outreach messages, follow up, and pass interested candidates to a recruiter with short notes on each person’s fit.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a call with a recruiter or hiring manager about what a role needs. Then come hours of searching, sending messages, tracking replies, scheduling screening calls, and updating candidate records so the team knows who has been contacted.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Sourcers use Boolean search on professional networking sites, job boards and general search engines. They also rely on an applicant tracking system, a recruiting CRM for outreach sequences, contact lookup tools, spreadsheets, and code or design sites when searching for technical talent.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with recruiters and hiring managers, and sometimes with recruiting coordinators who book interviews. Some sourcers work inside one company’s talent team, while others work for staffing or search firms that fill roles for many clients.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Sourcers are usually measured on reply rates to outreach, how many candidates they pass along, how many of those reach interviews, and how many get hired. Hiring managers’ feedback on candidate quality also counts, along with fair, nondiscriminatory search practices.

qa.q: What does a sourcer do day to day?
qa.a: A sourcer spends most of the day searching for people who match a job’s needs, often people who are happily employed. They write and send personal messages, follow up with those who do not answer, hold short intro calls, and hand interested candidates to a recruiter. They also keep records updated and adjust searches based on feedback from hiring managers.

qa.q: What is the difference between a sourcer and a recruiter?
qa.a: A sourcer focuses on the top of the hiring process: finding people and getting them interested in talking. A recruiter usually takes over from there, running screens, coordinating interviews, managing the hiring manager, and handling offers. On small teams one person may do both jobs, and some sourcers move into recruiter roles over time.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They do a regular job, such as customer service, sales, patient intake or banking, but in Spanish as well as English. They answer questions, explain bills, policies and products, solve problems, and write clear notes in English so the rest of the team can follow.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Common settings include call centers, clinics and hospitals, banks, schools, stores, government offices and remote home desks. Some roles serve customers in Spain or Latin America, so workers adjust to other time zones, currencies and local vocabulary.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days mean a steady line of calls, chats, emails or walk-in customers. Workers switch between Spanish and English many times an hour, translate short notices, and help coworkers who get a Spanish-speaking customer they can’t serve alone.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A headset, a customer or ticket system, scripts and approved Spanish templates, and a shared glossary of company terms. A keyboard set up for accents and the letter ñ helps, since written Spanish without them can look careless or change the meaning.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Many employers give a spoken and written Spanish test before hiring. On the job, managers review recorded calls or messages for accuracy, polite tone, and correct information, plus usual measures like problems solved and customer feedback.

qa.q: What does a Spanish speaking customer service worker do day to day?
qa.a: They take calls, chats or emails from customers who prefer Spanish. They verify accounts, answer questions, fix orders or billing issues, and explain next steps in plain language. They log each contact in English, pass hard cases to other teams, and often help English-only coworkers with Spanish-speaking customers.

qa.q: What is the difference between a bilingual Spanish speaking job and a Spanish interpreter?
qa.a: Bilingual staff do their own job in Spanish, like selling or scheduling. Interpreters carry meaning between two other people and follow a code of ethics on accuracy and confidentiality. Court interpreters must usually meet certification rules set by each state or the federal courts. Medical interpreter certification is voluntary nationally, but many hospitals require proof of training.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Procurement and spend analysts collect purchasing data from invoices, purchase orders and company cards, clean it and sort it into categories. They find where the company buys the same thing from many suppliers, pays above contract prices or spends outside approved contracts, and suggest ways to save.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include pulling data from ERP and procurement systems, fixing supplier names and categories, and building dashboards. Analysts also prepare bid comparisons for sourcing events, check contract compliance, and answer questions from category managers about price trends and supplier spend.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with category managers, buyers and sourcing leads, plus finance teams who confirm savings and accounts payable staff who own invoice data. They also support budget owners in IT, marketing or operations, and sometimes talk with suppliers about pricing and volumes.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include ERP systems such as SAP or Oracle, procurement suites like Coupa, SAP Ariba or Jaggaer, and spend analytics software. Excel, SQL and BI tools such as Power BI or Tableau do the heavy lifting for cleaning data and showing results.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Analysts are judged on the savings they help find and confirm, the accuracy of spend data, and how much spend runs through approved contracts. Leaders also value clear dashboards, fast answers for sourcing decisions and early warnings about price increases or supplier risk.

qa.q: What does a spend analyst do day to day?
qa.a: A spend analyst pulls purchasing data from finance and procurement systems, cleans and categorizes it, and looks for patterns. They spot duplicate suppliers, off-contract buying and prices above agreed rates. Then they build reports and dashboards, support bids and negotiations with data, and track the savings that procurement and finance agree on.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a procurement analyst?
qa.a: Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in supply chain, business, finance or a related field, but strong data skills can matter more than the major. Experience with Excel, SQL and BI tools helps most. Optional certifications in supply management or procurement can support promotion, but no license is required for the role.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Sponsorship managers sell or buy partnerships with events, teams, venues and athletes. On the selling side they build packages of signage, naming rights, hospitality and media. On the buying side they pick deals that fit the brand. Both sides track delivery of every promised benefit.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes calls with prospects or partners, building a proposal deck and negotiating contract terms. Other hours go to checking that logos, ads and on-site activations ran as promised, collecting proof photos and reports, and planning renewals for next season.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Sellers work with marketing, ticketing, event operations, legal and creative teams at teams, leagues, venues and events. Buyers work with brand managers, agencies and athletes’ agents. Deals with college athletes follow name, image and likeness rules that vary by state and school.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a CRM such as Salesforce, proposal decks in PowerPoint or Google Slides, and contract templates. Many teams use sponsorship valuation and media measurement services, social media analytics, and spreadsheets that track each deliverable, its due date and its proof of performance.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Sellers are judged on new revenue, renewals and partner satisfaction. Buyers are judged on the return a sponsorship brings, such as brand exposure, leads, hospitality value and sales. On both sides, delivering every contracted benefit on time protects the relationship and the renewal.

qa.q: What does a sponsorship manager do day to day?
qa.a: A sponsorship manager spends the day building and keeping partner deals. On the selling side, that means prospecting, pitching packages and negotiating contracts. After signing, they make sure every promised logo, ad, ticket and activation is delivered, then send recap reports. Brand-side managers do the reverse, choosing and measuring sponsorships for their company.

qa.q: What is the difference between sponsorship sales and partnership activation?
qa.a: Sponsorship sales focuses on finding partners and closing new or renewed contracts. Partnership activation, sometimes called partnership services, makes sure the signed deal is delivered: signage, events, social posts, hospitality and reports. Smaller organizations often combine both roles, while pro teams and large events usually keep separate sales and activation staff.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: SQL developers write the queries, views and stored procedures that pull answers out of company databases. They build reports and data feeds, load data from other systems, tune slow queries and make sure the numbers in reports match the source records.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes report requests from business teams, writing and testing queries, and checking results against known totals. Some hours go to fixing failed overnight data loads, reading query plans to speed up slow reports and documenting changes before they go live.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with business analysts and managers who need reports, database administrators who run the servers, and BI developers who build dashboards. They also coordinate with application developers whose software writes to the same database.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include SQL Server Management Studio, Oracle SQL Developer and DBeaver. Many write T-SQL or PL/SQL and build data loads in SSIS or similar ETL tools. Reports often go out through SSRS, Power BI, Tableau or Excel, and code is kept in Git.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on correct results first: report totals must match the source data. Next come query speed, how little load the code puts on shared databases, and clear, documented code. Meeting reporting deadlines, such as month-end close, also matters.

qa.q: What is the difference between a SQL developer and a database administrator?
qa.a: A SQL developer writes the code that uses the database: queries, stored procedures, views and reports. A database administrator keeps the database itself running, handling installs, backups, security, user access and server performance. The jobs overlap on query tuning, and in small companies one person may do both.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to become a SQL developer?
qa.a: Many postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems or a related field, but strong SQL skills often matter more. Some people move into the role from reporting, analyst or help desk jobs. Database certifications and sample projects can help show skill without a degree.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They help issue, redeem and manage stablecoins or tokenized assets such as Treasury bills, bonds and fund shares. They map how tokens move on a blockchain, tie them to off-chain records, and check that reserves or underlying assets match the tokens outstanding.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include reviewing smart contract changes, reconciling token supply against reserve or custody reports, and testing transfer limits such as wallet allowlists. It also means answering questions from legal and compliance teams and meeting with partners.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with blockchain engineers, lawyers, compliance officers and treasury or fund operations staff. Outside partners include custodians, transfer agents, banks, exchanges, wallet providers, auditors and accounting firms that review reserves.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include public and permissioned blockchains, token standards such as ERC-20, smart contract code and security audit reports, and custody and wallet platforms. They also use blockchain explorers, analytics tools for sanctions screening, and reconciliation spreadsheets.

day.label: Rules that shape the work
day.text: Tokenized stocks, bonds and fund shares are generally still securities, so federal securities rules apply. Payment stablecoins fall under the GENIUS Act of 2025, and regulators are still writing its rules. Anti-money laundering duties apply, and state money transmitter licensing varies by state.

qa.q: What does a stablecoin and tokenization specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They keep digital tokens and real assets in sync. That means checking token supply against reserves or custody records, reviewing smart contract updates, working with lawyers on securities and payment rules, and coordinating with custodians, transfer agents and exchanges. Many also design new products, such as tokenized money market fund shares, and explain how they work to clients.

qa.q: What is the difference between a stablecoin and a tokenized asset?
qa.a: A stablecoin aims to hold a steady value, usually one dollar, backed by reserves such as cash and short-term Treasuries. It is mainly used for payments. A tokenized asset is a blockchain record of ownership in something else, like a bond or fund share. Its value moves with that asset, and it is usually treated as a security.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They set technical direction for a group of teams. They design large systems, write design documents, review other engineers’ plans, and step in on the hardest bugs or outages. Principal engineers often shape strategy across a whole company or product line.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may mix design reviews, one-on-one mentoring, and deep focused work on a tricky problem. Many still write code, but less than before. Much of the time goes to writing, reading proposals, and helping teams agree on a path.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with engineering managers, directors, product managers, and other senior engineers. They mentor mid-level and senior engineers. They often act as the bridge between leadership goals and the teams that build the software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by impact beyond their own output. Leaders look at whether systems became more reliable, whether teams moved faster, whether big decisions held up over time, and whether other engineers grew under their guidance.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Beyond code editors and version control, they rely on design documents, architecture diagrams, monitoring and tracing tools, and incident reviews. Clear writing is one of their most important tools, since many decisions happen through written proposals.

qa.q: What does a staff engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A staff engineer spends the day guiding technical work rather than only doing it. They review designs, write proposals, mentor engineers, untangle hard problems, and help teams align on architecture. Some days involve deep coding or debugging an outage. Others are mostly meetings and writing. The mix depends on the company and on which problems need them most.

qa.q: What is the difference between a staff engineer and an engineering manager?
qa.a: A staff engineer leads through technical expertise and does not manage people. An engineering manager handles hiring, performance reviews, and team health. Both are senior roles, and many companies treat them as parallel career tracks. Staff engineers focus on architecture and technical decisions, while managers focus on the people and processes that deliver the work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Statisticians design studies, surveys and experiments, then analyze the data to answer specific questions. They choose sample sizes and methods, build statistical models, check assumptions and explain what the results can and cannot prove, including how much uncertainty remains.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day mixes writing and checking analysis code, meeting researchers about study plans and reviewing data for errors or missing values. Statisticians also write analysis plans, prepare tables and charts, and draft methods sections for reports or journal papers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with scientists, doctors, engineers, economists and managers who need answers from data. In clinical trials they work with physicians, data managers and regulatory staff, and in government with survey teams. They often explain results to people with no statistics training.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Statisticians mainly use R, SAS, Python and Stata, and sometimes SPSS. Clinical trial work often relies on SAS and CDISC data standards. Many also use SQL to pull data, Git for version control, and Quarto or R Markdown to write reproducible reports.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on sound design and correct methods that hold up to peer or regulatory review. Clear explanations of uncertainty and limits matter as much as the results. Reproducible code, careful documentation and meeting study deadlines also count.

qa.q: Do you need a master’s degree to be a statistician?
qa.a: Most statistician jobs ask for a master’s degree in statistics, mathematics or a related field, and research or academic roles often require a PhD. Some entry-level analyst jobs accept a bachelor’s degree. There is no state license for statisticians, though professional groups offer voluntary accreditation.

qa.q: What is the difference between a statistician and a data scientist?
qa.a: A statistician focuses on study design, probability and inference: deciding what data to collect and how sure anyone can be about a conclusion. A data scientist usually works with large existing datasets and builds prediction models and data products, with more programming and engineering. The fields overlap heavily, and many people move between them.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Design, build and run storage arrays, SAN and NAS systems, and cloud object storage. They create volumes, set up snapshots and replication, manage backups, and plan capacity so applications never run out of space.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Check overnight backup and replication jobs, review alerts for failing disks or nearly full volumes, handle requests for new storage, tune slow performance, and push a migration or upgrade forward. Many teams also share on-call shifts for after-hours outages.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Array management consoles, Fibre Channel switches and zoning, iSCSI, NFS and SMB protocols, RAID and erasure coding, backup software, cloud storage consoles, monitoring dashboards, and scripts in Python, PowerShell or Bash to automate routine tasks.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Server and virtualization admins, database administrators, network engineers, security teams and application owners. They also open support cases with hardware vendors and coordinate firmware updates and part replacements.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: No lost data, high uptime, backups that actually restore, meeting agreed recovery point and recovery time objectives, steady performance under load, and capacity forecasts accurate enough to avoid emergency purchases.

qa.q: Is storage engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. A storage problem can slow or stop many applications at once, and lost data is hard to get back, so outages bring real pressure. Migrations and upgrades often happen at night or on weekends, and many teams run on-call rotations. Good monitoring, tested restores and careful change plans keep most days calm.

qa.q: What is the difference between SAN and NAS storage?
qa.a: A SAN gives servers block-level storage over a dedicated network, often Fibre Channel or iSCSI, and each server sees it like a local disk. NAS shares files over a regular network using NFS or SMB, so many users and servers can open the same files. Storage engineers often manage both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A store manager hires, trains and schedules staff, tracks sales against targets, controls stock and shrink, and keeps the shop clean, safe and well stocked. They also handle customer complaints and make sure company policies are followed on every shift.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a walk of the sales floor and a look at yesterday’s numbers. Then come deliveries, staffing gaps, shift briefings and customer issues. It ends with cash counts, closing checks and planning for tomorrow.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They lead sales associates, cashiers, stock clerks and assistant managers. They report to a district or area manager, deal with vendors and delivery drivers, and talk with customers who need help or want to escalate a problem.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Point of sale systems, inventory and ordering software, scheduling apps, sales reports and handheld scanners are daily tools. Many also use planograms to set displays, plus keys, safes and alarm codes for opening and closing.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are usually measured by sales versus target, labor cost, inventory accuracy and shrink, customer feedback scores and staff turnover. Audit results for safety, cash handling and store standards also count toward reviews and bonuses.

qa.q: What does a store manager do day to day?
qa.a: A store manager checks sales results, sets priorities and makes sure the right people are on each shift. They coach staff, receive and count stock, fix display and pricing issues, and step in on tough customer problems. They also handle paperwork such as payroll approvals, orders and incident reports, and often work the floor during busy hours.

qa.q: What is the difference between a store manager and an assistant store manager?
qa.a: The store manager is responsible for the whole shop: its results, budget, hiring decisions and standards. The assistant store manager supports them, often running shifts, training staff and covering when the manager is off. Assistants usually have less authority over hiring, scheduling and spending, and the role is a common step toward becoming a store manager.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Analyze what the company spends in each category, find and vet possible suppliers, run requests for proposal, negotiate multi-year contracts, and then track whether suppliers meet the agreed price, quality and delivery terms.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Reviewing spend reports, drafting or scoring a request for proposal, holding a negotiation call with a supplier, meeting internal teams about upcoming needs, and checking which contracts are due for renewal or rebid.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Engineering, operations, quality, finance and legal teams inside the company, plus buyers who place orders and account managers at supplier firms. Senior leaders often sign off on large contract awards.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spend analysis software, e-sourcing platforms for bids and reverse auctions, contract management systems, the company’s ERP system, spreadsheets for cost models, and supplier scorecards that track performance over time.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By savings against a baseline, total cost of ownership, supplier on-time delivery and quality, lower supply risk, how much spend runs through approved contracts, and how satisfied internal teams are with suppliers.

qa.q: What does a strategic sourcing manager do day to day?
qa.a: They study company spending, decide which goods and services to put out for bid, and compare supplier offers on cost, quality and risk. They negotiate contract terms, work with legal on contract language, and hold regular reviews with key suppliers to fix problems and find further savings.

qa.q: What is the difference between strategic sourcing and purchasing?
qa.a: Strategic sourcing decides which suppliers to use and sets long-term contract terms. Purchasing handles routine buying under those contracts, such as issuing purchase orders and following up on late deliveries. Paying the invoices is usually done separately by accounts payable in finance, which keeps payment apart from ordering as a basic control.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Work out the loads a structure must carry, such as weight, wind, snow, earthquakes, pressure or vibration. Choose materials and member sizes, check designs against codes and standards, and produce the drawings, calculations and reports others build from.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Much of the day is spent at a computer running analysis models and checking results by hand. There are also design meetings, reviews of shop drawings, answers to contractor questions and, on some days, site visits to inspect work in progress.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Building engineers work closely with architects, mechanical and electrical engineers, contractors, steel fabricators and building officials. Aerospace and industrial structural engineers work with design, test and manufacturing teams, plus quality and certification staff.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Finite element analysis and structural design software, CAD and BIM models, spreadsheets and hand calculations. Common references include ASCE 7 for loads, ACI 318 for concrete and AISC standards for steel, as adopted through state and local building codes.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Designs must be safe, meet code and be practical to build. Building plans are typically sealed by a licensed professional engineer, and some states require a separate structural engineer (SE) license for certain buildings. Peer checks and plan review catch errors before construction.

qa.q: What does a structural engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix analysis with coordination. A structural engineer builds models of a structure, applies loads like gravity, wind and earthquakes, sizes beams, columns, connections and foundations, and writes up calculations. They also review drawings from other trades, answer builders’ questions and visit sites. Entry-level engineers usually work under a licensed engineer’s supervision.

qa.q: What is the difference between a structural engineer and a civil engineer?
qa.a: Structural engineering is a specialty that often falls under civil engineering. Civil engineers cover a wider field, including roads, water systems, drainage and site work. Structural engineers focus on how buildings, bridges and other structures carry loads. Many hold a PE license in civil engineering, and some states also offer or require a separate SE license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Summer interns take on a set project or support a team with real tasks. These can include research, data analysis, drafting reports, writing code, or helping with clients. Many programs end with the intern presenting results to managers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a team check-in, followed by project work and short meetings with a manager or mentor. Many programs add training sessions, lunch talks with leaders, and social events with other interns.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Interns report to a direct manager who assigns work. Many also get a mentor or buddy for everyday questions. A recruiting or early careers team usually runs the program, and interns spend time with others in their cohort.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Internships happen in corporate offices, labs, factories, hospitals, banks, nonprofits, and government agencies. Some are fully remote or hybrid. Many employers recruit in the fall or winter for the following summer.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Most programs hold a midsummer check-in and a final review. Managers look at work quality, reliability, how fast the intern learns, and how well they fit the team. The final review often decides whether a return offer is made.

qa.q: What does a summer intern do day to day?
qa.a: A summer intern works on assigned projects and supports their team. A day may include research, analysis, writing, coding, or meeting clients, plus check-ins with a manager or mentor. Many programs also include training and networking events. By the end of the summer, interns often present what they built or learned to the team and its leaders.

qa.q: Do summer interns have to be paid?
qa.a: At for-profit companies, interns must be paid at least minimum wage under federal law unless the intern, not the employer, is the primary beneficiary under the US Department of Labor’s test. Some states add stricter rules. Unpaid roles are more common at nonprofits and government agencies, where volunteer rules differ. Many company internships pay an hourly wage or a stipend.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A construction superintendent runs the jobsite every day. They schedule crews and subcontractors, check that work matches the plans and specs, enforce safety rules, track materials and deliveries, and fix problems on the spot so the project stays on time and on budget.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Days often start before the crews arrive with a site walk and a short safety or coordination meeting. The rest goes to walking the work, answering field questions, meeting inspectors, updating the short-term look-ahead schedule, and writing the daily log of weather, manpower, deliveries and issues.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the project manager, foremen, trade subcontractors, suppliers and equipment operators. They also deal with architects, engineers, owner’s representatives and local building inspectors, and often serve as the main point of contact for anyone on site.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Superintendents use drawings and specifications, scheduling software, project management apps on a tablet or phone, and digital daily reports. In the field they rely on tape measures, levels, laser layout tools, two-way radios, cameras and the site safety plan.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by finishing on schedule, passing inspections, keeping rework and punch lists short, and having no serious injuries. Clear daily records, good relationships with subcontractors and a satisfied owner at closeout also count heavily in how a superintendent is rated.

qa.q: What is the difference between a construction superintendent and a project manager?
qa.a: The superintendent runs the field: crews, subcontractors, safety, quality and the daily schedule on site. The project manager runs the business side from the office or trailer: contracts, budgets, change orders, billing and owner communication. They work as a team, and on smaller jobs one person may handle parts of both roles.

qa.q: Is being a construction superintendent a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Superintendents answer for schedule, safety and quality at once, and weather, late deliveries, failed inspections or short-handed crews can upset a whole week. Early starts and long days are common. People who stay organized, plan ahead and communicate clearly tend to handle the pressure well and often find the work rewarding.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A supervisor plans who does what on each shift, gives out tasks, checks that work meets the standard and fixes problems as they come up. They also train new staff, track hours and breaks, and report results to a manager.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The shift often starts with a short huddle to set goals and cover any gaps. Then the supervisor walks the floor, answers questions, moves people where they are needed, handles a complaint or two and writes up a handoff for the next shift.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Supervisors sit between the front-line team and upper management. They work daily with their crew, other shift leads, managers, human resources and sometimes customers, vendors or maintenance staff when equipment or orders need attention.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include scheduling and timekeeping software, radios or phones, checklists, shift logs, and email. Many also use inventory or point-of-sale systems, safety forms and simple spreadsheets to track output, quality and attendance.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Supervisors are judged on whether the team hits its targets safely and on time. Managers look at output, error rates, staff turnover, attendance, safety incidents and how well problems are handled before they grow.

qa.q: What does a supervisor do day to day?
qa.a: A supervisor runs the shift. They assign tasks, check the quality of work, cover for absent staff, answer questions and solve problems on the spot. They also train workers, enforce safety and company rules, approve time records and keep managers informed about what happened during the shift.

qa.q: What is the difference between a supervisor and a manager?
qa.a: A supervisor usually leads a shift or small team and spends most of the day on the floor with workers. A manager often oversees several supervisors or a whole department and focuses more on budgets, hiring, planning and policy. Titles vary by employer, so duties can overlap.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They audit supplier plants, approve new parts before production through PPAP or first article inspection, and issue corrective action requests when bad parts arrive. They then follow up until the supplier finds and fixes the root cause.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may start with a review of rejected parts and supplier scorecards. Later comes a call about an 8D report, a review of new part approval files, or a drive or flight to a supplier plant for a process audit.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: At their own company, they work with buyers, design engineers, manufacturing staff and receiving inspection. At supplier sites, they work with quality managers, process engineers and machine operators, sometimes in other countries.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Their tools include control plans, process FMEAs, SPC charts, capability studies and gauge studies. They also read inspection and CMM reports and use audit checklists based on standards such as ISO 9001, IATF 16949 in automotive or AS9100 in aerospace.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by fewer defective parts per million from suppliers and corrective actions closed on time. Part approvals ready for product launches and lower costs from supplier defects also count.

qa.q: What does a supplier quality engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They check that purchased parts meet the drawing and specification. Most days mix desk work and site work. At the desk, they review approval packages, track defects and push suppliers on corrective actions. On site, they audit processes, watch production runs and help fix weak spots such as poor gauging or missing process controls. Travel is common, and in some roles it is frequent.

qa.q: What is the difference between supplier quality and supplier development engineers?
qa.a: A supplier quality engineer mostly protects incoming quality. They approve parts, contain defects and drive corrective actions. A supplier development engineer works to make suppliers more capable over time, often by improving processes, capacity, cost or delivery, and by bringing new suppliers on board. Many companies combine both jobs under one title, which is why job postings often list them together.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Supply chain and logistics workers plan how parts and products move from suppliers to factories, warehouses and customers. They place orders, track shipments, manage stock levels and fix delays before they stop a production line or miss a delivery date.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with open orders, inventory reports and late shipments. The rest of the day goes to calls and emails with suppliers and carriers, updating forecasts, booking freight, and solving problems like damaged goods, short shipments or a truck held at a dock.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with suppliers, freight carriers, customs brokers, warehouse staff, production teams and sales. Much of the job is keeping all of these groups on the same schedule and passing clear, timely information between them.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most of the work runs through enterprise resource planning (ERP) software, warehouse and transportation management systems, and spreadsheets. Barcode scanners, carrier tracking portals and shared dashboards show where goods are and what stock is on hand.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured with numbers such as on-time delivery, order accuracy, inventory turns, freight costs and stockouts. Strong performers spot risks early, keep enough stock without tying up too much cash, and keep customers and production lines supplied.

qa.q: What does a supply chain and logistics coordinator do day to day?
qa.a: A coordinator checks orders and stock levels, schedules shipments with carriers, tracks deliveries and updates records in the company’s planning software. When something goes wrong, like a late supplier or a lost pallet, they find a fix, such as a backup source or faster freight, and tell everyone affected.

qa.q: What is the difference between supply chain management and logistics?
qa.a: Logistics is one part of the supply chain. It covers moving and storing goods: transportation, warehousing and distribution. Supply chain management is broader. It also includes sourcing suppliers, purchasing, demand planning and production scheduling. Many job titles blend both, so read each posting’s duties to see which side the role leans toward.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Supply chain planners compare sales forecasts with stock on hand and open orders. They decide what to buy, make or move, and when. They set reorder points and safety stock, and they flag shortages early so production and shipping stay on schedule.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with reports on inventory, late shipments and forecast changes. Planners adjust purchase orders and production schedules, chase suppliers about delays, and join planning meetings. Much of the afternoon goes to fixing exceptions, such as a part that will run out next week.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with buyers, suppliers, warehouse staff, production supervisors, sales teams and finance. In many companies they lead or join a monthly sales and operations planning meeting, where teams agree on one demand and supply plan.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Planners rely on ERP systems, demand planning software and spreadsheets, with Excel skills used almost daily. Many also use dashboards and reporting tools. Some hold optional certifications from professional supply chain associations, though no license is required.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by on-time delivery, fill rate, forecast accuracy, inventory turns and stockout counts. Good planners keep enough stock to meet demand without tying up too much cash in inventory sitting on shelves.

qa.q: What does a supply chain planner do day to day?
qa.a: A supply chain planner checks demand forecasts against inventory and incoming supply, then adjusts orders and schedules to close gaps. They review shortage and excess reports, talk with suppliers and internal teams about delays, and update plans in the company’s ERP system. The goal is having the right parts and products in the right place at the right time.

qa.q: What is the difference between a supply chain planner and a buyer?
qa.a: A planner decides how much of each item is needed and when, based on demand and inventory. A buyer places the orders with suppliers, negotiates terms and manages vendor relationships. In smaller companies one person often does both jobs, and titles like planner/buyer are common.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technical support engineers take escalated tickets that front-line support could not close. They read logs, check configurations, reproduce faults in a test setup, find the root cause, and either deliver a fix or a workaround or hand a clear bug report to developers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with reviewing the ticket queue and urgent cases. Then come customer calls or screen shares, log analysis, attempts to reproduce bugs, and written updates. Some time goes to writing knowledge base articles so the same issue gets solved faster next time.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with customers’ IT staff and developers, front-line support agents, software engineers, product managers and account managers. Good handoffs matter, because a clear reproduction and summary saves developers hours of guesswork.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a ticketing system, log search and monitoring tools, command-line shells, SQL for checking data, API testing tools, virtual machines or containers for reproducing issues, and remote session software. Basic scripting helps automate repeated checks.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is usually measured by response and resolution times against service level agreements, customer satisfaction scores, the number of escalations to engineering, and the quality of notes and bug reports. Fixing the real cause counts more than closing tickets quickly.

qa.q: What does a technical support engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They handle complex customer problems that basic support could not solve. Most days mean reading logs, asking targeted questions, reproducing the fault in a test environment, and testing fixes. They write updates to customers, document solutions, and send confirmed bugs to developers with clear steps to reproduce them. Some roles include on-call shifts for urgent outages.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technical support engineer and a help desk technician?
qa.a: A help desk technician usually handles first-line requests such as password resets, account access and common how-to questions, often following scripts. A technical support engineer takes the harder escalated cases, digs into logs, code behavior and system configuration, and works closely with developers to find root causes. The engineer role typically expects deeper technical skills.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A customer support manager hires and trains agents, builds shift schedules, and reviews tickets and calls for quality. They track response and resolution times, handle escalated customer issues, and coach agents through regular one-on-one meetings.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a look at overnight ticket volume and staffing gaps. Then come queue checks, a team huddle, quality reviews of recorded calls or chats, a few escalations, and planning for next week’s schedule.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in a help desk or ticketing system, a phone or contact center platform, and live chat software. Managers also use workforce scheduling tools, quality scorecards, dashboards, and a shared knowledge base.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Besides their own agents and team leads, they work with product, engineering, sales, and billing teams. They pass along common customer complaints, report bugs, and help shape help articles and support policies.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Managers are measured by team results such as first response time, resolution time, customer satisfaction scores, quality review scores, and backlog size. Agent turnover, attendance, and staying within budget also count.

qa.q: What does a customer support manager do day to day?
qa.a: They keep the support queue under control and the team working well. That means watching ticket and call volume, adjusting schedules, stepping in on difficult customer cases, scoring agent work for quality, and coaching people. They also report trends to other departments and hire and train new agents when the team grows or someone leaves.

qa.q: What is the difference between a support team lead and a customer support manager?
qa.a: A team lead usually still handles some tickets and guides a small group of agents during a shift. A customer support manager owns the whole team or several teams. They make hiring decisions, set schedules and goals, manage performance reviews, and answer to senior leaders for results. Titles and duties vary by company.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: System administrators keep a company’s servers, networks and user devices running. They create and remove user accounts, set access permissions, apply software updates and security patches, manage backups, and fix problems that stop people from working.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with checking monitoring alerts, overnight backup results and the help desk queue. Then come planned tasks such as patching servers or setting up laptops, mixed with urgent fixes when a login, printer or shared drive fails.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include directory services for accounts and permissions, remote management consoles, scripting languages such as PowerShell or Bash, monitoring dashboards, ticketing systems, virtualization platforms and cloud administration portals.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They support employees across the company, answer to an IT manager, and work with help desk staff, network engineers and security teams. They also deal with outside vendors for hardware, software licenses and support contracts.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in steady uptime, fast recovery from outages, backups that actually restore, and accounts that give each person only the access they need. Clear documentation and closed tickets also count.

qa.q: What does a system administrator do day to day?
qa.a: A system administrator watches servers and networks for problems, handles support tickets, creates and removes user accounts, and decides who can open which files and systems. They also install updates, check backups, set up new devices and write scripts to automate routine tasks. Some work after hours during planned maintenance or outages.

qa.q: What is the difference between a system administrator and a network administrator?
qa.a: A system administrator focuses on servers, operating systems, user accounts and the software people use. A network administrator focuses on the links between them, such as routers, switches, firewalls, Wi-Fi and VPNs. In smaller companies one person often does both jobs, while larger companies usually split them.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Systems engineers turn customer needs into clear, testable requirements. They define how subsystems connect, manage interfaces between teams, run trade studies to compare design options, and plan how the finished product will be verified and validated before delivery.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes design reviews, requirement updates and meetings with hardware, software and test teams. They chase down interface conflicts, update models or documents, assess change requests, and check test results against the original requirements.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They sit between many groups: electrical, mechanical and software engineers, test technicians, project managers, quality staff and customers. In defense and aerospace work, they often deal with government program offices, and some roles require a security clearance.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include requirements management software, model-based systems engineering tools using SysML, simulation software, spreadsheets for trade studies, and issue trackers. Many teams follow a lifecycle such as the V-model, plus standards their industry or customer requires.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows up as a system that passes integration and acceptance testing with few surprises. Reviewers look for traceable requirements, controlled interfaces, managed risks, and changes handled without breaking schedule, cost or safety goals.

qa.q: What does a systems engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A systems engineer spends most days keeping a complex product coherent. That means writing and tracing requirements, settling interface questions between teams, leading or attending design reviews, and reviewing test data. They link what the customer asked for with what each engineering group builds, catching conflicts early before they become costly integration problems.

qa.q: What is the difference between a systems engineer and a software engineer?
qa.a: A software engineer designs and writes code for a specific part of a product. A systems engineer looks at the whole product, including hardware, software and how people use it, and defines how the parts fit together. In IT job ads, though, the title can also mean someone who builds and maintains servers, networks and cloud infrastructure, so read each posting closely.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Systems software engineers write and maintain the low-level code other programs depend on. That includes operating system kernels, device drivers, database storage engines, compilers, runtimes and network stacks. They fix hard bugs, tune performance and keep these layers stable under heavy load.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes design reviews, writing code in C, C++ or Rust, and chasing a stubborn bug with a debugger or profiler. Engineers read crash dumps, run benchmarks, review teammates’ changes and test fixes across different hardware or operating system versions.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include compilers, debuggers such as GDB, profilers, tracing tools, version control and continuous integration systems. Engineers also use emulators, virtual machines and test hardware. Many read assembly, packet captures or kernel logs to see what the machine is really doing.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with other systems engineers, application developers who build on their code, hardware engineers, site reliability teams and security specialists. Some contribute to open source projects and review code from outside contributors.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by correctness, speed, memory use and reliability. A good change makes the system faster or safer without breaking anything above it. Clear code, solid tests and careful handling of edge cases matter more than shipping quickly.

qa.q: What does a systems software engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They write and debug the core software that applications run on, such as kernels, drivers, databases, compilers and networking code. Much of the day goes to reading code, profiling performance, tracking down crashes or race conditions, reviewing changes and running tests to make sure fixes hold up on real hardware.

qa.q: What is the difference between a systems software engineer and an application developer?
qa.a: An application developer builds programs people use directly, like websites or mobile apps. A systems software engineer builds the layers beneath them, such as operating systems, databases and compilers. Systems work needs deeper knowledge of memory, concurrency, hardware and performance, and bugs can affect every program that sits on top.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Tax staff work out the income tax a company owes in the US and in each foreign country where it operates. They prepare and file federal, state and foreign returns, track estimated payments, and calculate the tax numbers that go into the financial statements.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with pulling ledger data and booking book-to-tax adjustments. Later come reconciling tax accounts, answering a notice from a tax authority, and checking how a new law, acquisition or entity change affects what the company owes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with controllers and accounting teams, legal staff who manage the company’s entities, and outside advisers in each country. They also explain their figures to external auditors and respond to tax authorities during audits.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets are central, along with the company’s accounting system, tax compliance and provision software, and research databases for tax codes, regulations and rulings. Returns are usually filed electronically through government or vendor e-filing systems.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work means every return is accurate and filed on time, with no avoidable penalties or interest. Tax figures in the financial statements should hold up under audit, and positions such as transfer pricing need clear supporting documentation.

qa.q: What is the difference between tax compliance and tax provision?
qa.a: Compliance means preparing and filing tax returns and paying what is due to each tax authority. Provision means estimating income tax expense, including current and deferred taxes, for the company’s financial statements. US companies reporting under US GAAP follow the accounting standard known as ASC 740. Many corporate tax roles cover both.

qa.q: Do you need a CPA license to work in corporate tax?
qa.a: No license is generally required to prepare your own employer’s tax returns, but many employers prefer or require a CPA for senior roles. CPA licensing is handled by each state, and education and experience rules vary by state. Some tax professionals instead hold the IRS enrolled agent credential, and some are attorneys.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A tech lead plans how the team will build features, splits big projects into tasks, reviews code and makes design calls. They still write code, often the trickiest or most foundational parts, while making sure nobody on the team stays stuck for long.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a short standup, then a block of code reviews. Afternoons mix pairing with a stuck engineer, answering questions from product managers and writing code between meetings. Many leads guard a few hours a week for deep technical work.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with the engineers on their team, an engineering manager, product managers and designers. They also coordinate with other teams whose systems theirs depends on, plus quality assurance, security and operations staff when releases or incidents come up.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a version control system with pull requests, an issue tracker for planning, team chat, shared design documents and diagrams. They also use continuous integration pipelines, monitoring dashboards and the same code editors and debuggers the rest of the team uses.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in what the team ships, not just personal output. Leads are judged on delivery against plans, code quality, system reliability, how quickly teammates grow and get unblocked, and how clearly they explain technical tradeoffs to nontechnical partners.

qa.q: What is the difference between a tech lead and an engineering manager?
qa.a: A tech lead owns the technical direction of a team: design, code quality and day to day unblocking, while still coding. An engineering manager usually handles people matters such as hiring, performance reviews and career growth, and may code little or not at all. Some companies combine both roles in one team lead job.

qa.q: Is being a tech lead a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Leads juggle their own coding with reviews, meetings and helping others, so focus time gets fragmented. They often feel responsible when deadlines slip or production breaks. Stress drops when the team plans realistically, shares on call duties fairly and the lead learns to delegate instead of fixing everything personally.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A technical account manager is the named technical contact for a set of customers after the sale. They learn each customer’s setup, plan upgrades and rollouts, track open support issues, and push for fixes inside their own company.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a review of open tickets and escalations. Then come customer calls, a quarterly business review or upgrade planning session, and internal meetings with support or engineering to chase stuck problems. Notes and account plans get updated throughout.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: On the customer side, they work with IT managers, engineers and administrators. Inside their own company, they work with support engineers, product managers, developers and the account executive or customer success manager who owns the business relationship.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They live in ticketing systems, a CRM, shared account plans and video calls. Many also use the product’s admin consoles, log and monitoring tools, cloud dashboards and documentation to understand what the customer is seeing.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually measured by customer health and retention, renewal outcomes, how fast escalations get resolved, adoption of new features, and customer satisfaction scores. Clear communication during outages and upgrades counts heavily.

qa.q: What does a technical account manager do day to day?
qa.a: They check on their customers’ open issues, join calls to plan upgrades or migrations, and escalate bugs to engineering when a fix is needed. They keep notes on each customer’s environment, explain new releases, and act as a single point of contact so customers do not have to repeat their story to new support agents.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technical account manager and a customer success manager?
qa.a: Both work with existing customers after the sale. A customer success manager focuses more on business goals, adoption and renewals. A technical account manager goes deeper into the technical setup, upgrades and problem solving. Titles and duties vary by company, and at some smaller firms one person covers both roles.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technical product managers decide what a platform, API or infrastructure product should do next and why. They gather needs from engineering teams, write clear requirements, set priorities on the roadmap and make tradeoffs between new features, reliability, performance and technical debt.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a standup, then moves to backlog grooming, a design review with architects and calls with internal or external developers using the product. Afternoons may go to writing specs, reviewing API documentation, checking usage dashboards and answering questions in team chat.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work most closely with software engineers, engineering managers and architects. They also partner with site reliability, security, developer relations, technical writers and support teams. Their users are often other engineers, so feedback tends to be detailed and technical.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include issue trackers, roadmap software, shared docs and wikis, and diagramming apps.
