Many also use API testing tools, analytics dashboards, monitoring and logging tools, and SQL to pull their own data. Reading code is helpful, though writing production code is usually not expected.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by adoption and outcomes, not features shipped. Typical signals include developer adoption, API usage and error rates, uptime, time to integrate, internal team productivity, support ticket volume and whether roadmap goals land on schedule.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technical product manager and a product manager?
qa.a: Both own what gets built and why. A technical product manager focuses on products whose users are often engineers, such as APIs, platforms and infrastructure. The role needs deeper knowledge of system design, integrations and performance. A general product manager more often works on customer facing features and leans more on user research, design and market positioning.

qa.q: Do you need a computer science degree to be a technical product manager?
qa.a: No single degree is required, and no license applies. Many technical product managers studied computer science or engineering, or worked as software engineers first. Employers mostly look for proof you can discuss architecture, APIs and tradeoffs with engineers. Product experience, technical projects and strong writing can matter as much as the degree itself.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A technical program manager plans large engineering efforts that span several teams. They map dependencies, track risks, set milestones and keep dates honest. When teams disagree or a blocker appears, they bring the right people together and push for a decision.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with status checks across teams. Then come design reviews, risk discussions and planning meetings. Between meetings they update schedules, write status reports, chase open questions and flag slipping work to leaders before it becomes a surprise.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with software and hardware engineers, engineering managers, product managers and quality teams. They also deal with security, legal, operations and support groups, plus executives who need clear, short updates on progress and risk.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include issue trackers, project planning software, shared roadmaps, wikis and dashboards. Many also read code, system diagrams and test results well enough to spot technical risk. Clear writing and spreadsheets are daily tools too.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means programs ship on time with known tradeoffs and few surprises. Leaders look at whether risks were raised early, whether teams stayed aligned, and whether decisions and status were written down clearly for everyone involved.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technical program manager and a product manager?
qa.a: A product manager decides what to build and why, based on customer and business needs. A technical program manager focuses on how and when it gets built across teams. They manage schedules, dependencies and execution risk. The two roles work side by side, and on smaller teams one person may cover parts of both.

qa.q: Do you need to be an engineer to become a technical program manager?
qa.a: No license or specific degree is required. Many technical program managers have a computer science or engineering background, or spent years as engineers. Employers expect enough technical depth to follow architecture talks and judge risk. Some people also hold project management certifications, but these are optional and not required by law.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technical recruiters fill software, data and other engineering roles. They meet hiring managers to define each role, write job posts, search for candidates, run first-round screening calls and guide people through interviews to an offer.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often go to sourcing on professional networks, code-sharing sites and the company’s applicant database, then sending personal outreach messages. Afternoons bring screening calls, interview scheduling, debriefs with the hiring team and updates to candidates waiting on decisions.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with hiring managers, engineering interviewers who assess technical skills, HR partners who handle pay and onboarding, and candidates. In-house recruiters may also work with sourcers and coordinators. Agency recruiters answer to client companies.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: An applicant tracking system, professional networking sites, Boolean search strings, scheduling tools and video calls. A working vocabulary of job titles, languages, frameworks and seniority levels helps them read a resume and spot a likely fit before passing it to engineers.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Common measures include time to fill a role, how many screened candidates pass the technical interviews, offer acceptance, candidate feedback and how long new hires stay. Agency recruiters are often paid partly on placements.

qa.q: What does a technical recruiter do day to day?
qa.a: They find and contact engineers, hold short screening calls about experience, goals, location and pay expectations, and set up interviews. Engineers on the hiring team test technical skills. The recruiter keeps the process moving, shares feedback and helps close offers, following hiring laws. Rules on asking about salary history or posting pay ranges vary by state and city.

qa.q: Do technical recruiters need to know how to code?
qa.a: No. Most technical recruiters do not code. Many come from general recruiting, sales or HR and learn the basics of common languages, tools and job levels on the job. That knowledge helps them ask better screening questions and earn engineers’ trust, but the technical assessment is done by engineering interviewers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technical writers plan, draft and update user manuals, online help, release notes, installation guides and API reference pages. They turn engineering details into clear steps, keep content accurate as the product changes, and fix gaps that users or support teams report.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with checking tickets or a sprint board for new features. The writer then interviews an engineer, tests the feature in a staging build, drafts or revises pages, sends them for review, and publishes approved changes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with software engineers, product managers, designers, QA testers and customer support staff. Subject matter experts review drafts for accuracy, while editors or other writers check style, structure and consistency with the company’s style guide.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include Markdown, a docs-as-code setup with Git, static site generators, help authoring tools and XML formats like DITA. API writers read code samples, use OpenAPI specs and test calls with command-line or API client tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good documentation is accurate, findable and easy to follow. Teams judge it by fewer support tickets on covered topics, reviewer sign-off, user feedback ratings, page search data, and whether docs ship on time alongside each product release.

qa.q: What does a technical writer do day to day?
qa.a: A technical writer gathers facts from engineers and product teams, tries the product themselves, and writes clear instructions and reference pages. They revise drafts after technical review, update older pages when features change, and publish content to help sites or developer portals. Much of the day is spent asking questions, testing steps and editing for clarity.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technical writer and a copywriter?
qa.a: A technical writer explains how a product works so people can install, use or build on it. Accuracy and clarity matter most. A copywriter writes ads, web pages and emails meant to persuade people to buy or act. Technical writers usually work with engineers, while copywriters usually work with marketing teams.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technicians build, install, test, repair and maintain equipment such as machines, heating and cooling systems, vehicles, electronics or medical devices. They find faults, replace worn parts, adjust settings and record what they did, so each unit has a clear service history.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a list of work orders. A technician inspects equipment, runs diagnostic tests, swaps failed parts and confirms the fix works before signing off. Planned maintenance fills quieter hours, but a sudden breakdown can change the whole schedule.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Hand and power tools, multimeters, pressure gauges, torque wrenches and laptops running diagnostic software. Manuals, wiring diagrams and schematics guide the work. Gloves, eye protection and lockout/tagout devices are part of the daily routine.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Shops, factories, hospitals, data centers, homes, vehicle service bays and outdoor field sites. Some stay at one location, while others drive between customer calls. The work can involve standing, kneeling, lifting, tight spaces, ladders and noisy or hot areas.

day.label: Licenses and certifications
day.text: Rules depend on the specialty and often on the state. Technicians servicing stationary refrigeration or air conditioning need EPA Section 608 certification, while those servicing vehicle air conditioning need Section 609. Electrical work may require a state or local license. Many employers also value voluntary industry certifications.

qa.q: What does a technician do day to day?
qa.a: A technician works through assigned jobs, such as installing new equipment, doing scheduled maintenance or answering breakdown calls. They inspect the equipment, test it to find the fault, repair or replace parts, check that everything runs safely and write up the work. They also order parts, keep tools in shape and explain repairs to supervisors or customers.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technician and an engineer?
qa.a: Engineers mainly design and plan equipment and systems, and they often hold a bachelor’s degree in engineering. Technicians do the hands-on work of building, installing, testing and repairing that equipment. Technicians usually train through a certificate, an associate degree, an apprenticeship or on the job, and they often report field problems back to engineers.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Technology consultants study how a client’s business runs, find where systems fall short, and recommend fixes. They compare software and hardware options, plan rollouts, set up or configure systems, and train staff so the new tools actually get used.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often mixes client meetings, requirement notes, and hands-on work. A consultant might run a discovery workshop in the morning, write a recommendation or project plan after lunch, then test a system setting or fix a problem before an update call.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with business owners, managers, and end users who explain what they need. They also coordinate with in-house IT teams, software vendors, project managers, and sometimes security or compliance staff who must approve changes.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include cloud platforms, business software such as CRM and ERP systems, project tracking boards, diagramming apps, spreadsheets, and video calls. Many also use scripting or admin consoles to configure systems and check that data moved correctly.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether the project lands on time and within budget, whether the system works as promised, and whether staff adopt it. Client satisfaction, repeat work, and clear documentation also count heavily.

qa.q: What does a technology consultant do day to day?
qa.a: A technology consultant spends the day learning a client’s needs, comparing tools, and turning choices into working systems. That means meetings, writing plans and proposals, configuring software, testing, fixing issues, and training users. Some days are mostly analysis and slides. Others are hands-on setup and troubleshooting, depending on the project stage.

qa.q: What is the difference between a technology consultant and an IT support specialist?
qa.a: An IT support specialist keeps existing systems running and solves day-to-day problems for users. A technology consultant looks at the bigger picture. They advise on which systems to adopt or change, plan the project, and guide the rollout. Consultants usually work project to project, often for several clients, while support staff handle ongoing tickets.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Telecommunications engineers design, build and run the networks that carry phone calls and mobile data. They plan cell sites and radio coverage, design fiber and microwave links, configure core network equipment, troubleshoot outages and roll out new technology such as 5G.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might include reviewing coverage maps and drive test results, planning capacity for busy areas or configuring network equipment. Engineers also work tickets on dropped calls or slow data, join overnight maintenance windows and sometimes visit tower sites or equipment rooms.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with field technicians and tower crews, network operations center staff, equipment vendors, and site acquisition and permitting teams. They also coordinate with project managers, IT and security teams, and sometimes with landowners or local officials about new sites.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include RF planning software such as Atoll or Planet, drive test kits, spectrum analyzers and fiber testers like OTDRs. Core and transport work uses vendor management systems, Wireshark for protocol traces and Python scripts. Field visits need a laptop and console cables.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on network uptime, call and data quality, coverage and capacity in busy areas, and fast fixes during outages. Projects must meet deadlines and follow FCC rules on spectrum use and radio frequency exposure. Safety on towers and field sites is never optional.

qa.q: Do telecommunications engineers need a license?
qa.a: Most telecom engineers do not need a personal license. A Professional Engineer license, issued by each state, is needed only in some roles, such as sealing certain designs, and rules vary by state. Spectrum licenses from the FCC belong to the carrier, not the engineer. Anyone who climbs towers must be trained in fall protection under OSHA rules.

qa.q: What is the difference between a telecommunications engineer and a network engineer?
qa.a: A network engineer usually runs data networks inside companies, such as routers, switches, firewalls and Wi-Fi. A telecommunications engineer works on carrier networks that serve the public, including radio access, fiber transport and the mobile core. The fields overlap in IP routing, and many telecom engineers also hold networking certifications.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A territory sales manager owns revenue in one geographic area. They find new accounts, visit existing customers, quote prices, close orders and keep a pipeline of prospects moving toward the area’s sales target.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with route planning and CRM updates, then several in-person calls with buyers, store managers or business owners. Afternoons often bring follow-up emails, quotes, order problems and notes logged before the next day’s visits.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They deal with purchasing agents, owners, distributors and end users in their area. Inside the company they lean on inside sales, customer service, marketing and their regional sales manager for pricing, samples and support.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Expect a CRM system, a laptop or tablet, a phone, mapping and routing apps, product samples and price sheets. Many roles provide a company car or pay a mileage reimbursement, so a valid driver’s license and clean record are common requirements.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured against the territory quota: revenue, unit volume, new accounts won and customer retention. Managers also watch call activity, pipeline health and forecast accuracy, and pay often includes a commission or bonus tied to these numbers.

qa.q: What does a territory sales manager do day to day?
qa.a: They spend much of the day on the road visiting customers and prospects in their assigned area. Between visits they prospect for new accounts, prepare quotes, solve order or delivery issues, and log every call in the CRM. They also review progress toward the territory target and plan which accounts to see next.

qa.q: What is the difference between a territory sales manager and a regional sales manager?
qa.a: A territory sales manager usually sells directly and owns one area’s customers and quota, often without managing staff. A regional sales manager typically oversees several territories and leads the reps who cover them, focusing on coaching, hiring, forecasting and regional targets. Titles vary by company, so check each posting’s duties.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Writes test plans from the product’s requirements, builds fixtures, and runs units through heat, cold, humidity, vibration, shock and long life cycles. Records the data, finds the root cause of failures, and reports whether the design passes or needs changes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts by checking units that ran overnight in a thermal chamber or on a shaker table. Then comes reviewing logged data, tearing down a failed part, updating a test script, and meeting with designers to explain what broke and why.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Thermal and humidity chambers, vibration shakers, shock towers, oscilloscopes, multimeters, power supplies and data acquisition systems. Many write automation scripts in Python or a graphical test language. Most follow standards such as MIL-STD-810, IEC 60068 or JEDEC, depending on the industry.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Design, firmware and mechanical engineers, technicians who set up and run tests, and manufacturing and quality teams. They also work with outside accredited labs that handle certification testing. Customers or program managers often review the final reports.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By clear, repeatable tests that trace back to each requirement, and by catching failures before products ship. Good engineers write reports others can trust, keep equipment calibrated, and turn vague failures into a confirmed root cause.

qa.q: What does a test and validation engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They plan and run tests that stress hardware past normal use, such as temperature cycling, vibration, shock and accelerated life tests. Most days mix lab work with data analysis, failure investigation and report writing. They also build fixtures, automate test runs and meet with design teams to decide whether a design is ready for production.

qa.q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
qa.a: Verification checks that the hardware meets its written specifications, such as a voltage range or temperature rating. Validation checks that the product meets the user’s real needs in its intended environment. In simple terms, verification asks if it was built right, and validation asks if the right thing was built. Test engineers often do both.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Most roles involve answering customers, translating text, or interpreting conversations between Thai and English. Common jobs include bilingual customer support, content review, localization, sales for the Thai market, and interpreting in clinics, courts or community settings.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A support or review worker might clear a queue of chats, emails or calls in Thai and log each case in English. A translator might spend the day adapting product text and checking that the tone suits Thai readers.

day.label: Hours and time zones
day.text: Thailand is 11 or 12 hours ahead of US Eastern time and does not use daylight saving time. US jobs serving customers in Thailand often include night, early morning or split shifts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Workers use help desk and ticketing systems, call software, translation memory tools, glossaries and style guides. They need to type Thai script quickly and handle line breaks well, since Thai writes words without spaces between them.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers often test both languages before hiring. On the job, reviewers check accuracy, tone and correct polite forms such as khrap and kha. They also track speed, case resolution and customer ratings.

qa.q: Do you need a certification to work as a Thai interpreter?
qa.a: It depends on the setting. Most business and support jobs only require a language test from the employer. Court interpreter rules vary by state, and many courts use a registered or qualified status for languages without a full certification exam. Healthcare employers often want medical interpreter training, and some national credentials do not require a Thai oral exam.

qa.q: What is the difference between a Thai translator and a Thai interpreter?
qa.a: A translator works with written text, such as documents, websites or app screens, and usually has time to research terms. An interpreter works with spoken language in real time, by phone, video or in person, often in medical, legal or business settings. Many people do both, but the skills and hiring tests differ.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They work out how much heat a product makes and how to remove it. They size fans, pumps, pipes, heat exchangers and cold plates, run simulations, and check that parts stay within safe temperature and pressure limits.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A morning might go to building a computational fluid dynamics model or reviewing simulation results. An afternoon often means lab time: placing sensors on a prototype, running it in a test chamber, and comparing measured temperatures with predictions before suggesting design changes.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use CAD software, CFD and finite element tools, and spreadsheets or scripts for hand calculations. In the lab they work with thermocouples, flow meters, pressure sensors, infrared cameras, data loggers and environmental chambers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with mechanical designers, electrical engineers who set power loads, test technicians and manufacturing staff. They also talk with suppliers of fans, pumps and heat exchangers, and explain tradeoffs in size, cost and noise to project managers.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Jobs are found in electronics and data centers, electric vehicles and batteries, aerospace, power generation, HVAC and building systems, and industrial equipment. Most work happens in an office and lab, with some trips to test sites or factories.

qa.q: What does a thermal and fluids engineer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days mix analysis and testing. They model heat flow and fluid movement with simulation software, check results with hand calculations, and test prototypes with sensors in a lab. They then recommend changes, such as a larger heat sink, a different pump or a new airflow path, and share results in reports and design reviews.

qa.q: Do thermal and fluids engineers need a PE license?
qa.a: Usually not for product design work inside a company, since many states exempt that work. A Professional Engineer license is needed to sign and seal plans offered to the public, which is common in HVAC and building system design. Requirements vary by state, but the usual path includes an engineering degree, the FE and PE exams, and supervised experience.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Track hacker groups, ransomware crews, scam and phishing campaigns, and new malware. Collect signs of attack such as malicious domains, IP addresses and file hashes. Study how attackers operate, then write alerts and reports that tell defenders what to watch for and how to block it.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Start by reviewing overnight threat feeds, security advisories, news and underground forums. Check whether new indicators show up in company logs, update block lists and watchlists, and brief the security team. Later hours often go to deeper research on one group or a written assessment for leaders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Security operations center analysts, incident responders, threat hunters and vulnerability management teams use their findings daily. They also brief executives in plain language, support fraud and legal teams, and trade information with peers through industry sharing groups.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Threat intelligence platforms, log search tools in a SIEM, malware sandboxes, open-source intelligence tools, domain registration and passive DNS lookups, and shared frameworks that map attacker techniques. Strong writing skills and a habit of checking sources matter as much as any software.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good intelligence is timely, accurate and actionable. Analysts are judged on whether their warnings led to blocked attacks, faster detection or smarter patch priorities, and on how clearly they explain confidence levels and what the reader should do next.

qa.q: What does a threat intelligence analyst do day to day?
qa.a: They read threat feeds, advisories and forum chatter, then decide what matters to their company. They check if new attack signs appear in company systems, add them to block lists, and research the groups behind them. Much of the day is writing short alerts and longer reports that help other security teams act quickly.

qa.q: What is the difference between a threat intelligence analyst and a SOC analyst?
qa.a: A SOC analyst watches alerts inside the company’s own network and responds to suspicious activity as it happens. A threat intelligence analyst looks outward at attackers, their tools and their campaigns. The intelligence analyst’s findings give SOC analysts context, help tune detection rules, and show which threats deserve attention first.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Designs injection molds, stamping dies, jigs and fixtures that let a plant make the same part thousands of times. Reviews part drawings for moldability, plans gates, cooling and ejection, picks tool steels, and manages tool builds, trials and repairs.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start on the shop floor at a mold trial or with a die that is wearing out. The rest of the day goes to CAD models, design reviews, tool shop quotes, and fixing features that came out of tolerance.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Works closely with toolmakers, machinists, process technicians and quality inspectors. Also works with product designers to make parts easier to mold or stamp, and with outside tool shops and buyers on build schedules and cost.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: 3D CAD and CAM software, mold flow and forming simulation, GD&T drawings, calipers, micrometers and coordinate measuring machine reports. Daily work also calls for knowledge of tool steels, heat treating, EDM, hot runner systems and press tonnage.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in parts that meet print early in trials, short cycle times, low scrap, and tools that run a long time between repairs. In automotive and medical plants, tools must also pass formal part approval and validation before production.

qa.q: What does a tooling engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A tooling engineer splits time between the computer and the plant floor. They design or review molds, dies and fixtures in CAD, run simulations, and work with tool shops on builds. On the floor they attend tool trials, measure sample parts, troubleshoot defects like flash or short shots, and plan repairs and changes.

qa.q: What is the difference between a tooling engineer and a toolmaker?
qa.a: A tooling engineer designs the tool and decides how it should work, from steel choice to cooling and ejection. A toolmaker builds and repairs it by machining, grinding, EDM and fitting parts by hand. Engineers usually hold a mechanical or manufacturing engineering degree, while toolmakers often train through apprenticeships. Most tooling jobs need no state license.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Traders buy and sell stocks, bonds, currencies, commodities or derivatives for their firm or its clients. They fill orders at the best price they can get, manage open positions, stay within risk limits and make sure every trade is recorded correctly.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts before the market opens with a review of overnight news, economic data and current positions. During trading hours they watch prices, execute orders and adjust hedges. After the close they check trades with operations and review profit and loss.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Traders work closely with sales staff, portfolio managers, research analysts and risk managers. They also deal with compliance officers, operations teams that settle trades, and brokers or counterparties at other firms.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use several screens, order and execution management systems, market data terminals, spreadsheets and recorded phone or chat lines. Many also write code, often in Python, to build pricing models or automated trading strategies.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Performance is judged on profit and loss, execution quality against price benchmarks, and staying within assigned risk limits. Following best execution rules, trade reporting duties and market conduct rules matters just as much.

qa.q: Do traders need a license in the US?
qa.a: It depends on the role. Securities traders at broker-dealers usually must pass FINRA’s SIE exam and the Series 57, which requires firm sponsorship. People handling futures for customers often need the Series 3 and NFA registration. Some proprietary roles have different rules, so check with the employer.

qa.q: Is being a trader a stressful job?
qa.a: It often is. Traders make fast decisions with real money, and gains or losses show up right away. Volatile markets, tight risk limits and early starts add pressure. Many people still enjoy the pace, the clear feedback and the focus on numbers, but the job suits those who stay calm under pressure.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They build and tune the software that sends, routes and matches orders. This covers order gateways, matching engines, market data handlers, and pre-trade risk checks. They cut latency, keep systems stable under heavy volume, and fix problems fast when something breaks during market hours.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start before the market opens with system checks and a review of overnight logs. During trading hours they watch for errors and latency spikes. Later they write and test code, profile performance, and release changes in planned windows when markets are closed.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work in C++, Java or Rust on tuned Linux servers. They use the FIX protocol and exchange binary protocols, kernel bypass networking, and precise clock sync. Some firms use FPGAs and colocated servers placed inside exchange data centers to shave off microseconds.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with traders, quantitative researchers, and risk and compliance staff. They also deal with network engineers, site reliability teams, and the technical support desks at exchanges and brokers when connections or certifications need attention.

day.label: Rules they work under
day.text: Broker-dealers with market access must keep pre-trade risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5. At FINRA member firms, people primarily responsible for designing, developing or significantly modifying algorithmic strategies in equity, preferred or convertible debt securities must register as Securities Traders by passing the SIE and Series 57.

qa.q: What does a trading systems engineer do day to day?
qa.a: They keep trading software fast and reliable. Before the open they check systems and connections. During market hours they monitor latency, errors and risk limits, and respond quickly to incidents. The rest of the day goes to writing and testing code, measuring performance, and preparing releases that go out when markets are closed.

qa.q: What is the difference between a trading systems engineer and a quant developer?
qa.a: A trading systems engineer builds the infrastructure that moves orders, such as gateways, matching engines and market data feeds, with a focus on speed and stability. A quant developer works closer to strategy, turning researchers’ models into code, building backtests and pricing tools. Titles overlap a lot, and duties differ from firm to firm.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Training and enablement staff find out what people need to learn. They build courses, guides and practice exercises, then teach them live or online. They also update content when a product, process or policy changes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a live onboarding session for new hires or customers. Later comes time to edit a video module, answer learner questions and meet a product team about an upcoming release that needs new training.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with subject matter experts, managers, sales and support teams, and HR. For customer training, they also partner with product managers and customer success staff to learn what users struggle with most.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include a learning management system, video meeting software, slide decks, screen recording tools and e-learning authoring software. Many also use surveys, quizzes and simple reporting dashboards to track who finished what.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured by whether people can actually do the work after training. Teams look at course completion, quiz scores, learner feedback, time to get new hires productive and changes in errors, support tickets or sales results.

qa.q: What does a training and enablement specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They plan and deliver lessons for employees or customers. On a given day, they may teach a class, record a short video, write a how-to guide, interview an expert, review feedback and fix confusing material. Much of the job is turning complex information into clear, practical steps people can follow.

qa.q: What is the difference between training and enablement?
qa.a: Training usually means teaching specific skills or processes, often through courses and classes. Enablement is broader. It often refers to giving a team, commonly sales or support, everything they need to succeed, including training, reference content, tools and coaching. Many companies combine the two in one role, and titles vary by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Travel coordinators book and manage business trips for employees, teams or event groups. They arrange flights, hotels, rental cars and ground transport, apply company travel policy, check passport and visa needs, track spending and rebook travelers fast when flights are canceled or plans change.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with new trip requests and itinerary changes that came in overnight. Then come booking flights and hotels, checking fares against policy, sending confirmations and preparing visa letters. Weather delays or cancellations can take over the afternoon with urgent rebooking calls.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with travelers and their managers, executive assistants, finance and accounts payable teams, and event planners. Outside the company they deal with travel management agencies, airline and hotel sales staff, visa services and consulates.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most use corporate booking tools like SAP Concur, Navan or Egencia, and some use a reservation system such as Sabre or Amadeus. Expense software, Excel trackers, airline and hotel portals, flight tracking apps and shared calendars are everyday tools.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: They are judged on traveler safety and satisfaction, accurate bookings with no lost reservations, and fast fixes when plans break. Finance also watches policy compliance, use of negotiated rates and unused ticket credits, and whether travel spending stays on budget.

qa.q: What is the difference between a travel coordinator and a travel agent?
qa.a: A travel agent usually sells trips to the public or to many clients and is often paid partly by commission. A travel coordinator usually works inside one company, school or organization, booking work trips under its travel policy and budget. Coordinators also track spending and traveler safety, often alongside an outside travel management agency.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be a travel coordinator?
qa.a: No federal license is required, and in-house coordinators rarely need any license. A few states, including California, Florida and Hawaii, require businesses that sell travel to the public to register with the state. Employers mostly look for travel or hospitality experience, strong organization, calm problem solving and comfort with booking software.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Treasury staff track cash across every company bank account, forecast what will come in and go out, fund payments, and invest spare cash. They also manage borrowing, credit lines and debt covenants, and hedge risk from foreign currencies and interest rates.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The morning starts with cash positioning: checking bank balances, moving money between accounts and confirming that payroll and supplier payments are funded. Later work may include updating the cash forecast, placing currency trades, reviewing hedges, or answering bank and audit requests.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They report to a treasurer or the chief financial officer and work closely with accounting, accounts payable, tax and the business units. Outside the company, they deal with banks, lenders, investment managers and auditors.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most teams use a treasury management system, online bank portals, the company’s accounting software and spreadsheets. Payments move by wire, ACH and secure bank messaging. Market data screens help with currency and interest rate decisions.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success means the company never runs short of cash, payments go out on time and securely, forecasts land close to actual results, and losses from currency or rate swings stay within the limits set by policy.

qa.q: What does a treasury analyst do day to day?
qa.a: A treasury analyst checks daily bank balances, moves cash where it is needed, and makes sure payments are funded. They update short and long term cash forecasts, track debt and credit lines, prepare hedge and investment reports, and help set up bank accounts and payment controls to prevent fraud.

qa.q: What is the difference between treasury and accounting?
qa.a: Accounting records what already happened and produces financial statements. Treasury looks ahead. It manages the actual cash, decides where it is held and how it moves, arranges borrowing, and hedges currency and interest rate risk. The two teams work closely, since accounting records the results of treasury’s decisions.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Review user reports and flagged content against the platform’s policies. Remove or label posts that break the rules, suspend accounts, and decide appeals. Senior staff write and update policies, train reviewers, and investigate coordinated abuse such as scams, spam rings, and fake accounts.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A shift often starts in a review queue sorted by severity. Urgent items like threats of violence, self-harm, or child exploitation come first. Between cases, staff tag emerging trends, escalate unclear calls to policy leads, and flag gaps in the written rules.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Case management queues, moderation dashboards, and automated classifiers that flag likely violations. Hash-matching tools catch known illegal images. Investigators also use account history lookups, spreadsheets, SQL queries, and link analysis to connect related accounts.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Engineers who build detection tools, product teams launching new features, legal counsel, and outside review vendors. Some roles handle law enforcement requests, which must follow federal privacy law and the platform’s legal process.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Accuracy against policy, consistency across similar cases, and speed on high-priority queues. Quality reviewers audit samples of decisions. Appeal reversal rates show where rules or training need work. Teams also watch reviewer wellbeing because of exposure to disturbing material.

qa.q: What does a trust and safety specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They work through queues of reported or auto-flagged content and accounts, apply the platform’s written policies, and take action such as removal, warnings, or bans. They review appeals, escalate hard cases, and spot new abuse patterns. Apparent child sexual abuse material must be reported to the national CyberTipline under federal law, so those cases follow a strict process.

qa.q: Is trust and safety a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. Reviewers may see graphic violence, hate, and abuse, and must make fast calls with real consequences. Many employers offer counseling, wellness breaks, blurred or grayscale previews, and rotation off the hardest queues. Policy and investigations roles see less raw content but face pressure from public scrutiny and changing rules. Support varies widely by employer.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: UI and visual designers decide how each screen looks. They set layout grids, choose type and color, draw icons, and define the states of buttons, forms and menus so every part of an app or website feels consistent.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a team standup. Then come mockups in a design tool, feedback rounds with product managers, updates to the design system, and checks on test builds to see whether spacing, fonts and colors match the approved files.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with UX designers and researchers who shape user flows, product managers who set priorities, and front-end developers who build the screens. Brand and marketing teams often weigh in on visual style.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most work happens in vector-based interface design tools with shared component libraries. Designers also use prototyping features, icon and illustration software, color contrast checkers, and handoff specs that give developers exact sizes, colors and spacing.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good UI work is clear, consistent and accessible. Teams review it against the design system, brand guidelines and accessibility standards such as WCAG contrast rules, and by whether users can easily find and tap what they need.

qa.q: What does a UI and visual designer do day to day?
qa.a: Most days are spent turning wireframes into polished screens. A UI and visual designer picks fonts, colors and spacing, builds reusable components, drafts icons, and presents mockups for feedback. They also answer developer questions and review built screens to catch details that drifted from the design.

qa.q: What is the difference between a UI designer and a UX designer?
qa.a: A UX designer focuses on how a product works: user research, task flows, wireframes and testing whether people can reach their goals. A UI designer focuses on how it looks on screen: layout, type, color, icons and interaction states. Many jobs blend both roles, so read each posting closely.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Underwriters review applications for insurance or loans and judge the risk. They approve, decline, or change the terms. That can mean setting a premium, adding exclusions, requiring a bigger down payment, or asking for more documents before a final decision.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Most days mean working through a queue of files. An underwriter reads credit reports, income records, financial statements, inspection reports, loss histories, or medical records. They request missing items, weigh the facts against company guidelines, and write notes explaining each decision.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Underwriters work with agents, brokers, loan officers, and processors who send in applications. They also deal with appraisers, inspectors, and actuaries. Senior underwriters or managers sign off on files above an underwriter’s approval authority.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Underwriters rely on underwriting and rating software, automated underwriting systems, credit reports, and written guideline manuals. Spreadsheets, document portals, and third party data reports help them check facts and compare a file against the company’s rules.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are judged by how well approved policies or loans perform over time, such as losses or defaults. Quality audits check that files follow guidelines and regulations. Turnaround time and staying within approval authority also count.

qa.q: What does an underwriter do day to day?
qa.a: An underwriter spends the day reviewing applications for insurance or loans. They check documents, credit, income, property details, or loss history. They compare each file to company guidelines, ask for missing information, and decide whether to approve, decline, or change the terms or price. They also record clear notes so others can see why each decision was made.

qa.q: What is the difference between an underwriter and an actuary?
qa.a: An actuary uses statistics to study risk across large groups and helps set base rates and pricing models. An underwriter applies those rates and the company’s guidelines to one applicant at a time. In short, actuaries build the pricing framework, and underwriters decide whether a specific person or business fits it and on what terms.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Builds a pipeline of students and new graduates for internships and entry-level roles. Plans campus visits, career fairs and info sessions, screens resumes, schedules interviews, extends offers, and keeps candidates engaged until their start date.

day.label: The yearly cycle
day.text: The work follows the academic calendar. Fall is packed with career fairs and interviews for next summer’s interns and full-time graduates. Spring brings more offers and onboarding prep. Summer is spent running the intern program and turning strong interns into full-time hires.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Hiring managers who define each role, college career services offices, student clubs, professors, and campus ambassadors. Inside the company they work with HR, compensation and onboarding teams, plus employees who volunteer as interviewers or alumni speakers.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Applicant tracking systems, campus recruiting platforms linked to university career centers, video interview tools, candidate relationship and event software, and spreadsheets for tracking offers. Booth displays and branded giveaways come along to career fairs.

day.label: Rules to know
day.text: Hiring must follow federal equal employment opportunity laws. Unpaid internships at for-profit employers must meet the Department of Labor’s primary beneficiary test. International students often need work authorization such as CPT or OPT, and some states and cities add their own hiring rules.

qa.q: What does a university recruiter do day to day?
qa.a: It depends on the season. In fall and early spring they travel to campuses, staff career fair booths, host info sessions, and run interview days. Between events they screen resumes, coordinate interviews with hiring managers, make offers, and answer candidate questions. In summer they support interns, plan next year’s events, and push for intern-to-full-time offers.

qa.q: What is the difference between a university recruiter and a corporate recruiter?
qa.a: A corporate recruiter usually fills individual openings with experienced hires all year. A university recruiter hires groups of interns and new graduates on a schedule tied to the school year. Campus work leans more on employer branding, events, and school relationships, and candidates are judged on potential, coursework, and projects rather than past job results.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: UX designers map how people move through a product, then sketch flows, wireframes and prototypes. They run or join user research, test designs with real users, and revise screens until tasks feel clear and quick to finish.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a team standup, then time in a design tool refining a checkout flow. Afternoons often bring a user interview, a usability test, or a review where engineers and product managers question the design.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work closely with product managers, software engineers, UI and visual designers, and UX researchers. They also talk with customer support, marketing and real users to learn where people get stuck.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include collaborative design and prototyping software, whiteboard apps for journey maps, survey and usability testing platforms, analytics dashboards, and shared design systems that keep buttons, forms and patterns consistent.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success shows in whether users can finish tasks easily. Teams look at test results, task completion, error rates, support tickets and accessibility, often checked against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, plus how smoothly designs hand off to engineering.

qa.q: What is the difference between a UX designer and a UI designer?
qa.a: A UX designer focuses on how a product works: the steps, flows, structure and whether users can reach their goals. A UI designer focuses on how it looks: colors, type, icons and visual layout. Many jobs blend both, so postings often ask for UX/UI skills together.

qa.q: Do you need a degree or license to be a UX designer?
qa.a: No state license is required to work as a UX designer. Some employers prefer a degree in design, psychology, human-computer interaction or a related field, but many hire based on a portfolio. A strong portfolio shows your process, research, iterations and the problems your designs solved.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Plan studies, recruit participants, run interviews and usability tests, and watch people use products. Then analyze notes and recordings and turn findings into clear recommendations for design and product teams.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a remote usability session, then tagging quotes from yesterday’s interviews. Afternoons often go to writing a discussion guide, screening recruits, or presenting findings to designers and product managers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Designers, product managers, engineers, marketers and sometimes customer support staff. Study participants are customers, prospects or members of the public, who are often paid a small incentive for their time.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Video call and screen recording software, survey platforms, participant recruiting panels, clickable prototypes, spreadsheets, and shared digital whiteboards for sorting findings. Many teams also keep a research repository so past insights are easy to find.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether findings change real decisions. Strong researchers choose the right method, ask neutral questions, get informed consent, protect participant privacy, and report insights clearly enough that teams act on them.

qa.q: What does a UX researcher do day to day?
qa.a: They talk with and watch real users. A typical day mixes running interviews or usability tests, recruiting and scheduling participants, analyzing recordings and survey results, and sharing findings with designers and product managers. The goal is to show where a product confuses people and what they actually need.

qa.q: What is the difference between UX research and market research?
qa.a: UX research studies how people use and experience a product, often through usability tests and interviews, to guide design. Market research studies who buys, why and at what price, often through surveys and segmentation, to guide business and marketing choices. Many jobs blend both, especially at smaller companies.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Build business cases that show in numbers what a product will save or earn a specific customer. They gather data on the customer’s costs, time and risks, then turn it into return on investment, payback period and total cost of ownership figures that buyers can defend to their own finance team.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a discovery call beside an account executive, asking how many hours a process takes today. Then come updates to a value model in a spreadsheet, a short executive summary deck, and a review of results for a customer coming up for renewal.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Inside the company they work with account executives, sales engineers, customer success managers, product marketing and finance. On the customer side they talk with operations managers, finance staff and the executives who approve budgets and sign contracts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Spreadsheets do most of the heavy lifting, along with value calculators, slide decks and the company’s CRM system. They also rely on customer usage data, industry benchmarks, case studies and published research to back up their assumptions.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is usually measured by win rates and deal size on opportunities they support, plus renewals and expansions. Credibility matters too: whether customer finance teams accept the numbers, and whether projected savings hold up once the product is in use.

qa.q: What does a value engineer do day to day?
qa.a: A value engineer joins sales and renewal conversations to quantify a product’s impact. They interview customers about current costs and pain points, build models showing savings or revenue gains, and present the business case to decision makers. After the sale, they often track realized value so the customer success team can prove results at renewal time.

qa.q: What is the difference between a value engineer and a sales engineer?
qa.a: A sales engineer proves the product works technically, through demos, integrations and answering technical questions. A value engineer proves the product is worth buying, through financial models and business cases. Note that value engineering in construction and manufacturing is a different discipline focused on cutting project costs without losing function.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan shoots, film footage, and cut it into a finished video. That means picking the best takes, building a story, adding music and graphics, correcting color, cleaning up audio, and exporting files sized for each platform or screen.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a client call about a brief, then a few hours logging and syncing footage. Afternoons often go to rough cuts, revisions from notes, and rendering. Shoot days run long, with setup and teardown on each end.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: They use nonlinear editing software, color grading and motion graphics programs, and audio tools. On set they handle cameras, lenses, lights, microphones, and gimbals. Fast computers, large drives, and cloud storage keep big video files organized and backed up.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with clients, marketing teams, directors, writers, and on-camera talent. On bigger projects they hand off to colorists, sound mixers, and animators. Social media managers often send quick requests and expect fast turnarounds.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on whether the story is clear, the pacing holds attention, and the sound and picture look clean. Meeting deadlines, handling feedback well, and delivering files in the right formats matter as much as creative skill.

qa.q: What does a video editor and producer do day to day?
qa.a: They move a video from idea to finished file. Some days are spent filming on location or in a studio. Others are spent at a desk cutting footage, adding sound, graphics, and color, and making changes based on client or team notes. They also plan schedules, manage files, and deliver final versions for web, social, or broadcast.

qa.q: What is the difference between a video editor and a video producer?
qa.a: An editor works mainly in post-production, shaping raw footage into a finished cut. A producer handles the bigger picture: planning, budgets, scheduling, crew, locations, and client communication. Many smaller teams and freelancers do both jobs, which is why postings often combine the titles and ask for shooting skills too.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They plan, shoot, edit and animate short videos for ads, social posts, product demos and employee training. The work covers scripting and storyboards, filming, cutting footage, adding motion graphics and captions, mixing sound and exporting files for each platform.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day might start with a brief from marketing, then an hour of filming an interview or product shots. Afternoons often go to editing, building animated titles, color correcting, and sending a draft link for review comments.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include mirrorless or cinema cameras, lenses, lights, microphones and gimbals. On the computer they use nonlinear editing software, motion graphics and 3D programs, color grading tools, audio cleanup software and shared cloud storage for large files.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with marketing managers, social media teams, instructional designers, copywriters and subject experts. Freelancers and agency staff also deal directly with clients, on-camera talent, voice actors and sometimes legal reviewers who check music and image rights.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on clear storytelling, clean audio, on-brand design and meeting deadlines. For marketing and social videos, teams also look at views, watch time and clicks. Training videos are judged on whether learners understand and remember the material.

qa.q: What does a video and motion designer do day to day?
qa.a: They turn ideas into finished videos. That means reading the brief, writing or reviewing a script, filming or gathering footage, editing it into a story, and adding animated text, graphics and music. Much of the day is spent at the edit desk making revisions after feedback, then exporting versions sized for different platforms.

qa.q: What is the difference between a video editor and a motion graphics designer?
qa.a: A video editor mainly works with filmed footage, choosing shots, cutting for pace and fixing sound and color. A motion graphics designer creates animated elements like titles, logos, charts and explainer scenes, often from scratch. Many marketing and social media roles combine both skills, along with basic filming.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Most of these jobs are regular roles, such as bank teller, pharmacy technician, caseworker or support agent, with Vietnamese added. The person answers questions, explains bills, policies or forms, and helps customers finish tasks in Vietnamese. They then record notes in English for coworkers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They serve Vietnamese-speaking customers, patients and families, many of them older immigrants who are more comfortable in Vietnamese. Some roles deal with suppliers, factories or partners in Vietnam for import, manufacturing or travel work. They also work closely with English-only coworkers.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Jobs are found in call centers, remote home offices, hospitals, clinics, banks, insurance agencies, schools, social service offices and courts. Many openings are in areas with large Vietnamese communities, such as parts of California, Texas, Washington and Virginia.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Daily tools include phone and chat systems, customer records software, and a keyboard set up to type Vietnamese with correct tone marks. Translators use glossaries and translation memory software. Remote interpreters use headsets and video platforms.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Employers often test speaking and reading skill before hiring. On the job, work is judged on accuracy, clear and polite speech, call quality reviews and customer feedback. Knowing both Northern and Southern vocabulary helps, since many US speakers use Southern Vietnamese.

qa.q: Do I need a certification to work as a Vietnamese interpreter?
qa.a: It depends on the setting. Most bilingual customer service jobs only test your fluency. Medical interpreters usually need formal training, and voluntary national credentials exist. Court interpreting rules are set by each state, and many states offer Vietnamese credentials through written and oral exams. Federal courts certify only Spanish interpreters and use other qualification categories for Vietnamese.

qa.q: What is the difference between a bilingual employee and an interpreter?
qa.a: A bilingual employee does their own job, such as banking or support, directly in Vietnamese. An interpreter repeats what other people say between two languages without adding advice, and follows ethics rules on accuracy, impartiality and confidentiality. A translator works with written text instead of speech.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Keeps the largest accounts happy and growing. They onboard new funds and firms, guide them through account setup and know-your-customer checks, answer questions on fees, limits and products, and fix problems fast when trades, transfers or access go wrong.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with market news and a check of client activity. The rest of the day mixes calls and chats with clients, escalating urgent tickets, preparing account reviews and meeting internal teams. Busy markets can mean early starts or late messages.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Clients include hedge funds, asset managers, trading firms, family offices, corporate treasuries and high-volume individual traders. Inside the company they work with trading desks, compliance, operations, product, legal and support staff to solve client issues.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: A CRM system to track contacts and deals, client chat channels, trading and reporting dashboards, ticketing tools and spreadsheets. They must understand order types, fee tiers, settlement, custody and API access well enough to explain them clearly.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Results are measured by client retention, trading volume or assets from their book, new accounts brought in, and client satisfaction. Response time, a clean compliance record and accurate notes on every client conversation also count.

qa.q: What does a VIP relationship manager do day to day?
qa.a: They act as the main point of contact for top clients. Each day they answer client questions, solve account or trading problems, pass urgent issues to the right internal team, review client activity, and look for ways to grow the relationship, such as better fee tiers or new products. They also keep careful records for compliance.

qa.q: Do you need a license to be an institutional relationship manager?
qa.a: It depends on the employer and what is offered. At a broker-dealer, staff who solicit or service securities accounts usually must register through FINRA, often by passing the SIE and Series 7, and most states also require an exam such as the Series 63. Many crypto exchange and some bank roles need no license, so check each posting.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Visual merchandisers plan store layouts, window displays and product presentations that draw customers in and help them buy. They follow brand guidelines and planograms, set up seasonal and promotional displays, choose fixtures, signs and props and train store staff to keep displays right.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts with a walk of the sales floor to check displays against the plan. Then come moving fixtures, dressing mannequins and building new windows, often before or after store hours. They photograph finished work and review which products are selling.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with store managers and sales associates, buyers and merchandise planners who choose what the store sells, marketing and brand teams, regional managers, vendors and the builders who make fixtures and props.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include planogram software, Adobe Illustrator and Photoshop, SketchUp for store layouts and sales reports. On the floor they use ladders, tool kits, fixtures, mannequins, garment steamers and sign holders.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on sales in featured areas, how closely stores follow brand guidelines and planograms and finishing floor sets by the deadline. Staying within the display budget and keeping the store easy to shop also count.

qa.q: What is the difference between a visual merchandiser and a merchandise planner?
qa.a: A visual merchandiser decides how products look and where they sit in the store, through displays, windows and layouts. A merchandise planner or buyer decides which products the store carries, how many to order and how to price them. The two work closely, since a strong display only works if the right stock is on hand.

qa.q: Do you need a degree to be a visual merchandiser?
qa.a: Not always. Many visual merchandisers start as store associates and learn on the job. A degree in fashion merchandising, interior design or visual communication helps for corporate and regional roles. Employers look for a portfolio of displays, an eye for color and layout and the ability to lift and build things.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Sets technical direction for several engineering teams, hires and coaches engineering managers, plans headcount and budget, and decides how the organization designs, builds, tests and ships software. They balance new features against reliability, security and technical debt.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with one-on-ones with managers, then roadmap and planning meetings with product leaders. Afternoons may cover architecture reviews, hiring interviews, incident follow-ups and budget questions. Much of the day is meetings, so hands-on technical work is short or handed to senior engineers.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They usually report to a CTO or CEO and lead engineering managers, staff engineers and sometimes architects. Peers include product, design, security, finance, HR and sales leaders, plus outside vendors and, at times, customers with technical needs.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Issue tracking and planning tools, roadmap documents, engineering metrics dashboards, cloud cost reports, incident management systems and code review platforms. Budget spreadsheets, org charts and written design documents matter as much as any programming language.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether teams ship what was promised, system uptime and incident trends, delivery speed, hiring and retention, team engagement, and spending within budget. They are also judged on how well they grow managers and keep engineering aligned with business goals.

qa.q: What is the difference between a director of engineering and a VP of engineering?
qa.a: Titles vary by company. Usually a director leads a group of teams and their managers and focuses on delivery within one product area. A VP owns the whole engineering organization or a large part of it, sets strategy, owns the budget and headcount plan, and works as part of the executive team. In small companies one person may do both.

qa.q: Is being a VP of engineering a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be. They answer for outages, missed deadlines, layoffs and hiring gaps, and may be pulled in during major incidents at any hour. Much of the pressure comes from hard tradeoffs between speed, quality and cost. Strong managers beneath them, clear priorities and good incident processes make the load more manageable.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: A VP of sales sets the revenue target, builds the sales plan, and decides how territories, quotas, and commission plans are structured. They hire and coach sales managers, review the pipeline, and answer to the CEO or board for hitting the number.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Mornings often start with a forecast or pipeline review with front-line managers. The rest of the day mixes deal strategy on large opportunities, calls with key customers, hiring interviews, and meetings with marketing, finance, and product leaders.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They lead sales managers, account executives, sales development reps, and often sales operations staff. They work closely with the CEO, finance on budgets and compensation, marketing on lead flow, and customer success on renewals and expansion.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Most rely on a CRM system for pipeline and forecasting, dashboards for activity and conversion metrics, and spreadsheets for quota and territory models. Video calls, sales enablement content, and conversation recording tools support coaching and deal reviews.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Success is measured mainly by revenue against target and forecast accuracy. Leaders also watch win rates, sales cycle length, average deal size, quota attainment across the team, rep turnover, and the cost of acquiring each new customer.

qa.q: What does a VP of sales do day to day?
qa.a: They review the pipeline and forecast, coach managers on key deals, and join calls with large customers. They also hire, plan territories and quotas, and report results to the CEO or board. Much of the job is spotting risks early and moving people and resources to close the gap to the number.

qa.q: What is the difference between a sales manager and a VP of sales?
qa.a: A sales manager runs one team of reps and focuses on their daily activity and deals. A VP of sales leads the whole sales organization or a region, manages the managers, sets strategy, quotas, and compensation plans, and is personally accountable for the company’s or region’s overall revenue target.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Vulnerability management specialists find known security weaknesses across a company’s servers, laptops, cloud services and applications. They run scans, rank findings by real risk, assign fixes to system owners, track deadlines, confirm patches worked and report remaining exposure to security leaders.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A typical day includes reviewing new scan results, checking fresh advisories for flaws being exploited in the wild and deciding what gets fixed first. Specialists chase owners about overdue patches, handle exception requests and rescan systems to confirm fixes.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with system administrators, cloud and network engineers and application developers who apply the fixes. They also work with security operations, risk and compliance staff, auditors, and IT managers who approve maintenance windows.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common scanners include Tenable Nessus, Qualys and Rapid7 InsightVM, plus cloud security tools and code scanners for applications. Specialists use CVSS scores, CVE records and CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog to set priorities, and track work in Jira or ServiceNow.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Work is judged on how fast serious flaws get fixed, how much of the company is scanned and how few known exploited flaws stay open past deadline. Audits check the program against frameworks like PCI DSS or the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Good relationships with fix owners matter too.

qa.q: What is the difference between vulnerability management and penetration testing?
qa.a: Vulnerability management is an ongoing program that regularly scans everything for known flaws and makes sure they get fixed. Penetration testing is a time-limited exercise in which testers try to break in like a real attacker, often chaining weaknesses together. Pen test findings usually feed into the vulnerability management process for tracking and fixes.

qa.q: Do vulnerability management jobs require certifications?
qa.a: No certification is required by law, but many postings ask for one, such as CompTIA Security+, CySA+ or a GIAC certification. Defense and federal contractor roles often must meet Department of Defense cyber workforce rules, commonly through an approved certification, and may need a security clearance. Hands-on scanning and patching experience usually matters most.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Unload trucks, check incoming goods against packing lists, and put stock away in assigned locations. Pick items for orders, pack them securely, print and apply labels, and stage boxes for outbound carriers. Count inventory and report damaged or missing items.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Shifts often start with a short meeting on order volume and safety. Associates then work an assigned area, such as receiving, picking or packing, and may move between areas as orders peak. Many sites run day, night and weekend shifts.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Handheld scanners, pallet jacks, carts, tape guns and label printers are daily tools. Many sites use a warehouse management system that tells each worker what to pick next. Driving a forklift requires employer training and evaluation under OSHA rules.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Distribution centers, online order fulfillment centers, retail and grocery warehouses, factories and third-party logistics sites. Buildings are often large and loud. Some areas are hot in summer, and food warehouses may include cooler or freezer zones.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Supervisors look at accuracy, speed and safety. Many sites measure units picked or packed per hour against a set rate and check orders for errors. Some states require employers to tell workers in writing about any production quotas.

qa.q: What does a warehouse associate do day to day?
qa.a: A warehouse associate moves goods through a building. They unload and check deliveries, put items on shelves, pick products for orders with a scanner, pack and label boxes, and load outgoing trucks. They also count stock, keep aisles clear, and follow safety rules for lifting and equipment.

qa.q: Is warehouse associate a stressful job?
qa.a: It can be, mostly because of the pace and the physical load. Workers stand and walk for most of the shift, lift boxes, and may need to meet hourly rates. Peak seasons bring overtime. Many people like the clear tasks, steady routine, and the chance to leave work behind at the end of a shift.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Wealth management professionals plan and manage the finances of wealthy people and families. They build investment portfolios and coordinate tax planning, estate and trust planning, insurance, charitable giving and passing wealth to heirs. Senior advisors lead the relationship while associates prepare plans, reports and paperwork.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day may include client meetings to review goals and performance, rebalancing portfolios and preparing financial plans. Advisors also coordinate with a client’s CPA or estate attorney, process account paperwork and research investments. Associates spend more time on reports, data entry and meeting prep.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work directly with clients and their families. Teams include lead advisors, associates, portfolio managers, financial planners and client service staff. They also coordinate with outside CPAs, estate planning attorneys, trust officers, insurance specialists and the custodians that hold the assets.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include CRM systems such as Salesforce or Redtail, financial planning software like eMoney or MoneyGuidePro, portfolio management and rebalancing tools, and custodian platforms. Excel, e-signature tools, secure client portals and video meetings round out the day.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Advisors are judged on assets under management, new assets brought in, client retention and the quality of advice. Clients look at how well their goals are met, not just returns. Compliance reviews check best-interest or fiduciary standards, disclosures and records of every recommendation.

qa.q: Do you need a license to work in wealth management?
qa.a: Usually. Advisors who sell securities must pass the SIE and Series 7 exams and register through a broker-dealer. Those who give investment advice for pay typically register as investment adviser representatives, often by passing the Series 65 or 66. Selling insurance needs a state license. Rules vary by state, and the CFP certification is common but voluntary.

qa.q: What is the difference between a wealth manager and a financial planner?
qa.a: A financial planner helps clients with budgets, savings, retirement, insurance and goals, and may serve people at many income levels. A wealth manager usually serves wealthier clients and combines investment management with tax, estate, trust and charitable planning. Many wealth managers are also planners, and neither title is a license by itself.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Web developers write the code that makes websites work. They build page layouts, add features like forms and search, connect sites to databases, fix bugs, and update older code so pages stay fast, secure and easy to use on phones and computers.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Many days start with a short team check-in. Then a developer picks up tasks from a shared list, writes and tests code, reviews a teammate’s changes, and pushes finished work to a test site. Time also goes to tracking down bugs users have reported.

day.label: Tools of the trade
