day.text: Core tools include HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the parts people see, plus server languages and databases for the code behind them. Developers use code editors, version control such as Git, browser developer tools, and frameworks that speed up common tasks.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: Developers work closely with designers who plan how pages look, product managers who set priorities, and testers who check for problems. Some work directly with clients or business owners, turning plain requests into working features and explaining what is possible.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Good work means pages load quickly, look right on different screens, and work for people using assistive technology like screen readers. Code should be clean enough for others to read and change, and new releases should not break features that already worked.

qa.q: What is the difference between a front-end and a back-end web developer?
qa.a: A front-end developer builds what visitors see and click, using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A back-end developer builds the server side: databases, user accounts, and the logic that stores and sends data. A full-stack developer handles both. Smaller teams often expect one person to cover both sides.

qa.q: Do you need a degree or license to be a web developer?
qa.a: No license is required to work as a web developer in any US state. Many employers prefer a degree in computer science or a related field, but plenty hire based on skills shown in a portfolio of real projects. Self-study, coding bootcamps and community college courses are common paths into the work.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Welders read blueprints and weld symbols, then prepare metal by cutting, grinding and cleaning it. They fit and clamp parts in place, set up the welding machine and join the pieces. Afterward they check each weld for size, shape and visible flaws.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common processes include stick (SMAW), MIG (GMAW), TIG (GTAW) and flux-cored welding. Welders also use grinders, torches, clamps, fillet gauges and measuring tapes. Protective gear includes a welding helmet, gloves, a jacket and sometimes a respirator.

day.label: Where they work
day.text: Welders work in fabrication shops, factories, shipyards, refineries, pipelines and construction sites. Some weld outdoors, at heights or in tight spaces. Aerospace and other high-precision shops often do TIG work in clean, controlled settings.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Welds are checked against the job’s code or drawings, such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel or ASME rules for pressure piping. Inspectors may use visual checks, ultrasonic or X-ray testing. Flawed welds are usually repaired as the code allows, often by grinding out the defect and rewelding.

day.label: Certification and testing
day.text: Most employers require passing a weld test for each process and position. Many welders hold certifications from the American Welding Society or qualify under ASME Section IX. Some cities and states require extra licensing for structural work, so rules vary by location.

qa.q: What does a welder do day to day?
qa.a: A welder reviews drawings, preps and fits metal parts, and joins them using processes like MIG, TIG or stick. Through the day they adjust machine settings, clean between passes and inspect their own welds. They follow safety rules for fumes, sparks and hot work, and fix any defects found in inspection.

qa.q: What is the difference between a welder and a fabricator?
qa.a: A welder focuses on joining metal with heat and filler metal. A fabricator builds whole parts or structures, which includes cutting, bending, shaping and fitting metal from drawings. Many fabricators also weld, and many welders do some fitting, but the fabricator role usually covers more of the building process.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Configures business processes, security groups, and calculated fields in Workday. Builds custom reports, loads data, and fixes problems when a hire, pay change, or approval gets stuck. Keeps the setup matched to company policy as it changes.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: Starts by working the support queue for HR and finance users. Tests changes in a sandbox tenant before moving them to production. Payroll cutoffs, open enrollment, and year-end close make some weeks much busier than others.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: HR, payroll, benefits, and finance teams who own the processes. IT and integration staff who connect Workday to other systems. Outside consultants on big projects, plus Workday’s own support team when a bug needs escalating.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Workday’s report writer and calculated fields, the Enterprise Interface Builder for mass data loads, and integration tools for outbound files. Also a ticketing system, spreadsheets for data cleanup, and written test scripts for each change.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: By whether people get paid correctly and data stays accurate. Also by how fast tickets close, whether security access passes audits, and how smoothly the company handles Workday’s twice-yearly feature releases.

qa.q: What does a Workday specialist do day to day?
qa.a: They answer user tickets, change business process steps, update security access, and build reports for HR and finance leaders. They test every change in a sandbox first, then move it to production. Around Workday’s two major releases each year, they review new features and run regression tests so nothing breaks.

qa.q: What is the difference between a Workday specialist and a Workday consultant?
qa.a: A specialist usually works inside the company that uses Workday and supports one system long term. A consultant usually works for an implementation partner and sets up Workday for several clients on fixed projects. Consultants often travel and deploy new modules, while specialists keep things running after launch. Job titles vary, so read each posting.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: Workforce management analysts forecast how many calls, chats, emails or tasks a team will receive and turn that into staffing needs for each interval. They build schedules, plan breaks, training and time off, watch real-time service levels, and adjust staffing when volume or absences change.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: A day often starts by checking yesterday’s results against forecast and today’s staffing. Real-time analysts watch queues and move agents between channels or shift breaks. Others update forecasts, build next month’s schedules, approve time-off requests, and report on service level and adherence.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with contact center managers, team leads and agents, plus HR, finance and operations leaders who plan headcount. They also coordinate with recruiting and training teams on new hire classes, and with outsourcing partners when vendors handle part of the volume.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Common tools include workforce management software such as NICE CXone, Verint or Calabrio, contact center platforms like Genesys Cloud or Five9, and Excel for Erlang C staffing models. SQL and BI tools like Power BI or Tableau support forecasting and reporting.

day.label: How the work is judged
day.text: Analysts are judged on forecast accuracy, service level, average speed of answer and schedule adherence. Leaders also watch occupancy, overtime and idle time, since staffing too many or too few people both cost the business. Fair, workable schedules help keep agents and reduce turnover.

qa.q: What is the difference between workforce management and workforce planning?
qa.a: Workforce management works on short horizons: forecasting volume by interval, building schedules and adjusting staffing in real time. Workforce planning looks further ahead, estimating how many people a team needs over the coming months or years, when to hire and which skills to build. In contact centers, the two often sit in the same team.

qa.q: What skills do you need to be a workforce management analyst?
qa.a: Strong Excel and math skills come first, including forecasting methods and staffing models such as Erlang C. Analysts also need to learn WFM software, basic SQL or BI tools, and how contact centers run. Clear communication matters, since analysts explain staffing decisions to managers and agents. Many start as agents or team leads before moving into analysis.

day.label: Main duties
day.text: They keep the office running. That means managing space and seating, ordering supplies, greeting visitors, handling mail and deliveries, and booking meeting rooms. They also fix small problems before staff notice them. Many also plan office moves, new desk setups and small events.

day.label: A typical day
day.text: The day often starts with a walk-through to check kitchens, printers and meeting rooms. Then come vendor calls, a supply order, visitor check-ins, maintenance tickets and staff questions. Plans can change fast when something breaks or a big meeting lands on the calendar.

day.label: Who they work with
day.text: They work with almost everyone. Staff and managers bring requests. Building managers, landlords, cleaners, security, IT and outside vendors handle repairs and services. HR and finance often help with new hire setups, budgets and invoices.

day.label: Safety and compliance
day.text: They often keep emergency plans, evacuation maps and first aid kits up to date. They also help run fire drills where required. Federal OSHA rules set a baseline, but some states run their own safety plans and fire codes are set locally, so details vary by place.

day.label: Tools of the trade
day.text: Expect ticket systems, room booking and visitor sign-in software, spreadsheets, shared calendars and purchasing tools. Hands-on gear matters too, such as label makers, badge printers and a basic toolkit. A good list of trusted vendor contacts is just as important.

qa.q: What does an office manager do day to day?
qa.a: An office manager keeps the workplace ready for people to do their jobs. On a typical day they restock supplies and greet visitors. They also log repair requests, book rooms, sort mail and deliveries, and answer staff questions. They often track office budgets, manage vendor contracts and help with safety tasks like updating emergency contacts and first aid kits.

qa.q: What is the difference between an office manager and a facilities manager?
qa.a: An office manager focuses on daily operations and people: supplies, visitors, admin tasks and staff requests. A facilities manager focuses more on the building itself, such as heating and cooling, maintenance, leases, large vendor contracts and renovation projects. A facilities manager may also oversee several sites. In smaller companies, one person often does both jobs.
